Experiments are performed on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and show that the method has the potential to perform better than standard dropout and at the level of Monte Carlo Dropout (the standard method to compute the real dropout outputs consistently with the training assumption of an ensemble, of course quite expensive computationally) The study gives a very interesting theoretical model for dropout as a latent variable model where standard dropout is then a monte carlo approximation. This is very probably widely applicable to further studies of dropout. The framework for the study of the inference gap is interesting although maybe somewhat less widely applicable. The proposed model is convincing although 1. it is tested on simple datasets 2. the gains are relatively small and 3. there is an increased computational cost during training because a new hyper-parameter is introduced. p6 line 8 typo: expecatation

title: HyperNetworks | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###This work explores hypernetworks: an approach of using one network, also known as a hypernetwork, to generate the weights for another network. We apply hypernetworks to generate adaptive weights for recurrent networks. In this case, hypernetworks can be viewed as a relaxed form of weight-sharing across layers. In our implementation, hypernetworks are are trained jointly with the main network in an end-to-end fashion. Our main result is that hypernetworks can generate non-shared weights for LSTM and achieve state-of-the-art results on a variety of sequence modelling tasks including character-level language modelling, handwriting generation and neural machine translation, challenging the weight-sharing paradigm for recurrent networks.
review: A well known limitation in deep neural networks is that the same parameters are typically used for all examples, even though different examples have very different characteristics. For example, recognizing animals will likely require different features than categorizing flowers. Using different parameters for different types of examples has the potential to greatly reduce underfitting. This can be seen in recent results with generative models, where image quality is much better for less diverse datasets. However, it is difficult to use different parameters for different examples because we typically train using minibatches, which relies on using the same parameters for all examples in a minibatch (i.e. doing matrix multiplies in a fully-connected network). The hypernetworks paper cleverly proposes to get around this problem by adapting different *parameters* for different time steps in recurrent networks and different. The basic insight is that a minibatch will always include many different examples from the same time step or spatial position, so there is no computational issue involved with using different *parameters*. In this paper, the *parameters* are modified for different positions based on the output from a hypernetwork which conditions on the time step. Hypothetically, this hypernetwork could also condition on other features that are shared by all sequences in the minibatch. I expect this method to become standard for training RNNs, especially where the length of the sequences is the same during the training and testing phases. Penn Treebank is a highly competitive baseline, so the SOTA result reported here is impressive. The experiments on convolutional networks are less experimentally impressive. I suspect that the authors were aiming to achieve state of the art results here but settled with achieving a reduction in the number of parameters. It might even be worthwhile to consider a synthetic experiment where two completely different types of image are appended (i.e. birds on the left and flowers on the right) and show that the hypernetwork helps in this situation. It may be the case that for convnets, the cases where hypernetworks help are very specific. For RNNs, it seems to be the case that explicitly changing the nature of the computation depending on the position in the sequence greatly improves generalization. While a usual RNN could learn to store a counter (indicating the position in the sequence), the hypernetwork could be a more efficient way to add capacity. Applications to time series forecasting and modeling could be an interesting area for future work.

title: A Learned Representation For Artistic Style | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###The diversity of painting styles represents a rich visual vocabulary for the construction of an image. The degree to which one may learn and parsimoniously capture this visual vocabulary measures our understanding of the higher level features of paintings, if not images in general. In this work we investigate the construction of a single, scalable deep network that can parsimoniously capture the artistic style of a diversity of paintings. We demonstrate that such a network generalizes across a diversity of artistic styles by reducing a painting to a point in an embedding space. Importantly, this model permits a user to explore new painting styles by arbitrarily combining the styles learned from individual paintings. We hope that this work provides a useful step towards building rich models of paintings and offers a window on to the structure of the learned representation of artistic style.
review: This paper addresses the problem of efficient neural stylization. Instead of training a separate network for N different styles (as is done, e.g., in Johnson et al.), this paper extends the instance normalization work of Ulyanov et al. to train a single network and learn a smaller set â€œconditional instance normalizationâ€ parameters dependent on the desired output style. The conditional instance normalization applies a learnt affine transformation on normalized feature maps at each layer in the network. Qualitative results are shown. I have not worked in this area, but Iâ€™m generally aware of the main issues in transferring artistic style. The paper addresses a known challenge of incorporating different styles into the same net, which have a number of practical benefits. As far as I can tell the results look compelling. As Iâ€™m less confident in my expertise in this area, Iâ€™m happy to support another reviewer who is willing to champion this paper. My main comments are on the paper writing. As far as I understand, the main novelty of the approach starts in Section 2.2, and before that is review of prior art. If this is indeed the case, one suggestion is to remove the subsection heading for 2.1 so itâ€™s grouped with the first part of Section 2, and to cite related work for the feedforward network (e.g., Johnson et al.) in the text and in Fig 2 so itâ€™s clear. In fact, Iâ€™m wondering if Figs 2 and 3 can be combined somehow so that the contribution is clearer in the figures. I was at first confused by Eq (5) as x and z are not defined anywhere. Also, it may be helpful to write out everything explicitly as is done in the instance normalization paper. In Eq (4), perhaps you could write T_s to emphasize that there are separate networks for different styles. Fig 5 left: Iâ€™m assuming the different colors correspond to the different styles. If so, perhaps mention this in the caption. Also, this figure is hard to read. Maybe instead show single curves with error bars that are averages over the loss curves for N-styles and individual styles. Typos: Page 1: Shouldnâ€™t it be â€œVGG-16â€ network (not *VGG-19â€)? Page 2: â€œnewtorkâ€ => â€œnetworkâ€. Paragraph after Eq. (5): â€œmuch lessâ€ => â€œfewerâ€.

title: Hadamard Product for Low-rank Bilinear Pooling | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###Bilinear models provide rich representations compared with linear models. They have been applied in various visual tasks, such as object recognition, segmentation, and visual question-answering, to get state-of-the-art performances taking advantage of the expanded representations. However, bilinear representations tend to be high-dimensional, limiting the applicability to computationally complex tasks. We propose low-rank bilinear pooling using Hadamard product for an efficient attention mechanism of multimodal learning. We show that our model outperforms compact bilinear pooling in visual question-answering tasks with the state-of-the-art results on the VQA dataset, having a better parsimonious property.
review: Summary: The paper presents low-rank bilinear pooling that uses Hadamard product (commonly known as element-wise multiplication). The paper implements low-rank bilinear pooling on an existing model (Kim et al., 2016b) and builds a model for Visual Question Answering (VQA) that outperforms the current state-of-art by 0.42%. The paper presents various ablation studies of the new VQA model they built. Strengths: 1. The paper presents new insights into element-wise multiplication operation which has been previously used in VQA literature (such as Antol et al., ICCV 2015) without insights on why it should work. 2. The paper presents a new model for the task of VQA that beats the current state-of-art by 0.42%. However, I have concerns about the statistical significance of the performance (see weaknesses below). 3. The various design choices made in model development have been experimentally verified. Weaknesses/Suggestions: 1. When authors explicitly (keeping rest of the model architecture same) compared low-rank bilinear pooling with compact bilinear pooling, they found that low-rank bilinear pooling performs worse. Hence, it could not be experimentally verified that low-rank bilinear pooling is better in performance than compact bilinear pooling (at least for the task of VQA). 2. The authors argue that low-rank bilinear pooling uses 25% less parameters than compact bilinear pooling. So, could the authors please explain how does the reduction in number of parameters help experimentally? Does the training time of the model reduce significantly? Can we train the model with less data? 3. One of the contributions of the paper is that the proposed model outperforms the current state-of-art on VQA by 0.42%. However, I am skeptical that the performance of the proposed model is statistically significantly better than the current state-of-art. 4. I would like the authors to explicitly mention the differences between MRN, MARN and MLB. It is not very clear from reading the paper. 5. In the caption for Table 1, fix the following: â€œhave notâ€ -> â€œhave noâ€ Review Summary: I like the insights about low-rank bilinear pooling using Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication) presented in the paper. However, it could not be justified that low-rank bilinear pooling leads to better performance than compact biliear pooling. It does lead to reduction in number of parameters but it is not clear how much that helps experimentally. So, to be more convinced I would like the authors to provide experimental justification of why low-rank bilinear pooling is better than other forms of pooling.

title: Learning Continuous Semantic Representations of Symbolic Expressions | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###The question of how procedural knowledge is represented and inferred is a fundamental problem in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Recent work on program induction has proposed neural architectures, based on abstractions like stacks, Turing machines, and interpreters, that operate on abstract computational machines or on execution traces. But the recursive abstraction that is central to procedural knowledge is perhaps most naturally represented by symbolic representations that have syntactic structure, such as logical expressions and source code. Combining abstract, symbolic reasoning with continuous neural reasoning is a grand challenge of representation learning. As a step in this direction, we propose a new architecture, called neural equivalence networks, for the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of mathematical and logical expressions. These networks are trained to represent semantic equivalence, even of expressions that are syntactically very different. The challenge is that semantic representations must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures.
review: The authors propose a new model to learn symbolic expression representations. They do a reasonably extensive evaluation with similar approaches and motivate their approach well. As expressed in the preliminary questions, I think the authors could improve the motivation for their subexpforce loss. At the top of page 6 the authors mention that they compare to two-layer MLP w/o residual connections. I think having a direct comparison between a model with and w/o the subexpforce loss would be helpful too and should be included (i.e. keep the residual connections and normalization). My main concern is the evaluation *score*. It appears to be precision on a per query basis. I believe a more standard metric, precision-recall or roc would be more informative. In particular the chosen metric is expected to perform better when the equivalence classes are larger, since this isn*t taken into account in the denominator, but the likelihood of a random expression matching the query increases.

title: Discovering objects and their relations from entangled scene representations | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###Our world can be succinctly and compactly described as structured scenes of objects and relations. A typical room, for example, contains salient objects such as tables, chairs and books, and these objects typically relate to each other by virtue of their correlated features, such as position, function and shape. Humans exploit knowledge of objects and their relations for learning a wide spectrum of tasks, and more generally when learning the structure underlying observed data. In this work, we introduce relation networks (RNs) - a general purpose neural network architecture for object-relation reasoning. We show that RNs are capable of learning object relations from scene description data. Furthermore, we show that RNs can act as a bottleneck that induces the factorization of objects from entangled scene description inputs, and from distributed deep representations of scene images provided by a variational autoencoder. The model can also be used in conjunction with differentiable memory mechanisms for implicit relation discovery in one-shot learning tasks. Our results suggest that relation networks are a powerful architecture for solving a variety of problems that require object relation reasoning.
review: + Understanding relations between objects is an important task in domains like vision, language and robotics. However, models trained on real-life datasets can often exploit simple object properties (not relation-based) to identify relations (eg: animals of bigger size are typically predators and small-size animals are preys). Such models can predict relations without necessarily understanding them. Given the difficulty of the task, a controlled setting is required to investigate if neural networks can be designed to actually understand pairwise object relations. The current paper takes a significant step in answering this question through a controlled dataset. Also, multiple experiments are presented to validate the *relation learning* ability of proposed Relation Networks (RN). + The dataset proposed in the paper ensures that relation classification models can succeed only by learning the relations between objects and not by exploiting *predator-prey* like object properties. + The paper presents very thorough experiments to validate the claim that *RNs* truly learn the relation between objects. 1. In particular, the ability of the RN to force a simple linear layer to disentangle scene description from VAE latent space and permuted description is very interesting. This clearly demonstrates that the RN learns object relations. 2. The one-shot experiments again demonstrate this ability in a convincing manner. This requires the model to understand relations in each run, represent them through an abstract label and assign the label to future samples from the relationship graph. Some suggestions: - Is g_{psi}(.) permutation invariant as well. Since it works on pairs of objects, how did you ensure that the MLP is invariant to the order of the objects in the pair? - The RNs need to operate over pairs of objects in order to identify pairwise interactions. However, in practical applications there are more complicated group interactions. (eg. ternary interaction: *person* riding a *bike* wears *helmet*). Would this require g(.) of RN to not just operate on pairs but on every possible subset of objects in the scene? More generally, is such a pairwise edge-based approach scalable to larger number of objects? - The authors mention that * a deep network with a sufficiently large number of parameters and a large enough training set should be capable of matching the performance of a RN*. This is an interesting point, and could be true in practice. Have the authors investigated this effect by trying to identify the minimum model capacity and/or training examples required by a MLP to match the performance of RN for the provided setup? This would help in quantifying the significance of RN for practical applications with limited examples. In other words, the task in Sec. 5.1 could benefit from another plot: the performance of MLP and RN at different amounts of training samples. - While the simulation setup in the current paper is a great first-step towards analyzing the *relation-learning* ability of RNs, it is still not clear if this would transfer to real-life datasets. I strongly encourage the authors to experiment on real-life datasets like Coco, visual genome or HICO as stated in the pre-review stage. - Minor: Some terminologies in the paper such as *objects* and *scene descriptions* used to refer to abstract entities can be misleading for readers from the object detection domain in computer vision. This could be clarified early on in the introduction. - Minor: Some results like Fig. 8 which shows the ability of RN to generalize to unseen categories are quite interesting and could be moved to the main draft for completeness. The paper proposes a network which is capable of understanding relationships between objects in a scene. This ability of the RN is thoroughly investigated through a series of experiments on a controlled dataset. While, the model is currently evaluated only on a simulated dataset, the results are quite promising and could translate to real-life datasets as well.

title: Making Neural Programming Architectures Generalize via Recursion
abstract: Abstract:###Empirically, neural networks that attempt to learn programs from data have exhibited poor generalizability. Moreover, it has traditionally been difficult to reason about the behavior of these models beyond a certain level of input complexity. In order to address these issues, we propose augmenting neural architectures with a key abstraction: recursion. As an application, we implement recursion in the Neural Programmer-Interpreter framework on four tasks: grade-school addition, bubble sort, topological sort, and quicksort. We demonstrate superior generalizability and interpretability with small amounts of training data. Recursion divides the problem into smaller pieces and drastically reduces the domain of each neural network component, making it tractable to prove guarantees about the overall systemâ€™s behavior. Our experience suggests that in order for neural architectures to robustly learn program semantics, it is necessary to incorporate a concept like recursion.
review: This paper argues that recursion is the missing ingredient for neural program induction, enabling perfect out-of-distribution generalization and even formal verification by restricting the problem to base cases and reduction rules. Honestly, while the empirical results—100% accuracy on arbitrarily long inputs from a handful of traces—are undeniably impressive and the verification idea is a neat theoretical contribution, I have serious reservations about the actual novelty and significance of the approach. The paper is essentially an engineering tweak of the Reed & de Freitas NPI framework where the authors simply change the supervision to include recursive calls; the architecture itself doesn't learn to *discover* or *invent* recursion, it just imitates a pre-baked recursive trace. This effectively decouples the hard part of program synthesis (inducing compositional structure) from the execution modeling, which makes me question whether we've actually advanced the core problem or just proven that LSTMs are great at copying stack-based traces when you explicitly tell them where to push and pop. What really bugs me is the lack of discussion on what happens when the input domain is continuous or perceptual—say, sorting MNIST digits or performing arithmetic on handwritten numerals—where the base cases and reductions aren't just symbolic booleans but require robust perception. In that setting, the recursive logic might generalize, but the perceptual errors would compound, making the proof of perfect generalization practically useless. So I'm left wondering: can you name a single realistic, non-toy problem where we have full execution traces available, the environment is fully observable and discrete, yet the proposed method would actually fail to learn the recursive program from the provided traces? If the answer is no, then this result feels more like a testament to the power of heavy supervision than a breakthrough in neural program generalization.

title: End-to-end Optimized Image Compression
abstract: Abstract:###We describe an image compression method, consisting of a nonlinear analysis transformation, a uniform quantizer, and a nonlinear synthesis transformation. The transforms are constructed in three successive stages of convolutional linear filters and nonlinear activation functions. Unlike most convolutional neural networks, the joint nonlinearity is chosen to implement a form of local gain control, inspired by those used to model biological neurons. Using a variant of stochastic gradient descent, we jointly optimize the entire model for rate-distortion performance over a database of training images, introducing a continuous proxy for the discontinuous loss function arising from the quantizer. Under certain conditions, the relaxed loss function may be interpreted as the log likelihood of a generative model, as implemented by a variational autoencoder. Unlike these models, however, the compression model must operate at any given point along the rate-distortion curve, as specified by a trade-off parameter. Across an independent set of test images, we find that the optimized method generally exhibits better rate-distortion performance than the standard JPEG and JPEG 2000 compression methods. More importantly, we observe a dramatic improvement in visual quality for all images at all bit rates, which is supported by objective quality estimates using MS-SSIM.
review: This paper presents a fully end-to-end trainable nonlinear transform coding framework for image compression, using cascaded convolutions with generalized divisive normalization (GDN) nonlinearities and a continuous relaxation of quantization via additive uniform noise to enable stochastic gradient descent. The results are honestly quite impressive—the method consistently beats JPEG and JPEG 2000 in both PSNR and MS-SSIM across a range of bitrates, and more importantly, the visual quality is dramatically better, with none of the blocking or ringing artifacts that plague linear transform coders. The connection to variational autoencoders is a nice theoretical framing, though I'm not convinced it adds much beyond the standard rate-distortion formulation. My main gripes: the architecture choices (filter sizes, number of stages, channel counts) feel somewhat ad-hoc and underexplored—you just pick something and it works, but I'd like to see some ablation studies or justification. Also, while the comparison to JPEG and JPEG2000 is favorable, the entropy coder you implemented is more sophisticated than what JPEG typically uses, and the training set is massive, so the gains might be less about the nonlinear transform and more about having a better coder and more data. The fact that you trained separate models for each λ is computationally expensive and limits practical deployment—I'd be more excited if you'd shown a single model that can interpolate across the curve. That said, the work is technically solid, the empirical results are compelling, and the visual examples speak for themselves. I'm leaning accept, but I'd like to see more discussion on complexity and practical feasibility, and maybe some experiments with simpler nonlinearities to isolate the contribution of GDN.

title: Optimization as a Model for Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Though deep neural networks have shown great success in the large data domain, they generally perform poorly on few-shot learning tasks, where a model has to quickly generalize after seeing very few examples from each class. The general belief is that gradient-based optimization in high capacity models requires many iterative steps over many examples to perform well. Here, we propose an LSTM-based meta-learner model to learn the exact optimization algorithm used to train another learner neural network in the few-shot regime. The parametrization of our model allows it to learn appropriate parameter updates specifically for the scenario where a set amount of updates will be made, while also learning a general initialization of the learner network that allows for quick convergence of training. We demonstrate that this meta-learning model is competitive with deep metric-learning techniques for few-shot learning.
review:
This paper proposes an LSTM-based meta-learner that learns to optimize a classifier network for few-shot learning, framing gradient descent updates as analogous to LSTM cell state updates and training the meta-learner to produce effective parameter updates and a good initialization. The idea is clever and well-motivated—explicitly learning an optimization procedure tailored to the few-update regime is a natural fit for the problem. The results on Mini-ImageNet are solid, beating the fine-tuning baseline and performing competitively with Matching Networks, especially in the 5-shot setting where the gap is more pronounced. I also appreciate the visualization of the learned gates, which gives some insight into what the meta-learner is actually doing.

However, I have several concerns. First, the gradient independence assumption (ignoring the dependency of the learner's gradients on the meta-learner's parameters) is a significant simplification—you hand-wave it away by citing Andrychowicz et al., but in the few-shot setting where the meta-learner is explicitly controlling the learning dynamics, this could matter more than you acknowledge. Have you tried estimating the impact of this approximation, or is there a reason it's less problematic here than in the large-scale setting? Second, the model is trained separately for 1-shot and 5-shot with a fixed number of updates, which limits its generality—I'd like to see how it performs when the number of shots or updates varies at test time, or whether a single meta-learner can handle both settings. Third, the comparison to Matching Networks is somewhat undercooked; you implemented your own version and created your own Mini-ImageNet split, which makes it hard to directly compare to the published numbers or know if the implementation is faithful. The fact that your Matching Net results are lower than the original paper's suggests either implementation differences or dataset differences, and you don't discuss this adequately. Finally, the learner network is relatively small (4 conv layers, 32 filters); it's unclear how well this approach scales to deeper architectures or larger class counts. The paper is well-written and the idea is interesting, but the technical limitations and evaluation choices leave me with reservations. I'm leaning towards accept because the core contribution is novel and empirically validated, but I'd like to see a more thorough discussion of these issues.

title: Learning End-to-End Goal-Oriented Dialog
abstract: Abstract:###Traditional dialog systems used in goal-oriented applications require a lot of domain-specific handcrafting, which hinders scaling up to new domains. End- to-end dialog systems, in which all components are trained from the dialogs themselves, escape this limitation. But the encouraging success recently obtained in chit-chat dialog may not carry over to goal-oriented settings. This paper proposes a testbed to break down the strengths and shortcomings of end-to-end dialog systems in goal-oriented applications. Set in the context of restaurant reservation, our tasks require manipulating sentences and symbols, so as to properly conduct conversations, issue API calls and use the outputs of such calls. We show that an end-to-end dialog system based on Memory Networks can reach promising, yet imperfect, performance and learn to perform non-trivial operations. We confirm those results by comparing our system to a hand-crafted slot-filling baseline on data from the second Dialog State Tracking Challenge (Henderson et al., 2014a). We show similar result patterns on data extracted from an online concierge service.
review: This paper introduces a set of five synthetic goal-oriented dialog tasks in the restaurant reservation domain, along with two real-world datasets (DSTC2 and a concierge service), to systematically evaluate end-to-end dialog systems. The authors test Memory Networks, supervised embeddings, and IR baselines, showing that MemNNs can learn to issue API calls and track dialog state, but struggle with interpreting KB results and presenting options—per-dialog accuracy remains near zero on the harder tasks. I appreciate the effort to create a reproducible benchmark with explicit subtasks that isolate different capabilities, and the inclusion of OOV generalization and real data is a nice touch. However, I have several concerns. First, the synthetic tasks are quite simplistic—the language is templated, the dialog flow is deterministic, and the KB is tiny (600 restaurants)—so it's unclear how much these results tell us about real-world complexity. Second, the paper feels more like a resource/benchmark paper than a novel modeling contribution; the MemNN architecture is essentially unchanged from prior work, and the match-type features are a small engineering fix. Third, the performance on the full Task 5 is still abysmal (19.7% dialog accuracy with the best model), and the Concierge results are barely above random, which makes me question whether the benchmark is too hard or the methods are just not up to the task—either way, the paper doesn't provide much insight into why. The comparison to a hand-coded slot-filling baseline on DSTC2 is weak because the rules are ad-hoc and not a strong competitor. I'd be more enthusiastic if the paper proposed a new model that actually solved these tasks, or provided a deeper analysis of failure modes beyond accuracy numbers. As it stands, it's a useful resource but not a breakthrough, and I'm leaning towards reject due to limited novelty and incremental contribution.

title: Towards Principled Methods for Training Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###The goal of this paper is not to introduce a single algorithm or method, but to make theoretical steps towards fully understanding the training dynamics of gen- erative adversarial networks. In order to substantiate our theoretical analysis, we perform targeted experiments to verify our assumptions, illustrate our claims, and quantify the phenomena. This paper is divided into three sections. The first sec- tion introduces the problem at hand. The second section is dedicated to studying and proving rigorously the problems including instability and saturation that arize when training generative adversarial networks. The third section examines a prac- tical and theoretically grounded direction towards solving these problems, while introducing new tools to study them.
review: This paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of why GAN training is unstable, proving that when the data distribution and generator distribution lie on low-dimensional manifolds (which is almost always the case), the Jensen-Shannon divergence is always maxed out, the optimal discriminator is perfect and locally constant, and gradients either vanish (for the original cost) or become Cauchy-distributed with infinite variance (for the -log D alternative). The theoretical contributions are genuinely important—this is the first paper I've seen that actually explains the gradient instability phenomenon in a mathematically sound way, and the proofs are clean and convincing. I particularly like the geometric perspective on manifold alignment and the use of transversality; it finally gives us a principled reason why GANs are so finicky. The proposed fix—adding continuous noise to both distributions to smooth them out and then annealing—is elegant and theoretically grounded, and the bound relating the Wasserstein distance of the original distributions to the JSD of the noisy ones is a nice piece of work. My main criticism is that the empirical validation is quite limited; the paper mostly shows gradient norm plots on a fixed DCGAN, but doesn't actually train a full model with the noise annealing strategy and compare it to standard GANs on a real benchmark like CIFAR-10. The paper also doesn't provide practical guidance on how to schedule the noise decay or tune the noise variance, which limits its immediate impact. That said, the theoretical insights are so foundational that I think this should be accepted despite the weak experiments—the analysis alone is a significant contribution that will influence how the community thinks about GAN training. I'd like to see the authors add at least one full training experiment in the final version to demonstrate that the proposed method actually works in practice. Strong accept on the theory, but I'd bump it down to accept if the experiments remain this sparse.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Unsupervised Auxiliary Tasks
abstract: Abstract:###Deep reinforcement learning agents have achieved state-of-the-art results by directly maximising cumulative reward. However, environments contain a much wider variety of possible training signals. In this paper, we introduce an agent that also maximises many other pseudo-reward functions simultaneously by reinforcement learning. All of these tasks share a common representation that, like unsupervised learning, continues to develop in the absence of extrinsic rewards. We also introduce a novel mechanism for focusing this representation upon extrinsic rewards, so that learning can rapidly adapt to the most relevant aspects of the actual task. Our agent significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on Atari, averaging 880\% expert human performance, and a challenging suite of first-person, three-dimensional emph{Labyrinth} tasks leading to a mean speedup in learning of 10 and averaging 87\% expert human performance on Labyrinth.
review: This paper introduces the UNREAL agent, which augments A3C with auxiliary tasks—pixel control (learning policies to maximize local pixel changes), reward prediction (classifying immediate rewards from a skewed replay buffer), and value function replay—all sharing the same representation. The results are honestly quite staggering: on Labyrinth, UNREAL achieves 87% human-normalized performance versus 54% for A3C with a 10x speedup, and on Atari it hits 880% mean human-normalized score, crushing prior state-of-the-art. I love the intuition behind pixel control—learning to manipulate the visual stream as an intrinsic objective is a genuinely clever way to learn useful motor skills without extrinsic rewards, and the fact that it outperforms reconstruction or prediction baselines validates the "control, don't just predict" philosophy. The reward prediction with skewed replay is also a nice pragmatic trick to focus representation on sparse rewards without biasing the policy. My main concerns are: (1) the computational cost is non-trivial—the pixel control head with deconv layers and multiple Q-learning updates per step adds significant overhead, and you don't discuss wall-clock time or FLOPs; (2) the ablation results are somewhat murky—while you show each component helps, the relative contribution of pixel control vs. reward prediction vs. VR isn't systematically disentangled across all levels, and the hyperparameter sensitivity of the combined agent is still present (just less so); (3) the theoretical justification for why pixel changes are a good auxiliary task is hand-wavy—you appeal to babies and redness, but a more rigorous argument about which intrinsic rewards are universally useful would strengthen the paper; (4) the Labyrinth environment is custom and not widely available, making reproducibility harder, though the Atari results mitigate this. Overall, this is a strong empirical paper with a simple, effective idea that clearly advances the state of the art—I'm leaning accept, but I'd like to see more discussion on computational trade-offs and a clearer breakdown of what each auxiliary task contributes in different regimes.

title: Multi-Agent Cooperation and the Emergence of (Natural) Language
abstract: Abstract:###The current mainstream approach to train natural language systems is to expose them to large amounts of text. This passive learning is problematic if we are in- terested in developing interactive machines, such as conversational agents. We propose a framework for language learning that relies on multi-agent communi- cation. We study this learning in the context of referential games. In these games, a sender and a receiver see a pair of images. The sender is told one of them is the target and is allowed to send a message to the receiver, while the receiver must rely on it to identify the target. Thus, the agents develop their own language interactively out of the need to communicate. We show that two networks with simple configurations are able to learn to coordinate in the referential game. We further explore whether the â€œword meaningsâ€ induced in the game reflect intuitive semantic properties of the objects depicted in the image, and we present a simple strategy for grounding the agentsâ€™ code into natural language, a necessary step in developing machines that should eventually be able to communicate with humans.
review: This paper explores how two simple neural agents can develop a communication protocol from scratch through referential games, where a sender must produce a symbol to help a receiver identify a target image among distractors. I think the core idea—using multi-agent cooperation as a driver for emergent language—is compelling and aligns well with the broader push towards interactive, functional language learning. The results are solid: the agents reliably converge to near-perfect coordination, and the informed sender architecture with a convolutional bias yields more diverse symbol usage and higher semantic purity with respect to object categories. The manipulation of common knowledge (showing different image instances of the same class) is a nice touch, and the grounding experiment using supervised ImageNet labels to make the emergent code human-interpretable is clever, especially the finding that humans can guess the target 68% of the time even for images not containing the supervised categories. However, I have some reservations. The game setup is quite simplistic—single-symbol messages, two images, no turn-taking or dialogue—so the "language" that emerges is more of a labeling scheme than anything resembling natural language syntax or compositionality. The comparison between agnostic and informed senders is interesting, but the informed architecture essentially hard-codes a comparison between the two images, which is a strong inductive bias that may be doing most of the work. Also, the purity numbers, while significant, are still far from perfect, and the t-SNE visualizations show a lot of intermixing between categories. The paper claims to be about the "emergence of (natural) language," but what we see is closer to a rudimentary signaling system; the jump to natural language is huge and not really addressed. That said, the paper is well-written, the experiments are carefully designed, and the grounding experiment with human subjects is a strong contribution. I'd lean towards accept because it opens up a promising research direction and provides a clean framework for studying emergent communication, but I'd encourage the authors to be more cautious in framing this as "natural language" and to discuss the limitations of the single-symbol setting more explicitly. I'd also like to see a bit more analysis of why the informed sender leads to more semantically coherent symbols—is it purely the dimension-wise comparison, or something else? Overall, a solid paper with a clear contribution, though not a breakthrough.

title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
abstract: Abstract:###Despite their massive size, successful deep artificial neural networks can exhibit a remarkably small difference between training and test performance. Conventional wisdom attributes small generalization error either to properties of the model family, or to the regularization techniques used during training. Through extensive systematic experiments, we show how these traditional approaches fail to explain why large neural networks generalize well in practice. Specifically, our experiments establish that state-of-the-art convolutional networks for image classification trained with stochastic gradient methods easily fit a random labeling of the training data. This phenomenon is qualitatively unaffected by explicit regularization, and occurs even if we replace the true images by completely unstructured random noise. We corroborate these experimental findings with a theoretical construction showing that simple depth two neural networks already have perfect finite sample expressivity as soon as the number of parameters exceeds the number of data points as it usually does in practice. We interpret our experimental findings by comparison with traditional models.
review: This is a genuinely important paper that systematically demolishes a lot of conventional wisdom about why deep networks generalize. The central finding—that state-of-the-art CNNs can perfectly fit completely random labels and even random pixels with zero training error, while still achieving near-zero training loss with standard optimization—is a massive blow to the idea that model complexity or explicit regularization explains generalization. I love the experimental design: the randomization tests are clean, the interpolation between no noise and full noise shows a smooth degradation in test performance, and the ImageNet results with 95% top-1 accuracy on random labels are just absurd. The theoretical construction showing that a depth-2 network with 2n+d parameters can represent any labeling of n points is elegant and directly supports the empirical findings. The paper also does a good job systematically ruling out VC-dimension, Rademacher complexity, and uniform stability as explanations, and the discussion of implicit regularization via SGD (with the kernel analogy) is thought-provoking. My main criticisms: the paper is a bit light on proposing what *does* explain generalization—it's largely a demolition job without a clear replacement theory, though I appreciate the tentative directions. The "implicit regularization" section on linear models is interesting but feels somewhat disconnected from the main narrative, and the claim that "SGD converges to the minimum norm solution" is only true for linear models with specific initialization; for deep nets it's not established. Also, the paper doesn't deeply address why some architectures (e.g., Inception) generalize better than others despite all being able to fit random labels. That said, the experimental rigor is outstanding, the implications for the field are profound, and the writing is clear. This is exactly the kind of paper that forces the community to re-evaluate its assumptions. I'm recommending a strong accept—this will be highly cited and debated.

title: Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Neural networks are powerful and flexible models that work well for many difficult learning tasks in image, speech and natural language understanding. Despite their success, neural networks are still hard to design. In this paper, we use a recurrent network to generate the model descriptions of neural networks and train this RNN with reinforcement learning to maximize the expected accuracy of the generated architectures on a validation set. On the CIFAR-10 dataset, our method, starting from scratch, can design a novel network architecture that rivals the best human-invented architecture in terms of test set accuracy. Our CIFAR-10 model achieves a test error rate of 3.65, which is 0.09 percent better and 1.05x faster than the previous state-of-the-art model that used a similar architectural scheme. On the Penn Treebank dataset, our model can compose a novel recurrent cell that outperforms the widely-used LSTM cell, and other state-of-the-art baselines. Our cell achieves a test set perplexity of 62.4 on the Penn Treebank, which is 3.6 perplexity better than the previous state-of-the-art model. The cell can also be transferred to the character language modeling task on PTB and achieves a state-of-the-art perplexity of 1.214.
review:
This paper introduces Neural Architecture Search, where a recurrent network (the controller) generates model descriptions and is trained via reinforcement learning to maximize validation accuracy of the child networks. The approach is elegantly simple—use an RNN to output architectural hyperparameters as a sequence, train with REINFORCE, and scale with distributed asynchronous training. The empirical results are genuinely impressive: on CIFAR-10, the controller discovers a 39-layer network achieving 3.65% test error, which at the time beats the best human-designed architectures like DenseNet, and on Penn Treebank it finds a recurrent cell that outperforms LSTM with 62.4 perplexity, which transfers to character-level modeling and even improves GNMT translation by 0.5 BLEU. The skip connection mechanism via set-selection attention is a clever way to handle variable connectivity, and the tree-based formulation for recurrent cells is well-thought-out. I also appreciate the control experiments showing that policy gradient outperforms random search, and that the discovered cell is robust to adding new functions like max and sin.

However, I have some reservations. First, the computational cost is astronomical—800 GPUs concurrently training 800 child networks to convergence is completely impractical for most researchers, and the paper glosses over this by saying "we use distributed training." Second, the search space, while larger than previous work, is still quite constrained (limited filter sizes, only certain layer types, fixed depth schedules), and the controller essentially does a guided hyperparameter search over a predefined space rather than discovering genuinely novel architectural paradigms. Third, the REINFORCE gradient has high variance; the baseline helps, but the paper doesn't deeply analyze the variance or explore more sophisticated policy gradient methods. Fourth, the comparison to random search, while favorable, only shows results after 400 models—I'd like to see the asymptotic behavior. Finally, the paper doesn't provide much insight into *why* the discovered architectures work—the visualization of the RNN cell shows similarities to LSTM, but there's no analysis of what the controller has learned about good design principles.

That said, this is a pioneering work that popularized the idea of architecture search with RL, and the empirical results on CIFAR-10 and PTB are strong. It's well-written, the method is clearly described, and the transfer learning results are a nice bonus. I'm leaning accept—the paper opens up a new research direction, even if it's computationally heavy and somewhat limited in search space. I'd like to see the authors address the computational cost and provide more analysis on the learned search strategy in the final version.

title: Q-Prop: Sample-Efficient Policy Gradient with An Off-Policy Critic
abstract: Abstract:###Model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been successful in a wide variety of simulated domains. However, a major obstacle facing deep RL in the real world is their high sample complexity. Batch policy gradient methods offer stable learning, but at the cost of high variance, which often requires large batches. TD-style methods, such as off-policy actor-critic and Q-learning, are more sample-efficient but biased, and often require costly hyperparameter sweeps to stabilize. In this work, we aim to develop methods that combine the stability of policy gradients with the efficiency of off-policy RL. We present Q-Prop, a policy gradient method that uses a Taylor expansion of the off-policy critic as a control variate. Q-Prop is both sample efficient and stable, and effectively combines the benefits of on-policy and off-policy methods. We analyze the connection between Q-Prop and existing model-free algorithms, and use control variate theory to derive two variants of Q-Prop with conservative and aggressive adaptation. We show that conservative Q-Prop provides substantial gains in sample efficiency over trust region policy optimization (TRPO) with generalized advantage estimation (GAE), and improves stability over deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), the state-of-the-art on-policy and off-policy methods, on OpenAI Gym*s MuJoCo continuous control environments.
review:
This paper presents Q-Prop, a policy gradient method that uses an off-policy critic as a control variate via its first-order Taylor expansion, combining the stability of on-policy Monte Carlo gradients with the sample efficiency of off-policy TD learning. The core idea—adding a residual REINFORCE term to correct the deterministic critic gradient—is elegant and theoretically well-grounded, and the adaptive variants (conservative and aggressive) that modulate the control variate strength based on estimated correlation are a nice practical touch. The empirical results are strong: conservative Q-Prop consistently outperforms TRPO-GAE in sample efficiency across several MuJoCo domains, often by an order of magnitude, and achieves better or comparable final performance to DDPG while being significantly more stable and less sensitive to hyperparameters, particularly on the challenging Humanoid task where DDPG fails entirely. I appreciate the detailed variance analysis and the unifying view that connects policy gradient and actor-critic methods.

However, I have some reservations. First, the computational cost is nontrivial—you're fitting an off-policy critic with replay and a separate value function for GAE, then taking multiple critic gradient steps per policy update, which makes the per-iteration cost higher than TRPO and roughly comparable to DDPG, though the paper argues this is fine when data collection is the bottleneck. Second, the "unbiased" claim relies on the critic being a true Taylor expansion around the mean action, but in practice the critic is an approximation trained off-policy, so the control variate is only approximately unbiased—the paper acknowledges this but doesn't quantify the bias. Third, while the conservative variant is empirically more stable, the heuristic of setting η=1 when covariance is positive and 0 otherwise feels somewhat ad-hoc; I'd like to see a more principled way to estimate the optimal η or at least a sensitivity analysis. Fourth, the experiments focus on locomotion tasks with low-dimensional state spaces—it's unclear how Q-Prop scales to high-dimensional visual inputs or discrete action spaces, where the Taylor expansion of the critic would be less straightforward.

Overall, this is a well-executed paper with a theoretically sound and practically effective contribution. The gains in sample efficiency and stability over TRPO and DDPG are meaningful, and the control variate perspective is insightful. I'm recommending accept—the paper advances the state of the art in continuous control RL, even if the method is computationally heavier and the theoretical unbiasedness is somewhat idealized. I'd encourage the authors to discuss the limitations more explicitly and provide some guidance on when to use conservative vs. aggressive variants in practice.

title: Learning to Act by Predicting the Future
abstract: Abstract:###We present an approach to sensorimotor control in immersive environments. Our approach utilizes a high-dimensional sensory stream and a lower-dimensional measurement stream. The cotemporal structure of these streams provides a rich supervisory signal, which enables training a sensorimotor control model by interacting with the environment. The model is trained using supervised learning techniques, but without extraneous supervision. It learns to act based on raw sensory input from a complex three-dimensional environment. The presented formulation enables learning without a fixed goal at training time, and pursuing dynamically changing goals at test time. We conduct extensive experiments in three-dimensional simulations based on the classical first-person game Doom. The results demonstrate that the presented approach outperforms sophisticated prior formulations, particularly on challenging tasks. The results also show that trained models successfully generalize across environments and goals. A model trained using the presented approach won the Full Deathmatch track of the Visual Doom AI Competition, which was held in previously unseen environments.
review:
This paper presents a surprisingly simple yet effective approach to sensorimotor control: instead of learning a policy or value function via RL, train a network to predict future measurements (health, ammo, frags) conditioned on current sensory input, current measurements, and a goal vector, then at test time just pick the action that maximizes the predicted outcome. I have to admit, the results are genuinely impressive—DFP outperforms DQN, A3C, and DSR on Doom tasks, with a multiplicative gap on the harder Battle scenarios, and it won the Full Deathmatch track of the Visual Doom AI Competition by a 50% margin over a more complex LSTM-based system that used extra supervision. The ability to train with randomized goals and then generalize to new goals at test time is a nice demonstration of the framework's flexibility, and the ablation showing that predicting multiple measurements beats scalar reward is a solid empirical validation of the core intuition. I also appreciate the architectural choices like the dueling-style split into expectation and action streams—it's a clean way to handle the action-conditional predictions.

However, I have some reservations. First, the method is essentially a learned forward model with a planning-by-argmax step, which is a form of model-based RL or Monte Carlo control, but the paper frames it as a departure from RL, which feels a bit disingenuous—you're still maximizing a reward-like objective, just not via Bellman backups. Second, the "no fixed goal" training is cool, but it's basically goal-conditioned behavior cloning on predicted outcomes, which has been explored before; the novelty is the architecture and the specific application, not the conceptual framework. Third, the architecture is quite task-specific—it assumes measurements are scalar and goals are linear combinations, and it's not obvious how to extend this to complex goals or tasks where the relevant measurements aren't obvious. Fourth, the comparison to A3C is somewhat unfair because A3C was given the same dense reward signal derived from the measurements, but DFP is directly predicting the measurements themselves, which is a richer training signal—so the advantage might be more about the supervision format than the algorithm. Finally, the paper doesn't provide much theoretical analysis—why does predicting future measurements work so well, and are there failure cases where it would break down?

Overall, I think this is a solid empirical paper with compelling results, but I'm not convinced it fundamentally rethinks RL as the title suggests. It's more of a clever and effective application of supervised learning to control. I'm leaning accept because the results are strong and the method is simple and reproducible, but I'd like to see a more honest discussion of the relationship to model-based RL and a clearer analysis of when this approach would fail. Also, the lack of memory or temporal abstraction is a limitation that the authors acknowledge but don't address. I'd recommend acceptance with the caveat that the theoretical framing is somewhat overstated.

title: On Large-Batch Training for Deep Learning: Generalization Gap and Sharp Minima
abstract: Abstract:###The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method and its variants are algorithms of choice for many Deep Learning tasks. These methods operate in a small-batch regime wherein a fraction of the training data, say -- data points, is sampled to compute an approximation to the gradient. It has been observed in practice that when using a larger batch there is a degradation in the quality of the model, as measured by its ability to generalize. We investigate the cause for this generalization drop in the large-batch regime and present numerical evidence that supports the view that large-batch methods tend to converge to sharp minimizers of the training and testing functions---and as is well known, sharp minima lead to poorer generalization. In contrast, small-batch methods consistently converge to flat minimizers, and our experiments support a commonly held view that this is due to the inherent noise in the gradient estimation. We discuss several strategies to attempt to help large-batch methods eliminate this generalization gap.
review:
This paper tackles a well-known practical problem: large-batch training in deep learning often leads to worse generalization than small-batch training, even when training accuracy is comparable. The authors provide compelling empirical evidence that this generalization gap correlates with LB methods converging to sharp minima (characterized by large Hessian eigenvalues) while SB methods find flat minima. I appreciate the systematic experiments across multiple architectures and datasets, the introduction of a computationally feasible sharpness metric (even if heuristic), and the warm-starting experiments that nicely illustrate how SB exploration phase seems necessary before LB fine-tuning works. The paper also thoughtfully explores several attempted remedies—data augmentation, conservative training, adversarial training—and honestly reports that none fully solve the problem, which is an important negative result for the community.

However, I have some concerns. First, the sharpness metric (Equation 4) is somewhat ad-hoc; it's a local perturbation measure with arbitrary parameters (epsilon, number of L-BFGS iterations, random subspace dimension), and the paper doesn't justify why these specific choices are appropriate or how sensitive the results are to them. Second, the experimental setup uses ADAM for both SB and LB, but ADAM itself has adaptive per-parameter learning rates that might interact with batch size in ways not discussed—I'd like to see similar experiments with plain SGD to ensure the phenomenon isn't optimizer-specific. Third, the paper frames "sharp vs. flat minima" as the cause of the generalization gap, but the evidence is correlational, not causal; it's possible that both sharpness and poor generalization are consequences of some other factor. Fourth, the paper doesn't provide a theoretical explanation for why noise in SB gradients leads to flat minima—it's treated as an empirical observation, but some analysis or intuition would strengthen the argument. Fifth, the performance model in Appendix C suggests LB could be much faster, but the paper doesn't actually demonstrate a wall-clock speedup; without that, the practical motivation feels incomplete.

Overall, I think this is a solid empirical paper that makes an important observation and will be useful for the community to think about. The results are clear, the experiments are reasonably thorough, and the negative results on attempted fixes are valuable. I'm recommending accept, but I'd like to see the authors address the limitations of the sharpness metric, provide more discussion on the causal interpretation, and ideally include some wall-clock timing results to substantiate the parallelism argument. It's not a theoretical breakthrough, but it's a well-executed empirical study that advances our understanding of a practical problem.

title: Semi-supervised Knowledge Transfer for Deep Learning from Private Training Data
abstract: Abstract:###Some machine learning applications involve training data that is sensitive, such as the medical histories of patients in a clinical trial. A model may inadvertently and implicitly store some of its training data; careful analysis of the model may therefore reveal sensitive information. To address this problem, we demonstrate a generally applicable approach to providing strong privacy guarantees for training data: Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles (PATE). The approach combines, in a black-box fashion, multiple models trained with disjoint datasets, such as records from different subsets of users. Because they rely directly on sensitive data, these models are not published, but instead used as **teachers** for a **student** model. The student learns to predict an output chosen by noisy voting among all of the teachers, and cannot directly access an individual teacher or the underlying data or parameters. The student*s privacy properties can be understood both intuitively (since no single teacher and thus no single dataset dictates the student*s training) and formally, in terms of differential privacy. These properties hold even if an adversary can not only query the student but also inspect its internal workings. Compared with previous work, the approach imposes only weak assumptions on how teachers are trained: it applies to any model, including non-convex models like DNNs. We achieve state-of-the-art privacy/utility trade-offs on MNIST and SVHN thanks to an improved privacy analysis and semi-supervised learning.
review:
This paper presents PATE (Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles), a framework for training machine learning models with differential privacy guarantees on training data. The core idea is elegant and intuitive: train an ensemble of teachers on disjoint subsets of sensitive data, then use noisy voting among teachers to label public unlabeled data for training a student model that is ultimately released. The paper makes several nice contributions: (1) it removes the convexity restrictions of prior work (Hamm et al. 2016), making the approach applicable to arbitrary models including DNNs; (2) it applies the moments accountant in a novel data-dependent way to tighten privacy bounds when teacher quorums are strong; (3) it demonstrates impressive empirical results—98% accuracy on MNIST with epsilon ~2 (vs. Abadi et al.'s 97% with epsilon 8) and 90.66% on SVHN with epsilon 8.19, which is a meaningful privacy guarantee (unlike Shokri & Shmatikov's per-parameter epsilon). The use of GAN-based semi-supervised learning to dramatically reduce the number of teacher queries is clever and effective.

That said, I have some reservations. First, the approach relies on a substantial amount of unlabeled public data that is assumed to be available. While this is often true for image benchmarks, it's not guaranteed in many sensitive domains (e.g., medical data). Second, the data-dependent privacy analysis technically makes epsilon itself a function of the data, which means the reported epsilon values are not themselves differentially private unless noise is added—the paper hand-waves this by saying the noise would be small, but it's a subtle point that deserves more discussion. Third, the method requires training a large number of teachers (250 in their experiments), which is computationally expensive and may not scale to very large datasets or tasks with many classes where partitioning would leave each teacher with too little data. Fourth, the paper doesn't deeply explore failure modes—what happens when teachers disagree strongly, or when the public unlabeled data distribution differs significantly from the private data distribution? Finally, while the black-box nature is a strength, it also means the privacy analysis is conservative—it assumes any teacher's predictions can change arbitrarily when one training example changes, which may be overly pessimistic in practice.

Overall, I think this is a strong paper that makes a significant contribution to privacy-preserving machine learning. The intuitive appeal of the approach combined with formal guarantees and strong empirical results makes it compelling. I'm recommending accept—the approach is novel, well-executed, and the results are state-of-the-art. I'd like to see the authors address the limitations around data-dependent epsilon and the assumptions on unlabeled data in the final version, but these don't undermine the core contribution.

title: Amortised MAP Inference for Image Super-resolution
abstract: Abstract:###Image super-resolution (SR) is an underdetermined inverse problem, where a large number of plausible high resolution images can explain the same downsampled image. Most current single image SR methods use empirical risk minimisation, often with a pixel-wise mean squared error (MSE) loss. However, the outputs from such methods tend to be blurry, over-smoothed and generally appear implausible. A more desirable approach would employ Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) inference, preferring solutions that always have a high probability under the image prior, and thus appear more plausible. Direct MAP estimation for SR is non-trivial, as it requires us to build a model for the image prior from samples. Here we introduce new methods for emph{amortised MAP inference} whereby we calculate the MAP estimate directly using a convolutional neural network. We first introduce a novel neural network architecture that performs a projection to the affine subspace of valid SR solutions ensuring that the high resolution output of the network is always consistent with the low resolution input. We show that, using this architecture, the amortised MAP inference problem reduces to minimising the cross-entropy between two distributions, similar to training generative models. We propose three methods to solve this optimisation problem: (1) Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) (2) denoiser-guided SR which backpropagates gradient-estimates from denoising to train the network, and (3) a baseline method using a maximum-likelihood-trained image prior. Our experiments show that the GAN based approach performs best on real image data. Lastly, we establish a connection between GANs and amortised variational inference as in e.g. variational autoencoders.
review: This paper attempts to tackle image super-resolution via amortized MAP inference, arguing that it yields more plausible results than MSE-based averaging. The authors introduce a neat architectural trick—an affine projection layer that enforces exact consistency with the downsampled input—which is arguably the paper's strongest technical contribution and clearly works well even with MSE training, leading to faster convergence and lower LR-consistency error. However, I have serious reservations about the broader claims and the empirical validation. The paper proposes three methods (GAN, denoiser-guided, density-guided), but two of them (AffDG and AffLL) are empirical failures in the image domain, producing consistently blurry results and unstable training despite extensive heuristic annealing; the paper essentially abandons them after the grass texture experiment. This effectively reduces the contribution to "AffGAN works, the rest don't," which feels thin given the theoretical framing. Moreover, the AffGAN outputs on ImageNet are concerning—the famous "snake to water" hallucination shows the model aggressively prioritizes prior density over fidelity, which is exactly the sort of dangerous behavior that makes MAP inference questionable in the first place. The authors themselves acknowledge in Section 5.6 that MAP estimates are representation-dependent and can be highly atypical (e.g., the mode of a high-dimensional Gaussian has zero norm), which directly undermines the core motivation that MAP yields "plausible" solutions. The connection to variational inference in Appendix F is interesting but under-explored and not empirically validated. Overall, I find the paper technically competent but conceptually muddled: it proposes a principled objective, shows it fails for two out of three proposed optimizers, and the one that "works" produces visually sharp but often semantically incorrect outputs. The affine projection is a useful engineering contribution, but the MAP inference framing adds little beyond what we already know from GAN-based SR, and the empirical evidence does not convincingly demonstrate that this approach is well-posed or superior.

title: Learning Graphical State Transitions
abstract: Abstract:###Graph-structured data is important in modeling relationships between multiple entities, and can be used to represent states of the world as well as many data structures. Li et al. (2016) describe a model known as a Gated Graph Sequence Neural Network (GGS-NN) that produces sequences from graph-structured input. In this work I introduce the Gated Graph Transformer Neural Network (GGT-NN), an extension of GGS-NNs that uses graph-structured data as an intermediate representation. The model can learn to construct and modify graphs in sophisticated ways based on textual input, and also to use the graphs to produce a variety of outputs. For example, the model successfully learns to solve almost all of the bAbI tasks (Weston et al., 2016), and also discovers the rules governing graphical formulations of a simple cellular automaton and a family of Turing machines.
review: This paper proposes the Gated Graph Transformer Neural Network (GGT-NN), an extension of Li et al.'s GGS-NNs that uses graph-structured data as an intermediate representation and can learn to construct and modify graphs from textual input or to simulate dynamical systems like cellular automata and Turing machines. The authors introduce a set of differentiable graph transformations (node addition, state update, edge update, propagation, aggregation) and demonstrate strong performance on the bAbI tasks, achieving near-perfect accuracy on most tasks with relatively few training examples, as well as on synthetic tasks involving Rule 30 and arbitrary 4-state Turing machines. I think the core idea of using explicitly graph-structured internal states is compelling and the modular transformation framework is a neat engineering contribution, but I have some serious concerns. First, the model relies heavily on strong supervision—the correct graph is provided at every timestep during training—which makes the bAbI results feel more like a demonstration that the architecture can learn to copy a provided graph structure from a knowledge base rather than truly "understanding" or extracting semantics from the text. The authors acknowledge this supervision requirement, but without it, I'm skeptical the model would learn anything meaningful, and the paper doesn't explore how to relax this assumption. Second, the model's computational complexity scales quadratically with the number of nodes, which severely limits its applicability to larger graphs; this is mentioned in passing but not addressed with any clever sparsity or approximation techniques. Third, the failure on bAbI task 17 (Positional Reasoning) is a notable red flag—this task requires relational reasoning about order, which is precisely what a graph-based model should excel at, yet it couldn't reach 95% accuracy even with 10,000 examples. The connection to existing memory-augmented architectures like DNC and HAM is discussed but the comparison is superficial; the paper doesn't provide a clear argument for why a distributed graph representation is superior to sequential attention mechanisms beyond hand-wavy claims about parallel processing. Overall, I find the paper technically solid but the novelty is incremental—it's essentially GGS-NNs plus a set of well-designed but not groundbreaking transformations—and the empirical evaluation, while extensive, doesn't convincingly demonstrate that GGT-NNs are solving problems that existing architectures couldn't also solve with appropriate supervision. I'd recommend acceptance if the authors can more clearly articulate what problems this architecture uniquely enables and demonstrate its advantage on tasks where graph structure is truly essential and not just a convenient way to represent a knowledge base.

title: Maximum Entropy Flow Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Maximum entropy modeling is a flexible and popular framework for formulating statistical models given partial knowledge. In this paper, rather than the traditional method of optimizing over the continuous density directly, we learn a smooth and invertible transformation that maps a simple distribution to the desired maximum entropy distribution. Doing so is nontrivial in that the objective being maximized (entropy) is a function of the density itself. By exploiting recent developments in normalizing flow networks, we cast the maximum entropy problem into a finite-dimensional constrained optimization, and solve the problem by combining stochastic optimization with the augmented Lagrangian method. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, and applications to finance and computer vision show the flexibility and accuracy of using maximum entropy flow networks.
review: This paper proposes Maximum Entropy Flow Networks (MEFN), a framework that uses normalizing flows and the augmented Lagrangian method to solve continuous maximum entropy problems. The core idea—replacing the intractable direct density optimization with learning an invertible transformation from a simple distribution—is clever and addresses the long-standing issues of sampling and density evaluation in ME modeling. I appreciate the connection drawn between ME and modern deep generative models, and the texture synthesis application nicely demonstrates the practical benefit of maximizing entropy for sample diversity, which is often overlooked in moment-matching approaches. The technical execution is solid: using normalizing flows ensures tractable density computation, the augmented Lagrangian handles the constrained optimization cleanly, and the stochastic gradient estimator for entropy is unbiased and efficient. However, I have several concerns. First, the computational cost of the augmented Lagrangian outer loop with full SGD inner optimizations is substantial, and the paper doesn't discuss runtime or scalability compared to simpler alternatives; for high-dimensional problems like images, this seems prohibitively expensive, and I'm skeptical that the real NVP structure with only 3 residual blocks has sufficient capacity to capture complex image distributions accurately. Second, while the Dirichlet example is a nice sanity check, it's a low-dimensional toy problem where the ME solution is already known and easy to sample; the paper would benefit from a more challenging high-dimensional ME problem with ground truth to really stress-test the algorithm. Third, the theoretical justification for the augmented Lagrangian convergence relies on regularity conditions that are hand-waved away; the authors admit these aren't proven, which is fine for an empirical paper, but then they should lean harder on the empirical results, which are mixed—the entropy improvement over the texture net is clear, but visual diversity isn't always guaranteed (as the authors acknowledge in Appendix C with the brick texture failure). The risk-neutral asset pricing application is interesting but the comparison to the Gibbs method is somewhat superficial; the Q-Q plot shows close agreement, but it's unclear which distribution is actually more accurate given the limited data, and the heavy-tail mismatch isn't fully explained. I also worry about the novelty—the use of normalizing flows for generative modeling and the augmented Lagrangian for constrained optimization are both well-established techniques; the contribution is their combination, which is neat but perhaps not groundbreaking. Overall, I find the paper promising and well-written, but the practical limitations and lack of compelling high-dimensional results leave me unconvinced that this is a significant advance over existing approaches like GANs or VAEs with moment-matching penalties. I would lean toward borderline accept with a strong recommendation to demonstrate scalability on more challenging problems and to provide a clearer comparison to state-of-the-art generative models.

title: Topology and Geometry of Half-Rectified Network Optimization
abstract: Abstract:###The loss surface of deep neural networks has recently attracted interest in the optimization and machine learning communities as a prime example of high-dimensional non-convex problem. Some insights were recently gained using spin glass models and mean-field approximations, but at the expense of strongly simplifying the nonlinear nature of the model. In this work, we do not make any such approximation and study conditions on the data distribution and model architecture that prevent the existence of bad local minima. Our theoretical work quantifies and formalizes two important folklore facts: (i) the landscape of deep linear networks has a radically different topology from that of deep half-rectified ones, and (ii) that the energy landscape in the non-linear case is fundamentally controlled by the interplay between the smoothness of the data distribution and model over-parametrization. Our main theoretical contribution is to prove that half-rectified single layer networks are asymptotically connected, and we provide explicit bounds that reveal the aforementioned interplay. The conditioning of gradient descent is the next challenge we address. We study this question through the geometry of the level sets, and we introduce an algorithm to efficiently estimate the regularity of such sets on large-scale networks.
