Our empirical results show that these level sets remain connected throughout all the learning phase, suggesting a near convex behavior, but they become exponentially more curvy as the energy level decays, in accordance to what is observed in practice with very low curvature attractors.
review: This paper tackles the loss landscape of neural networks, specifically asking whether ReLU networks have bad local minima and how the geometry of level sets changes with overparameterization. I think the main theoretical contribution—showing that single-layer ReLU networks' level sets become connected as overparameterization increases, with the energy gap scaling as \(O(m^{-1/n})\)—is genuinely interesting and provides a formal justification for a widely held intuition. The proof technique, which exploits local linearization of the ReLU activation and covers the weight space with \(\epsilon\)-nets, is clever and technically sound, though it's quite dense and relies on quantities like \(\delta_{W}(l,\alpha;m)\) that are hard to interpret or compute in practice. The extension to deeper networks is only conjectured, which limits the immediate impact of the result. On the empirical side, the Dynamic String Sampling algorithm is a neat heuristic for probing connectivity and geodesic length, and the results across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and PTB show a consistent pattern—level sets are connected up to very low loss, but the geometry becomes increasingly non-convex (i.e., longer geodesics) as the loss decreases. That said, I'm not fully convinced by the empirical methodology. The algorithm only certifies connectivity if it converges; failure to converge could just mean the heuristic is stuck, not that a disconnection exists. The paper acknowledges this, but it's a serious limitation when claiming "near convex behavior." The counterexample in Appendix E is a nice sanity check, but it's a highly contrived task (permuting three points) and doesn't really mirror real-world difficulty. I'm also concerned that the paper overclaims: showing connected level sets up to low loss doesn't imply optimization is easy—saddle points and ill-conditioning can still cause slowdowns, and the paper doesn't address this. The theoretical results are asymptotic and don't provide practical guidance on, say, how many hidden units are "enough" to avoid bad local minima on a given dataset. On balance, I find the paper thought-provoking and the proof of the single-layer result is a solid piece of work, but the empirical contribution is more of a diagnostic tool than a definitive characterization, and the gap between theory and practice remains substantial. I'd lean toward acceptance because the theoretical insights are valuable and the paper stimulates discussion, but I'd want to see more careful treatment of the algorithm's limitations and a clearer statement of what the results imply for practitioners.

title: Paying More Attention to Attention: Improving the Performance of Convolutional Neural Networks via Attention Transfer
abstract: Abstract:###Attention plays a critical role in human visual experience. Furthermore, it has recently been demonstrated that attention can also play an important role in the context of applying artificial neural networks to a variety of tasks from fields such as computer vision and NLP. In this work we show that, by properly defining attention for convolutional neural networks, we can actually use this type of information in order to significantly improve the performance of a student CNN network by forcing it to mimic the attention maps of a powerful teacher network. To that end, we propose several novel methods of transferring attention, showing consistent improvement across a variety of datasets and convolutional neural network architectures.
review: This paper proposes a simple but effective idea: transfer knowledge from a teacher CNN to a student CNN by making the student mimic the teacher's spatial attention maps, defined as channel-wise aggregated activations (e.g., sum of squared activations) or input gradients. The intuition is that attention maps encode where the network "looks," and forcing the student to attend similarly should improve its representations. I find the core idea quite appealing and the experimental validation is extensive—across CIFAR-10, CUB, Scenes, and ImageNet, activation-based attention transfer consistently improves student performance, often outperforming full-activation transfer (FitNets-style hints) and knowledge distillation. The gains on ImageNet (1.1% top-1 improvement for ResNet-18 using ResNet-34 as teacher) are particularly impressive and, to my knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a knowledge transfer method that actually works on ImageNet at scale. The gradient-based attention transfer is less practical due to double backpropagation cost, but the symmetry regularization trick is a neat side contribution. That said, I have some concerns. First, the definition of attention maps is somewhat ad-hoc—the authors try a few aggregation functions (sum, sum of squares, max) but don't provide a strong theoretical justification for why one works better than others, and the choice of \(F_{\text{sum}}^2\) feels somewhat arbitrary. Second, the method is essentially a regularizer, and the improvement is sensitive to hyperparameters like \(\beta\) and placement of transfer losses—the paper doesn't provide a principled way to tune these. Third, the comparison to full-activation transfer is interesting but not fully explained; why does attention transfer work better than transferring full activations? The authors speculate but don't analyze deeply. Fourth, the gradient-based AT section feels incomplete—it's only tested on a small NIN without batch norm and the results are modest; I'm not convinced it's worth the extra computation. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with clear empirical value, and the attention transfer idea is likely to be adopted by practitioners. The novelty is moderate—it's essentially knowledge distillation applied to spatial attention maps—but the results speak for themselves. I'd recommend acceptance, with the suggestion that the authors provide more insight into why attention maps are a better transfer target than activations, and perhaps clarify the practical guidelines for choosing transfer layers and hyperparameters.

title: Learning Visual Servoing with Deep Features and Fitted Q-Iteration
abstract: Abstract:###Visual servoing involves choosing actions that move a robot in response to observations from a camera, in order to reach a goal configuration in the world. Standard visual servoing approaches typically rely on manually designed features and analytical dynamics models, which limits their generalization capability and often requires extensive application-specific feature and model engineering. In this work, we study how learned visual features, learned predictive dynamics models, and reinforcement learning can be combined to learn visual servoing mechanisms. We focus on target following, with the goal of designing algorithms that can learn a visual servo using low amounts of data of the target in question, to enable quick adaptation to new targets. Our approach is based on servoing the camera in the space of learned visual features, rather than image pixels or manually-designed keypoints. We demonstrate that standard deep features, in our case taken from a model trained for object classification, can be used together with a bilinear predictive model to learn an effective visual servo that is robust to visual variation, changes in viewing angle and appearance, and occlusions. A key component of our approach is to use a sample-efficient fitted Q-iteration algorithm to learn which features are best suited for the task at hand. We show that we can learn an effective visual servo on a complex synthetic car following benchmark using just 20 training trajectory samples for reinforcement learning. We demonstrate substantial improvement over a conventional approach based on image pixels or hand-designed keypoints, and we show an improvement in sample-efficiency of more than two orders of magnitude over standard model-free deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Videos are available at http://rll.berkeley.edu/visual_servoing.
review:
This paper presents a method for learning visual servoing policies that combines pre-trained deep features (from VGG), a bilinear dynamics model, and a sample-efficient fitted Q-iteration algorithm to weight the features. The core idea is clever: instead of learning a policy from scratch with RL, use off-the-shelf visual features and a simple predictive model, then learn only the feature weights and control costs via FQI. I think the approach is well-motivated and the experimental setup—a challenging car-following simulation with distractors, occlusions, and novel cars—is appropriate for testing generalization. The results are strong: the VGG conv4_3 features with FQI weights substantially outperform pixel-based baselines, classical IBVS, and even a state-of-the-art tracker, all while being far more sample-efficient than TRPO (20 trajectories vs. thousands). The multiscale bilinear dynamics model is sensible and the FQI formulation is elegant, making the optimization computationally tractable. I also appreciate the careful ablation comparing different feature layers and optimization methods.

That said, I have some concerns. First, the method relies heavily on the pre-trained VGG features being suitable for the task—this works here because ImageNet features are good for car detection, but it's not clear how well this would generalize to completely novel objects or domains where no such pre-trained model exists. Second, the bilinear dynamics model is quite restrictive; it assumes linearity in controls and local spatial structure, which works for camera motion but likely wouldn't hold for more complex robot dynamics (e.g., manipulation with joint angles). Third, the FQI algorithm, while efficient, learns only a linear weighting of features; this is a significant limitation if the optimal weighting is non-linear or context-dependent. Fourth, the comparison to TRPO is a bit unfair—TRPO is trained from scratch on raw pixels, while the proposed method uses a pre-trained feature extractor and a learned dynamics model; the sample efficiency gain is impressive but partly due to the inductive bias already baked in. Finally, the paper lacks a real-world experiment; the simulation is rich but still synthetic, and the gap to physical robots with noisy sensors and unmodeled dynamics remains unexplored.

Overall, I find the paper technically solid and the results compelling, but the contributions are somewhat incremental—combining known components (VGG features, bilinear models, FQI) in a principled way. The sample efficiency is the main selling point, and the authors demonstrate it convincingly. I'd lean toward acceptance, but I'd like to see a discussion of limitations and potential failure cases, and ideally some indication of how the method might extend to more complex dynamics or real-world settings.

title: Stochastic Neural Networks for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Deep reinforcement learning has achieved many impressive results in recent years. However, tasks with sparse rewards or long horizons continue to pose significant challenges. To tackle these important problems, we propose a general framework that first learns useful skills in a pre-training environment, and then leverages the acquired skills for learning faster in downstream tasks. Our approach brings together some of the strengths of intrinsic motivation and hierarchical methods: the learning of useful skill is guided by a single proxy reward, the design of which requires very minimal domain knowledge about the downstream tasks. Then a high-level policy is trained on top of these skills, providing a significant improvement of the exploration and allowing to tackle sparse rewards in the downstream tasks. To efficiently pre-train a large span of skills, we use Stochastic Neural Networks combined with an information-theoretic regularizer. Our experiments show that this combination is effective in learning a wide span of interpretable skills in a sample-efficient way, and can significantly boost the learning performance uniformly across a wide range of downstream tasks.
review: This paper proposes a two-stage framework for hierarchical reinforcement learning: first, pre-train a diverse set of skills using a stochastic neural network with a mutual information bonus in a proxy environment; second, use those skills as fixed primitives for a high-level policy to solve downstream sparse-reward tasks. I think the core idea—learning a rich repertoire of behaviors with minimal supervision and then reusing them hierarchically—is compelling and practically relevant. The use of SNNs with bilinear integration and the MI regularizer is clever, and the results on the Swimmer mazes and Gather tasks show clear improvements over baselines, especially in sample efficiency. The visitation plots nicely demonstrate that the skills are interpretable and diverse. However, I have several concerns that prevent me from being fully enthusiastic. First, the pre-training phase still requires a carefully designed proxy reward (e.g., speed for locomotion), which is not truly "unsupervised" and encodes significant domain knowledge—this limits the generality of the approach. Second, the MI bonus estimation via discretization of the state space is crude and unlikely to scale to high-dimensional continuous spaces; the paper doesn't address this limitation. Third, the failure on the Ant robot (Appendix D) is a serious red flag—the method breaks down on unstable agents due to switching between skills, which is exactly the kind of challenging robot where hierarchical RL is most needed. Fourth, the comparison to baselines is somewhat unfair: the "Gaussian noise" baseline is trivial, and the intrinsic motivation baseline (CoM reward) is not a state-of-the-art exploration method like VIME or count-based exploration, which were shown to make progress on these tasks. Fifth, the paper lacks theoretical analysis or even a clear discussion of why the MI bonus encourages diversity—the connection to InfoGAN is mentioned but not rigorously justified. The writing is clear overall, but the paper feels like a solid empirical demonstration rather than a fundamental advance; the contributions are mostly heuristic and the failure modes are significant. title: Nonparametric Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Automatically determining the optimal size of a neural network for a given task without prior information currently requires an expensive global search and training many networks from scratch. In this paper, we address the problem of automatically finding a good network size during a single training cycle. We introduce {it nonparametric neural networks}, a non-probabilistic framework for conducting optimization over all possible network sizes and prove its soundness when network growth is limited via an penalty. We train networks under this framework by continuously adding new units while eliminating redundant units via an penalty. We employ a novel optimization algorithm, which we term ``Adaptive Radial-Angular Gradient Descent** or {it AdaRad}, and obtain promising results.
review: This paper tackles the important problem of automatically determining neural network size during a single training run, proposing a "nonparametric" framework that dynamically adds and removes units using a fan-in \(\ell_2\) regularizer, a novel CapNorm layer, and a new optimizer called AdaRad. I find the core idea compelling—the theoretical result (Theorem 1) showing that the objective attains a finite global minimum under fan-in/out regularization is a genuine contribution and provides a solid foundation for the approach. The AdaRad optimizer is also clever: decomposing gradients into radial (length-changing) and angular (direction-changing) components to handle the interaction between the regularizer and new unit initialization is a neat technical solution. The detailed analysis of a single training run (Figure 3) is illuminating and demonstrates that the dynamics of unit lifetimes, fan-in lengths, and CapNorm interplay work as intended. However, I have several reservations. First, the method is computationally expensive—adding units one by one per epoch and requiring multiple training phases (with and without regularization, step size annealing) makes this significantly slower than standard parametric training, and the paper doesn't provide wall-clock comparisons. Second, the algorithm is laden with heuristics: the unit addition rate \(\nu\), the frequency \(\nu_{\text{freq}}\), the radial step size \(\alpha_r = 1/(50\lambda)\), the angular step size annealing schedule—these all require tuning and their optimal values likely depend on the dataset and architecture, undermining the "automatic" claim. Third, the empirical results are mixed: on MNIST and rectangles images the method is competitive or better than random search, but on convex it fails badly, converging to networks that are too small and underperforming parametric counterparts. The poker result is impressive (0% test error) but that dataset is relatively easy and the comparison to decision trees is a strawman—modern deep learning baselines would likely also achieve near-perfect accuracy. Fourth, the comparison to parametric networks is not entirely fair: parametric networks are trained with RMSprop/Adam and separate hyperparameter tuning, while the nonparametric networks use AdaRad with a specific schedule; a more controlled ablation isolating the effect of AdaRad vs. the growth/shrinkage mechanism would strengthen the paper. Finally, the proof of Theorem 1 is long and complex, and while I appreciate the rigor, it assumes differentiability and uses a linearization argument that is mathematically intricate—I worry that practitioners will find it inaccessible and that the assumptions may not hold for modern architectures with skip connections or batch normalization (CapNorm is not covered by the theorem). Overall, I find the paper interesting and technically solid, but the practical utility is unclear given the computational cost, heuristic-heavy algorithm, and mixed results. I'd lean toward borderline acceptance, with a strong recommendation that the authors provide clearer guidance on hyperparameter settings, wall-clock comparisons, and a more honest discussion of when the method fails (e.g., convex) and why.

title: Distributed Second-Order Optimization using Kronecker-Factored Approximations
abstract: Abstract:###As more computational resources become available, machine learning researchers train ever larger neural networks on millions of data points using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Although SGD scales well in terms of both the size of dataset and the number of parameters of the model, it has rapidly diminishing returns as parallel computing resources increase. Second-order optimization methods have an affinity for well-estimated gradients and large mini-batches, and can therefore benefit much more from parallel computation in principle. Unfortunately, they often employ severe approximations to the curvature matrix in order to scale to large models with millions of parameters, limiting their effectiveness in practice versus well-tuned SGD with momentum. The recently proposed K-FAC method(Martens and Grosse, 2015) uses a stronger and more sophisticated curvature approximation, and has been shown to make much more per-iteration progress than SGD, while only introducing a modest overhead. In this paper, we develop a version of K-FAC that distributes the computation of gradients and additional quantities required by K-FAC across multiple machines, thereby taking advantage of methodâ€™s superior scaling to large mini-batches and mitigating its additional overheads. We provide a Tensorflow implementation of our approach which is easy to use and can be applied to many existing codebases without modification. Additionally, we develop several algorithmic enhancements to K-FAC which can improve its computational performance for very large models. Finally, we show that our distributed K-FAC method speeds up training of various state-of-the-art ImageNet classification models by a factor of two compared to Batch Normalization(Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015).
review:
This paper presents a distributed asynchronous implementation of K-FAC, a second-order optimization method based on Kronecker-factored approximations to the Fisher information matrix, and demonstrates speedups on large-scale ImageNet models. The core idea—distributing the computation of gradients, second-order statistics, and Fisher block inversions across multiple workers—is a natural and practical extension of Martens and Grosse's original K-FAC work. I find the engineering contributions solid: the asynchronous inversion of curvature matrices and the dedicated stats worker both make sense given the different computational characteristics of these operations, and the doubly-factored Kronecker approximation for wide convolutional layers is a clever way to handle the AlexNet-style fully connected layer with 9k input units. The empirical results on GoogLeNet, AlexNet, and ResNet-50 show that distributed K-FAC can achieve roughly 2x wall-clock speedups over a well-tuned SGD with Batch Normalization baseline, and the mini-batch scaling experiment (Figure 6) convincingly demonstrates that K-FAC makes better use of large batches than SGD. I also appreciate the step-size selection based on Fisher norm clipping and the automatic graph construction in TensorFlow—these are practical contributions that make the method more usable.

That said, I have several concerns that temper my enthusiasm. First, the asynchronous updates introduce staleness in both the curvature statistics and the inverses, and while the paper claims this doesn't hurt performance, there's no systematic analysis of how staleness affects convergence or how sensitive the method is to the update frequency of the Fisher blocks. Second, the doubly-factored approximation is a significant additional approximation on top of the already-strong K-FAC assumptions, and the paper doesn't provide any theoretical justification or error bounds for it—only empirical results on AlexNet, which is a single data point. Third, the comparison to SGD baselines is somewhat cherry-picked: the "standard BN" baseline uses small chunks (rbz=32) which intentionally introduces noise, making the comparison look better; the improved BN baseline with larger chunks is closer to a fair comparison, but even then, the hyperparameters for SGD (learning rate schedules, momentum, etc.) are not thoroughly tuned, and it's unclear if the speedup is due to K-FAC's better curvature modeling or simply better hyperparameter choices. Fourth, the paper claims distributed K-FAC is "2x faster" than SGD+BN, but the wall-clock time plots show the gap narrowing over time, and the final validation errors are often similar—so the benefit is primarily in early training, which is useful but less dramatic than claimed. Fifth, the algorithm complexity is substantial: the paper introduces multiple approximations (standard K-FAC, cheaper K-FAC for conv layers, doubly-factored K-FAC), asynchronous updates, and a specialized step-size selection method—this is a lot of moving parts, and it's unclear how robust the method is to hyperparameter variations or how easily it can be adopted by practitioners without significant tuning.

Overall, I find the paper technically sound and the results promising, but the contributions are primarily engineering and empirical rather than theoretical, and the comparison to baselines could be more rigorous. I'd recommend acceptance, but with a strong suggestion that the authors provide a more thorough ablation study on the effects of staleness, a clearer discussion of the trade-offs of each approximation, and a more careful hyperparameter tuning methodology for the SGD baselines to ensure a fair comparison.

title: Pruning Filters for Efficient ConvNets
abstract: Abstract:###The success of CNNs in various applications is accompanied by a significant increase in the computation and parameter storage costs. Recent efforts toward reducing these overheads involve pruning and compressing the weights of various layers without hurting original accuracy. However, magnitude-based pruning of weights reduces a significant number of parameters from the fully connected layers and may not adequately reduce the computation costs in the convolutional layers due to irregular sparsity in the pruned networks. We present an acceleration method for CNNs, where we prune filters from CNNs that are identified as having a small effect on the output accuracy. By removing whole filters in the network together with their connecting feature maps, the computation costs are reduced significantly. In contrast to pruning weights, this approach does not result in sparse connectivity patterns. Hence, it does not need the support of sparse convolution libraries and can work with existing efficient BLAS libraries for dense matrix multiplications. We show that even simple filter pruning techniques can reduce inference costs for VGG-16 by up to 34% and ResNet-110 by up to 38% on CIFAR10 while regaining close to the original accuracy by retraining the networks.
review:
This paper addresses the important problem of reducing inference costs in CNNs by pruning entire filters (and their corresponding feature maps) based on the \(\ell_1\)-norm of the filter weights, rather than pruning individual weights. The core idea is appealing—structured pruning that maintains dense matrix operations, which is immediately practical with existing BLAS libraries, unlike irregular weight pruning that requires sparse libraries or specialized hardware. I appreciate the simplicity of the approach and the extensive empirical evaluation on VGG-16, ResNet-56/110 on CIFAR-10, and ResNet-34 on ImageNet. The results are solid: achieving ~34% FLOP reduction on VGG-16 and ~38% on ResNet-110 with minimal accuracy loss, and the one-shot pruning+retraining strategy is much more practical than iterative layer-by-layer retraining. The sensitivity analysis across layers is also useful, particularly the observation that in ResNets the layers near the shortcut connections are more sensitive, which provides guidance for practitioners. The comparison showing that \(\ell_1\)-norm pruning outperforms random or largest-filter pruning, and even activation-based criteria in many cases, is a nice empirical justification for the heuristic.

That said, I have some concerns. First, the \(\ell_1\)-norm criterion is rather ad-hoc—while it works empirically, the paper doesn't provide a theoretical justification for why filter weight magnitude correlates with importance, especially given that Batch Normalization rescales activations and can make weight magnitudes less meaningful. Second, the comparison to related work is somewhat superficial: the authors mention group-sparsity regularization but don't compare against it experimentally, which would be a more natural baseline since that method also induces structured sparsity during training. Third, the retraining strategy is simplified (constant learning rate, fixed epochs) and the paper doesn't systematically study how retraining hyperparameters affect the final accuracy, which is critical for reproducibility. Fourth, the ResNet pruning strategy—pruning the first layer of each residual block only—is a limitation; the authors acknowledge that pruning the second layer is harder due to the identity shortcut, but they don't explore alternatives like pruning both layers with careful alignment, which could yield further speedups. Finally, the wall-clock speedups on GPU are somewhat less than the FLOP reduction suggests (e.g., 24.2% FLOP reduction on ResNet-34 but only 22.9% time saving), due to cuDNN overhead and non-convolution operations; the paper should be more transparent about this gap.

Overall, I find the paper technically sound and the results are useful for practitioners, but the novelty is moderate—the approach is a straightforward application of magnitude-based pruning to the filter level, and similar ideas have appeared concurrently (e.g., group-sparsity methods). I'd recommend acceptance, but with the suggestion that the authors strengthen the theoretical justification or provide a more thorough comparison to structured regularization methods, and be more careful in reporting wall-clock speedups versus FLOP reductions.

title: Learning to Generate Samples from Noise through Infusion Training
abstract: Abstract:###In this work, we investigate a novel training procedure to learn a generative model as the transition operator of a Markov chain, such that, when applied repeatedly on an unstructured random noise sample, it will denoise it into a sample that matches the target distribution from the training set. The novel training procedure to learn this progressive denoising operation involves sampling from a slightly different chain than the model chain used for generation in the absence of a denoising target. In the training chain we infuse information from the training target example that we would like the chains to reach with a high probability. The thus learned transition operator is able to produce quality and varied samples in a small number of steps. Experiments show competitive results compared to the samples generated with a basic Generative Adversarial Net.
review:
This paper introduces "infusion training," a method for learning a generative model as a Markov chain transition operator that progressively denoises noise into data samples. The core idea is clever—instead of reversing a fixed diffusion process (as in Sohl-Dickstein et al.), the authors train the model to denoise samples from an "infusion chain" that is slightly biased towards a target data point. This allows the model to learn to make large jumps in a small number of steps, which is a practical advantage over diffusion models that require thousands of tiny steps. I appreciate the simplicity of the approach and the strong empirical results: the generated samples on MNIST, TFD, CIFAR-10, and CelebA look sharp and varied, the inpainting experiments are convincing, and the likelihood estimates (though approximate) are competitive with or better than GANs and GSNs. The connection to GSNs and variational autoencoders is well-articulated, and the paper does a good job situating the contribution in the broader literature.

However, I have several concerns that prevent me from being fully enthusiastic. First, the training procedure is heavily heuristic—the infusion rate schedule (increasing \(\alpha\) over steps) and the choice of \(\omega = 0.01\) or 0.02 are not justified theoretically, and the paper shows that results are quite sensitive to these hyperparameters (see Appendix Table 4). Second, the lower-bound-based training variant is mentioned but not thoroughly explored; most experiments use the denoising-based surrogate loss, which lacks a clear probabilistic interpretation. Third, the comparison to GANs is a bit unfair: the GAN baselines in Table 3 are from Salimans et al. (2016) and use different architectures and semi-supervised training; a controlled comparison with the same generator architecture would be more convincing. Fourth, the Parzen-window log-likelihood estimates are known to be unreliable (as the authors acknowledge), and while the AIS comparisons are better, the importance sampling estimates still rely on the same heuristic proposal distribution, which may not be tight. Fifth, the paper doesn't address the scalability of the approach—training on 15-20 denoising steps with a large network might be computationally expensive, and the authors don't provide training times or convergence analysis.

Overall, I find the idea interesting and the results promising, but the theoretical grounding is thin and the empirical evaluation has some weaknesses. I'd recommend borderline acceptance, with the suggestion that the authors provide a clearer theoretical justification for the infusion training objective, a more thorough comparison to GANs and VAEs under controlled conditions, and a discussion of the computational cost and practical limitations. If these issues are addressed, the paper could be a solid contribution to the generative modeling community.

title: FILTER SHAPING FOR CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORKS
abstract: Abstract:###Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are powerful tools for classification of visual inputs. An important property of CNN is its restriction to local connections and sharing of local weights among different locations. In this paper, we consider the definition of appropriate local neighborhoods in CNN. We provide a theoretical analysis that justifies the traditional square filter used in CNN for analyzing natural images. The analysis also provides a principle for designing customized filter shapes for application domains that do not resemble natural images. We propose an approach that automatically designs multiple layers of different customized filter shapes by repeatedly solving lasso problems. It is applied to customize the filter shape for both bioacoustic applications and gene sequence analysis applications. In those domains with small sample sizes we demonstrate that the customized filters achieve superior classification accuracy, improved convergence behavior in training and reduced sensitivity to hyperparameters.
review:
This paper proposes a data-driven method to design non-rectangular convolutional filter shapes based on correlation analysis, with applications to bioacoustic spectrograms and gene sequences. I think the core idea—that standard square filters may not be optimal for domains with different spatial correlation structures—is intuitive and practically important, especially for small-sample scientific applications where domain-agnostic defaults can underperform. The theoretical connection to Gaussian complexity bounds is a nice touch, linking filter shape to generalization capacity, and the empirical results on three tasks are reasonably convincing: the custom-shaped filters consistently outperform fixed-shape baselines (e.g., ~5% absolute improvement on birdsong) and show better robustness to learning rate variations. The filter shapes themselves are interpretable—horizontal stripes for wingbeats, vertical stripes for songs—which adds credibility. I also appreciate the stability analysis showing that performance is not overly sensitive to the DFMax parameter.

That said, I have several reservations. First, the theory relies on two-layer networks with contraction mappings and doesn't extend to deep CNNs with ReLU, batch norm, or multiple convolutional layers—the repeated lasso heuristic for multi-layer shapes is pragmatic but lacks theoretical backing. Second, the comparison to baselines is narrow: the paper compares to fixed \(3\times3\) and \(3\times5\) filters and an \(L_1\)-regularized \(5\times5\), but doesn't benchmark against more modern adaptive methods like deformable convolutions, graph-based CNNs, or learned filter masks via group sparsity during training. Third, the improvement on the gene sequence data is a mere 0.8%, and the filter shapes there are essentially \(1\times9\) after pooling—so the contribution for that domain is marginal. Fourth, the treatment of max-pooling by "average pooling" in the covariance analysis is hand-wavy; max-pooling is nonlinear and its effect on correlation structure isn't fully justified. Finally, the paper doesn't provide clear practical guidelines on how to choose the number of layers or DFMax for a new domain beyond the small sweep shown.

Overall, I find the idea compelling and the empirical validation solid for the bioacoustic tasks, but the theoretical and algorithmic contributions are somewhat incremental. The method is essentially a data-driven heuristic for filter shape design, and while it works well on the tested domains, it's unclear how broadly applicable it is or how it compares to other structured filter learning approaches. I'd lean toward acceptance, but with the suggestion that the authors strengthen the theoretical connection to deep networks, provide a more thorough comparison to state-of-the-art adaptive filter methods, and offer clearer practical guidelines for applying the method to new domains.

title: Normalizing the Normalizers: Comparing and Extending Network Normalization Schemes
abstract: Abstract:###Normalization techniques have only recently begun to be exploited in supervised learning tasks. Batch normalization exploits mini-batch statistics to normalize the activations. This was shown to speed up training and result in better models. However its success has been very limited when dealing with recurrent neural networks. On the other hand, layer normalization normalizes the activations across all activities within a layer. This was shown to work well in the recurrent setting. In this paper we propose a unified view of normalization techniques, as forms of divisive normalization, which includes layer and batch normalization as special cases. Our second contribution is the finding that a small modification to these normalization schemes, in conjunction with a sparse regularizer on the activations, leads to significant benefits over standard normalization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our unified divisive normalization framework in the context of convolutional neural nets and recurrent neural networks, showing improvements over baselines in image classification, language modeling as well as super-resolution.
review:
This paper proposes a unified view of normalization techniques, framing batch normalization, layer normalization, and divisive normalization as different choices of summation and suppression fields in a general framework. The authors then propose two simple modifications: adding a smoothing term \(\sigma\) to the denominator of the normalizer, and adding an L1 regularizer on the centered activations. They show that these modifications consistently improve performance across CNNs (CIFAR), RNNs (Penn Treebank), and super-resolution tasks. I find the unified perspective helpful—it clarifies the relationships between methods and highlights the design choices that matter. The empirical results are reasonably strong: the modified LN (\(\mathrm{LN}^*\)) and DN (\(\mathrm{DN}^*\)) often outperform standard BN and LN, particularly on RNNs where BN struggles. The ablation studies (Table 7) are thorough and clearly demonstrate the separate contributions of \(\sigma\) and the L1 regularizer. The super-resolution results are also compelling, showing that DN outperforms the strong SRCNN baseline while BN actually degrades performance—this is a nice illustration of the method's practical utility.

However, I have several concerns. First, the novelty is somewhat limited—the modifications are largely engineering tweaks (adding a smoothing term and an L1 penalty) to existing normalization schemes, and the theoretical justification (e.g., the L1 regularizer encouraging decorrelation) is hand-wavy and not rigorously analyzed. Second, the paper claims a "unified framework" but the connection to divisive normalization is primarily conceptual; the proposed DN is not the same as the canonical divisive normalization used in neuroscience (which typically involves local pooling with learned weights and exponent parameters), but rather a simplified local version of LN with a smoothing term. Third, the ResNet results are underwhelming—DN still lags behind BN (91.3% vs 92.6% on CIFAR-10), which suggests that the method does not fully generalize to state-of-the-art architectures without careful tuning. Fourth, the paper doesn't provide a clear analysis of why \(\sigma\) helps—the hand-wavy explanation about "implicit noise injection" and "invertibility" is not backed by experiments or theory. Finally, the computational cost of DN in CNNs (local pooling across filter channels) is not discussed, and it's unclear how this scales compared to BN or LN.

Overall, I think the paper makes a useful empirical contribution—the modifications are simple, easy to implement, and clearly help in certain settings—but the theoretical depth is shallow and the gains over BN on standard CNN tasks are modest. The paper would benefit from a more rigorous analysis of the mechanisms behind the improvements, and a clearer delineation of when DN is preferable to BN or LN. I'd lean toward acceptance but with reservations about the novelty and theoretical grounding.

title: Multilayer Recurrent Network Models of Primate Retinal Ganglion Cell Responses
abstract: Abstract:###Developing accurate predictive models of sensory neurons is vital to understanding sensory processing and brain computations. The current standard approach to modeling neurons is to start with simple models and to incrementally add interpretable features. An alternative approach is to start with a more complex model that captures responses accurately, and then probe the fitted model structure to understand the neural computations. Here, we show that a multitask recurrent neural network (RNN) framework provides the flexibility necessary to model complex computations of neurons that cannot be captured by previous methods. Specifically, multilayer recurrent neural networks that share features across neurons outperform generalized linear models (GLMs) in predicting the spiking responses of parasol ganglion cells in the primate retina to natural images. The networks achieve good predictive performance given surprisingly small amounts of experimental training data. Additionally, we present a novel GLM-RNN hybrid model with separate spatial and temporal processing components which provides insights into the aspects of retinal processing better captured by the recurrent neural networks.
review:
This paper applies deep recurrent neural networks to model the spiking responses of retinal ganglion cells to natural scenes, showing that a shared two-layer RNN significantly outperforms standard generalized linear models in predicting firing rates. I find the work compelling—it's a clean, well-executed application of modern deep learning to a classic neuroscience problem, and the results are striking: RNNs capture around 80% of explainable variance, a substantial jump over LNs and GLMs. The multitask learning framework (sharing features across neurons) is a sensible choice that improves both performance and stability, and the data efficiency result (good performance with surprisingly little training data) is reassuring for experimentalists with limited recordings. The hybrid GLM-RNN model is a nice diagnostic tool, showing that temporal nonlinearities account for most of the improvement, though spatial nonlinearities also play a role. I also appreciate the careful experimental setup, including the use of explainable variance normalized by trial-to-trial variability, which is the right metric for this domain.

That said, I have some reservations. First, the novelty is somewhat limited from a machine learning perspective—the architecture is a standard stacked RNN with shared parameters, and the training procedure (MSE loss with Adam) is straightforward. The paper doesn't introduce any new algorithmic ideas; it's primarily an application of existing tools to a new domain. Second, the RNN is largely a black box, and while the authors acknowledge this, the paper doesn't go far enough in trying to understand what the network has learned—the filters from image to first-layer RNN units are interpretable (resembling classical receptive fields), but the recurrent dynamics and the higher-layer representations are not analyzed. Third, the comparison to GLMs is somewhat unfair in that the GLMs are highly constrained (rank-1 filters, simple spike history), while the RNN has vastly more parameters and nonlinearities; a more careful ablation controlling for model capacity would strengthen the argument that the RNN architecture specifically, rather than just increased capacity, is responsible for the improvement. Fourth, the paper doesn't address the correlations between neurons; the model treats each neuron independently, which ignores a key aspect of retinal coding (Pillow et al., 2008 showed that modeling correlations improves predictions). Finally, while the results are impressive, the paper is written primarily for a neuroscience audience and could benefit from a clearer explanation of the model architecture and training details for a machine learning reader.

Overall, I think this is a solid contribution that bridges deep learning and systems neuroscience, and the empirical results are convincing. However, the machine learning novelty is modest, and the paper would be stronger with more mechanistic analysis of the RNN's internal representations. I'd recommend acceptance, but with the suggestion that the authors provide more insight into what the RNN is learning and consider modeling correlations across neurons in future work.

title: Improving Generative Adversarial Networks with Denoising Feature Matching
abstract: Abstract:###We propose an augmented training procedure for generative adversarial networks designed to address shortcomings of the original by directing the generator towards probable configurations of abstract discriminator features. We estimate and track the distribution of these features, as computed from data, with a denoising auto-encoder, and use it to propose high-level targets for the generator. We combine this new loss with the original and evaluate the hybrid criterion on the task of unsupervised image synthesis from datasets comprising a diverse set of visual categories, noting a qualitative and quantitative improvement in the ``objectness** of the resulting samples.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles the persistent and frustrating issue of mode collapse and low visual fidelity in unsupervised GANs, particularly when confronted with diverse datasets like ImageNet, which is a crucial problem for the community. The core idea of using the discriminator's own feature space to estimate a density via a denoising auto-encoder, and subsequently regressing the generator towards these "denoised" targets, is both elegant and intuitively appealing; I genuinely like the shift from simple first-moment matching to a full density-guided target. The empirical results speak for themselves: a jump from 4.36 to 7.72 on CIFAR-10 (unsupervised) is substantial, and the qualitative samples clearly demonstrate improved objectness without resorting to semi-supervised labels. I also appreciate the theoretical detour connecting the DAE residual to the score of the data distribution in the feature space, even if it relies on shaky assumptions. Cons - My main gripe is the non-stationarity elephant in the room. You are effectively training a density estimator (the DAE) on a moving target—the discriminator's features are shifting throughout training—so the denoising targets you feed to the generator are inherently stale. The paper acknowledges this but offers no robust solution beyond a hand-wave at historical averaging (which didn't work), making me worry this is a fundamental flaw rather than a minor implementation detail. The theoretical justification regarding \(\Phi\)'s effect is also a bit hand-wavy; since \(\Phi\) is a non-invertible deep convnet, the gradient you backpropagate is a distorted version of the true score plus an intractable volume expansion term, so the method ultimately reads more like a clever heuristic than a principled modification of the GAN objective. Furthermore, the computational overhead of training a separate deep, fully-connected denoiser alongside G and D is non-trivial and scales poorly, and while you claim robustness to collapse, the reliance on Inception score (which primarily rewards class clarity over intra-class diversity) doesn't convincingly prove you've solved mode coverage—I'd have liked to see a recall metric or FID to back that claim. Overall, it's a solid empirical contribution with a neat idea, but the theoretical gaps and training instabilities give me pause; I'd lean towards a weak accept given the clear empirical gains, but I'm not fully convinced this is the right way forward.

title: Efficient Vector Representation for Documents through Corruption
abstract: Abstract:###We present an efficient document representation learning framework, Document Vector through Corruption (Doc2VecC). Doc2VecC represents each document as a simple average of word embeddings. It ensures a representation generated as such captures the semantic meanings of the document during learning. A corruption model is included, which introduces a data-dependent regularization that favors informative or rare words while forcing the embeddings of common and non-discriminative ones to be close to zero. Doc2VecC produces significantly better word embeddings than Word2Vec. We compare Doc2VecC with several state-of-the-art document representation learning algorithms. The simple model architecture introduced by Doc2VecC matches or out-performs the state-of-the-art in generating high-quality document representations for sentiment analysis, document classification as well as semantic relatedness tasks. The simplicity of the model enables training on billions of words per hour on a single machine. At the same time, the model is very efficient in generating representations of unseen documents at test time.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a very practical and important problem: how to learn document representations that are both semantically meaningful and computationally efficient, especially for large-scale deployment. The key insight of using a corruption mechanism on the input document to enforce that a simple average of word embeddings captures document semantics is clever and well-motivated. I really like the theoretical analysis showing that the corruption acts as a data-dependent regularizer that naturally suppresses frequent but uninformative words while preserving rare, discriminative ones—this explains both the performance gains and the speedup, since you can train with high corruption rates (q=0.9) and still improve over baselines. The empirical results are solid: Doc2VecC matches or beats Paragraph Vectors on IMDB sentiment (10.48% vs 10.81% error) while being dramatically faster at test time (7 seconds vs 4+ minutes for inference on 25k documents), and the word analogy results showing ~20% uplift over Word2Vec on several tasks are genuinely impressive. The simplicity of the final representation—just a plain average—makes this highly practical. Cons - That said, I have some serious reservations. The Skip-thought comparison on IMDB is borderline unfair: you report 17.42% error for Skip-thought, but that's using a generic model trained on a different corpus (books) without fine-tuning, while Doc2VecC is trained on the IMDB unlabeled data. Of course it performs better—this is an apples-to-oranges comparison, and you should at least acknowledge this more honestly. More importantly, the method essentially reduces to learning word embeddings that are optimized to be average-able, which is neat, but the novelty over Word2Vec with post-hoc IDF weighting is thinner than the paper suggests. The Taylor expansion analysis is elegant, but in practice the corruption regularization is just a more sophisticated way of doing what subsampling and IDF already do, and the performance gap between Doc2VecC and Word2Vec+IDF is often small (e.g., 11.28% vs 10.48% on IMDB with test excluded). On the semantic relatedness task (SICK), Doc2VecC significantly underperforms LSTM-based methods and even Skip-thought (Pearson 0.838 vs 0.858), and the hand-wavy explanation about sentence length doesn't fully convince me—if your method is supposed to be a general-purpose document encoder, it should handle short sentences too. Finally, while I appreciate the efficiency, the representation is still just a bag-of-embeddings average, which inherently loses word order and syntactic structure; the paper would be stronger if it discussed scenarios where this failure mode matters. Overall, it's a solid engineering contribution with good empirical results on some tasks, but the theoretical novelty is moderate and the experimental design has some glaring weaknesses. I'd lean towards a borderline accept, mostly for the practical efficiency gains and the interesting regularization perspective.

title: Learning Invariant Feature Spaces to Transfer Skills with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###People can learn a wide range of tasks from their own experience, but can also learn from observing other creatures. This can accelerate acquisition of new skills even when the observed agent differs substantially from the learning agent in terms of morphology. In this paper, we examine how reinforcement learning algorithms can transfer knowledge between morphologically different agents (e.g., different robots). We introduce a problem formulation where twp agents are tasked with learning multiple skills by sharing information. Our method uses the skills that were learned by both agents to train invariant feature spaces that can then be used to transfer other skills from one agent to another. The process of learning these invariant feature spaces can be viewed as a kind of ``analogy making,** or implicit learning of partial correspondences between two distinct domains. We evaluate our transfer learning algorithm in two simulated robotic manipulation skills, and illustrate that we can transfer knowledge between simulated robotic arms with different numbers of links, as well as simulated arms with different actuation mechanisms, where one robot is torque-driven while the other is tendon-driven.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely hard and underexplored problem: transferring skills between robots with different morphologies and even different actuation mechanisms, where the state spaces are completely misaligned. The core idea of learning an invariant embedding space via a proxy task, using a Siamese-style contrastive loss combined with autoencoder reconstruction to avoid degenerate solutions, is clever and biologically plausible—I appreciate the nod to mirror neurons and tool-use adaptation in the intro. The empirical results are quite compelling: transferring from a 3-link to a 4-link arm on a sparse-reward button pressing task, and especially from torque-driven to tendon-driven actuation, where the state representations have totally different semantics, is no small feat. The fact that the method allows the target agent to succeed where learning from scratch completely fails speaks volumes. I also like the image-based experiment—showing that the embedding can be learned directly from pixels via convnets makes the approach much more practical. The comparison to CCA, KCCA, and UMA is reasonable, and the neural embedding clearly outperforms these linear/shallow alternatives when the correspondence is nonlinear. Cons - My biggest concern is the alignment procedure. The time-based pairing assumption is extremely brittle—it essentially requires both agents to execute the proxy task at the same speed and with synchronized phase, which is rarely true in practice. The EM-style DTW alternation is a step in the right direction, but the paper barely evaluates it (just one sentence saying it "does not hurt performance" on the tendon experiment), and the ablation on the button task suggests it doesn't actually improve over time-based alignment. This feels like a major unaddressed weakness: if the correspondence is wrong, the embedding will be wrong, and transfer will fail or even hurt. The method also requires optimal or near-optimal trajectories for the proxy tasks in both domains, which assumes you already have working policies for those skills—that's a strong assumption that limits applicability. The comparison to "direct mapping" is somewhat unfair because you're learning a deterministic state-to-state mapping, which is obviously harder when state spaces differ in dimensionality; a more sophisticated baseline like learning a probabilistic mapping or using GAN-based domain adaptation would have been more convincing. Additionally, the reinforcement learning algorithm used (iLQG with local linear models) is quite specific and not the standard deep RL used in most modern work; it's unclear how well the transfer reward would work with model-free algorithms like TRPO or DDPG, especially since the transfer reward is dense but potentially misleading. The ablation over number of proxy tasks is interesting, but the paper doesn't dig into why three tasks works better than one—is it just more data, or is diversity of skills important? Finally, the theoretical justification for why the shared feature space should enable transfer is hand-wavy: the assumption that optimal state distributions match under f and g is strong, and there's no discussion of what happens when this assumption is violated. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a neat idea and impressive demos, but the alignment issue and the strong assumptions about having pre-learned skills make me hesitant. I'd lean towards a borderline accept—the results are good enough, but the method needs more robustness and a clearer theoretical grounding before I'd be fully convinced.

title: Transfer of View-manifold Learning to Similarity Perception of Novel Objects
abstract: Abstract:###We develop a model of perceptual similarity judgment based on re-training a deep convolution neural network (DCNN) that learns to associate different views of each 3D object to capture the notion of object persistence and continuity in our visual experience. The re-training process effectively performs distance metric learning under the object persistency constraints, to modify the view-manifold of object representations. It reduces the effective distance between the representations of different views of the same object without compromising the distance between those of the views of different objects, resulting in the untangling of the view-manifolds between individual objects within the same category and across categories. This untangling enables the model to discriminate and recognize objects within the same category, independent of viewpoints. We found that this ability is not limited to the trained objects, but transfers to novel objects in both trained and untrained categories, as well as to a variety of completely novel artificial synthetic objects. This transfer in learning suggests the modification of distance metrics in view- manifolds is more general and abstract, likely at the levels of parts, and independent of the specific objects or categories experienced during training. Interestingly, the resulting transformation of feature representation in the deep networks is found to significantly better match human perceptual similarity judgment than AlexNet, suggesting that object persistence could be an important constraint in the development of perceptual similarity judgment in biological neural networks.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a fundamental and cognitively rich problem: how object persistence (continuity across views) can shape perceptual similarity judgments, and whether we can transfer this ability to novel objects. The core idea—fine-tuning AlexNet with a Siamese triplet loss using multi-view renderings from ShapeNet—is clean, well-motivated, and biologically plausible. The empirical results are genuinely impressive: OPnet achieves a massive boost in instance retrieval MAP on novel instances (0.856 vs AlexNet's 0.529) and even transfers reasonably to synthetic objects and Pokemons, suggesting the learned feature space captures something abstract about parts and shape beyond category-level semantics. I particularly like the analysis of the view-manifold structure—the LDA-style intra/inter-object distance ratio and the TSNE visualizations convincingly show that OPnet contracts within-object variation while preserving between-object separation, and the hierarchical clustering matching human perception data (Spearman 0.659 vs AlexNet's 0.460) is a nice validation of the cognitive hypothesis. The paper is also refreshingly honest about limitations and carefully ablates different feature layers and baselines. Cons - My main concern is the evaluation setup: the training and testing both use rendered images from 3D models with controlled camera rotations, which is a big leap from natural images. When you tested on real-world datasets (Geusebroek et al.), the improvement over AlexNet was only "slight"—this is buried in Section 4 and should be front and center, as it suggests the transfer might be partly an artifact of the synthetic domain. The assumption that views of the same object should always be more similar than views of different objects is reasonable but breaks down for highly symmetric objects or when the viewpoint change is extreme; the paper doesn't discuss how the method handles these edge cases. The training uses only 12 discrete azimuthal views at a fixed elevation, which is a coarse sampling of the view manifold—does the method still work with continuous view sequences or more realistic ego-motion? The comparison to the joint embedding model (Li et al.) is a bit unfair because that model is trained for a different purpose (cross-view retrieval) and only on chairs; a stronger baseline would be a Siamese network trained with the same data but without the triplet margin tuned properly. I'm also skeptical about the margin parameter M=0.1 being selected by cross-validation on the training set—since the test sets are so different, this might not generalize, and there's no sensitivity analysis. Finally, the paper claims this work is about "transfer of learning," but the network is still fine-tuned on 200 objects from 29 categories; calling it "zero-shot" would be a stretch. Overall, I find the core idea elegant and the results on synthetic data compelling, but the lack of real-world validation and the controlled nature of the experiments make me cautious. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the paper contributes a neat demonstration of how object persistence can shape similarity, but the practical impact is still unclear.

title: What does it take to generate natural textures?
abstract: Abstract:###Natural image generation is currently one of the most actively explored fields in Deep Learning. Many approaches, e.g. for state-of-the-art artistic style transfer or natural texture synthesis, rely on the statistics of hierarchical representations in supervisedly trained deep neural networks. It is, however, unclear what aspects of this feature representation are crucial for natural image generation: is it the depth, the pooling or the training of the features on natural images? We here address this question for the task of natural texture synthesis and show that none of the above aspects are indispensable. Instead, we demonstrate that natural textures of high perceptual quality can be generated from networks with only a single layer, no pooling and random filters.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper asks a deceptively simple but powerful question: what actually *matters* for texture synthesis in deep networks? The answer—surprisingly little—is delivered with a clean, systematic ablation that cuts through the hype around deep hierarchical features. The demonstration that a single-layer CNN with *random* filters can synthesize textures that rival the VGG-based state-of-the-art (Gatys et al.) is genuinely eye-opening. I really appreciate the thorough exploration of design choices: filter size, number of feature maps, filter type (random, Fourier, k-means, PCA), and the clear finding that multi-scale random filters are the key, not learned representations. The introduction of the VGG-loss as a quantitative proxy for perceptual quality is a sensible move, though I have reservations (see below). The paper is also refreshingly honest about the finite-size effects and the trade-off between perceptual similarity and sample variability, and the discussion linking practical texture synthesis to the MaxEnt framework with an epsilon-environment is a nice theoretical contribution that elevates the paper beyond just empirical tinkering. The quality of the generated textures, especially for regular structures like brick walls and grids, is genuinely impressive. Cons - My main gripe is the evaluation. While the VGG-loss is a useful heuristic, the paper still relies heavily on qualitative visual inspection, and Figure 4 shows several cases where the multi-scale model clearly produces worse textures than VGG (e.g., the pebbles and the stone wall) despite the authors' claim of "often rivaling" it. The use of VGG-loss as a "quantitative" measure is circular when the baseline (Gatys) is *defined* by that same loss—of course it's a good approximation, but that doesn't make it an independent ground truth. I'd have liked to see a proper human psychophysics experiment (e.g., two-alternative forced choice) to back up the perceptual claims, especially since the authors themselves discuss the need for better perceptual metrics. The computational inefficiency of the multi-scale model is also a major practical concern: using 55x55 filters directly is orders of magnitude slower than the hierarchical VGG approach, and the paper's dismissal of this ("not necessary but can improve efficiency") feels like a hand-wave—if the only advantage of depth is speed, that's worth demonstrating quantitatively. The random multi-scale model also seems to *overfit* perceptually: samples are often too close to the reference (low variability), which the authors acknowledge, but they don't explore how to tune the optimization to increase variability without sacrificing quality—this is a critical missing piece for a practical texture model. Finally, the paper's title asks "what does it take," but the answer is still somewhat incomplete: we know random filters + multi-scale + ReLU works, but *why* does it work? The intuition about the Gram matrix capturing pairwise correlations is hand-wavy, and there's no analysis of what these random filters are actually detecting or why they generalize across such diverse textures. Overall, I find this to be a strong, thought-provoking paper that challenges conventional wisdom with clean experiments, but the evaluation is a bit too casual and the practical limitations (speed, variability control) are under-addressed. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the core result is important, but the paper needs a more rigorous evaluation and a clearer path to practical use before I'd be fully convinced.

title: Emergence of foveal image sampling from learning to attend in visual scenes
abstract: Abstract:###We describe a neural attention model with a learnable retinal sampling lattice. The model is trained on a visual search task requiring the classification of an object embedded in a visual scene amidst background distractors using the smallest number of fixations. We explore the tiling properties that emerge in the model*s retinal sampling lattice after training. Specifically, we show that this lattice resembles the eccentricity dependent sampling lattice of the primate retina, with a high resolution region in the fovea surrounded by a low resolution periphery. Furthermore, we find conditions where these emergent properties are amplified or eliminated providing clues to their function.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a fascinating and biologically-grounded question: can a learnable retinal sampling lattice emerge from task-driven training, and does it resemble the foveated structure of the primate retina? The core idea—parameterizing individual kernel positions and spreads as learnable Gaussian filters within an attention framework, and training end-to-end on a visual search task—is elegant and well-executed. The main result is genuinely striking: when the model can only translate its glimpse window (like an eye), the kernels converge to a fovea-like layout with high resolution at the center and coarser sampling in the periphery, with the sampling interval growing linearly with eccentricity just like in primate retina. The comparison to the "Translation and Zoom" model is also insightful—showing that zoom effectively replaces the need for a fovea, which supports the functional interpretation that the fovea acts as an implicit zoom mechanism. The temporal rollouts in Figure 7 clearly demonstrate that the model learns to detect the target with the low-resolution periphery and then refine with the high-resolution fovea, which is a beautiful demonstration of the utility of the emergent structure. The paper is also refreshingly concise and clear, with well-designed ablations. Cons - My main concern is the simplicity of the task and dataset. Cluttered MNIST with 144 fixed-position kernels is a far cry from natural scenes, and it's unclear whether this result would generalize to more complex, naturalistic visual search tasks where textures, colors, and object categories matter. The model uses only 144 kernels total, which is orders of magnitude fewer than the ~1.5 million ganglion cells in the retina, so the comparison is more qualitative than quantitative. The paper also doesn't explore whether the emergent fovea is truly *optimal* for the task or just one of many local minima—a control experiment with a uniform lattice but more kernels or a learned non-foveated layout would have strengthened the claim. The "Fixed Lattice" baseline in Table 2 shows that learning the lattice helps, but it doesn't ablate whether the specific *foveated* structure is necessary, or whether any learned non-uniform layout would work. The analysis of the emergent properties is also somewhat shallow: beyond plotting sampling interval vs eccentricity, there's no investigation of whether the learned filters are actually encoding different spatial frequency bands or whether the fovea's higher resolution is being used for fine discrimination vs the periphery for coarse detection. Finally, the connection back to biology is intriguing but speculative—the model doesn't incorporate realistic eye movement costs, saccade latencies, or the fact that the retina is fixed and cannot be "retrained" in an individual lifetime, so the claim that this is "optimal design" needs more careful framing. Overall, I think this is a neat and thought-provoking paper that opens an interesting direction, but the results are still at the proof-of-concept stage on a very simplified domain. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the core idea is solid and the fovea emergence is compelling, but the paper needs more thorough analysis and validation on more challenging tasks before the biological conclusions hold water.

title: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Fast and Robust Unsupervised Learning via Neural Population Infomax
abstract: Abstract:###A framework is presented for unsupervised learning of representations based on infomax principle for large-scale neural populations. We use an asymptotic approximation to the Shannon*s mutual information for a large neural population to demonstrate that a good initial approximation to the global information-theoretic optimum can be obtained by a hierarchical infomax method. Starting from the initial solution, an efficient algorithm based on gradient descent of the final objective function is proposed to learn representations from the input datasets, and the method works for complete, overcomplete, and undercomplete bases. As confirmed by numerical experiments, our method is robust and highly efficient for extracting salient features from input datasets. Compared with the main existing methods, our algorithm has a distinct advantage in both the training speed and the robustness of unsupervised representation learning. Furthermore, the proposed method is easily extended to the supervised or unsupervised model for training deep structure networks.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a fundamental and notoriously difficult problem: learning useful representations from high-dimensional data via the infomax principle, with a specific focus on scalability to large neural populations. The theoretical framework is impressively comprehensive—the asymptotic approximation to mutual information for large populations is elegant, and the hierarchical infomax approach provides a principled way to escape local minima in a nonconvex optimization landscape. I particularly appreciate the analytical solutions for the initial whitening transformation and the way the method naturally handles complete, overcomplete, and undercomplete bases without the usual algorithmic gymnastics. The low-rank approximation via the effective rank \(K_0\) is a clever regularization mechanism that simultaneously reduces overfitting and computational cost, and the biological grounding in cortical columnar structure gives the work a nice interdisciplinary flavor. The empirical results are strong: the filters learned on natural images are genuinely Gabor-like, the convergence speed is dramatically faster than IICA and sparse coding (often by an order of magnitude), and the ability to learn overcomplete bases (1024 filters on 144-dimensional patches) is impressive. The image denoising example in the appendix, where 14 bases from your method outperform 100 bases from dictionary learning, is a striking demonstration of the quality of the learned representation. Cons - That said, this paper has some serious exposition problems. The main text is dense to the point of being almost unreadable—you introduce a massive amount of notation and mathematical machinery (Propositions, Lemmas, multiple appendices) without giving the reader much intuition for what's actually happening. The key insight—that you can approximate the MI via a Fisher information matrix and then decompose the optimization into two stages (whitening + nonlinearity learning)—gets buried under layer upon layer of derivations. The comparison to existing methods is also somewhat unfair: you compare to IICA, FICA, and SRBM, but the experimental setup (batch size, learning rate schedules) seems heavily tuned for your method while the baselines are given default parameters. The claim that SRBM "could not easily learn Gabor-like filters" is suspicious—with proper sparsity tuning and sufficient training, SRBM (Lee et al., 2008) absolutely learns Gabor filters, so I suspect the issue is with your implementation rather than a fundamental limitation of the method. The evaluation metrics (coefficient entropy and conditional entropy) are also somewhat self-serving—they measure properties that your method explicitly optimizes, so it's not surprising that you do well on them, but they don't tell us whether the learned features are actually *useful* for downstream tasks like classification or transfer learning. The paper would be much stronger with a simple supervised evaluation (e.g., train a linear classifier on the learned features for CIFAR-10 or MNIST) to demonstrate practical utility. Finally, the connection to deep learning is tantalizing but hand-wavy—you suggest the framework can be extended to deep networks, but there's no actual implementation or results on multi-layer architectures, which feels like a missed opportunity. Overall, I think this is a technically solid paper with a genuinely interesting theoretical contribution and impressive empirical results on filter learning, but the presentation is too dense and the evaluation is too narrowly focused on entropy-based metrics. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the core ideas are strong, but the paper needs major revision to be accessible and to convincingly demonstrate the broader impact of the method.

title: PixelCNN++: Improving the PixelCNN with Discretized Logistic Mixture Likelihood and Other Modifications
abstract: Abstract:###PixelCNNs are a recently proposed class of powerful generative models with tractable likelihood. Here we discuss our implementation of PixelCNNs which we make available at https://github.com/openai/pixel-cnn. Our implementation contains a number of modifications to the original model that both simplify its structure and improve its performance. 1) We use a discretized logistic mixture likelihood on the pixels, rather than a 256-way softmax, which we find to speed up training. 2) We condition on whole pixels, rather than R/G/B sub-pixels, simplifying the model structure. 3) We use downsampling to efficiently capture structure at multiple resolutions. 4) We introduce additional short-cut connections to further speed up optimization. 5) We regularize the model using dropout. Finally, we present state-of-the-art log likelihood results on CIFAR-10 to demonstrate the usefulness of these modifications.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper is a textbook example of how to take a strong existing model and make it significantly better through thoughtful engineering. The discretized logistic mixture likelihood is a genuine improvement—it's more parameter-efficient than the 256-way softmax (1536 outputs per pixel vs. a handful of parameters per mixture component), trains faster, and achieves better log-likelihood. The simplification to conditioning on whole pixels rather than sub-pixels is the right call; the cross-channel dependencies are simple enough to model with linear coefficients, and removing the sub-pixel masking complexity makes the code cleaner and the architecture more accessible. The downsampling + upsampling with shortcut connections (U-Net style) is a sensible way to capture multi-scale structure while keeping computational costs manageable, and the ablation showing that dropout is crucial for both generalization and perceptual quality is a useful practical insight. The state-of-the-art result of 2.92 bits per sub-pixel on CIFAR-10 (unconditional) and 2.92 class-conditional speaks for itself, and the samples in Figures 3 and 4 look qualitatively much better than the original PixelCNN—the global coherence is noticeably improved. The paper is also refreshingly honest about the surprising finding that small receptive fields can achieve competitive likelihood scores, even if samples lack global structure, which is an important diagnostic for the community. Cons - That said, I'm a bit torn because this paper reads more like a high-quality tech report or blog post than a full ICLR paper. The contributions are mostly engineering modifications without a unifying theoretical insight—the logistic mixture is a better output distribution, downsampling is more efficient than dilation, shortcuts help optimization, dropout prevents overfitting. Each modification is sensible, and the cumulative result is impressive, but there's no single "aha" moment or deep conceptual breakthrough.
