The ablation experiments are appreciated but somewhat thin—for example, the logistic mixture is compared to a softmax in a *different architecture* (with linear dependencies between channels), so it's not a clean apples-to-apples comparison; the memory and speed improvements are mentioned qualitatively but not quantified. The small receptive field experiments are intriguing, but the paper doesn't dig into *why* likelihood and perceptual quality decouple—this could have been a more substantial contribution. The class-conditional result (2.94 bpd) actually gets *worse* than the unconditional model (2.92), which is odd and deserves more discussion—is the conditioning information just too weak, or is the model overfitting? Finally, the paper's scope is narrow: only CIFAR-10 is evaluated, with no experiments on larger datasets (e.g., ImageNet) or other modalities, which limits the generality of the claims. Overall, I think this is a solid, well-executed piece of engineering that pushes the state of the art and provides a valuable open-source implementation, but it lacks the depth and breadth I'd expect from a top-tier conference paper. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the improvements are real and the code release is a significant community contribution, but the paper itself feels a bit lightweight for ICLR.

title: Mode Regularized Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Although Generative Adversarial Networks achieve state-of-the-art results on a variety of generative tasks, they are regarded as highly unstable and prone to miss modes. We argue that these bad behaviors of GANs are due to the very particular functional shape of the trained discriminators in high dimensional spaces, which can easily make training stuck or push probability mass in the wrong direction, towards that of higher concentration than that of the data generating distribution. We introduce several ways of regularizing the objective, which can dramatically stabilize the training of GAN models. We also show that our regularizers can help the fair distribution of probability mass across the modes of the data generating distribution during the early phases of training, thus providing a unified solution to the missing modes problem.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a central pain point in GAN training—mode collapse and instability—with a refreshingly practical approach. The core idea of using an autoencoder-based regularizer is intuitive and well-motivated: adding an encoder to map data points to the latent space and back creates a point-to-point correspondence between manifolds, and the mode regularizer term \(\log D(G(E(x)))\) cleverly forces the generator to cover even minor modes by explicitly reconstructing training examples. The grid search experiment on MNIST (Figure 3) is genuinely compelling—showing that regularized GANs achieve higher MODE scores across a wide range of hyperparameters is strong evidence that the method improves stability, not just peak performance. The compositional MNIST experiment with 1000 modes (Figure 5) is a nice stress test, and the result that Reg-GAN covers significantly more modes than DCGAN is convincing. I also appreciate the MODE score as a correction to Inception score's blind spot—penalizing the KL divergence between the generated label distribution and the true label distribution is a sensible fix. The qualitative samples on CelebA (Figures 6-7) show that MDGAN produces sharper, less distorted faces with better side-face coverage, which is genuinely impressive. Cons - That said, I have some significant concerns. The paper is quite messy and hard to follow—the exposition jumps between the metric regularizer, mode regularizer, and MDGAN without a clear unifying narrative, and the notation in Equation (1) is confusing (you use \(G\) ambiguously for both the generator and the decoder). The manifold-diffusion training (MDGAN) is introduced as a separate two-stage algorithm, but the paper never clearly explains *why* this two-step procedure works better than the single-stage regularized GAN—the intuition about "matching manifolds first, then diffusing probability mass" is hand-wavy and lacks theoretical grounding. More critically, the comparison to VAEGAN in Appendix D is deeply unfair: you admit you only ran their official code for 30 epochs with default settings, while your model was carefully tuned and trained for 20 epochs—this is not a controlled comparison, and the claim that VAEGAN "performs very bad" is undermined by your own admission that their generated samples are of "low quality" in your metric because they're too far from the modes, which is circular reasoning. The ablation studies are also weak: you never systematically vary \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) to show the trade-off between reconstruction quality and mode coverage, and you don't ablate the two regularizers separately to see which one is doing the heavy lifting. The third-party discriminator metric for missing modes is sensitive to the choice of noise level \(\sigma\) (Table 4 shows different \(\sigma\) values for different models, which is sketchy), and the human evaluation is mentioned but never quantified—"five individuals agreed" is not a rigorous result. Finally, the method adds significant complexity (an encoder, two discriminators in MDGAN, multiple loss terms) but the gains on CelebA, while noticeable, still leave ~40-400 images on missing modes even with regularization—so the problem isn't fully solved. Overall, I think the core idea is solid and the empirical results on MNIST are strong, but the presentation is disorganized, the comparisons are not always fair, and the method is more of a collection of heuristics than a principled solution. I'd lean towards a borderline accept—the work is valuable for the community, but it needs substantial revision to clarify the contributions and strengthen the empirical evaluation.

title: Highway and Residual Networks learn Unrolled Iterative Estimation
abstract: Abstract:###The past year saw the introduction of new architectures such as Highway networks and Residual networks which, for the first time, enabled the training of feedforward networks with dozens to hundreds of layers using simple gradient descent. While depth of representation has been posited as a primary reason for their success, there are indications that these architectures defy a popular view of deep learning as a hierarchical computation of increasingly abstract features at each layer. In this report, we argue that this view is incomplete and does not adequately explain several recent findings. We propose an alternative viewpoint based on unrolled iterative estimation---a group of successive layers iteratively refine their estimates of the same features instead of computing an entirely new representation. We demonstrate that this viewpoint directly leads to the construction of highway and residual networks. Finally we provide preliminary experiments to discuss the similarities and differences between the two architectures.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper offers a genuinely refreshing conceptual contribution to a field that's been flooded with empirical tweaks. The central claim—that Highway and Residual networks should be understood not as building new representations at each layer but as performing unrolled iterative estimation of the same representation—is elegant, well-argued, and remarkably well-supported by evidence that has been puzzling the community. The explanation for why lesioning or shuffling layers barely hurts performance is the clearest I've seen: if each block is just refining an already-good estimate, then removing a few refiners leaves the core representation intact. The mathematical derivation connecting the iterative estimation view to the ResNet and Highway architectures is genuinely satisfying—Equation 1 (\(\mathbb{E}[a_i^k - A_i] = 0\)) directly implies the residual form, and the optimal linear estimator derivation recovers the Highway gating mechanism. The experimental corroboration in Figure 3, showing that the mean estimation error across Residual blocks stays near zero while the variance decreases, is a powerful validation of the theory. The visualization from Chu et al. (2017) showing a single filter refining from "light sources + specular highlights" to just "specular highlights" across blocks is the kind of evidence that makes the iterative view click. I also appreciate the comparative case studies—the ImageNet experiments refuting the claim that Highway networks are hard to train, and the language modeling results showing that gating matters when you need to dynamically replace features. Cons - That said, this paper reads more like a position paper or opinion piece than a full ICLR contribution. The core idea is compelling, but the empirical validation is quite thin: the primary experimental evidence for the iterative view comes from analyzing a *pre-trained* ResNet (from He et al.), not from a controlled experiment designed to test the theory. The derivation of Highway networks from the optimal linear estimator is clever, but it assumes the covariance structure is known and that the network can learn to compute the mixing coefficients—this feels more like a post-hoc justification than a proof. The language modeling experiment (Table 1a) shows that Residual performs worse than Highway variants, but the authors dismiss this by saying "if the task requires dynamically replacing individual features, gating is beneficial"—which is a post-hoc rationalization rather than a principled explanation. The claim that "batch normalization provides regularization benefits that can't be easily explained by either improved optimization nor by the inductive bias for Residual networks" is interesting but not explored. The paper also lacks a clear definition of what constitutes a "stage" versus a "block" beyond dimensionality changes—this seems central to the theory but is left somewhat vague. Finally, the paper doesn't address the elephant in the room: if layers are just iteratively refining the same representation, why do deeper ResNets (e.g., 1001 layers) still outperform shallower ones? Is it simply more refinement iterations? If so, why does performance saturate? Overall, I think this is a thought-provoking and valuable conceptual contribution that will likely influence how people think about these architectures, but as an ICLR paper it feels underdeveloped empirically and somewhat informal. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the idea is important enough to warrant publication, but the paper needs stronger experimental validation and a tighter theoretical treatment to be fully convincing.

title: Improving Neural Language Models with a Continuous Cache
abstract: Abstract:###We propose an extension to neural network language models to adapt their prediction to the recent history. Our model is a simplified version of memory augmented networks, which stores past hidden activations as memory and accesses them through a dot product with the current hidden activation. This mechanism is very efficient and scales to very large memory sizes. We also draw a link between the use of external memory in neural network and cache models used with count based language models. We demonstrate on several language model datasets that our approach performs significantly better than recent memory augmented networks.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper presents a remarkably simple and elegant idea that works surprisingly well. The neural cache model—storing previous hidden states and retrieving them via dot product with the current state—is about as lightweight as you can get while still being effective, and the fact that it requires no training and can be slapped onto any pre-trained RNN language model with negligible cost is a huge practical advantage. The empirical results are convincing: on wikitext2, you get a 30% relative improvement over the LSTM baseline (99.3 → 68.9 perplexity) just by adding a cache of 2000 words, and the gains on LAMBADA (408 → 138 on development set) are genuinely impressive for a dataset specifically designed to be hard for language models. I also appreciate the thorough comparison with the unigram cache baseline—the neural cache clearly outperforms, especially at larger cache sizes, showing that the hidden states are capturing much richer contextual information than simple word counts. The connection to traditional cache models is well-explained and grounds the work in established literature, and the discussion of global normalization vs. linear interpolation is a nice ablation. The scalability argument is strong: no learned memory lookup operator means you can use caches of thousands of words without the computational overhead of pointer networks or memory-augmented architectures. Cons - That said, the novelty is somewhat thin. This is essentially an attention mechanism over a fixed memory of past hidden states, which has been explored extensively in the pointer network and memory-augmented network literature. The key difference is that you're not learning the attention weights or the memory representations—which is exactly why it's efficient, but also why it's limited. The paper claims to "surpass the performance of memory augmented networks," but the comparison is apples-to-oranges: your model is a test-time add-on to a pre-trained LSTM, while the MemNN baseline is a full trained model with different architecture and capacity. The lack of learning also means the cache representation is frozen—you can't adapt the memory to the task or learn better keys, which might limit performance on more complex domains. The ablation on cache size is informative, but there's no analysis of what the cache is actually doing—are the retrieved words always from the immediate past, or are they capturing longer-range semantic relationships? A qualitative analysis of attention patterns would have been really useful. The hyperparameter sensitivity (θ, λ, α) seems non-trivial from Figures 2 and 3, and the fact that the optimal λ differs between the development and control sets on LAMBADA (Figure 5) is a red flag—it suggests the model's performance is brittle to the prevalence of target words in the context. Finally, the paper is quite short and feels more like a technical report than a full ICLR paper; the experimental section is solid but lacks depth, and there's no discussion of failure cases or limitations beyond the brief mention of the λ mismatch. Overall, I think this is a neat, practical contribution with strong empirical results, but the conceptual novelty is modest and the paper feels a bit lightweight. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the simplicity and effectiveness make it a valuable addition to the toolkit, but I'd like to see more analysis and a clearer positioning relative to existing work.

title: Unsupervised Cross-Domain Image Generation
abstract: Abstract:###We study the problem of transferring a sample in one domain to an analog sample in another domain. Given two related domains, S and T, we would like to learn a generative function G that maps an input sample from S to the domain T, such that the output of a given representation function f, which accepts inputs in either domains, would remain unchanged. Other than f, the training data is unsupervised and consist of a set of samples from each domain, without any mapping between them. The Domain Transfer Network (DTN) we present employs a compound loss function that includes a multiclass GAN loss, an f preserving component, and a regularizing component that encourages G to map samples from T to themselves. We apply our method to visual domains including digits and face images and demonstrate its ability to generate convincing novel images of previously unseen entities, while preserving their identity.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely novel and practically important problem: unsupervised cross-domain image generation where you want to preserve high-level semantics (like identity) while transferring to a visually distinct target domain. The core idea of composing the generator as \(G = g \circ f\), where \(f\) is a fixed feature extractor, is elegant and practically motivated—it forces the generator to operate in a semantic space rather than pixel space, which is exactly what you want for identity-preserving transfer. The compound loss is well-designed: the GAN term ensures domain realism, the \(f\)-constancy term preserves semantics, and the \(L_{TID}\) regularization stabilizes training by encouraging the network to map target samples to themselves. The empirical results are genuinely impressive: on SVHN→MNIST transfer, you achieve 90.66% accuracy (vs 13.71% for the baseline), and the unsupervised domain adaptation result beating DANN (84.44% vs 73.85%) with a simple nearest neighbor classifier is a strong demonstration of the method's utility. The face-to-emoji application is compelling and the retrieval results (median rank 16 out of 100k with 22.88% rank-1 accuracy) show that the generated emoji preserve identity surprisingly well, even outperforming human-created emoji in discriminability—that's a striking result. The ablation studies are thorough and clearly demonstrate the contribution of each loss component. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The method feels like a clever engineering combination of existing pieces—GANs, perceptual losses, identity preservation—rather than a fundamentally new conceptual contribution. The paper's framing as "domain transfer" is broad, but the actual solution is quite specific to settings where you have a good semantic feature extractor \(f\) pretrained on one of the domains, which limits generality. The comparison to style transfer (Gatys et al.) in Figure 5 is a bit of a strawman—style transfer was never designed to map to a specific target distribution like emoji, so showing it fails is unsurprising. The face-to-emoji evaluation is impressive but also somewhat problematic: the "manual emoji" created by annotators were constrained by a web interface and not optimized for identity preservation, so the comparison isn't entirely fair. The retrieval metric uses VGG face, which is a different network from \(f\) (good for avoiding bias), but it's still a face recognition network—so you're essentially measuring whether the emoji preserve face identity, not whether they're "good emoji" in a broader sense. The domain adaptation experiment, while strong, uses a nearest neighbor classifier, which is a weak baseline—it would be more convincing to show that features learned from the transferred images can train a standard classifier. The paper also doesn't discuss failure cases or limitations in much depth—what happens when \(f\) is poor on the target domain, or when the domains are too far apart? The results on reverse transfer (MNIST→SVHN, emoji→faces) are hand-waved as "less appealing," which suggests the method isn't symmetric and the asymmetry is a real limitation. Overall, I think this is a well-executed paper with strong empirical results and a clear application, but the conceptual novelty is moderate and the evaluation could be more rigorous. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the face-to-emoji demo is impressive enough to warrant publication, but I'd like to see a cleaner framing of the contributions and a more honest discussion of the method's limitations.

title: Third Person Imitation Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Reinforcement learning (RL) makes it possible to train agents capable of achieving sophisticated goals in complex and uncertain environments. A key difficulty in reinforcement learning is specifying a reward function for the agent to optimize. Traditionally, imitation learning in RL has been used to overcome this problem. Unfortunately, hitherto imitation learning methods tend to require that demonstrations are supplied in the first-person: the agent is provided with a sequence of states and a specification of the actions that it should have taken. While powerful, this kind of imitation learning is limited by the relatively hard problem of collecting first-person demonstrations. Humans address this problem by learning from third-person demonstrations: they observe other humans perform tasks, infer the task, and accomplish the same task themselves. In this paper, we present a method for unsupervised third-person imitation learning. Here third-person refers to training an agent to correctly achieve a simple goal in a simple environment when it is provided a demonstration of a teacher achieving the same goal but from a different viewpoint; and unsupervised refers to the fact that the agent receives only these third-person demonstrations, and is not provided a correspondence between teacher states and student states. Our methods primary insight is that recent advances from domain confusion can be utilized to yield domain agnostic features which are crucial during the training process. To validate our approach, we report successful experiments on learning from third-person demonstrations in a pointmass domain, a reacher domain, and inverted pendulum.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely hard and practically important problem: learning to imitate from demonstrations when the demonstrator and the imitator have different viewpoints, which is exactly what humans do all the time. The core idea of combining GAIL with domain confusion to learn a feature representation that is invariant to the "domain" (first-person vs third-person viewpoint) is clever and well-motivated—it's a natural extension of domain adaptation ideas to the imitation learning setting, and the formulation in Equation 5 is clean. The empirical results are solid: the method works on three simple MuJoCo tasks, and the ablation studies convincingly show that both domain confusion and the multi-time-step input are important for good performance. The learning curves in Figure 3 show that the method is actually competitive with first-person GAIL (Figure 9), which is a strong result considering the added difficulty of the viewpoint change. I also appreciate the sensitivity analysis on camera angle (Figure 8) and the domain confusion coefficient λ (Figure 6)—these help build confidence in the method's robustness. The baselines are reasonable, and the failure of applying a first-person policy to a third-person agent (Figure 9) nicely illustrates why this problem is nontrivial. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The domain differences in the experiments are quite small—a 40-degree camera rotation and a color change—which is a far cry from the kinds of cross-domain imitation that would be practically useful, like imitating a human from video with a robot that has completely different morphology and dynamics. The method also requires expert *failures* in the source domain to train the discriminator, which is a strong assumption—in most real-world settings, we only have successful demonstrations, not labeled failures. The paper's framing as "unsupervised" is a bit misleading: you're not using labels for the target task, but you are using domain labels (first-person vs third-person) and explicit failure trajectories, which is still supervision. The architecture is extremely simple (two conv layers + two FC layers) and the images are tiny (50x50), so it's unclear how well this would scale to more complex visual domains. The comparison to "first-person features applied to third-person agent" is a bit of a strawman—of course it fails, since the features aren't domain-invariant—a more meaningful baseline would be using a domain adaptation method like Tzeng et al. (2015) to adapt the features *before* applying the first-person policy. The paper also doesn't discuss failure cases—when does the method break? What happens if the camera angle difference is 90 degrees, or if the background changes completely? Finally, the writing is a bit rough in places—the notation is occasionally confusing (e.g., using \(\mathcal{D}\) for both the discriminator and the domain confusion network), and the "velocity" term is introduced without a clear explanation of why the discriminator needs access to future frames. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a good idea and clean experiments on simple domains, but the scope is quite narrow and the practical applicability to real-world cross-domain imitation (e.g., human to robot) is still a long way off. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the contribution is valuable and the community should be thinking about this problem, but the paper feels like a proof of concept rather than a mature solution.

title: Variational Recurrent Adversarial Deep Domain Adaptation
abstract: Abstract:###We study the problem of learning domain invariant representations for time series data while transferring the complex temporal latent dependencies between the domains. Our model termed as Variational Recurrent Adversarial Deep Domain Adaptation (VRADA) is built atop a variational recurrent neural network (VRNN) and trains adversarially to capture complex temporal relationships that are domain-invariant. This is (as far as we know) the first to capture and transfer temporal latent dependencies in multivariate time-series data. Through experiments on real-world multivariate healthcare time-series datasets, we empirically demonstrate that learning temporal dependencies helps our model*s ability to create domain-invariant representations, allowing our model to outperform current state-of-the-art deep domain adaptation approaches.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: unsupervised domain adaptation for multivariate time-series data, specifically in the healthcare domain where age-group differences create distribution shifts. The core idea of combining a Variational Recurrent Neural Network (VRNN) with adversarial domain adaptation is elegant and well-motivated—the VRNN captures temporal latent dependencies across time steps, while the adversarial component (borrowed from DANN) encourages those representations to be domain-invariant. The empirical results are strong and convincing: on both the AHRF mortality prediction and ICD9 code prediction tasks, VRADA consistently outperforms DANN, R-DANN (DANN with an LSTM), and VFAE, often by 4-5% in AUC. The t-SNE visualizations in Figure 1 are compelling—they clearly show that VRADA produces better mixing of source and target distributions than DNN or R-DANN, which is a nice qualitative validation of the domain-invariance claim. I also appreciate the thorough ablation studies: Table 3 shows that joint training (rather than pretraining the VRNN) works best, Table 5 demonstrates that the reconstruction loss helps, and Figure 3 provides a nice visualization of the temporal latent dependencies, showing that VRADA's neuron activations are more consistent across time steps than R-DANN's. The application to healthcare is timely and practical, and the paper is well-written and easy to follow. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The novelty is somewhat incremental—this is essentially VRNN + DANN, which is a natural combination of two existing techniques rather than a fundamentally new idea. The paper claims to be "the first to capture and transfer temporal latent dependencies," but R-DANN (LSTM + DANN) also captures temporal dependencies, just without the variational component. The paper doesn't clearly articulate why the variational aspect is crucial—is it the stochasticity, the KL regularization, or the reconstruction objective? The ablation in Table 5 shows that reconstruction loss helps, but that's not a new insight (autoencoders have long been used for domain adaptation). The evaluation is also somewhat narrow: the results are only on two healthcare datasets, and the time-series are short (4 days for AHRF, 24 hours for ICD9) and relatively low-dimensional (20 and 99 features). It's unclear how well VRADA would scale to longer sequences or higher-dimensional data. The R-DANN baseline is a sensible comparison, but it's essentially the same architecture as VRADA without the variational component—this is good for ablation, but it also means the improvement is modest (1-2% AUC on ICD9), which raises questions about whether the added complexity of the VRNN is worth it. The paper also doesn't discuss the computational cost of VRADA compared to R-DANN—the variational component adds significant complexity, and it would be good to know if the performance gain justifies the overhead. Finally, the discussion of "temporal latent dependencies" is somewhat hand-wavy—the visualizations in Figures 3 and 4 show activation patterns, but it's not clear what those patterns actually mean or why VRADA's patterns are "better" beyond being more consistent. Overall, I think this is a solid, well-executed paper with strong empirical results, but the conceptual contribution is modest and the evaluation is limited to a single domain (healthcare) with relatively simple time-series. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the work is valuable for the community and the results are convincing, but I'd like to see a clearer articulation of the theoretical contribution and broader validation on more diverse time-series datasets.

title: Program Synthesis for Character Level Language Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a statistical model applicable to character level language modeling and show that it is a good fit for both, program source code and English text. The model is parameterized by a program from a domain-specific language (DSL) that allows expressing non-trivial data dependencies. Learning is done in two phases: (i) we synthesize a program from the DSL, essentially learning a good representation for the data, and (ii) we learn parameters from the training data - the process is done via counting, as in simple language models such as n-gram. Our experiments show that the precision of our model is comparable to that of neural networks while sharing a number of advantages with n-gram models such as fast query time and the capability to quickly add and remove training data samples. Further, the model is parameterized by a program that can be manually inspected, understood and updated, addressing a major problem of neural networks.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored direction: can we build interpretable, efficient language models that are competitive with neural networks by synthesizing programs from a domain-specific language? The core idea is elegant—learn a program that dynamically selects which simple counting-based model to use for each prediction context, essentially building a decision tree of specialized n-gram-like models. The results on the Linux Kernel dataset are genuinely impressive: 1.53 BPC and 23.5% error rate, significantly beating both n-gram (2.23 BPC, 37.7%) and LSTM (2.05 BPC, 38.1%). The fact that the model can be manually inspected and understood is a major advantage over black-box neural networks, and the ability to quickly add/remove training data (since the model is just counts) is a practical benefit that neural networks don't offer. The query time is also excellent (3,000-62,000 queries/second), making this suitable for deployment. The ablation studies clearly show the contribution of cache and backoff, and the example programs synthesized (e.g., detecting the first character of a word, distinguishing comments from code) provide concrete evidence that the DSL captures meaningful linguistic structure. The paper is well-structured and the formal semantics of the DSL are thorough. Cons - That said, I have several reservations. The performance on unstructured text (Hutter Prize Wikipedia) is only "competitive" with neural networks (Table 2), not superior, and the paper acknowledges that the model is "less suitable" for natural language. This suggests the method is really a win for structured data like source code, where the regularities are more amenable to the kind of discrete, rule-based patterns the DSL can capture. The synthesis procedure is quite complex—MCMC, genetic programming, decision tree learning, and brute-force search—and the paper doesn't provide enough detail on the hyperparameters or the sensitivity of the results to the search procedure. The claim that the model is "interpretable" is somewhat undermined by the sheer size of the synthesized program: 700 BranchPrograms, 2200 SimplePrograms, and over 8600 instructions. That's not a program a human can easily inspect, and the interactive visualization is a nice gesture but doesn't fully solve the interpretability problem. The comparison to LSTM is also not entirely apples-to-apples: the LSTM uses 2×512 units and 50 epochs, while the DSL model uses a cache and backoff to n-gram models, which are additional sources of information. The training time (8 hours) is still substantial, and the paper doesn't discuss how the synthesis scales to larger datasets or longer sequences. Finally, the DSL is hand-crafted for character-level language modeling, which raises the question of how general this approach is—if we have to design a new DSL for every domain, the method doesn't really solve the problem of learning representations, it just shifts the engineering effort. Overall, I think this is a clever and well-executed paper with strong results on structured data, but the limited generality, the complexity of the synthesis procedure, and the questionable interpretability of the final program give me pause. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the work is novel and the results are compelling, but the practical applicability beyond source code modeling is still unclear.

title: Episodic Exploration for Deep Deterministic Policies for StarCraft Micromanagement
abstract: Abstract:###We consider scenarios from the real-time strategy game StarCraft as benchmarks for reinforcement learning algorithms. We focus on micromanagement, that is, the short-term, low-level control of team members during a battle. We propose several scenarios that are challenging for reinforcement learning algorithms because the state- action space is very large, and there is no obvious feature representation for the value functions. We describe our approach to tackle the micromanagement scenarios with deep neural network controllers from raw state features given by the game engine. We also present a heuristic reinforcement learning algorithm which combines direct exploration in the policy space and backpropagation. This algorithm collects traces for learning using deterministic policies, which appears much more efficient than, e.g., ?-greedy exploration. Experiments show that this algorithm allows to successfully learn non-trivial strategies for scenarios with armies of up to 15 agents, where both Q-learning and REINFORCE struggle.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely hard and practically important problem: reinforcement learning in large-scale multi-agent settings with huge action spaces, using StarCraft micromanagement as a testbed. The problem formulation is well-motivated—the action space complexity (24^15 actions at the start of a battle) makes naive random exploration infeasible, and the durative, coordinated nature of the task demands a different approach. The greedy MDP reduction (Section 4.2) is a clever way to break the joint action inference into sequential unit-by-unit decisions while preserving optimality, and the normalized cumulative rewards (Section 4.3) address the issue of state-dependent reward scales. The feature representation and deep network architecture are thoughtfully designed to handle variable-size inputs and relational actions (attack unit X, move to position Y) without hand-crafted cross-features. The main contribution—the zero-order (ZO) exploration algorithm—is intuitive and empirically effective: randomize the last-layer weights at the start of an episode to explore deterministically, then use the cumulative reward to update both the weights and the embedding network. The results are strong: ZO consistently outperforms DQN and REINFORCE on most maps (e.g., 90% win rate on dragoons_zealots vs 61% for DQN, 79% on m15v16 vs 13% for DQN), and generalizes better to out-of-distribution unit counts (Table 2). The ablation showing that ZO training is much more stable and less initialization-dependent than DQN (Figure 1) is a significant practical advantage. The paper is also refreshingly honest about the limitations and the heuristic nature of the algorithm. Cons - That said, I have some serious reservations. The ZO algorithm is presented as a principled combination of finite-difference gradient estimation and backpropagation, but the update rule for the embedding network parameters (using \(\text{sign}(w / \Psi_\theta(s,a))\)) is a crude heuristic with no theoretical justification—it's essentially a hand-crafted gradient approximation that happens to work. The paper acknowledges this ("crude approximation," "heuristic") but doesn't provide any analysis of why it works or when it might fail. The comparison to DQN and REINFORCE is also somewhat unfair: DQN uses experience replay with the last episode only (not random batches from a large replay buffer), which is known to be suboptimal, and the hyperparameter search is extensive but the best results are reported without cross-validation or statistical significance. The feature engineering is also quite elaborate—17 features per unit, including distance computations and one-hot encodings—which undermines the claim of "raw state features" and makes the approach less general than implied. The model architecture is specific to the unit-based representation and doesn't leverage spatial structure (e.g., convolutional networks over 2D maps), which might be more natural for RTS games. The generalization experiments (Table 2) are encouraging, but the performance drops significantly on some maps (e.g., m18v20 from 63% heuristic to 17% ZO), suggesting the learned policies are still brittle. Finally, the paper doesn't compare to more recent exploration methods like bootstrapped DQN or parameter noise, which would be natural baselines. Overall, I think this is a solid empirical paper with a clever exploration heuristic and strong results on a challenging domain, but the theoretical grounding is weak and the approach feels like a bag of tricks rather than a principled algorithm. I'd lean towards a borderline accept—the problem is important, the results are compelling, but the contribution is more heuristic than fundamental.

title: Soft Weight-Sharing for Neural Network Compression
abstract: Abstract:###The success of deep learning in numerous application domains created the desire to run and train them on mobile devices. This however, conflicts with their computationally, memory and energy intense nature, leading to a growing interest in compression. Recent work by Han et al. (2016) propose a pipeline that involves retraining, pruning and quantization of neural network weights, obtaining state-of-the-art compression rates. In this paper, we show that competitive compression rates can be achieved by using a version of *soft weight-sharing* (Nowlan & Hinton, 1991). Our method achieves both quantization and pruning in one simple (re-)training procedure. This point of view also exposes the relation between compression and the minimum description length (MDL) principle.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a practically important problem—neural network compression for on-device deployment—with a principled Bayesian approach that connects directly to the minimum description length (MDL) principle. The core idea of using soft weight-sharing (a mixture of Gaussians prior) to simultaneously achieve pruning and quantization in one training procedure is elegant and conceptually clean. The connection to variational learning and the bits-back argument is well-explained, and the empirical results are strong: on LeNet-300-100 and LeNet-5-Caffe, you achieve compression rates of 64x and 62x respectively, which are state-of-the-art and competitive with Han et al.'s pipeline, all with a simpler, one-step procedure. The visualization in Figure 3 showing the mixture components collapsing and merging during training is a nice demonstration of the method's dynamics—the network effectively learns how many quantization levels it needs. I also appreciate the ablation with Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning (Figure 2), which gives a sense of the method's robustness across different settings. The paper is well-written and the connection to existing work is clear. Cons - That said, I have some significant concerns. The scalability issue is a major red flag—you acknowledge in Appendix C that the algorithm is "too slow to get usable results" for large networks like VGG with 138M parameters, and your proposed solution (sampling a subset of weights for the prior gradient) is untested. This severely limits the practical impact of the method, since compression is most needed for large modern architectures. The hyperparameter tuning using Bayesian optimization over 13 parameters feels like a crutch—if the method requires that much tuning to work, it's not really a practical drop-in replacement for the Han et al. pipeline, which has a clearer set of steps. The comparison to Han et al. is also somewhat unfair: you use the same post-processing storage format (CSC with Huffman encoding), so the compression gains are largely coming from the quantization and pruning induced by your prior, but the error rates on LeNet-5-Caffe (0.97% vs 0.74% for Han et al.) are slightly worse, and on ResNet the accuracy drop is significant (6.48% → 8.50%, a 2% absolute drop). The method also introduces a new hyperparameter \(\tau\) to weigh the complexity loss, and the paper doesn't provide clear guidance on how to set it—0.005 is used, but why? The connection to "soft weight-sharing" is historically interesting, but the method is essentially just empirical Bayes with a mixture prior, which is not new; the novelty is in applying it to compression rather than regularization. Finally, the paper doesn't compare to more recent compression methods like variational dropout (Molchanov et al., 2017) or dynamic network surgery (Guo et al., 2016) in a systematic way—you mention them but don't include them in the comparison table. Overall, I think this is a well-written paper with a clever idea and strong results on small networks, but the scalability issues and the complexity of hyperparameter tuning make me skeptical about its practical utility for modern deep learning. I'd lean towards a borderline accept—the idea is nice and the MDL framing is elegant, but the method needs to demonstrate scalability and simpler tuning before I'd be fully convinced.

title: Neural Program Lattices
abstract: Abstract:###We propose the Neural Program Lattice (NPL), a neural network that learns to perform complex tasks by composing low-level programs to express high-level programs. Our starting point is the recent work on Neural Programmer-Interpreters (NPI), which can only learn from strong supervision that contains the whole hierarchy of low-level and high-level programs. NPLs remove this limitation by providing the ability to learn from weak supervision consisting only of sequences of low-level operations. We demonstrate the capability of NPL to learn to perform long-hand addition and arrange blocks in a grid-world environment. Experiments show that it performs on par with NPI while using weak supervision in place of most of the strong supervision, thus indicating its ability to infer the high-level program structure from examples containing only the low-level operations.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: learning hierarchical program abstractions from weak supervision consisting only of flat sequences of elementary operations, rather than requiring the full program trace annotations that NPI demands. The core technical contribution—combining ideas from CTC (for alignment) and StackRNNs (for differentiable stacks) into a lattice structure that approximates the marginalized likelihood over all possible program hierarchies—is clever and well-engineered. The lattice formulation is a nice middle ground between the exponential cost of enumerating all paths and the oversimplification of collapsing all paths into a single state; grouping by call depth and elementary operation index is a sensible design choice that balances computational cost against representational accuracy. The empirical results are strong: on the NANOCRAFT task, NPL significantly outperforms both NPI (when only a subset of samples have full annotations) and seq2seq baselines, and on the ADDITION task, NPL with just one fully-annotated sample per digit length generalizes to 1000-digit numbers, matching the performance of NPI trained with full supervision on all samples. The generalization from 10-digit to 1000-digit addition is genuinely impressive and highlights the power of learning the latent program structure. The paper is well-written, the connection to prior work is clear, and the ablation studies are informative. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The method is quite complex—combining CTC, differentiable stacks, and a lattice DP with soft-argmax approximations is a lot of moving parts, and the paper doesn't provide a clear intuition for why all this machinery is necessary beyond "it works." The approximation quality is also unclear: the paper acknowledges that the lattice only approximately computes the marginal likelihood, but there's no analysis of how close this approximation is to the exact (intractable) marginal, or in what regimes it fails. The weak supervision setting is still quite strong—you assume access to a small number of fully-annotated program traces (e.g., 1 per digit length for ADDITION) to bootstrap learning, which is a significant assumption. The paper claims this is "weak supervision" relative to NPI, but it's still a form of semi-supervision; a truly unsupervised setting would have no full program traces at all. The tasks are also relatively simple: ADDITION is a well-structured algorithmic task, and NANOCRAFT is a grid-world with a fixed set of programs. It's unclear how well this would scale to more complex, noisy domains (e.g., real-world action sequences) where the number of possible programs is large and the supervision is truly ambiguous. The comparison to seq2seq baselines is somewhat unfair—the S2S-Easy baseline is specifically designed for addition and still underperforms, but a more modern Transformer or attention-based model might do better. Finally, the computational cost of the lattice grows with the product of the number of timesteps, elementary operations, and call depths, which could be prohibitive for long sequences or deep programs. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a clever idea and impressive results on two well-chosen tasks, but the complexity of the method and the remaining need for some strong supervision make it feel like a step forward rather than a complete solution. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the contribution is valuable and the results are strong, but the method is over-engineered for the tasks and the generalization to more realistic settings is unclear.

title: Tracking the World State with Recurrent Entity Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a new model, the Recurrent Entity Network (EntNet). It is equipped with a dynamic long-term memory which allows it to maintain and update a rep- resentation of the state of the world as it receives new data. For language under- standing tasks, it can reason on-the-fly as it reads text, not just when it is required to answer a question or respond as is the case for a Memory Network (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015). Like a Neural Turing Machine or Differentiable Neural Computer (Graves et al., 2014; 2016) it maintains a fixed size memory and can learn to perform location and content-based read and write operations. However, unlike those models it has a simple parallel architecture in which several memory loca- tions can be updated simultaneously. The EntNet sets a new state-of-the-art on the bAbI tasks, and is the first method to solve all the tasks in the 10k training examples setting. We also demonstrate that it can solve a reasoning task which requires a large number of supporting facts, which other methods are not able to solve, and can generalize past its training horizon. It can also be practically used on large scale datasets such as Childrenâ€™s Book Test, where it obtains competitive performance, reading the story in a single pass.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper introduces a genuinely elegant and biologically-inspired architecture for maintaining a dynamic world state while reading text. The core idea—a bank of gated RNNs with shared parameters, each corresponding to a latent entity, with content-based and location-based addressing—is conceptually clean and well-motivated. The results speak for themselves: the EntNet is the first model to solve all 20 bAbI tasks in the 10k training setting, achieving a 0.5% mean error with zero failed tasks, which significantly outperforms MemN2N (4.2% mean error, 3 failed), DNC (3.8%, 2 failed), and DMN+ (2.8%, 1 failed). The synthetic world model task is also a strong demonstration—the EntNet maintains near-perfect accuracy even at sequence length 20 while MemN2N degrades to ~0.45 error and LSTM to ~0.35, and the generalization to sequences 4× longer than training (Table 1b) is genuinely impressive, suggesting the model has learned the underlying dynamics rather than memorizing patterns. The interpretability experiment in Table 3 is a highlight—showing that the memory slots actually encode coherent entity-level representations (e.g., the "milk" slot storing "garden") provides concrete evidence that the model is building the kind of world model the authors claim. The CBT results are also solid: the simplified EntNet achieves 61.6% on Named Entities and 58.8% on Common Nouns, outperforming all other single-pass models including LSTMs and window LSTMs. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The model has a lot of moving parts—gates with content and location terms, key vectors, candidate updates, normalization—and the paper doesn't provide a clear ablation study to show which components are essential and which are just bells and whistles. The performance on the 1k bAbI setting (Appendix, Table 6) is actually quite poor (29.6% mean error, 15 failed tasks), significantly worse than MemN2N (13.9%, 11 failed), which suggests the model is data-hungry and relies on the larger training set to learn the complex gating mechanics. The weight-tying variant (Table 5) also doesn't consistently help, and in some cases hurts performance, which undermines the "entity" interpretation—if the model isn't actually using entity-specific keys as intended, the interpretability story becomes less convincing. The comparison to DNC in Table 7 is a bit cherry-picked: the EntNet's best-seed performance is worse than DNC's best-seed (7.38% vs 3.8% mean error), and the paper leans on the "mean performance" comparison to make the EntNet look better, which is a bit disingenuous since the DNC results are from a single paper and the variance is high. The model also doesn't handle inter-memory communication, which seems like a significant limitation—if entities interact (e.g., John gives the ball to Mary), a purely parallel independent-update model might struggle to capture the relational dynamics. Finally, the CBT results, while strong for single-pass models, still lag significantly behind multi-pass models like AoA Reader (72.0% vs 61.6%), suggesting the "read-once" constraint is a real limitation. Overall, I think this is a strong paper with a clever architecture and impressive empirical results on synthetic and benchmark tasks, but the data efficiency concerns, the lack of a clean ablation, and the gap to multi-pass models on real data give me pause. I'd lean towards a strong accept—the bAbI result alone is a significant contribution, but I'd like to see a more thorough analysis of the model's components and failure modes.

title: Steerable CNNs
abstract: Abstract:###It has long been recognized that the invariance and equivariance properties of a representation are critically important for success in many vision tasks. In this paper we present Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks, an efficient and flexible class of equivariant convolutional networks. We show that steerable CNNs achieve state of the art results on the CIFAR image classification benchmark. The mathematical theory of steerable representations reveals a type system in which any steerable representation is a composition of elementary feature types, each one associated with a particular kind of symmetry. We show how the parameter cost of a steerable filter bank depends on the types of the input and output features, and show how to use this knowledge to construct CNNs that utilize parameters effectively.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper presents a beautifully elegant and mathematically rigorous framework for constructing equivariant convolutional networks, generalizing previous work on group equivariant CNNs (G-CNNs) to arbitrary steerable feature representations. The core insight—that steerable representations decompose into irreducible feature types, and that the parameter cost of an equivariant filter bank is determined by the intertwining number between input and output representation types—is a significant theoretical contribution that both explains why equivariant networks are parameter-efficient and provides a practical recipe for designing them. The "type system" analogy is particularly useful: just as you wouldn't add meters to seconds, you shouldn't mix feature types that transform differently under symmetries. The experimental results are compelling: on CIFAR-10 with full data, the steerable CNN achieves 3.64% error, outperforming Wide ResNet (4.17%), DenseNet (4.51%), and even the previous state-of-the-art (3.74% from Huang et al.); on CIFAR-100, 19.38% vs 20.28% for Wide ResNet. The gains are even more pronounced in the small-data regime (2k and 4k labels), where steerable CNNs achieve 24.48% and 14.91% error respectively, convincingly demonstrating that equivariance as an inductive bias improves sample efficiency. The construction of regular and quotient capsules, and the discussion of admissible nonlinearities (CReLU, etc.), bridges the gap between abstract representation theory and practical implementation. I also appreciate the computational efficiency trick—using the block structure of intertwiners to avoid storing full basis matrices—which makes the method scalable. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The paper is quite dense and assumes a high level of mathematical maturity; while the theory is elegant, the barrier to entry for practitioners is substantial, and the paper doesn't provide enough intuitive explanations to make the method accessible. The experiments, while strong, are limited to CIFAR (and one small-data ablation); it would be more convincing to see results on ImageNet or other large-scale benchmarks to demonstrate that the method scales. The choice of capsules (regular, qm, qmr2, qmr3, and irreps A1, A2, B1, B2, E) is somewhat ad hoc—the paper doesn't provide a systematic way to choose which capsules to use for a given task, and the final architecture uses a mix of quotient capsules with ReLU and irreducible capsules with CReLU, which feels more like engineering than a principled design. The claim that the method "decouples computational cost from group size" is a bit misleading: while the number of parameters is independent of group size, the convolution operation itself still needs to be applied over the group or over the induced representation, which can be computationally expensive. The comparison to ResNets is also slightly unfair because the steerable CNN uses a different architecture (with capsules and specialized nonlinearities) and more careful tuning; it would be helpful to see an ablation where a standard ResNet is augmented with the same capacity. Finally, the paper focuses on discrete groups (specifically D4), and while the theory extends to continuous groups, the implementation details for that case are not provided, so it's unclear how practical the method is beyond small discrete symmetries. Overall, I think this is an excellent paper with a beautiful theoretical contribution and strong empirical results, but the practical usability and scalability are still somewhat unclear. I'd lean towards a strong accept—the paper is a significant step forward for equivariant deep learning, and the results on CIFAR are genuinely impressive, but I'd like to see a clearer path to applying the method to larger groups and datasets.

title: Learning to Query, Reason, and Answer Questions On Ambiguous Texts
abstract: Abstract:###A key goal of research in conversational systems is to train an interactive agent to help a user with a task. Human conversation, however, is notoriously incomplete, ambiguous, and full of extraneous detail. To operate effectively, the agent must not only understand what was explicitly conveyed but also be able to reason in the presence of missing or unclear information. When unable to resolve ambiguities on its own, the agent must be able to ask the user for the necessary clarifications and incorporate the response in its reasoning. Motivated by this problem we introduce QRAQ (*crack*; Query, Reason, and Answer Questions), a new synthetic domain, in which a User gives an Agent a short story and asks a challenge question. These problems are designed to test the reasoning and interaction capabilities of a learning-based Agent in a setting that requires multiple conversational turns. A good Agent should ask only non-deducible, relevant questions until it has enough information to correctly answer the User*s question. We use standard and improved reinforcement learning based memory-network architectures to solve QRAQ problems in the difficult setting where the reward signal only tells the Agent if its final answer to the challenge question is correct or not. To provide an upper-bound to the RL results we also train the same architectures using supervised information that tells the Agent during training which variables to query and the answer to the challenge question. We evaluate our architectures on four QRAQ dataset types, and scale the complexity for each along multiple dimensions.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely important and understudied problem: multi-turn reasoning in ambiguous contexts where the agent must actively query for missing information, not just answer questions from a static story. The QRAQ domain is a nice extension of the bAbI framework, introducing variables, deducibility, relevance, and the need to decide when to query versus answer. The problem is well-motivated and the dataset design is thoughtful—the four dataset types (Loc, +obj, +alias, +par) systematically probe different aspects of reasoning. The impRL architecture, with soft attention over multiple memory hops, is a sensible improvement over the base memory network, and the empirical results show that it consistently improves answer accuracy on the harder datasets (e.g., 75.6% vs 69.7% on the hardest Loc dataset). The curriculum learning approach—first rewarding queries to encourage exploration, then penalizing them to reduce unnecessary queries—is a pragmatic solution to the exploration problem in this setting. I also appreciate the use of multiple evaluation metrics (answer accuracy, trajectory accuracy, trajectory completeness, query accuracy), which provide a nuanced view of agent performance beyond just final answer correctness. The paper is well-written and the related work section is comprehensive. Cons - That said, I have some significant concerns. The gap between supervised and RL performance is enormous—on the hardest Loc dataset, impSL achieves 92.4% answer accuracy while impRL gets only 64.2%. This suggests the RL agent is not learning a robust query policy, and the paper doesn't provide a convincing explanation for why this gap persists despite the impRL improvements. The trajectory-completeness metric (46.9% for impRL on the hardest Loc) is particularly damning—it means the agent is making irrelevant queries, missing relevant ones, or both, more than half the time. The action masking and curriculum learning feel like band-aids for a fundamentally weak policy gradient approach; the paper doesn't explore more sophisticated RL methods (e.g., PPO, A2C) or compare to them. The datasets are synthetic and relatively small-scale (100k training examples), so it's unclear how these results would transfer to more realistic, noisy natural language. The "depth" concept is central to problem complexity, but the dataset generation algorithm is described only vaguely ("detailed description ... when we release"), making it hard to assess the difficulty or reproducibility. The comparison to bAbI-dialog (Weston, 2016) is also somewhat superficial—that paper explores many different supervision regimes, while QRAQ focuses on a single RL setting with a sparse reward, so the claimed "significant increase in difficulty" isn't directly substantiated. Finally, the paper claims the agent must "learn unstated constraints," but the problems are actually generated from a known graph-based algorithm, so the agent is really learning to mimic a specific inference procedure rather than discovering general logical principles. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a well-designed dataset and some interesting architectural improvements, but the RL results are underwhelming and the gap between supervised and RL performance suggests the problem may be too hard for current RL methods. I'd lean towards a borderline accept—the dataset contribution is valuable, but the learning results feel preliminary and the method doesn't convincingly solve the problem it sets out to address.

title: Deep Predictive Coding Networks for Video Prediction and Unsupervised Learning
abstract: Abstract:###While great strides have been made in using deep learning algorithms to solve supervised learning tasks, the problem of unsupervised learning - leveraging unlabeled examples to learn about the structure of a domain - remains a difficult unsolved challenge. Here, we explore prediction of future frames in a video sequence as an unsupervised learning rule for learning about the structure of the visual world. We describe a predictive neural network (*PredNet*) architecture that is inspired by the concept of *predictive coding* from the neuroscience literature. These networks learn to predict future frames in a video sequence, with each layer in the network making local predictions and only forwarding deviations from those predictions to subsequent network layers. We show that these networks are able to robustly learn to predict the movement of synthetic (rendered) objects, and that in doing so, the networks learn internal representations that are useful for decoding latent object parameters (e.g. pose) that support object recognition with fewer training views. We also show that these networks can scale to complex natural image streams (car-mounted camera videos), capturing key aspects of both egocentric movement and the movement of objects in the visual scene, and the representation learned in this setting is useful for estimating the steering angle. These results suggest that prediction represents a powerful framework for unsupervised learning, allowing for implicit learning of object and scene structure.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles the fundamental challenge of unsupervised learning through video prediction, and the proposed PredNet architecture is both biologically inspired and technically well-grounded. The core idea—using predictive coding with separate positive and negative error populations, local recurrence, and top-down connections—is elegant and aligns nicely with theories of cortical function. The empirical results are strong across both synthetic and natural domains: on rotating faces, PredNet achieves 0.0152 MSE vs 0.0180 for a CNN-LSTM encoder-decoder and 0.125 for copy-last-frame, and on CalTech Pedestrian, it achieves 3.13e-3 MSE vs 3.67e-3 for the control model. More importantly, the paper convincingly demonstrates that learning to predict enables useful representation learning—the latent variable decoding experiments show that PredNet's representations are better for decoding pose, rotation speed, and identity than randomly initialized networks, and the orientation-invariant classification experiment (Figure 3, right) shows that 5-shot learning from PredNet representations beats autoencoders and ladder networks. The steering angle estimation results (74% variance explained with just 1K labeled examples) are a compelling demonstration that the representations transfer to a real-world regression task. The architecture is also computationally efficient, using convolutional LSTMs and a single forward/backward pass, unlike some prior work. I appreciate the thorough ablation studies in the appendix (Table 3), showing that the error-passing mechanism and the positive/negative splitting both contribute to performance. The paper is well-written and the connection to neuroscience is thoughtfully integrated. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The hyperparameter sensitivity is a concern—the best model for prediction (L0, loss only on lowest layer) differs from the best model for representation learning (Lall, with loss on all layers), and the paper doesn't provide a principled way to choose this trade-off for a given downstream task. The comparison to Finn et al.'s DNA model on Human3.6M (Table 5) is underwhelming—PredNet gets 38.9 PSNR vs DNA's 42.1, and the authors don't dig into why, beyond noting they didn't optimize hyperparameters. The claim that prediction "requires knowledge of object structure" is intuitive but not rigorously tested—the experiments show correlation between prediction accuracy and representation quality, but don't establish causation. The model is fundamentally deterministic and doesn't handle stochasticity or multi-modal futures, which is a significant limitation for real-world video where multiple outcomes are possible; recent work on stochastic video prediction (e.g., Vondrick et al., 2016; Denton & Fergus, 2018) addresses this, and the paper doesn't discuss how PredNet could be extended. The multiple-step prediction results (Figure 6) show the model degrades quickly beyond 2-3 steps, which limits its utility for planning or long-horizon tasks. Finally, the training data scale is relatively modest (41K frames for KITTI), and it's unclear how well the approach scales to larger datasets or higher resolutions. Overall, I think this is a strong paper with a compelling architecture, solid empirical results, and a nice connection to neuroscience, but the stochasticity limitation and the gap to state-of-the-art on Human3.6M give me some pause. I'd lean towards a strong accept—the work is a significant step forward for prediction-based unsupervised learning, and the steering angle and classification results are genuinely impressive, but I'd like to see a more systematic treatment of the representation vs. prediction trade-off and a discussion of how to handle uncertainty.

title: Diet Networks: Thin Parameters for Fat Genomics
abstract: Abstract:###Learning tasks such as those involving genomic data often poses a serious challenge: the number of input features can be orders of magnitude larger than the number of training examples, making it difficult to avoid overfitting, even when using the known regularization techniques. We focus here on tasks in which the input is a description of the genetic variation specific to a patient, the single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), yielding millions of ternary inputs. Improving the ability of deep learning to handle such datasets could have an important impact in medical research, more specifically in precision medicine, where high-dimensional data regarding a particular patient is used to make predictions of interest. Even though the amount of data for such tasks is increasing, this mismatch between the number of examples and the number of inputs remains a concern. Naive implementations of classifier neural networks involve a huge number of free parameters in their first layer (number of input features times number of hidden units): each input feature is associated with as many parameters as there are hidden units. We propose a novel neural network parametrization which considerably reduces the number of free parameters. It is based on the idea that we can first learn or provide a distributed representation for each input feature (e.g. for each position in the genome where variations are observed in data), and then learn (with another neural network called the parameter prediction network) how to map a feature*s distributed representation (based on the feature*s identity not its value) to the vector of parameters specific to that feature in the classifier neural network (the weights which link the value of the feature to each of the hidden units). This approach views the problem of producing the parameters associated with each feature as a multi-task learning problem. We show experimentally on a population stratification task of interest to medical studies that the proposed approach can significantly reduce both the number of parameters and the error rate of the classifier.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: applying deep learning to high-dimensional genomic data where the number of features (SNPs) far exceeds the number of training examples, a regime where standard neural networks massively overfit. The core idea—using an auxiliary network to predict the parameters of the first layer based on feature embeddings—is elegant and well-motivated. The "Diet Network" framing as a multi-task learning problem where each input feature is a separate task is conceptually clean, and the reduction in parameters is dramatic: from 30M to 50K in your example, a factor of 600. The empirical results on the 1000 Genomes ancestry prediction task are strong: the per-class histogram embedding with reconstruction yields 97.37% accuracy (vs 94.45% for the basic model) while reducing parameters by nearly 4000x, and the confusion matrix shows near-perfect separation at the continental level. The ablation over different embeddings (random projections, SNP2Vec, histograms) is thorough and informative, and the use of a reconstruction loss to regularize the model is a nice touch that reduces variance. The application to population stratification is timely and practically relevant, and the paper is well-written and accessible to non-genomics readers. Cons - That said, I have some reservations. The comparison to PCA is somewhat weak—you compare to a linear classifier on PCA features, but you don't compare to standard MLPs with strong regularization (dropout, weight decay) on the raw data, which would be a more direct baseline for whether the Diet Network actually improves over standard deep learning. The best results use a per-class histogram embedding that exploits the class labels to construct the embedding—this feels like a form of leakage, since the embedding uses information about the distribution of each feature across classes, which is exactly what the classifier is trying to predict. A truly unsupervised embedding (like SNP2Vec or random projections) would be more principled, and indeed these perform worse (91-94% vs 97%). The method also adds significant architectural complexity—two auxiliary networks—which makes training more difficult, as evidenced by the fact that end-to-end learning of the embeddings performed worse than using pre-computed ones. The paper doesn't explore how this method would generalize to other domains, or whether the parameter reduction is worth the added complexity when simpler methods like PCA or L1-regularized logistic regression might suffice. Finally, the paper claims this is a "novel" parametrization, but the idea of using a network to predict the weights of another network has been explored in Hypernetworks (Ha et al., 2016) and other works—the novelty is more in the application to genomics and the emphasis on parameter reduction rather than capacity expansion, but this distinction is somewhat subtle. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a clever idea and impressive results on a real-world genomic task, but the reliance on label-informed embeddings and the weak baseline comparisons give me some pause. I'd lean towards a weak accept—the contribution is valuable for the genomics community, and the parameter reduction is genuinely impressive, but the method's generality and the fairness of the comparison need more work.

title: Deep Biaffine Attention for Neural Dependency Parsing
abstract: Abstract:###This paper builds off recent work from Kiperwasser & Goldberg (2016) using neural attention in a simple graph-based dependency parser. We use a larger but more thoroughly regularized parser than other recent BiLSTM-based approaches, with biaffine classifiers to predict arcs and labels. Our parser gets state of the art or near state of the art performance on standard treebanks for six different languages, achieving 95.7% UAS and 94.1% LAS on the most popular English PTB dataset. This makes it the highest-performing graph-based parser on this benchmarkâ€”outperforming Kiperwasser & Goldberg (2016) by 1.8% and 2.2%â€”and comparable to the highest performing transition-based parser (Kuncoro et al., 2016), which achieves 95.8% UAS and 94.6% LAS. We also show which hyperparameter choices had a significant effect on parsing accuracy, allowing us to achieve large gains over other graph-based approaches.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper is a model of clarity and empirical rigor in an area—neural dependency parsing—that's been moving fast. The core technical contribution is clean and well-motivated: replacing the standard MLP-based attention with a biaffine classifier, and further applying dimension-reducing MLPs before the biaffine transformation, both speeds things up and improves accuracy. The results speak for themselves: 95.7% UAS and 94.1% LAS on PTB-SD 3.3.0, which is state-of-the-art among graph-based parsers and competitive with the best transition-based parsers (Kuncoro et al.'s 95.8/94.6). I really appreciate the thorough hyperparameter analysis—the ablation showing that β2=0.9 instead of 0.999 makes a big difference, and that 3-4 LSTM layers are better than 2, is the kind of practical insight that helps the community. The deep vs shallow bilinear comparison (Table 2) is also nicely done, showing that the reduced MLP dimension doesn't hurt accuracy while improving speed substantially. The parser also generalizes well across languages, achieving SOTA on CoNLL 2009 across six languages, which is a strong validation of the approach. The writing is excellent—the paper is easy to follow and the connection to traditional affine classifiers makes the biaffine idea intuitive. Cons - That said, the novelty is somewhat incremental. The biaffine attention mechanism is essentially a small twist on Hashimoto et al.'s bilinear attention, and the label classifier is a straightforward extension. The "deep" part (MLPs before the biaffine) is sensible but not surprising. The paper also doesn't address the limitations of graph-based parsers relative to transition-based ones—transition parsers can use rich structural features during decoding, while graph parsers are essentially doing arc factorization with an MST post-processing. The gap in LAS (94.1 vs 94.6 for Kuncoro et al.) suggests that label prediction, where structural context matters more, is where the approach still lags. The paper also doesn't explore more challenging settings like low-resource languages or domain adaptation, where the strong regularization might shine. Finally, while the hyperparameter analysis is thorough, it's all on English PTB, and it's unclear if the optimal settings transfer to other languages. Overall, I think this is a solid, well-executed paper that makes a clear contribution to the parsing literature, but the conceptual leap is modest and the paper feels more like a high-quality engineering paper than a breakthrough. I'd lean towards a strong accept—the results are state-of-the-art, the analysis is rigorous, and the code release will be valuable, but the contribution is primarily empirical rather than conceptual.

title: PixelVAE: A Latent Variable Model for Natural Images
abstract: Abstract:###Natural image modeling is a landmark challenge of unsupervised learning. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) learn a useful latent representation and model global structure well but have difficulty capturing small details. PixelCNN models details very well, but lacks a latent code and is difficult to scale for capturing large structures. We present PixelVAE, a VAE model with an autoregressive decoder based on PixelCNN. Our model requires very few expensive autoregressive layers compared to PixelCNN and learns latent codes that are more compressed than a standard VAE while still capturing most non-trivial structure. Finally, we extend our model to a hierarchy of latent variables at different scales. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on binarized MNIST, competitive performance on 64 Ã— 64 ImageNet, and high-quality samples on the LSUN bedrooms dataset.
review: Thank you for an interesting read. Pros - This paper presents a clean and elegant synthesis of two powerful generative modeling paradigms: VAEs and PixelCNNs. The core insight—using a PixelCNN as the conditional output distribution in a VAE decoder—is intuitively appealing and well-executed, and the results speak for themselves: state-of-the-art on binarized MNIST (79.02 nats), competitive performance on 64x64 ImageNet (3.61 bits/dim), and high-quality samples on LSUN bedrooms that are globally coherent in a way that PixelCNN samples often aren't. I really appreciate the analysis in Figure 4 showing that PixelVAE needs far fewer autoregressive layers than PixelCNN to achieve strong performance—this is a practical advantage that makes the model more computationally tractable. The breakdown of KL divergence vs. reconstruction cost as a function of autoregressive layers is also illuminating: it shows that the latent variables are freed from encoding small-scale details, learning a more compressed representation that captures global structure while the PixelCNN handles local texture and edge alignment. The hierarchical extension with multiple stochastic layers is natural and effective, and the visual inspection in Figure 5—showing that different layers capture different levels of scene structure (room geometry vs. objects/colors vs. pixel-level details)—is a beautiful demonstration of the model's representational hierarchy.
