The paper is well-written, the related work is thorough, and the results are convincingly presented. Cons - That said, the novelty is somewhat incremental. Combining a VAE with an autoregressive decoder is a natural idea that has been explored in other domains (e.g., sentence modeling with Bowman et al., 2016), and the paper doesn't fully address why previous attempts failed in image modeling while this one succeeds. The ImageNet results, while competitive, are not state-of-the-art—PixelRNN achieves 3.00 bits/dim vs. your 3.61—and the paper doesn't provide a deep analysis of why your model lags behind on this more challenging dataset. The LSUN samples in Figure 1 are impressive, but there's no quantitative comparison to other models on LSUN (e.g., DCGAN, Improved GAN) beyond visual inspection. The hierarchical model adds complexity, but the paper doesn't ablate the hierarchy systematically—e.g., how much does the second stochastic layer actually improve over a single-layer PixelVAE? The paper also doesn't discuss the computational cost of sampling from PixelVAE compared to PixelCNN or standard VAE, which is an important practical consideration. Finally, the MNIST results are reported as upper bounds from importance sampling, but the paper doesn't provide the actual estimated NLL with confidence intervals, making it hard to compare directly to other work. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a clever idea and strong empirical results, but the conceptual contribution is modest and the analysis could be deeper. I'd lean towards a strong accept—the work is clearly a step forward for generative modeling, and the hierarchical decomposition is genuinely interesting, but I'd like to see more thorough ablation and analysis of the failure cases.

title: Snapshot Ensembles: Train 1, Get M for Free
abstract: Abstract:###Ensembles of neural networks are known to be much more robust and accurate than individual networks. However, training multiple deep networks for model averaging is computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose a method to obtain the seemingly contradictory goal of ensembling multiple neural networks at no additional training cost. We achieve this goal by training a single neural network, converging to several local minima along its optimization path and saving the model parameters. To obtain repeated rapid convergence, we leverage recent work on cyclic learning rate schedules. The resulting technique, which we refer to as Snapshot Ensembling, is simple, yet surprisingly effective. We show in a series of experiments that our approach is compatible with diverse network architectures and learning tasks. It consistently yields lower error rates than state-of-the-art single models at no additional training cost, and compares favorably with traditional network ensembles. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 our DenseNet Snapshot Ensembles obtain error rates of 3.4% and 17.4% respectively.
review: This paper argues that you can get an ensemble of neural networks for the price of a single one by using cyclic learning rate schedules and saving snapshots at the end of each cycle. The idea is simple and elegant, and the experimental results are quite strong — the Snapshot Ensembles consistently beat standard single-model baselines and often come close to traditional ensembles trained independently at a fraction of the cost. What I like is the clever exploitation of SGD's non-convex dynamics: the cosine annealing forces the optimizer to visit multiple local minima, and the snapshots are diverse enough to make averaging worthwhile. The results on CIFAR-100 (17.4%) and Tiny ImageNet are particularly impressive. My main concern is that the paper doesn't sufficiently address the "no free lunch" aspect — the cyclic schedule effectively gives the model more opportunities to converge to a good minimum, but the total training iterations are fixed. If you just trained a single model for longer with a well-tuned learning rate decay, would you match the ensemble's performance? The paper shows the ensemble beats the standard schedule, but the standard schedule isn't exactly optimized for this budget. I'd like to see a comparison where you take the best snapshot from the cyclic run (not the ensemble) and compare it to the standard model — Figure 7 suggests the ensemble is always better than its individual members, but the margin varies. Also, the method seems to work best when the cycles are long enough for convergence (45+ epochs on ImageNet), which limits its applicability to very large datasets. The diversity analysis is nice, but I wish they'd computed the pairwise disagreement rate explicitly. Overall, this is a solid contribution with immediate practical impact, and I'd recommend acceptance. The idea is borderline obvious in hindsight, but that's often the mark of a good paper.

title: Training Agent for First-Person Shooter Game with Actor-Critic Curriculum Learning
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we propose a novel framework for training vision-based agent for First-Person Shooter (FPS) Game, in particular Doom. Our framework combines the state-of-the-art reinforcement learning approach (Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) model) with curriculum learning. Our model is simple in design and only uses game states from the AI side, rather than using opponents* information. On a known map, our agent won 10 out of the 11 attended games and the champion of Track1 in ViZDoom AI Competition 2016 by a large margin, 35\% higher score than the second place.
review:
This paper presents a practical engineering tour de force for training a Doom-playing agent, combining A3C with curriculum learning and a bunch of reward shaping tricks to win the ViZDoom competition. The results speak for themselves — the agent crushes the competition with 559 frags versus 413 for the second-place system, and the ablation studies are thorough and informative. What I appreciate is the sheer amount of engineering effort and the careful design of the curriculum, which progressively increases bot difficulty in a sensible way. The adaptive curriculum that shifts the task distribution based on performance is a nice touch, and the visualizations of the learned filters and the correlation analysis are genuinely useful for understanding what the network is doing.

That said, I'm not convinced this is ICLR material. The core algorithmic contribution is minimal — it's essentially A3C with a well-tuned curriculum and reward function, plus some post-processing hacks. The paper acknowledges that the curriculum design is hand-crafted and map-specific, which limits the generalizability of the approach. The reliance on privileged information like ground-truth location for reward shaping (even if not used at test time) feels a bit like cheating, and the post-training rules are ad-hoc engineering that undermines the "end-to-end" narrative. The claim that "our approach requires no opponent's information" is technically true but somewhat misleading given the extensive use of other game variables.

My biggest concern is that the paper doesn't really advance our understanding of RL — it's a case study in how to win a competition with lots of tuning and domain-specific hacks. The curriculum learning component is interesting but the paper doesn't provide a principled way to design curricula beyond "make the bots progressively harder." I'd like to see a comparison with a pure A3C baseline on the final map (which they claim doesn't work but don't show numbers for), and a discussion of how this approach would transfer to other FPS games or environments. The adaptive curriculum is under-explained — how exactly is the distribution updated? The paper says it shifts "when the agent performs well" but doesn't specify the update rule.

Overall, this is solid engineering work with impressive empirical results, but the intellectual contribution is thin. I'd recommend rejection for ICLR and suggest the authors target a more applied venue like ICRA or a conference on game AI. If the authors could generalize the curriculum framework or provide theoretical insights into why it works, I'd reconsider. For now, though, it feels more like a competition report than a research paper.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis
abstract: Abstract:###Recent years have seen the proposal of a number of neural architectures for the problem of Program Induction. Given a set of input-output examples, these architectures are able to learn mappings that generalize to new test inputs. While achieving impressive results, these approaches have a number of important limitations: (a) they are computationally expensive and hard to train, (b) a model has to be trained for each task (program) separately, and (c) it is hard to interpret or verify the correctness of the learnt mapping (as it is defined by a neural network). In this paper, we propose a novel technique, Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis, to overcome the above-mentioned problems. Once trained, our approach can automatically construct computer programs in a domain-specific language that are consistent with a set of input-output examples provided at test time. Our method is based on two novel neural modules. The first module, called the cross correlation I/O network, given a set of input-output examples, produces a continuous representation of the set of I/O examples. The second module, the Recursive-Reverse-Recursive Neural Network (R3NN), given the continuous representation of the examples, synthesizes a program by incrementally expanding partial programs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the rich and complex domain of regular expression based string transformations. Experiments show that the R3NN model is not only able to construct programs from new input-output examples, but it is also able to construct new programs for tasks that it had never observed before during training.
review: This paper tackles program synthesis from input-output examples using a two-part neural architecture: a cross-correlation encoder that learns a representation of the I/O pairs, and an R3NN that incrementally expands a partial program tree by selecting which non-terminal to expand. The core idea — training a single model that can synthesize programs for multiple tasks at test time without retraining — is appealing and addresses a genuine limitation of prior work like Neural Programmer-Interpreters. What I find interesting is the cross-correlation I/O encoder, which explicitly tries to discover alignments between input and output strings, and the R3NN's bidirectional message-passing to give each leaf a global context. The results on the FlashFill benchmarks (38% solved, 83% for programs up to size 13) are decent but not mind-blowing — the method still struggles with programs requiring more than 3 concatenations, and the 94% accuracy on held-out synthetic tasks comes from sampling 100 programs per task, which is effectively doing search with a learned proposal distribution rather than truly "synthesizing" a unique program. My main concern is that the training procedure assumes access to the ground-truth program for supervision, which limits applicability to settings where you have a large corpus of labeled programs (not just I/O examples). The paper also doesn't compare against FlashFill's actual search algorithm, only against its own baselines, so it's unclear if the neural approach actually improves over the hand-engineered heuristics. I'm also skeptical of the R3NN's complexity — the recursive-reverse-recursive pass is computationally heavy and seems like overkill when a simple LSTM baseline gets 88% on the same task. Overall, this is solid work with interesting ideas, but the empirical gains over simpler models are modest, and the reliance on program supervision makes the claimed "neuro-symbolic" synthesis less impressive than it first appears. I'd lean towards borderline acceptance, but I'd want to see a stronger comparison to FlashFill and a clearer demonstration that this approach can scale to larger programs or more complex DSLs.

title: Decomposing Motion and Content for Natural Video Sequence Prediction
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a deep neural network for the prediction of future frames in natural video sequences. To effectively handle complex evolution of pixels in videos, we propose to decompose the motion and content, two key components generating dynamics in videos. Our model is built upon the Encoder-Decoder Convolutional Neural Network and Convolutional LSTM for pixel-level prediction, which independently capture the spatial layout of an image and the corresponding temporal dynamics. By independently modeling motion and content, predicting the next frame reduces to converting the extracted content features into the next frame content by the identified motion features, which simplifies the task of prediction. Our model is end-to-end trainable over multiple time steps, and naturally learns to decompose motion and content without separate training. We evaluate the pro- posed network architecture on human activity videos using KTH, Weizmann action, and UCF-101 datasets. We show state-of-the-art performance in comparison to recent approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end trainable network architecture with motion and content separation to model the spatio-temporal dynamics for pixel-level future prediction in natural videos.
review: This paper proposes a neat idea for video prediction: split the problem into two separate encoders — one for motion (taking frame differences) and one for content (taking the last observed frame) — and then combine them to predict the next frame. The intuition that decoupling these factors simplifies the prediction task is solid, and the results on KTH, Weizmann, and UCF-101 are reasonably strong, especially on the SSIM metric where they beat both the ConvLSTM baseline and Mathieu et al.'s multi-scale adversarial approach. I appreciate that the network learns this decomposition without explicit supervision, and the residual skip connections at multiple scales are a sensible addition. The generalization result — where a model trained on Sports-1M performs comparably to one trained on UCF-101 — is genuinely interesting and suggests the motion representations are somewhat transferable. That said, I have a few concerns. First, the motion encoder takes simple image differences, which is a crude approximation of motion — it's not clear why this wouldn't just encode high-frequency temporal changes rather than true "motion." Second, the copy-last-frame baseline is surprisingly competitive on UCF-101, and the authors' post-hoc motion-masking analysis, while reasonable, feels like a defensive maneuver rather than a clean experimental design. Third, the paper claims "state-of-the-art" but the comparison to Mathieu et al. is only on a single-step prediction setup with relatively few frames, and the gains over ConvLSTM on KTH are marginal at best. The adversarial training is lifted directly from prior work with little novelty. Overall, I like the core idea and the decomposition is elegant, but the empirical evidence isn't as compelling as I'd hope for a top conference — I'd lean towards borderline accept, with a strong recommendation to clean up the evaluation and provide a clearer ablation of what the content vs. motion pathways are actually learning.

title: Towards a Neural Statistician
abstract: Abstract:###An efficient learner is one who reuses what they already know to tackle a new problem. For a machine learner, this means understanding the similarities amongst datasets. In order to do this, one must take seriously the idea of working with datasets, rather than datapoints, as the key objects to model. Towards this goal, we demonstrate an extension of a variational autoencoder that can learn a method for computing representations, or statistics, of datasets in an unsupervised fashion. The network is trained to produce statistics that encapsulate a generative model for each dataset. Hence the network enables efficient learning from new datasets for both unsupervised and supervised tasks. We show that we are able to learn statistics that can be used for: clustering datasets, transferring generative models to new datasets, selecting representative samples of datasets and classifying previously unseen classes. We refer to our model as a neural statistician, and by this we mean a neural network that can learn to compute summary statistics of datasets without supervision.
review: This paper introduces a clever hierarchical VAE that learns to compute summary statistics of datasets in an unsupervised manner, using a "statistic network" that maps sets of data points to a latent context vector which then conditions the generative model for each datapoint. The core idea — treating datasets as first-class objects and learning to compress them into a fixed-dimensional representation — is elegant and potentially impactful, especially for few-shot learning and transfer learning scenarios. I like the flexibility of the approach: the statistic network is exchangeable by construction, the model is parameter-efficient since the context space is fixed regardless of dataset count, and the whole thing is trained end-to-end without explicit supervision about dataset similarities. The results are solid across a range of tasks: clustering synthetic distributions, few-shot generation and classification on OMNIGLOT and MNIST, and even a proof-of-concept for faces. The OMNIGLOT 5-way 1-shot classification accuracy (97.3%) is competitive with matching networks, though the 20-way results lag behind, and the authors are upfront about this. My main concerns are: (1) the statistic network uses a simple elementwise mean as the pooling operation, which is surprisingly effective but seems almost too simple — I'd like to see an ablation comparing it to more complex pooling like max or attention-based pooling; (2) the model is dataset-hungry during training, and it's unclear how well it would perform with only a small number of training datasets; (3) the YouTube Faces results are visually impressive but the images are blurry and the identity transfer is inconsistent — it's a nice demo but not a rigorous benchmark. Overall, this is a strong paper with a clean idea, thorough experiments, and a clear contribution to the growing literature on meta-learning and transfer learning. I'd recommend acceptance with the caveat that the authors should be more honest about the limitations of the simple pooling mechanism and the data requirements. This is one of the more interesting papers I've reviewed this cycle, and I suspect it will inspire follow-up work on learning better dataset representations.

title: Generative Models and Model Criticism via Optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a method to optimize the representation and distinguishability of samples from two probability distributions, by maximizing the estimated power of a statistical test based on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). This optimized MMD is applied to the setting of unsupervised learning by generative adversarial networks (GAN), in which a model attempts to generate realistic samples, and a discriminator attempts to tell these apart from data samples. In this context, the MMD may be used in two roles: first, as a discriminator, either directly on the samples, or on features of the samples. Second, the MMD can be used to evaluate the performance of a generative model, by testing the modelâ€™s samples against a reference data set. In the latter role, the optimized MMD is particularly helpful, as it gives an interpretable indication of how the model and data distributions differ, even in cases where individual model samples are not easily distinguished either by eye or by classifier.
review:
This paper presents a principled and well-executed framework for optimizing the MMD two-sample test by directly maximizing its statistical power rather than just the MMD value itself. The core technical contribution — deriving a differentiable estimator of the test power ratio \(\text{MMD}^2 / \sqrt{V_m}\) and optimizing over kernel parameters using gradient descent — is solid and addresses a genuine gap in the literature. I particularly appreciate the careful treatment of the variance estimator (Equation 5), the efficient permutation test implementation that makes this practical, and the clear demonstration that maximizing MMD alone is suboptimal. The model criticism results on GAN-generated MNIST are a highlight — the ARD kernel visualization showing that the GAN overproduces slanted digits while underproducing vertical 1s is exactly the kind of subtle distribution mismatch that human evaluators would miss, and this is a compelling argument for using optimized MMD as a diagnostic tool. The synthetic experiments cleanly illustrate the superiority of power maximization over median heuristic or MMD maximization.

That said, I'm not entirely convinced by the GAN training experiments. The MMD-based GAN criterion is presented as a novel contribution, but the results are somewhat preliminary — the generated digits in Figure 4 look decent but not state-of-the-art, and there's no systematic comparison to other GAN variants beyond a brief mention. The connection to feature matching is acknowledged, but the empirical advantage over Salimans et al.'s minibatch discrimination isn't clearly demonstrated. I'd also like to see a more thorough discussion of the computational cost of optimizing the kernel parameters, especially for high-dimensional data like images, and whether the two-sample split for kernel selection significantly reduces test power in practice. The asymptotic justification for maximizing the t-statistic is fine, but the paper could do more to address finite-sample regimes where the permutation threshold term matters.

Overall, this is a strong paper with a clear theoretical contribution and practical utility for model evaluation. The writing is clear, the experiments are well-designed, and the code release is appreciated. I'd recommend acceptance, with a suggestion to either strengthen or de-emphasize the GAN training component and focus more on the model criticism angle, which is where the method really shines. The corrected variance estimator appendix is a nice touch — shows the authors care about correctness.

title: Generalizing Skills with Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can acquire complex behaviors from low-level inputs, such as images. However, real-world applications of such methods require generalizing to the vast variability of the real world. Deep networks are known to achieve remarkable generalization when provided with massive amounts of labeled data, but can we provide this breadth of experience to an RL agent, such as a robot? The robot might continuously learn as it explores the world around it, even while it is deployed and performing useful tasks. However, this learning requires access to a reward function, to tell the agent whether it is succeeding or failing at its task. Such reward functions are often hard to measure in the real world, especially in domains such as robotics and dialog systems, where the reward could depend on the unknown positions of objects or the emotional state of the user. On the other hand, it is often quite practical to provide the agent with reward functions in a limited set of situations, such as when a human supervisor is present, or in a controlled laboratory setting. Can we make use of this limited supervision, and still benefit from the breadth of experience an agent might collect in the unstructured real world? In this paper, we formalize this problem setting as semi-supervised reinforcement learning (SSRL), where the reward function can only be evaluated in a set of â€œlabeledâ€ MDPs, and the agent must generalize its behavior to the wide range of states it might encounter in a set of â€œunlabeledâ€ MDPs, by using experience from both settings. Our proposed method infers the task objective in the unlabeled MDPs through an algorithm that resembles inverse RL, using the agentâ€™s own prior experience in the labeled MDPs as a kind of demonstration of optimal behavior. We evaluate our method on challenging, continuous control tasks that require control directly from images, and show that our approach can improve the generalization of a learned deep neural network policy by using experience for which no reward function is available. We also show that our method outperforms direct supervised learning of the reward.
review: This paper introduces a compelling problem setting—semi-supervised reinforcement learning—where the reward function is only available in a subset of MDPs, and the goal is to generalize to a wider range of unlabeled MDPs using experience from both. The proposed S3G algorithm, which uses inverse RL to infer rewards in the unlabeled settings by treating the agent's own prior experience in labeled MDPs as "demonstrations," is elegant and practically motivated. The results on continuous control tasks with vision and dynamics variations show that S3G consistently outperforms both the standard RL policy and a reward regression baseline, often approaching oracle performance. I especially like the insight that the learned reward can actually provide better shaping than the true reward, which is a nice nod to the reward design literature. That said, I have a few reservations. First, the problem setting feels somewhat contrived—in practice, if the reward function is the same across MDPs and you have a simulator, why wouldn't you just use the true reward everywhere? The paper would benefit from a clearer real-world scenario where this assumption holds. Second, the method builds heavily on guided cost learning (Finn et al., 2016), and the novelty largely lies in the problem formulation rather than the algorithmic contribution—the algorithm is essentially GCL with the demonstrations coming from the agent's own RL policy rather than an expert. Third, the experiments are on relatively simple tasks (reacher, obstacle, cheetah) and the generalization gap is moderate; it's not clear how this scales to more complex domains like those with partial observability or high-dimensional action spaces. Also, the sample complexity table shows S3G uses significantly more samples than RL in the unlabeled phase, which is fine but should be discussed more honestly as a trade-off. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a well-defined problem and reasonable empirical validation, but I'd like to see a clearer articulation of the practical setting, stronger baselines (e.g., simply fine-tuning the RL policy with RL in the unlabeled MDP using the learned reward regression), and perhaps a discussion of how to avoid degenerate reward functions that could lead to policy collapse. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors address these points in the final version.

title: Learning Curve Prediction with Bayesian Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Different neural network architectures, hyperparameters and training protocols lead to different performances as a function of time. Human experts routinely inspect the resulting learning curves to quickly terminate runs with poor hyperparameter settings and thereby considerably speed up manual hyperparameter optimization. Exploiting the same information in automatic Bayesian hyperparameter optimization requires a probabilistic model of learning curves across hyperparameter settings. Here, we study the use of Bayesian neural networks for this purpose and improve their performance by a specialized learning curve layer.
review: This paper tackles the practically important problem of predicting learning curves for hyperparameter optimization, and does so with a solid empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks. The core idea — using Bayesian neural networks with a specialized "learning curve layer" that predicts parameters of parametric basis functions — is sensible and builds nicely on Domhan et al.'s earlier work. I appreciate the thorough comparison of different Bayesian inference methods (SGLD vs SGHMC) and the careful analysis of heteroscedastic noise. The results are mostly convincing: SGHMC with the learning curve layer consistently improves predictive performance, and the extension to Hyperband shows meaningful speedups over both vanilla Hyperband and standard Bayesian optimization. That said, I'm not entirely convinced the specialized architecture is a game-changer. The improvements over standard Bayesian neural networks are modest in many cases, and the LastSeenValue baseline is embarrassingly competitive on the extrapolation task — which suggests the problem might be easier than the paper implies. The fact that random forests often match or exceed the neural approaches for mean predictions (though not uncertainties) raises questions about whether the added complexity is justified. I also found the evaluation somewhat over-claimed: the VAE results are mixed, and the model's advantage over Bayesian optimization on the LR benchmark is marginal. The paper could be strengthened by a clearer discussion of when the learning curve layer actually helps and when it doesn't. Overall, I think this is a solid, well-executed paper that makes a meaningful but incremental contribution to the hyperparameter optimization literature. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors tone down the claims and provide a more nuanced discussion of the limitations. It's not groundbreaking, but it's a useful piece of work that the community will likely build on.

title: Learning to Optimize
abstract: Abstract:###Algorithm design is a laborious process and often requires many iterations of ideation and validation. In this paper, we explore automating algorithm design and present a method to learn an optimization algorithm. We approach this problem from a reinforcement learning perspective and represent any particular optimization algorithm as a policy. We learn an optimization algorithm using guided policy search and demonstrate that the resulting algorithm outperforms existing hand-engineered algorithms in terms of convergence speed and/or the final objective value.
review: This paper tackles the ambitious goal of learning an optimization algorithm from scratch using reinforcement learning, framing any iterative optimizer as a policy that maps historical gradient and objective information to a step vector. The core idea is compelling — why hand-engineer algorithms when we can learn them from data? — and the guided policy search framework is a reasonable choice for this continuous control problem. The empirical results on logistic regression, robust regression, and a tiny neural net are impressive: the learned optimizer often outperforms gradient descent, momentum, conjugate gradient, and even L-BFGS on the training distribution, converging faster and to better optima. I particularly like the observation that the learned algorithm can generalize beyond the 40-step training horizon and that it seems to discover adaptive step-sizing behavior implicitly. That said, I have serious concerns about the experimental setup. The problems are extremely low-dimensional (2-3 dimensions for logistic regression, 2 hidden units for the neural net), and it's unclear whether this approach scales to high-dimensional problems where optimization is actually hard. The state representation only includes the last 25 gradients and objective improvements, which seems insufficient for capturing curvature information in higher dimensions. The comparison to L-BFGS and conjugate gradient is also somewhat unfair — these algorithms have known limitations on non-convex problems, and the autonomous optimizer is trained specifically on the test distribution, giving it a huge advantage. The paper doesn't compare to modern adaptive methods like Adam or RMSprop, which would be a more relevant baseline for deep learning. I'm also skeptical of the broader claim that this "learns a better algorithm" — it learns a specialized heuristic for a specific class of functions, not a general-purpose optimizer. The lack of theoretical analysis or even a qualitative description of what the learned policy actually does is a missed opportunity. Overall, this is a provocative and interesting proof-of-concept, but the toy experiments and narrow scope make it hard to judge the real significance. I'd lean towards borderline reject, but I'd be happy to be proven wrong if the authors can demonstrate scalability to higher-dimensional problems and provide insight into the learned behavior.

title: A Compare-Aggregate Model for Matching Text Sequences
abstract: Abstract:###Many NLP tasks including machine comprehension, answer selection and text entailment require the comparison between sequences. Matching the important units between sequences is a key to solve these problems. In this paper, we present a general *compare-aggregate* framework that performs word-level matching followed by aggregation using Convolutional Neural Networks. We particularly focus on the different comparison functions we can use to match two vectors. We use four different datasets to evaluate the model. We find that some simple comparison functions based on element-wise operations can work better than standard neural network and neural tensor network.
review: This paper presents a "compare-aggregate" framework for text sequence matching, with a thorough empirical evaluation across four diverse tasks (MovieQA, InsuranceQA, WikiQA, and SNLI). The core contribution is a systematic comparison of six different word-level comparison functions within the same general architecture, and the finding that simple element-wise operations like subtraction and multiplication often outperform more complex neural network or neural tensor network comparators. I appreciate the breadth of the evaluation — it's rare to see a single model tested on such different datasets with competitive results, and the ablation over comparison functions is useful for practitioners. The model achieves state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on three of the four datasets, which is impressive given the simplicity of the approach. However, I'm not convinced the paper offers much beyond an empirical study. The framework is largely a synthesis of existing ideas — attention mechanisms and CNNs for aggregation are standard, and the element-wise comparison functions have been used before (e.g., Tai et al., 2015). The novelty boils down to "we tried these six functions on four datasets and found SubMult+NN works best," which is useful but not particularly deep or surprising. The baselines are also somewhat inconsistent — on SNLI, the comparison is to the state-of-the-art EBIM+TreeLSTM which outperforms the model, while on other datasets the comparisons are to older baselines, making the claimed "state-of-the-art" feel cherry-picked. I also found the visualization in Figure 2 to be quite hand-wavy and not particularly illuminating. The model also requires a fair bit of task-specific engineering — the MovieQA setup with triple sequences is awkward and suggests the framework doesn't generalize as cleanly as claimed. Overall, this is a solid engineering paper with useful empirical results, but the intellectual contribution is modest. I'd recommend borderline accept, with the expectation that the authors tone down the novelty claims and provide more rigorous baseline comparisons. The findings on comparison functions are valuable for the community, but this feels more like an EMNLP paper than an ICLR paper.

title: Data Noising as Smoothing in Neural Network Language Models
abstract: Abstract:###Data noising is an effective technique for regularizing neural network models. While noising is widely adopted in application domains such as vision and speech, commonly used noising primitives have not been developed for discrete sequence-level settings such as language modeling. In this paper, we derive a connection between input noising in neural network language models and smoothing in n-gram models. Using this connection, we draw upon ideas from smoothing to develop effective noising schemes. We demonstrate performance gains when applying the proposed schemes to language modeling and machine translation. Finally, we provide empirical analysis validating the relationship between noising and smoothing.
review: This paper draws a neat connection between input noising for neural network language models and classical n-gram smoothing, then leverages this to propose more sophisticated noising schemes that mimic interpolation and Kneser-Ney smoothing. The core idea is elegant — by analyzing the expected pseudocounts under noising, the authors show that unigram noising corresponds to linear interpolation, and then adapt this to derive an adaptive noising probability and a proposal distribution based on continuation counts. The empirical results are solid: the Kneser-Ney-inspired noising scheme achieves state-of-the-art single-model perplexity on Penn Treebank (73.4) matching Gal's variational dropout, and gives a +1.4 BLEU gain on IWSLT English-German translation. I particularly appreciate the validation of the smoothing effect via KL divergence analysis and the unseen n-gram perplexity evaluation — this goes beyond just reporting numbers and actually tests the claimed mechanism. The adaptive discounting ratio that scales γ based on the number of continuations is a nice touch and seems to make the method more robust to hyperparameter choice. That said, the novelty is somewhat incremental — the paper is essentially applying well-understood smoothing ideas from n-gram models to RNNs through the lens of noising, and while the connection is insightful, the method itself is a straightforward extension. The translation gains are modest (+0.7 to +1.4 BLEU), and it's unclear whether these improvements are statistically significant. I'd also like to see a comparison to other recent regularization methods for RNNs beyond Gal's variational dropout, such as recurrent dropout with memory loss (Semeniuta et al.) or zoneout, to better contextualize the gains. The paper is well-written and the theoretical analysis is sound, but the contribution feels more like a clever application of existing ideas than a breakthrough. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide more discussion of limitations and perhaps a more extensive ablation of the adaptive discounting. Overall, a solid paper that bridges classical and neural approaches in a thoughtful way, but not a game-changer.

title: Training Compressed Fully-Connected Networks with a Density-Diversity Penalty
abstract: Abstract:###Deep models have achieved great success on a variety of challenging tasks. How- ever, the models that achieve great performance often have an enormous number of parameters, leading to correspondingly great demands on both computational and memory resources, especially for fully-connected layers. In this work, we propose a new â€œdensity-diversity penaltyâ€ regularizer that can be applied to fully-connected layers of neural networks during training. We show that using this regularizer results in significantly fewer parameters (i.e., high sparsity), and also significantly fewer distinct values (i.e., low diversity), so that the trained weight matrices can be highly compressed without any appreciable loss in performance. The resulting trained models can hence reside on computational platforms (e.g., portables, Internet-of-Things devices) where it otherwise would be prohibitive.
review: This paper introduces a clever regularizer — the density-diversity penalty — that encourages weight matrices in fully-connected layers to be both sparse and low-diversity (i.e., having few distinct values), making them highly compressible. The key technical innovation is the "sorting trick" that reduces the computational cost of the pairwise L1 diversity penalty from O(n^4) to O(n log n), which is what makes this practical. I like the idea — it's a straightforward way to bake compression directly into training, and the two-phase training procedure (regularize first, then fine-tune with tied weights) is sensible. The results on MNIST and TIMIT are solid, achieving 20-200x compression on fully-connected layers with negligible performance loss, and the method compares favorably to Han et al.'s "deep compression" pipeline, especially on fully-connected layers where it achieves higher sparsity. That said, I have some concerns. The paper feels quite incremental — the density-diversity penalty is essentially a global total variation penalty combined with L1/L2 regularization, and the sorting trick, while neat, is the main algorithmic contribution. The weight-tying phase is a bit ad-hoc; it's not clear why alternating phases works better than a single joint optimization, and the paper doesn't provide a rigorous convergence analysis. The experiments are on relatively small models (LeNet, 3-layer MLP) and datasets; it's unclear how this scales to modern architectures like ResNet or Transformers, where fully-connected layers are less dominant. The comparison to "deep compression" is somewhat unfair because deep compression includes Huffman coding in its final compression rate, while the paper reports compression using a simpler sparse matrix representation with 11 bits for both value and index, which seems inflated. Also, the regularizer introduces a hyperparameter lambda_j for each layer, and the paper's scaling heuristic is hand-wavy — tuning this for large networks could be a pain. Overall, this is a solid contribution for model compression, but the novelty and scope feel more appropriate for a compression workshop or NeurIPS than ICLR. I'd lean towards borderline reject, but I'd be happy to see a follow-up with more extensive experiments on larger models and a cleaner theoretical justification.

title: Autoencoding Variational Inference For Topic Models
abstract: Abstract:###Topic models are one of the most popular methods for learning representations of text, but a major challenge is that any change to the topic model requires mathematically deriving a new inference algorithm. A promising approach to address this problem is autoencoding variational Bayes (AEVB), but it has proven diffi- cult to apply to topic models in practice. We present what is to our knowledge the first effective AEVB based inference method for latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), which we call Autoencoded Variational Inference For Topic Model (AVITM). This model tackles the problems caused for AEVB by the Dirichlet prior and by component collapsing. We find that AVITM matches traditional methods in accuracy with much better inference time. Indeed, because of the inference network, we find that it is unnecessary to pay the computational cost of running variational optimization on test data. Because AVITM is black box, it is readily applied to new topic models. As a dramatic illustration of this, we present a new topic model called ProdLDA, that replaces the mixture model in LDA with a product of experts. By changing only one line of code from LDA, we find that ProdLDA yields much more interpretable topics, even if LDA is trained via collapsed Gibbs sampling.
review: This paper presents the first effective application of autoencoding variational Bayes (AEVB) to latent Dirichlet allocation, addressing two key challenges: the non-reparameterizable Dirichlet prior (handled via a Laplace approximation in the softmax basis) and component collapsing (mitigated through high-momentum Adam, batch norm, and dropout). The resulting AVITM method achieves topic coherence comparable to collapsed Gibbs sampling and standard mean-field variational inference, with dramatically faster training and the major advantage that the inference network eliminates the need for per-document variational optimization at test time — a genuinely useful property for deployment. The paper also introduces ProdLDA, a novel topic model that replaces the mixture of multinomials with a product of experts in the natural parameter space, and shows that this simple change (one line of code) yields substantially more coherent topics than standard LDA, even when LDA is trained with Gibbs sampling. The empirical results are convincing: ProdLDA consistently beats LDA and NVDM on topic coherence across 20 Newsgroups and RCV1, and the ablation study in Table 5 clearly demonstrates that both the Dirichlet approximation and the high-momentum training are necessary for good performance. I appreciate the careful treatment of the component collapsing problem — it's a known issue in VAEs and the paper provides a practical solution that works. That said, I have some concerns. The Laplace approximation to the Dirichlet prior feels a bit ad-hoc; the paper claims it's a "standard" approximation but the diagonal covariance derivation for large K is not rigorously justified, and it's unclear how well this approximation holds for small K or asymmetric Dirichlet parameters. The comparison to NVDM is somewhat unfair because NVDM uses a standard Gaussian prior, while AVITM uses a Laplace-approximated Dirichlet that promotes sparsity — the improved coherence might simply be due to the prior rather than the inference method. The product-of-experts idea in ProdLDA is elegant, but it's essentially exponential-family PCA with a Dirichlet prior, which has been explored before in different forms. The paper also doesn't provide a clear guideline for practitioners on how to choose between LDA, ProdLDA, and NVDM — is ProdLDA always better, or does it depend on the dataset? Finally, the theoretical contribution is somewhat thin: the paper is primarily empirical and engineering-oriented, which is fine, but for ICLR I'd expect a bit more insight into why the product-of-experts assumption yields better topics (e.g., is it because it produces sharper posterior distributions?). Overall, this is a well-executed and practically useful piece of work, and I'd recommend acceptance, but I'd encourage the authors to provide more analysis of the approximation quality and to clarify the relationship between ProdLDA and existing exponential-family models. The code release is a nice bonus.

title: Optimal Binary Autoencoding with Pairwise Correlations
abstract: Abstract:###We formulate learning of a binary autoencoder as a biconvex optimization problem which learns from the pairwise correlations between encoded and decoded bits. Among all possible algorithms that use this information, ours finds the autoencoder that reconstructs its inputs with worst-case optimal loss. The optimal decoder is a single layer of artificial neurons, emerging entirely from the minimax loss minimization, and with weights learned by convex optimization. All this is reflected in competitive experimental results, demonstrating that binary autoencoding can be done efficiently by conveying information in pairwise correlations in an optimal fashion.
review: This paper presents a theoretically elegant approach to binary autoencoding, framing it as a minimax game where the decoder only has access to pairwise correlations between input and hidden units. The key result is that the optimal decoder emerges as a single logistic layer, with weights learned via convex optimization, which is refreshingly different from the usual non-convex backpropagation hell. The biconvex alternating minimization algorithm is clean, the proof of worst-case optimality is solid, and the extension to general losses via the monotonicity assumption is a nice touch. I like the reinterpretation of artificial neurons as minimax optimal decision rules given limited statistical information — it's a perspective that ties back to classical statistical decision theory and gives some theoretical grounding to why these architectures work. The empirical results are decent but not mind-blowing: PC-AE beats vanilla autoencoders on reconstruction loss, but the gap narrows as H increases, and deeper architectures would likely outperform both. The paper also feels somewhat isolated from modern autoencoding practice — there's no comparison to variational autoencoders, denoising autoencoders, or even stacked autoencoders, and the experiments are on relatively simple binarized datasets. The claim that pairwise correlations are "all the information needed" for worst-case optimality is mathematically true under the minimax formulation, but it's unclear whether this formulation captures the right inductive biases for real data, especially when reconstructions are evaluated by human judgment rather than cross-entropy. The encoding function ENC is a convex optimization problem that needs to be solved per example, which is fine for small datasets but could be a bottleneck at scale. I'd also like to see a deeper discussion of the trade-offs: when would you choose PC-AE over a standard autoencoder? The paper argues that PC-AE avoids non-convex optimization, but standard AEs train just fine with Adam these days. Overall, this is a clever and theoretically grounded paper that I'd recommend for acceptance, but I'd encourage the authors to be more upfront about the practical limitations and to provide more extensive comparisons to modern autoencoding variants. The theory is the star here — it's a nice contribution to the foundations of representation learning, even if the empirical impact is modest.

title: On the Quantitative Analysis of Decoder-Based Generative Models
abstract: Abstract:###The past several years have seen remarkable progress in generative models which produce convincing samples of images and other modalities. A shared component of some popular models such as generative adversarial networks and generative moment matching networks, is a decoder network, a parametric deep neural net that defines a generative distribution. Unfortunately, it can be difficult to quantify the performance of these models because of the intractability of log-likelihood estimation, and inspecting samples can be misleading. We propose to use Annealed Importance Sampling for evaluating log-likelihoods for decoder-based models and validate its accuracy using bidirectional Monte Carlo. Using this technique, we analyze the performance of decoder-based models, the effectiveness of existing log-likelihood estimators, the degree of overfitting, and the degree to which these models miss important modes of the data distribution.
review: This paper provides a much-needed reality check on how we evaluate decoder-based generative models, and honestly, it's about time someone did this properly. The authors use annealed importance sampling with bidirectional Monte Carlo validation to get accurate log-likelihood estimates for VAEs, GANs, and GMMNs on MNIST, and the results are striking: KDE is wildly inaccurate (often underestimating by hundreds of nats), the IWAE bound can be off by tens of nats, and VAEs massively outperform GANs and GMMNs on log-likelihood (300+ nat gaps) even though samples look visually similar. The finding that GANs and GMMNs don't simply memorize training data (their train-test gaps are smaller than VAEs) is genuinely interesting, and the posterior visualization analysis showing GANs missing modes of digit '2' is a concrete demonstration of a failure mode that samples alone can't reveal. I buy the methodology — BDMC validation on simulated data shows the AIS estimates are tight (usually <1 nat gap), and the observation model analysis (Table 3) convincingly argues that the likelihood gap isn't just an artifact of the Gaussian noise assumption. That said, I have some reservations. The analysis is largely confined to MNIST, and it's unclear whether these findings generalize to higher-dimensional data like CIFAR or ImageNet where GANs are more competitive visually. The AIS evaluation is computationally expensive (10,000 intermediate distributions, HMC tuning), making it impractical for routine benchmarking. The paper also doesn't provide a clear recommendation — should the field abandon GANs because of their poor likelihoods, or should we accept that likelihood isn't the right metric for them? The authors acknowledge this but don't grapple with the implications. I'd also like to see a comparison to more modern GAN variants (DCGAN, WGAN) and a discussion of whether the posterior visualization approach could be used as a diagnostic during training. Overall, this is a valuable contribution that exposes serious flaws in current evaluation practices, and the methodology is sound enough that I trust the findings. I'd recommend acceptance, but with the expectation that the authors be more explicit about the practical takeaways and limitations. This paper won't settle the debate about whether likelihood is the right metric, but it will force people to be more honest about what their estimators are actually measuring.

title: Trained Ternary Quantization
abstract: Abstract:###Deep neural networks are widely used in machine learning applications. However, the deployment of large neural networks models can be difficult to deploy on mobile devices with limited power budgets. To solve this problem, we propose Trained Ternary Quantization (TTQ), a method that can reduce the precision of weights in neural networks to ternary values. This method has very little accuracy degradation and can even improve the accuracy of some models (32, 44, 56-layer ResNet) on CIFAR-10 and AlexNet on ImageNet. And our AlexNet model is trained from scratch, which means itâ€™s as easy as to train normal full precision model. We highlight our trained quantization method that can learn both ternary values and ternary assignment. During inference, only ternary values (2-bit weights) and scaling factors are needed, therefore our models are nearly 16Ã— smaller than full- precision models. Our ternary models can also be viewed as sparse binary weight networks, which can potentially be accelerated with custom circuit. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show that the ternary models obtained by trained quantization method outperform full-precision models of ResNet-32,44,56 by 0.04%, 0.16%, 0.36%, respectively. On ImageNet, our model outperforms full-precision AlexNet model by 0.3% of Top-1 accuracy and outperforms previous ternary models by 3%.
review: This paper introduces Trained Ternary Quantization (TTQ), a method that learns asymmetric ternary values (+W_p, 0, -W_n) per layer rather than using fixed symmetric scaling, and crucially, learns both the codebook values and the assignment of weights to those values through gradient descent. The core idea is clever and practically effective: by maintaining latent full-precision weights during training and backpropagating scaled gradients to both the latent weights and the scaling factors, the model can adaptively adjust quantization decisions. The empirical results are genuinely impressive — TTQ achieves near full-precision accuracy on ResNet variants on CIFAR-10 (even improving over full precision for deeper ResNets) and outperforms prior ternary methods (TWN) by 3% on AlexNet ImageNet, achieving 42.5% top-1 error compared to 45.5% for TWN. The fact that they train AlexNet from scratch with ternary weights and still beat the full-precision baseline is a strong endorsement of the method. I also appreciate the sparsity analysis showing that 30-50% zero weights gives the best trade-off, and the kernel visualizations confirming that edge/corner detectors emerge even with ternary weights. That said, I have some reservations. The technical novelty is somewhat incremental — TWN already used ternary weights with scaling factors, and TTQ's main contribution is making the positive and negative scales asymmetric and trainable, which is neat but not a game-changer. The thresholding heuristic (Δ = t * max|w| with t=0.05) feels arbitrary and isn't thoroughly justified; the paper would benefit from a sensitivity analysis or a principled way to set this. The comparison to Deep Compression is a bit misleading — Deep Compression achieves higher compression rates (35-49x) with pruning+quantization+Huffman coding, while TTQ gives ~16x, so the claim of "better than Deep Compression" is only true if you ignore pruning. The paper also doesn't address the inference speedup from sparsity in any detail — skipping zero weights requires irregular memory access patterns that aren't always friendly to hardware, and the energy savings from reduced multiplications might be offset by control overhead. I'd also like to see results on more modern architectures like ResNet-50 or MobileNet to understand scalability. Overall, this is a solid, well-executed paper with practical results that will be useful for model compression practitioners, but the intellectual contribution is modest and the theoretical grounding is thin. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide a more thorough ablation of the threshold hyperparameter and a clearer discussion of the practical trade-offs between TTQ, pruning, and other compression methods.

title: DSD: Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Modern deep neural networks have a large number of parameters, making them very hard to train. We propose DSD, a dense-sparse-dense training flow, for regularizing deep neural networks and achieving better optimization performance. In the first D (Dense) step, we train a dense network to learn connection weights and importance. In the S (Sparse) step, we regularize the network by pruning the unimportant connections with small weights and retraining the network given the sparsity constraint. In the final D (re-Dense) step, we increase the model capacity by removing the sparsity constraint, re-initialize the pruned parameters from zero and retrain the whole dense network. Experiments show that DSD training can improve the performance for a wide range of CNNs, RNNs and LSTMs on the tasks of image classification, caption generation and speech recognition. On ImageNet, DSD improved the Top1 accuracy of GoogLeNet by 1.1%, VGG-16 by 4.3%, ResNet-18 by 1.2% and ResNet-50 by 1.1%, respectively. On the WSJâ€™93 dataset, DSD improved DeepSpeech and DeepSpeech2 WER by 2.0% and 1.1%. On the Flickr-8K dataset, DSD improved the NeuralTalk BLEU score by over 1.7. DSD is easy to use in practice: at training time, DSD incurs only one extra hyper-parameter: the sparsity ratio in the S step. At testing time, DSD doesnâ€™t change the network architecture or incur any inference overhead. The consistent and significant performance gain of DSD experiments shows the inadequacy of the current training methods for finding the best local optimum, while DSD effectively achieves superior optimization performance for finding a better solution. DSD models are available to download at https://songhan.github.io/DSD.
review: This paper introduces Dense-Sparse-Dense (DSD) training, a simple but surprisingly effective method that regularizes neural networks by pruning low-magnitude weights during training and then restoring them for a final dense fine-tuning phase. The core idea is intuitive: first train a dense model to identify important connections, then enforce sparsity to regularize and escape poor local minima, and finally restore the pruned connections to regain model capacity. The empirical results are genuinely impressive and remarkably consistent across a wide range of architectures and tasks — CNNs (GoogLeNet, VGG, ResNet on ImageNet), LSTMs (NeuralTalk on Flickr-8K), and RNNs (DeepSpeech on WSJ). The improvements are substantial: 4.3% top-1 error reduction on VGG-16, 2.0% WER improvement on DeepSpeech, and a 1.7 BLEU boost on NeuralTalk. I particularly appreciate the thorough validation showing DSD outperforms conventional fine-tuning (LLR) with statistical significance (p<0.001), and the ablation showing that multiple DSD iterations can yield diminishing but real gains. The paper is well-written and the method is trivially easy to implement — just one extra hyperparameter (sparsity) — and doesn't affect inference at all. That said, I have some reservations. The theoretical justification for why DSD works is hand-wavy ("escape saddle points," "break symmetry") and not rigorously grounded. The comparison to conventional training with the same number of epochs (LLR) is important, but the learning rate schedules aren't perfectly matched — DSD uses a more aggressive learning rate decay pattern that might explain some of the improvement. The method also seems to work best with moderate sparsity (30-50%), which is less aggressive than pruning for compression, raising the question of whether the gains are simply due to the extra training epochs and the regularization effect of temporarily reducing model capacity. I'd like to see a more systematic ablation isolating the contribution of each phase, and a comparison to other regularization techniques like weight decay or dropout in the same training budget. The captioning examples in the appendix are visually compelling but the paper doesn't provide a rigorous human evaluation. Overall, this is a practical, well-executed paper with strong empirical results that will be widely applicable, but the theoretical understanding lags behind the empirical success. I'd recommend acceptance — it's a solid contribution that practitioners will appreciate, even if it's not a theoretical breakthrough.

title: A Compositional Object-Based Approach to Learning Physical Dynamics
abstract: Abstract:###We present the Neural Physics Engine (NPE), a framework for learning simulators of intuitive physics that naturally generalize across variable object count and different scene configurations. We propose a factorization of a physical scene into composable object-based representations and a neural network architecture whose compositional structure factorizes object dynamics into pairwise interactions. Like a symbolic physics engine, the NPE is endowed with generic notions of objects and their interactions; realized as a neural network, it can be trained via stochastic gradient descent to adapt to specific object properties and dynamics of different worlds. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach on simple rigid body dynamics in two-dimensional worlds. By comparing to less structured architectures, we show that the NPE*s compositional representation of the structure in physical interactions improves its ability to predict movement, generalize across variable object count and different scene configurations, and infer latent properties of objects such as mass.
review: This paper introduces the Neural Physics Engine (NPE), a hybrid symbolic-neural architecture for learning physical dynamics that generalizes across variable object counts and scene configurations by explicitly modeling objects and their pairwise interactions. The core idea is elegant and biologically plausible: factorize the scene into object-based representations, select context objects via a spatial neighborhood mask, model dynamics as a sum of pairwise interactions, and compose these computations in a modular, reusable fashion. The empirical results are quite strong — the NPE consistently outperforms less structured baselines (No-Pairwise and LSTM) on prediction, generalization to 6-8 balls, and mass inference (90% accuracy), often by an order of magnitude in velocity error. I particularly like the ablation showing that removing the neighborhood mask degrades performance dramatically, validating that the spatial attention mechanism is doing real work, and the demonstration that the NPE can generalize to complex "U" and "I" wall geometries after training only on simpler "O" and "L" shapes. The paper is well-written and the connection to cognitive science (Spelke, Battaglia) grounds the approach in a compelling framework. That said, I have some concerns. The NPE is quite similar to the Interaction Network (Battaglia et al., 2016) published around the same time, and the differences — learning relations implicitly via attention rather than taking them as input, and inferring latent properties via optimization rather than a separate classifier — feel incremental rather than transformative. The experiments are on a highly simplified 2D physics engine (matter.js) with perfect state information; it's unclear how well this would work with real visual input, and the paper punts on the vision component entirely. The mass inference task uses only three discrete mass values, which is a bit toy — I'd like to see continuous masses or more challenging inference scenarios. The LSTM baseline is arguably weak; a more structured sequence model or a transformer with attention might fare better. The paper also doesn't compare to a conventional physics engine that's been learned via system identification, which would be a natural baseline. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a clear contribution to the growing literature on learning physical simulators, but the novelty is modest relative to concurrent work and the experimental scope is limited. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide a clearer comparison to Interaction Networks and a more honest discussion of the gap between perfect state inputs and real-world vision. It's a step in the right direction, but not the final word.

title: Learning to Remember Rare Events
abstract: Abstract:###Despite recent advances, memory-augmented deep neural networks are still limited when it comes to life-long and one-shot learning, especially in remembering rare events. We present a large-scale life-long memory module for use in deep learning. The module exploits fast nearest-neighbor algorithms for efficiency and thus scales to large memory sizes. Except for the nearest-neighbor query, the module is fully differentiable and trained end-to-end with no extra supervision. It operates in a life-long manner, i.e., without the need to reset it during training. Our memory module can be easily added to any part of a supervised neural network. To show its versatility we add it to a number of networks, from simple convolutional ones tested on image classification to deep sequence-to-sequence and recurrent-convolutional models. In all cases, the enhanced network gains the ability to remember and do life-long one-shot learning. Our module remembers training examples shown many thousands of steps in the past and it can successfully generalize from them. We set new state-of-the-art for one-shot learning on the Omniglot dataset and demonstrate, for the first time, life-long one-shot learning in recurrent neural networks on a large-scale machine translation task.
review: This paper introduces a simple but surprisingly effective memory module for neural networks that enables life-long one-shot learning by storing key-value pairs of activations and target labels, retrieving via nearest-neighbor lookups, and updating via a margin-based loss and age-based replacement. The core idea is elegant — just augment any network with an external memory that can be written to and queried during training, and suddenly you get the ability to remember rare examples seen thousands of steps ago. The empirical results are genuinely impressive: state-of-the-art on Omniglot (98.4% 5-way 1-shot), a synthetic task where standard seq2seq fails catastrophically (71% vs 12% accuracy), and a large-scale GNMT translation model that can correctly translate rare words like "Dostoevsky" and improves BLEU by 0.5 points when shown a context set. I particularly appreciate the versatility — the module works with CNNs, attention-based RNNs, and even the Neural GPU, and the efficient LSH approximation makes scaling to large memories practical. The loss function is essentially a margin-based triplet loss, which is well-motivated and works well in practice. That said, I have some reservations. The paper feels a bit rushed in places — the translation evaluation is clever but unconventional (splitting the test set into even/odd lines), and the "whole test context" BLEU score of 31.11 seems suspiciously high and isn't explained well. The synthetic task, while a nice demonstration, is also somewhat contrived and doesn't reflect real-world one-shot learning scenarios. The memory update rule (averaging keys) is simple but might not be optimal — I'd like to see an ablation comparing it to alternatives like learning the update or using a weighted average. The paper also doesn't compare to other memory-augmented approaches like MANN or differentiable neural computers on the same tasks, making it hard to judge relative performance. Overall, this is a solid and practical contribution that will likely be widely adopted, but the novelty is somewhat incremental given the existing literature on memory networks and matching networks. I'd recommend acceptance — the results speak for themselves and the module is clearly useful — but I'd encourage the authors to provide more rigorous comparisons and a clearer discussion of the limitations. The fact that it's open-source and easy to integrate is a big plus.

title: Transfer Learning for Sequence Tagging with Hierarchical Recurrent Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recent papers have shown that neural networks obtain state-of-the-art performance on several different sequence tagging tasks. One appealing property of such systems is their generality, as excellent performance can be achieved with a unified architecture and without task-specific feature engineering. However, it is unclear if such systems can be used for tasks without large amounts of training data. In this paper we explore the problem of transfer learning for neural sequence taggers, where a source task with plentiful annotations (e.g., POS tagging on Penn Treebank) is used to improve performance on a target task with fewer available annotations (e.g., POS tagging for microblogs). We examine the effects of transfer learning for deep hierarchical recurrent networks across domains, applications, and languages, and show that significant improvement can often be obtained. These improvements lead to improvements over the current state-of-the-art on several well-studied tasks.
review: This paper presents a systematic study of transfer learning for neural sequence taggers, proposing three architectures that share different levels of the hierarchical RNN — character-level, word-level, and CRF — depending on whether the transfer is cross-domain, cross-application, or cross-lingual. The core idea is sensible: if different tasks share alphabets, morphological patterns, or syntactic structures, then the lower layers of the network should capture transferable representations. The experiments are extensive and well-designed, covering POS tagging, chunking, and NER across English, Spanish, and Dutch, with both large benchmark datasets and low-resource settings. I particularly appreciate the ablation over labeling rates (0.001 to 1.0) and the clear validation that transfer gains are largest when the target task is data-starved and when the source-target relationship is close — T-A (shared CRF with label mapping) > T-B (separate CRF) > T-C (only character-level sharing) > no transfer. The results are solid: up to 8.85% absolute improvement on Twitter POS with 0.1 labels, and new state-of-the-art on CoNLL 2000 chunking (95.41 F1), CoNLL 2003 English NER (91.26 F1), and Spanish/Dutch NER. That said, I have some reservations. The novelty is somewhat incremental — the architectures are straightforward parameter-sharing variants of existing hierarchical taggers, and the transfer learning framework doesn't introduce new training algorithms or regularization beyond joint training. The gains on full datasets are modest (0.2-0.7%), which is fine for state-of-the-art claims but not transformative. The cross-lingual transfer is limited to similar alphabets (English-Spanish), and it's unclear how well this would work for languages with very different morphology or scripts. The paper also doesn't explore multi-source transfer (e.g., using multiple source tasks simultaneously), which would be a natural next step. I'm also a bit skeptical of the label mapping for T-A — the paper assumes PTB POS tags can be mapped to Twitter POS tags, but this mapping is non-trivial and the paper doesn't describe how it's done, which could affect reproducibility. The choice of GRU over LSTM is mentioned but not motivated, and I'd like to see an ablation comparing the two. Overall, this is a well-executed and practical piece of work that will be useful for practitioners dealing with low-resource sequence tagging, but the technical contribution is solid rather than groundbreaking. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide more details on label mapping and perhaps discuss the limitations of their cross-lingual setting.

title: Words or Characters? Fine-grained Gating for Reading Comprehension
abstract: Abstract:###Previous work combines word-level and character-level representations using concatenation or scalar weighting, which is suboptimal for high-level tasks like reading comprehension. We present a fine-grained gating mechanism to dynamically combine word-level and character-level representations based on properties of the words. We also extend the idea of fine-grained gating to modeling the interaction between questions and paragraphs for reading comprehension. Experiments show that our approach can improve the performance on reading comprehension tasks, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Children*s Book Test and Who Did What datasets. To demonstrate the generality of our gating mechanism, we also show improved results on a social media tag prediction task.
review: This paper introduces a fine-grained gating mechanism for dynamically combining word-level and character-level representations in reading comprehension models, conditioning the gate on linguistic features like POS tags, NER labels, and document frequencies. The core idea is simple but effective: instead of concatenating or using a scalar gate, they learn a per-dimension vector gate that selectively blends the two representations based on token properties. I like the intuition — rare tokens and named entities should rely more on character morphology, while frequent function words should use word embeddings — and the visualization in Figure 3 convincingly validates this behavior. The results are strong: new SOTA on CBT (74.64% on NE test) and WDW, and solid gains on SQuAD (71.25 F1) and Twitter tag prediction. The extension to document-query gating via element-wise products with attention is also sensible and clearly improves over the gated attention reader. My main concern is that the novelty is somewhat incremental — gating between word and char representations has been explored before (Miyamoto & Cho), and the main contribution is making it vector-valued and conditioning on richer features. The document-query gating is also a natural extension of prior attention mechanisms. The paper would benefit from a more thorough ablation isolating the contribution of each feature type (POS vs NER vs frequency), and the SQuAD results, while good, are not competitive with the best published models on the leaderboard (though the paper acknowledges this). The writing is clear and the experiments are well-executed, but I'm not convinced the technical contribution is substantial enough for ICLR — this feels more like a solid EMNLP paper than a top-tier conference breakthrough. I'd recommend borderline acceptance, with the caveat that the authors should provide a more detailed analysis of when and why the gating helps, and perhaps explore whether the learned gates transfer across tasks. The practical value is undeniable, but the intellectual novelty is modest.

title: A Simple but Tough-to-Beat Baseline for Sentence Embeddings
abstract: Abstract:###The success of neural network methods for computing word embeddings has motivated methods for generating semantic embeddings of longer pieces of text, such as sentences and paragraphs. Surprisingly, Wieting et al (ICLR*16) showed that such complicated methods are outperformed, especially in out-of-domain (transfer learning) settings, by simpler methods involving mild retraining of word embeddings and basic linear regression. The method of Wieting et al. requires retraining with a substantial labeled dataset such as Paraphrase Database (Ganitkevitch et al., 2013). The current paper goes further, showing that the following completely unsupervised sentence embedding is a formidable baseline: Use word embeddings computed using one of the popular methods on unlabeled corpus like Wikipedia, represent the sentence by a weighted average of the word vectors, and then modify them a bit using PCA/SVD. This weighting improves performance by about 10% to 30% in textual similarity tasks, and beats sophisticated supervised methods including RNN*s and LSTM*s. It even improves Wieting et al.*s embeddings. This simple method should be used as the baseline to beat in future, especially when labeled training data is scarce or nonexistent. The paper also gives a theoretical explanation of the success of the above unsupervised method using a latent variable generative model for sentences, which is a simple extension of the model in Arora et al. (TACL*16) with new *smoothing* terms that allow for words occurring out of context, as well as high probabilities for words like and, not in all contexts.
review: This paper presents a refreshingly simple unsupervised method for sentence embeddings: smooth inverse frequency weighting of word vectors followed by removing the first principal component. The core idea is embarrassingly straightforward — just weight each word by a/(a+p(w)) and subtract the common component — yet the empirical results are genuinely impressive. On textual similarity tasks, this method beats or matches sophisticated supervised models like RNNs and LSTMs, and improves over Wieting et al.'s PSL embeddings by a few points. The theoretical justification via a modified random walk generative model with smoothing terms is elegant and gives some principled grounding to what is essentially a reweighted average with PCA denoising. I particularly like the insight connecting word2vec's subsampling to implicit reweighting — that's a nice observation that explains why CBOW with sub-sampling works better than a naive average. The method is remarkably robust to the choice of the weighting parameter and the corpus used to estimate word frequencies, which is a practical boon. That said, the paper oversells the "tough-to-beat" claim — the method falls short on sentiment analysis and supervised tasks where word order and negation matter, as the authors acknowledge. The ablation showing that both reweighting and common component removal are important is useful. The theoretical model, while plausible, relies on the assumption that word vectors are uniformly dispersed, which is convenient but not fully justified. I'm also a bit skeptical about the "beat LSTM" narrative — the RNN/LSTM baselines in Wieting et al. were not heavily optimized for these tasks, and modern attention-based models would likely outperform this simple baseline. Overall, this is a solid, practical contribution that will be widely used as a baseline, and the paper is well-written and clearly argued.
