The novelty is moderate — it's essentially a more principled TF-IDF with a PCA trick — but the empirical validation is thorough and the theoretical connection to Arora et al.'s generative model is a nice touch. I'd recommend acceptance; it's not groundbreaking, but it's a genuinely useful paper that will save people a lot of unnecessary RNN training.

title: Capacity and Trainability in Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Two potential bottlenecks on the expressiveness of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are their ability to store information about the task in their parameters, and to store information about the input history in their units. We show experimentally that all common RNN architectures achieve nearly the same per-task and per-unit capacity bounds with careful training, for a variety of tasks and stacking depths. They can store an amount of task information which is linear in the number of parameters, and is approximately 5 bits per parameter. They can additionally store approximately one real number from their input history per hidden unit. We further find that for several tasks it is the per-task parameter capacity bound that determines performance. These results suggest that many previous results comparing RNN architectures are driven primarily by differences in training effectiveness, rather than differences in capacity. Supporting this observation, we compare training difficulty for several architectures, and show that vanilla RNNs are far more difficult to train, yet have slightly higher capacity. Finally, we propose two novel RNN architectures, one of which is easier to train than the LSTM or GRU for deeply stacked architectures.
review: This paper presents a massive empirical study comparing the capacity and trainability of various RNN architectures — vanilla RNN, IRNN, UGRNN, GRU, LSTM, and a newly proposed +RNN — across a wide range of tasks and depths. The main finding is that all architectures can store roughly 5 bits of task information per parameter, and that per-unit memory capacity is not a practical bottleneck. The paper also shows that performance differences between architectures are primarily driven by trainability rather than capacity, with gated architectures being much easier to train, especially at greater depths. I appreciate the sheer scale of the experiments — thousands of hyperparameter optimization runs across multiple tasks and depths — and the careful methodology to disentangle capacity from trainability. The results are informative: the 5 bits per parameter estimate is striking and aligns well with recent biological findings, and the observation that gating slightly reduces capacity but greatly improves trainability is a useful practical takeaway. The UGRNN and +RNN architectures, while not revolutionary, perform competitively and the +RNN seems particularly promising for deep stacking. That said, I have some reservations. The paper is largely empirical and descriptive — it reports what happens but doesn't provide a deep theoretical explanation for why the capacity is 5 bits or why gating hurts capacity. The "capacity" measure is also somewhat artificial: it's a memorization task with random inputs and labels, which may not reflect the capacity needed for more structured tasks like language modeling. The claim that all architectures are "nearly identical" in capacity is interesting, but the differences shown in Figure 1i (e.g., needing 1.3x more parameters for LSTM vs RNN) are not negligible in practice. The paper also doesn't compare to more recent architectures like attention mechanisms or transformer-based models, which might have very different capacity properties. The writing is clear and the figures are well-designed, but the paper feels more like a technical report than a breakthrough. Overall, I think this is a solid and useful empirical contribution that will help practitioners choose architectures, but the novelty is moderate and the theoretical depth is limited. I'd recommend acceptance, but with the caveat that the authors should tone down the claims and acknowledge that the capacity results are specific to the tasks studied. title: Learning to Perform Physics Experiments via Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###When encountering novel objects, humans are able to infer a wide range of physical properties such as mass, friction and deformability by interacting with them in a goal driven way. This process of active interaction is in the same spirit as a scientist performing experiments to discover hidden facts. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have yielded machines that can achieve superhuman performance in Go, Atari, natural language processing, and complex control problems; however, it is not clear that these systems can rival the scientific intuition of even a young child. In this work we introduce a basic set of tasks that require agents to estimate properties such as mass and cohesion of objects in an interactive simulated environment where they can manipulate the objects and observe the consequences. We found that deep reinforcement learning methods can learn to perform the experiments necessary to discover such hidden properties. By systematically manipulating the problem difficulty and the cost incurred by the agent for performing experiments, we found that agents learn different strategies that balance the cost of gathering information against the cost of making mistakes in different situations. We also compare our learned experimentation policies to randomized baselines and show that the learned policies lead to better predictions.
review: This paper presents an interesting and well-motivated study on using deep reinforcement learning to train agents to perform physical experiments in order to infer hidden object properties like mass and cohesion. The core idea — that agents should actively interact with objects rather than passively observe them — is compelling and grounded in developmental psychology. The two environments, "Which is Heavier" and "Towers," are well-designed to require interaction, and the results show that A3C agents learn sensible experiment policies that adapt to task difficulty and information cost, often outperforming randomized interaction baselines. I appreciate the thorough analysis of how discount factor and mass gap affect episode length and accuracy, and the qualitative behavior of the agents — e.g., poking all blocks before deciding in harder tasks — is intuitively correct. That said, I have some reservations. The paper explicitly states it does not present a new model or algorithm, and the contribution is primarily empirical and problem-framing. While that's fine, the novelty is limited compared to other ICLR papers. The tasks are also quite simplified — direct actuation on blocks in a physics simulator — and it's unclear how well these results would generalize to more complex, real-world scenarios where manipulation itself is a challenge. The comparison to randomized baselines is useful, but a comparison to a more structured baseline, like a policy that systematically probes each object, would strengthen the claims. Finally, the paper doesn't address how the learned experimentation policies could be reused or transferred to new tasks, which is a key aspect of scientific reasoning. Overall, I think this is a solid and thought-provoking paper with nice qualitative insights, but the technical contribution is modest and the scope is narrow. I'd lean towards acceptance with the expectation that the authors discuss these limitations more openly and perhaps suggest concrete directions for scaling up. title: Improving Policy Gradient by Exploring Under-appreciated Rewards
abstract: Abstract:###This paper presents a novel form of policy gradient for model-free reinforcement learning (RL) with improved exploration properties. Current policy-based methods use entropy regularization to encourage undirected exploration of the reward landscape, which is ineffective in high dimensional spaces with sparse rewards. We propose a more directed exploration strategy that promotes exploration of under-appreciated reward regions. An action sequence is considered under-appreciated if its log-probability under the current policy under-estimates its resulting reward. The proposed exploration strategy is easy to implement, requiring only small modifications to the standard REINFORCE algorithm. We evaluate the approach on a set of algorithmic tasks that have long challenged RL methods. We find that our approach reduces hyper-parameter sensitivity and demonstrates significant improvements over baseline methods. Notably, the approach is able to solve a benchmark multi-digit addition task. To our knowledge, this is the first time that a pure RL method has solved addition using only reward feedback.
review: This paper introduces UREX, a policy gradient method that promotes exploration by encouraging the model to increase probability mass on action sequences whose rewards are under-appreciated relative to their current log-probability. The core idea is elegant and practically effective: combine the standard REINFORCE objective with a mean-seeking RAML-style term, using self-normalized importance sampling to approximate the gradient. I really like the formulation — it's a principled way to bridge mode-seeking and mean-seeking behavior, and the connection to the optimal policy and KL divergence is well-motivated. The experimental results on algorithmic tasks are genuinely impressive: UREX consistently outperforms entropy-regularized REINFORCE and Q-learning, often by large margins, and is the first pure RL method I've seen that can solve multi-digit addition with generalization to 2000-digit sequences. The robustness to hyperparameters is also a significant practical advantage. That said, I have some reservations. The paper is essentially applying an existing idea (RAML) to the RL setting, and while the adaptation is clever, the novelty is somewhat incremental. The experiments are focused on algorithmic tasks with episodic total rewards, which is a niche setting — it's unclear how well UREX would perform on more standard RL benchmarks like Atari or continuous control. The paper also doesn't provide a deep theoretical analysis of why UREX works better than alternative exploration strategies, beyond the KL divergence argument. The connection to RWR is mentioned but not explored in depth, and the optimal policy derivation in Appendix A is interesting but not discussed in the main text. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a clear contribution and strong empirical results, but the scope is limited and the theoretical novelty is modest. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide more intuition about when and why UREX works, and perhaps a comparison to other directed exploration methods like intrinsic motivation. It's a useful addition to the policy gradient toolkit, but it's not a game-changer.This paper introduces UREX, a policy gradient method that promotes exploration by encouraging the model to increase probability mass on action sequences whose rewards are under-appreciated relative to their current log-probability. The core idea is elegant and practically effective: combine the standard REINFORCE objective with a mean-seeking RAML-style term, using self-normalized importance sampling to approximate the gradient. I really like the formulation — it's a principled way to bridge mode-seeking and mean-seeking behavior, and the connection to the optimal policy and KL divergence is well-motivated. The experimental results on algorithmic tasks are genuinely impressive: UREX consistently outperforms entropy-regularized REINFORCE and Q-learning, often by large margins, and is the first pure RL method I've seen that can solve multi-digit addition with generalization to 2000-digit sequences. The robustness to hyperparameters is also a significant practical advantage. That said, I have some reservations. The paper is essentially applying an existing idea (RAML) to the RL setting, and while the adaptation is clever, the novelty is somewhat incremental. The experiments are focused on algorithmic tasks with episodic total rewards, which is a niche setting — it's unclear how well UREX would perform on more standard RL benchmarks like Atari or continuous control. The paper also doesn't provide a deep theoretical analysis of why UREX works better than alternative exploration strategies, beyond the KL divergence argument. The connection to RWR is mentioned but not explored in depth, and the optimal policy derivation in Appendix A is interesting but not discussed in the main text. Overall, I think this is a solid paper with a clear contribution and strong empirical results, but the scope is limited and the theoretical novelty is modest. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide more intuition about when and why UREX works, and perhaps a comparison to other directed exploration methods like intrinsic motivation. It's a useful addition to the policy gradient toolkit, but it's not a game-changer.

title: Deep Learning with Dynamic Computation Graphs
abstract: Abstract:###Neural networks that compute over graph structures are a natural fit for problems in a variety of domains, including natural language (parse trees) and cheminformatics (molecular graphs). However, since the computation graph has a different shape and size for every input, such networks do not directly support batched training or inference. They are also difficult to implement in popular deep learning libraries, which are based on static data-flow graphs. We introduce a technique called dynamic batching, which not only batches together operations between different input graphs of dissimilar shape, but also between different nodes within a single input graph. The technique allows us to create static graphs, using popular libraries, that emulate dynamic computation graphs of arbitrary shape and size. We further present a high-level library of compositional blocks that simplifies the creation of dynamic graph models. Using the library, we demonstrate concise and batch-wise parallel implementations for a variety of models from the literature.
review: This paper tackles the important problem of implementing neural networks with dynamic computation graphs (DCGs) — models like TreeRNNs or graph convolutions where each input has a different shape — in static-graph frameworks like TensorFlow. The core contribution is "dynamic batching," a clever algorithm that batches operations at the same depth across different input graphs, then uses concat/gather ops inside a tf.while_loop to emulate the dynamic graph. This is a genuinely practical solution that addresses a real pain point, and the speedup numbers are compelling: 120x faster than a batch size of 1 on GPU, with only ~20% overhead relative to fully manual batching. The authors also introduce a high-level combinator library (TensorFlow Fold) that makes it much easier to write these models, with concise implementations for feed-forward attention, Tree-LSTMs, and graph convolutions. The Tree-LSTM results on the Stanford Sentiment Treebank set new SOTA (90.2% binary), which is a nice validation. I like the engineering contributions — dynamic batching is a solid algorithmic trick, and the combinator library seems genuinely useful. That said, I have some reservations. The paper is primarily an engineering contribution; the novelty is in the batching algorithm and the library design, not in the ML models themselves. The benchmarking is a bit generous — the comparison to manual batching uses trees of the same shape, which is a best-case scenario for manual batching and masks the fact that manual batching is impossible for different shapes. The library also introduces complexity: the gather/concat overhead is non-trivial, and the type system and combinators have a learning curve. The paper doesn't compare to alternative approaches like SPINN (Bowman et al.) or dynamic batching implementations in PyTorch, which would help contextualize the contribution. Overall, I think this is a useful and well-engineered piece of work that will be valuable to practitioners, but the technical contribution is more about tooling than about advancing the core ML methodology. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors provide a clearer comparison to existing approaches and a more honest discussion of the overhead and limitations. It's a solid systems paper for a conference that's increasingly accepting such contributions, but it's not a breakthrough in ML theory.

title: Calibrating Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we propose to equip Generative Adversarial Networks with the ability to produce direct energy estimates for samples. Specifically, we propose a flexible adversarial training framework, and prove this framework not only ensures the generator converges to the true data distribution, but also enables the discriminator to retain the density information at the global optimal. We derive the analytic form of the induced solution, and analyze the properties. In order to make the proposed framework trainable in practice, we introduce two effective approximation techniques. Empirically, the experiment results closely match our theoretical analysis, verifying the discriminator is able to recover the energy of data distribution.
review: This paper tackles a fundamental limitation of GANs: the discriminator becomes degenerate at the global optimum, losing any meaningful density information. The authors propose a clever fix — adding a convex regularizer K(p_gen) to the generator's objective, which provides an additional training signal that allows the discriminator to retain energy estimates while still ensuring the generator converges to the data distribution. The theoretical analysis is rigorous and elegant: they show via convex duality that the optimal discriminator takes the form c*(x) = -∂K(p_gen)/∂p_gen|_(p_gen=p_data) + bias, which for K = negative entropy gives exactly -log p_data(x) — the true energy. This is a beautiful result that connects adversarial training to maximum entropy IRL and energy-based models. The synthetic experiments beautifully validate the theory, with EGAN-Ent-NN recovering the correct energy contours on 2D mixtures where GAN and EBGAN degenerate to flat functions. The NIST digit ranking experiment is compelling — EGAN-Ent-NN's top-ranked images look like the mean digit while bottom-ranked ones are rotated or stylized, clearly demonstrating calibrated density information. That said, I have some concerns. The approximations for the entropy gradient in high dimensions feel a bit hacky — the nearest-neighbor method relies on Euclidean distance which is problematic in high-dimensional spaces, and the variational approximation seems to fail on the biased Gaussian mixture, incorrectly weighting the modes. The CIFAR-10 inception score (7.07) is decent but not state-of-the-art, and the paper doesn't compare to more recent GAN variants like WGAN or spectral normalization. The connection to EBGAN is interesting but the paper's critique feels a bit unfair — EBGAN wasn't designed to produce calibrated energies, and the authors' own EGAN-Const (which is essentially EBGAN) also degenerates. Overall, I think this is a solid theoretical contribution with convincing synthetic validation, but the practical approximations need more work before this becomes a go-to method for density estimation. I'd lean towards acceptance — the theory is novel and the problem is important — but I'd like to see a more thorough discussion of the limitations of the entropy approximations and a clearer path forward for high-dimensional settings. It's not a game-changer yet, but it's a significant step in the right direction.

title: Pruning Convolutional Neural Networks for Resource Efficient Inference
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a new formulation for pruning convolutional kernels in neural networks to enable efficient inference. We interleave greedy criteria-based pruning with fine-tuning by backpropagation-a computationally efficient procedure that maintains good generalization in the pruned network. We propose a new criterion based on Taylor expansion that approximates the change in the cost function induced by pruning network parameters. We focus on transfer learning, where large pretrained networks are adapted to specialized tasks. The proposed criterion demonstrates superior performance compared to other criteria, e.g. the norm of kernel weights or feature map activation, for pruning large CNNs after adaptation to fine-grained classification tasks (Birds-200 and Flowers-102) relaying only on the first order gradient information. We also show that pruning can lead to more than 10x theoretical reduction in adapted 3D-convolutional filters with a small drop in accuracy in a recurrent gesture classifier. Finally, we show results for the large-scale ImageNet dataset to emphasize the flexibility of our approach.
review: This paper tackles the practical problem of pruning convolutional neural networks for efficient inference, focusing on structured pruning of entire feature maps rather than individual weights to actually achieve speedups on modern hardware. The key contribution is a new pruning criterion based on a first-order Taylor expansion that approximates the change in loss when removing a feature map — essentially using the product of the activation and its gradient, which is computationally cheap since it's already computed during backprop. I really like the Taylor criterion; it's elegant, efficient, and empirically outperforms weight norms, activation statistics, and even OBD in terms of Spearman correlation with the oracle ranking. The experiments are thorough and convincing: pruning VGG-16 on Birds-200, AlexNet on Flowers-102, a 3D-CNN for gesture recognition, and even ImageNet, with up to 10x FLOPs reduction for modest accuracy drops. The FLOPs-regularized pruning is a sensible addition to bias pruning toward computationally expensive layers. The paper is well-written and the results are solid. That said, I have some reservations. The iterative pruning procedure — removing one feature map at a time with fine-tuning between — is computationally expensive; pruning to 50% of feature maps requires thousands of iterations, each with fine-tuning steps, which is impractical for very large networks unless you have serious compute resources. The comparison to OBD is somewhat hand-wavy; the authors claim OBD is slower but don't provide a clean implementation or timing comparison in the main text. The correlation analysis is useful but doesn't fully capture the dynamics of iterative pruning, where criteria that correlate well with the oracle at the first step might not correlate well after several pruning iterations. Finally, the method is not compared to more recent structured pruning techniques like network slimming or group sparsity regularization, which achieve similar results with a single training pass rather than iterative pruning. Overall, this is a solid and practical contribution, but the novelty is somewhat incremental and the computational cost of the procedure is a significant practical limitation. I'd recommend acceptance with the expectation that the authors discuss these limitations more honestly and perhaps suggest ways to reduce the cost of iterative pruning.

title: Query-Reduction Networks for Question Answering
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we study the problem of question answering when reasoning over multiple facts is required. We propose Query-Reduction Network (QRN), a variant of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that effectively handles both short-term (local) and long-term (global) sequential dependencies to reason over multiple facts. QRN considers the context sentences as a sequence of state-changing triggers, and reduces the original query to a more informed query as it observes each trigger (context sentence) through time. Our experiments show that QRN produces the state-of-the-art results in bAbI QA and dialog tasks, and in a real goal-oriented dialog dataset. In addition, QRN formulation allows parallelization on RNN*s time axis, saving an order of magnitude in time complexity for training and inference.
review: This paper tackles the important and challenging problem of multi-hop reasoning for question answering, and I think the proposed Query-Reduction Network is a clever and solid contribution. The key idea of treating context sentences as state-changing triggers to iteratively reduce the original query into a more informed one is intuitive and, as the paper shows, effective. I'm particularly impressed by the architectural novelty—sitting between attention mechanisms and RNNs, QRN seems to capture the best of both worlds by handling time dependencies while addressing the long-term memory issues that plague standard RNNs. The parallelization trick is also a nice practical bonus that gives it a real computational edge. The results are strong across the board, with QRN achieving state-of-the-art on both bAbI QA and dialog tasks, including the more challenging OOV and DSTC2 datasets. I also appreciate the interpretability analysis through gate visualizations and intermediate query decoding—it provides genuine insight into how the model reasons, which is rare in this field. My main criticism is that the experiments, while thorough on the bAbI suite, are somewhat limited to synthetic or heavily structured domains; I'd have liked to see how QRN performs on more naturalistic multi-hop QA datasets like HotpotQA to really test its generalizability. Additionally, the ablation studies could be more systematic—the paper mentions extensions like reset gates and vector gates but doesn't deeply analyze their individual contributions across tasks. That said, the core idea is elegant, the theoretical grounding is sound, and the empirical results convincingly demonstrate QRN's effectiveness. This is a well-written paper on a timely topic with clear practical implications for dialog systems and QA. I recommend acceptance.

title: Designing Neural Network Architectures using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###At present, designing convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures requires both human expertise and labor. New architectures are handcrafted by careful experimentation or modified from a handful of existing networks. We introduce MetaQNN, a meta-modeling algorithm based on reinforcement learning to automatically generate high-performing CNN architectures for a given learning task. The learning agent is trained to sequentially choose CNN layers using -learning with an -greedy exploration strategy and experience replay. The agent explores a large but finite space of possible architectures and iteratively discovers designs with improved performance on the learning task. On image classification benchmarks, the agent-designed networks (consisting of only standard convolution, pooling, and fully-connected layers) beat existing networks designed with the same layer types and are competitive against the state-of-the-art methods that use more complex layer types. We also outperform existing meta-modeling approaches for network design on image classification tasks.
review: This paper tackles the increasingly important problem of automating neural network architecture design, and honestly, I think it's a solid step in the right direction. The core idea of framing architecture search as a Markov Decision Process and using Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration is simple but effective—I'm genuinely impressed that the agent can discover networks that not only beat all prior hand-crafted CNNs using the same standard layer types but also compete with more complex state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and MNIST. The results are convincing: the top MetaQNN model achieves 6.92% error on CIFAR-10, which beats All-CNN and VGGnet, and the ensemble hits 0.28% on MNIST without data augmentation, which is essentially state-of-the-art. However, I'm a bit skeptical about the practical cost—8-10 days on 10 GPUs is hefty, and while the paper acknowledges this, it doesn't really explore how to make the search more efficient. Also, the state-action space is quite constrained (only standard convolution, pooling, and FC layers, with heavily discretized parameters), so I wonder how well this would scale to more exotic layer types or much larger datasets like ImageNet. The transfer learning experiment is a nice touch, showing that the CIFAR-10 model transfers decently to other tasks, though the finetuning results are noticeably worse than training from scratch on CIFAR-100, which raises questions about how generalizable these discovered architectures really are. The Q-learning analysis is thorough—I appreciate the visualizations of Q-values and accuracy distributions—but the method is essentially doing random search with guided exploitation, and I'd like to see a more rigorous comparison to Bayesian optimization or evolutionary strategies to really understand where the advantage comes from. That said, the paper is well-written, the experiments are reproducible, and the code is available, which I always appreciate. Overall, this is a well-executed piece of work that demonstrates reinforcement learning can be a viable tool for architecture design, even if the computational cost and constrained search space limit its immediate practical impact. I recommend acceptance, with the caveat that the authors should discuss scalability and potential improvements more explicitly.

title: Machine Comprehension Using Match-LSTM and Answer Pointer
abstract: Abstract:###Machine comprehension of text is an important problem in natural language processing. A recently released dataset, the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), offers a large number of real questions and their answers created by humans through crowdsourcing. SQuAD provides a challenging testbed for evaluating machine comprehension algorithms, partly because compared with previous datasets, in SQuAD the answers do not come from a small set of candidate answers and they have variable lengths. We propose an end-to-end neural architecture for the task. The architecture is based on match-LSTM, a model we proposed previously for textual entailment, and Pointer Net, a sequence-to-sequence model proposed by Vinyals et al. (2015) to constrain the output tokens to be from the input sequences. We propose two ways of using Pointer Net for our tasks. Our experiments show that both of our two models substantially outperform the best results obtained by Rajpurkar et al. (2016) using logistic regression and manually crafted features. Besides, our boundary model also achieves the best performance on the MSMARCO dataset (Nguyen et al. 2016).
review: This paper tackles the challenging SQuAD dataset for machine comprehension, and I think it's a solid piece of work with a practical and effective approach. The key idea of combining match-LSTM, which I liked in their previous entailment work, with a Pointer Network is natural and well-motivated—especially since SQuAD answers are variable-length spans from the passage. The boundary model, which predicts start and end positions, is clearly the right design choice here; the sequence model that treats answers as unordered tokens is conceptually neat but practically flawed for this task, and the results bear that out (61.1% vs 54.4% exact match). I appreciate the search mechanism they add to the boundary model—it's a simple but clever way to enforce consecutivity and boost performance to 63.0%, and the ensemble pushing it to 67.6% exact match and 77.0% F1 is genuinely competitive for that time. However, I have some reservations. The improvement from the bidirectional preprocessing LSTM and larger hidden dimensions is disappointingly small—barely a point—which makes me wonder if the match-LSTM layer is already capturing most of the useful signal, or if the model is hitting a ceiling that requires more fundamental changes. The analysis on question types and answer lengths is useful but superficial; they note "why" questions are hard, but they don't really dig into why or propose fixes. Also, the model essentially treats the problem as a span extraction task, which works for SQuAD but limits generalization to other QA formats where answers might not be verbatim spans—I'd like to see some discussion of that limitation. The comparisons to logistic regression and DCR are fine, but the field was moving fast, and the state-of-the-art at the time (like the Salesforce model they mention) was already ahead, so this isn't groundbreaking—it's a solid incremental contribution. Overall, I think this is a well-written, technically sound paper that demonstrates the effectiveness of match-LSTM + Pointer Networks for span-based QA, with clear results and reproducible code. I'd recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to think more about why their model struggles with certain question types and how to generalize beyond extractive QA.

title: DeepDSL: A Compilation-based Domain-Specific Language for Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract:###In recent years, Deep Learning (DL) has found great success in domains such as multimedia understanding. However, the complex nature of multimedia data makes it difficult to develop DL-based software. The state-of-the-art tools, such as Caffe, TensorFlow, Torch7, and CNTK, while are successful in their applicable domains, are programming libraries with fixed user interface, internal representation, and execution environment. This makes it difficult to implement portable and customized DL applications. In this paper, we present DeepDSL, a domain specific language (DSL) embedded in Scala, that compiles deep networks written in DeepDSL to Java source code. Deep DSL provides (1) intuitive constructs to support compact encoding of deep networks; (2) symbolic gradient derivation of the networks; (3) static analysis for memory consumption and error detection; and (4) DSL-level optimization to improve memory and runtime efficiency. DeepDSL programs are compiled into compact, efficient, customizable, and portable Java source code, which operates the CUDA and CUDNN interfaces running on NVIDIA GPU via a Java Native Interface (JNI) library. We evaluated DeepDSL with a number of popular DL networks. Our experiments show that the compiled programs have very competitive runtime performance and memory efficiency compared to the existing libraries.
review: This paper presents DeepDSL, a domain-specific language embedded in Scala that compiles deep learning network definitions into Java source code, and honestly, I think it's a well-executed piece of systems work with real practical value. The core idea—moving beyond the "library as API" paradigm that dominates frameworks like Caffe, TensorFlow, and Torch, and instead treating network definitions as compilable programs—is compelling. I particularly like the static analysis capabilities: detecting dimension mismatches before runtime, analyzing memory consumption statically, and reordering computation to free tensors early. The memory efficiency gains are genuinely impressive—they show DeepDSL handling ResNet with batch size 64 on a 12GB GPU where both Caffe and TensorFlow OOM, and the memory-efficient mode shaving off 10-30% memory with reasonable runtime overhead. The runtime performance is also competitive: faster than Caffe on AlexNet, Overfeat, and GoogLeNet, and faster than TensorFlow on AlexNet, GoogLeNet, and ResNet. However, I have some reservations. First, the compilation time for complex networks like ResNet takes "a few minutes," which isn't terrible but isn't trivial either, and the paper doesn't really discuss how this scales to even larger models or what the compilation bottlenecks are. Second, the generated Java code depends on JCuda, which is a JNI wrapper around CUDA—this adds a layer of indirection that could introduce overhead, and the paper doesn't analyze the JNI overhead compared to native C++ frameworks. Third, the claim that DeepDSL is "more flexible" than Theano because of its two-phase optimization and clean separation between IR and code generation is a bit hand-wavy; Theano also does extensive optimization, and I'd like to see a more concrete comparison of what DeepDSL's optimization passes actually do that Theano doesn't. Also, the "human readable" generated Java code is a nice selling point, but let's be real—nobody is going to manually edit 10,000 lines of generated convolution code; the real value is the portability and customizability, not readability per se. The related work section is thorough, and the experiments are extensive across five networks and two batch sizes each, though the TensorFlow tests have some inconsistencies (random data vs. real images, incomplete GoogLeNet) that make direct comparisons a bit apples-to-oranges. Overall, I think this is a solid systems paper that demonstrates the benefits of a compilation-based approach for DL—better memory management, early error detection, and competitive performance. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to be more transparent about the compilation overhead and to discuss the limitations of the Java/JNI approach more critically.

title: Bidirectional Attention Flow for Machine Comprehension
abstract: Abstract:###Machine comprehension (MC), answering a query about a given context paragraph, requires modeling complex interactions between the context and the query. Recently, attention mechanisms have been successfully extended to MC. Typically these methods use attention to focus on a small portion of the context and summarize it with a fixed-size vector, couple attentions temporally, and/or often form a uni-directional attention. In this paper we introduce the Bi-Directional Attention Flow (BIDAF) network, a multi-stage hierarchical process that represents the context at different levels of granularity and uses bi-directional attention flow mechanism to obtain a query-aware context representation without early summarization. Our experimental evaluations show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art results in Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) and CNN/DailyMail cloze test.
review: This paper introduces BiDAF, and honestly, I think it's one of the most well-executed and impactful papers on machine comprehension I've seen in a while. The core innovation—a bi-directional attention flow mechanism that doesn't squash the context into a fixed vector early but instead lets attention vectors flow through to subsequent modeling layers—is both simple and profoundly effective. I really appreciate the hierarchical design: character embeddings via CNNs handle OOV words, contextual LSTMs capture temporal dependencies, and the attention layer computes both query-to-context and context-to-query similarities using that nice α(h,u) = w^T[h;u;h∘u] formulation. The memory-less attention is a clever choice—by not making attention depend on previous time steps, they force the attention layer to focus purely on alignment while the modeling layer handles contextual reasoning, and the results bear this out (static attention beats dynamic by 3+ F1 points). The ablation study is thorough and honest: C2Q attention is absolutely critical (10+ point drop without it), Q2C attention helps, character embeddings matter, and the ensemble pushes to 73.3 EM / 81.1 F1 on SQuAD, which was state-of-the-art at the time. The visualization of feature spaces using t-SNE is genuinely insightful—seeing the contextual embedding layer disambiguate "May" as a month versus a verb, or aligning "When" to years and "Who" to names, gives real confidence that the model is learning meaningful representations. The error analysis is also useful, though I wish they'd dug deeper into why 50% of errors are boundary imprecision—that suggests the start/end prediction mechanism, while effective, has fundamental limitations that might require more structured output layers. The cloze test results on CNN/DailyMail are impressive too, beating all previous single models and even some ensembles, though the 60-hour training time on 8 GPUs is a bit steep—I'd have liked to see some discussion of efficiency trade-offs. My main criticism is that the model is quite heavyweight and over-engineered for what is essentially a span extraction task; simpler models like the Attention Sum Reader were closing the gap, and I wonder if the complexity is truly justified or if similar performance could be achieved with a leaner architecture. Also, the paper claims "state-of-the-art" but the SQuAD leaderboard was moving fast even then, and some concurrent work like DCN was also hitting similar numbers, so the margin wasn't massive. That said, the design principles—hierarchical representation, bidirectional attention, no early summarization—have proven influential and are now standard in QA systems. This is a well-written, technically sound paper with strong empirical results, clear ablations, and meaningful insights. I recommend acceptance without hesitation.

title: Incorporating long-range consistency in CNN-based texture generation
abstract: Abstract:###Gatys et al. (2015) showed that pair-wise products of features in a convolutional network are a very effective representation of image textures. We propose a simple modification to that representation which makes it possible to incorporate long-range structure into image generation, and to render images that satisfy various symmetry constraints. We show how this can greatly improve rendering of regular textures and of images that contain other kinds of symmetric structure. We also present applications to inpainting and season transfer.
review: This paper tackles an important limitation of the Gatys et al. texture synthesis method—its inability to capture long-range spatial structure—and honestly, I think the proposed solution is both simple and surprisingly effective. The core idea of computing shifted Gram matrices to capture spatial co-occurrences between feature maps at different offsets is elegant; it's essentially a high-level, CNN-based analog of GLCMs, and the fact that it can be dropped into the existing framework with minimal changes is a real strength. The results on structured textures like brick walls, woven patterns, and faces are visually compelling—the model clearly preserves alignment and periodicity that the original method completely loses. The inpainting application is a nice demonstration of how these long-range constraints can enforce consistency between the generated region and the surrounding context, and the season transfer examples show that the approach generalizes beyond pure texture synthesis. That said, I have some reservations. First, the method introduces a significant computational overhead (roughly 80% increase in generation time), and the paper doesn't really discuss whether this trade-off is worth it in practice, especially given that feed-forward alternatives like Texture Networks exist. Second, the choice of δ values per layer is pretty ad hoc—the paper essentially says "here's a fixed set that works for 384x384 images," but there's no principled way to adapt this to different image sizes or textures, and I worry about how robust this configuration is across diverse inputs. Third, while the results look good qualitatively, there's no quantitative evaluation or user study to back up the claims of improvement; a simple perceptual study or even a comparison to patch-based methods like Efros & Freeman would have strengthened the paper considerably. Fourth, the method seems to work best when the reference texture has clear periodic structure, but for more stochastic textures, the additional terms don't help much (and the paper acknowledges this). I also think the connection to MRFs could have been explored more deeply—the approach is reminiscent of a mean-field style of enforcing consistency, but the paper doesn't draw that connection explicitly or discuss how it relates to existing work on learning image priors. Overall, though, this is a well-executed piece of work that addresses a real limitation of a popular method, with clear visual improvements and interesting applications. I recommend acceptance, but I'd encourage the authors to provide more systematic evaluation and to address the computational cost and parameter selection issues in the final version.

title: Dynamic Coattention Networks For Question Answering
abstract: Abstract:###Several deep learning models have been proposed for question answering. How- ever, due to their single-pass nature, they have no way to recover from local maxima corresponding to incorrect answers. To address this problem, we introduce the Dynamic Coattention Network (DCN) for question answering. The DCN first fuses co-dependent representations of the question and the document in order to focus on relevant parts of both. Then a dynamic pointer decoder iterates over potential answer spans. This iterative procedure enables the model to recover from initial local maxima corresponding to incorrect answers. On the Stanford question answering dataset, a single DCN model improves the previous state of the art from 71.0% F1 to 75.9%, while a DCN ensemble obtains 80.4% F1.
review: This paper introduces the Dynamic Coattention Network for QA, and honestly, I think it's a significant step forward for the SQuAD leaderboard. The coattention encoder that jointly represents question and document is elegant—the bidirectional affinity matrix with sentinel vectors captures interactions nicely, and the fusion via bidirectional LSTM produces a rich representation. But the real star is the dynamic pointing decoder: iteratively refining start and end predictions lets the model escape local maxima, and the results speak for themselves—75.9% F1 for a single model and 80.4% for an ensemble, comfortably beating the previous state of the art. I appreciate the Highway Maxout Network design, though I'm not entirely convinced it's pulling its weight—the ablation shows dropping it for a 2-layer MLP only costs about 1.2 F1 points, which makes me wonder if the complexity is justified. The dynamic iterations are more impactful, but even there the gain over a single-pass decoder is only ~1.6 F1 points, so the improvement is real but not massive. The analysis is thorough: performance across document/question length is surprisingly stable (coattention seems to handle long contexts well), and the breakdown by question type shows consistent gains across all categories. The error analysis is honest—50% of errors are boundary imprecision, and the model sometimes oscillates between plausible answers, suggesting the iterative refinement isn't always converging. I'm also a bit concerned about computational cost; they don't report training time, but with 200-dim hidden states, maxout pools of 16, and up to 4 iterations per example, this must be expensive. That said, the ensemble result of 80.4% F1 was genuinely state-of-the-art at the time, and the model's ability to handle multi-sentence reasoning (as shown in the appendix) is impressive. The paper is well-written, the architecture is novel, and the empirical validation is strong. I'd recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to discuss the computational trade-offs more explicitly and to consider whether the HMN complexity is truly necessary given the modest gains.

title: SampleRNN: An Unconditional End-to-End Neural Audio Generation Model
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper we propose a novel model for unconditional audio generation task that generates one audio sample at a time. We show that our model which profits from combining memory-less modules, namely autoregressive multilayer perceptron, and stateful recurrent neural networks in a hierarchical structure is de facto powerful to capture the underlying sources of variations in temporal domain for very long time on three datasets of different nature. Human evaluation on the generated samples indicate that our model is preferred over competing models. We also show how each component of the model contributes to the exhibited performance.
review: This paper presents SampleRNN for unconditional raw audio generation, and I think it's a genuinely solid contribution that addresses a real limitation of models like WaveNet—the inability to capture very long-range dependencies without massive receptive fields. The hierarchical architecture, with frame-level RNNs operating at different temporal resolutions and a sample-level MLP handling local structure, is clever and well-motivated. The key insight that different modules can run at different clock rates, with the higher-level RNNs summarizing long-term context and upsampling via learned projections to condition the lower levels, is both elegant and practical. The results are convincing: SampleRNN consistently beats their WaveNet re-implementation on all three datasets in terms of NLL, and the human evaluation on Blizzard shows a clear preference for the 3-tier model over both the 2-tier version and WaveNet—89% preference over WaveNet is a landslide. I also appreciate the memory experiment where they injected a second of silence and showed the model maintains speaker consistency 83% of the time, which is strong evidence that the frame-level RNNs are actually learning and retaining long-term information. However, I have some concerns. First, the WaveNet comparison is a bit shaky—they admit their implementation might not match the original due to missing details and computational constraints, and their WaveNet has only 40 dilated layers with 64 channels versus the original's 30 layers with 256-512 channels, so this isn't exactly apples-to-apples. Second, the NLL improvements over a simple RNN are modest (1.387 vs 1.434 on Blizzard), which makes me wonder if the added complexity is truly paying off in terms of raw likelihood, even if the human evaluation suggests it is. Third, the Onomatopoeia results are the weakest—SampleRNN barely beats the RNN and actually does worse than WaveNet on the test set, suggesting the model might not generalize as well to more diverse, shorter sequences. Fourth, the computational cost is steep; they don't report exact training times, but the 3-tier model with GRUs running at multiple scales must be expensive, and the 60-hour training on eight GPUs for WaveNet-like models is nontrivial. The absence of a fully convolutional alternative in the final model (the hybrid is mentioned but dismissed as preliminary) is a missed opportunity—a dilated convolution-based sample-level module with RNNs at higher levels could have been a nice middle ground. Overall, I think this is a well-executed paper with a novel architecture, strong empirical results (especially on the human evaluation), and clear practical significance for audio generation. The hierarchical multi-scale approach is principled and likely to influence future work. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to be more transparent about the WaveNet comparison limitations and to explore the hybrid further in future work.

title: Metacontrol for Adaptive Imagination-Based Optimization
abstract: Abstract:###Many machine learning systems are built to solve the hardest examples of a particular task, which often makes them large and expensive to run---especially with respect to the easier examples, which might require much less computation. For an agent with a limited computational budget, this *one-size-fits-all* approach may result in the agent wasting valuable computation on easy examples, while not spending enough on hard examples. Rather than learning a single, fixed policy for solving all instances of a task, we introduce a metacontroller which learns to optimize a sequence of *imagined* internal simulations over predictive models of the world in order to construct a more informed, and more economical, solution. The metacontroller component is a model-free reinforcement learning agent, which decides both how many iterations of the optimization procedure to run, as well as which model to consult on each iteration. The models (which we call *experts*) can be state transition models, action-value functions, or any other mechanism that provides information useful for solving the task, and can be learned on-policy or off-policy in parallel with the metacontroller. When the metacontroller, controller, and experts were trained with *interaction networks* (Battaglia et al., 2016) as expert models, our approach was able to solve a challenging decision-making problem under complex non-linear dynamics. The metacontroller learned to adapt the amount of computation it performed to the difficulty of the task, and learned how to choose which experts to consult by factoring in both their reliability and individual computational resource costs. This allowed the metacontroller to achieve a lower overall cost (task loss plus computational cost) than more traditional fixed policy approaches. These results demonstrate that our approach is a powerful framework for using rich forward models for efficient model-based reinforcement learning.
review: This paper tackles an important and under-explored problem—how to adaptively allocate computation in a model-based optimization loop—and honestly, I think the proposed metacontroller framework is a clever and promising step forward. The core idea of learning a meta-level policy that decides when to stop "pondering" and which approximate model ("expert") to consult is elegant, and the connection to bounded rationality and human metacognition gives it conceptual depth. The experimental setup—a challenging continuous control task with non-linear gravitational dynamics—is well-chosen, and the results are convincing: the metacontroller learns to take more steps on harder episodes, fewer on easier ones, and achieves a lower total cost (performance + computation) than fixed-iteration iterative agents by about 11-15%. The ability to trade off between an accurate but expensive expert (IN) and a cheap but poor one (MLP) is also demonstrated, with the metacontroller sensibly favoring the IN expert most of the time. I particularly appreciate the thorough ablation: the reactive agent fails entirely, the iterative agents show diminishing returns, and the metacontroller's adaptive behavior emerges naturally from the REINFORCE training. However, I have some reservations. First, the task is a one-shot decision problem, which is a far cry from the sequential decision-making settings where this kind of adaptive imagination would really shine—I'd have liked to see at least a proof-of-concept in a multi-step control or planning domain. Second, the gain from using multiple experts over a single expert is surprisingly modest (only 9% of configurations beat the best iterative baseline), which suggests the metacontroller isn't fully exploiting the expert diversity; the entropy regularizer seems to be hurting performance at high computational costs, and the paper acknowledges this but doesn't offer a satisfying fix. Third, the training procedure is complex and somewhat brittle—learning rates had to be carefully tuned for each condition (as shown in the extensive hyperparameter tables), and the authors note convergence issues for larger numbers of ponder steps, which limits the generality of the approach. Fourth, while the comparison to iterative agents is solid, I'm curious how this compares to simpler adaptive strategies like early stopping based on validation loss or threshold-based termination—the paper doesn't provide such baselines. Fifth, the computational cost of training the metacontroller alongside the experts and the critic is not discussed; given the complexity of the architecture, I worry about scalability to larger models and more expensive experts. That said, the paper is well-written, the idea is novel and well-motivated, and the empirical results, while limited in scope, do demonstrate the core claim that adaptive computation allocation can improve speed-accuracy trade-offs. I recommend acceptance with encouragement to address the limitations in future work—particularly extending to sequential tasks and improving the multi-expert selection mechanism.

title: Exploring Sparsity in Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recurrent neural networks (RNN) are widely used to solve a variety of problems and as the quantity of data and the amount of available compute have increased, so have model sizes. The number of parameters in recent state-of-the-art networks makes them hard to deploy, especially on mobile phones and embedded devices. The challenge is due to both the size of the model and the time it takes to evaluate it. In order to deploy these RNNs efficiently, we propose a technique to reduce the parameters of a network by pruning weights during the initial training of the network. At the end of training, the parameters of the network are sparse while accuracy is still close to the original dense neural network. The network size is reduced by 8Ã— and the time required to train the model remains constant. Additionally, we can prune a larger dense network to achieve better than baseline performance while still reducing the total number of parameters significantly. Pruning RNNs reduces the size of the model and can also help achieve significant inference time speed-up using sparse GEMMs. Benchmarks show that using our technique model size can be reduced by 90% and speed-up is around 2Ã— to 7Ã—.
review: This paper tackles the increasingly important problem of model compression for RNNs, and honestly, I think it's a solid and practical piece of work. The core idea—progressively pruning weights during training using a monotonically increasing threshold—is refreshingly simple, and the fact that it doesn't increase training time is a huge practical advantage over methods that require retraining after pruning. The results on speech recognition are convincing: they achieve 90% sparsity with modest accuracy loss, and by starting with a larger dense model and pruning down, they can actually beat the baseline dense model's accuracy while still having fewer parameters (e.g., the sparse 3072-unit model achieves 3.95% relative improvement over the 1760-unit dense baseline with only 16.7M parameters versus 67M). The speedups from sparse matrix operations are real, though I'm a bit underwhelmed—cuSPARSE only gives 2-7x speedup despite 95% sparsity, which suggests the library is leaving a lot of performance on the table; a better implementation could likely do much better, and the paper acknowledges this. The observation that earlier layers get pruned more aggressively than later ones is interesting and suggests the final layers are more sensitive, which is worth investigating further. I also appreciate the comparison to hard pruning, showing that gradual pruning is 7-9% better—that's a useful guideline for practitioners. However, I have some reservations. First, the hyperparameter tuning for the pruning schedule seems quite heuristic—choosing start_itr, ramp_itr, end_itr, and the slopes based on "we use" rather than a principled method feels ad hoc, and the need to pre-train a model to estimate the 90th percentile weight value for q adds an extra step that isn't fully justified. Second, the experiments are limited to speech recognition; I'd like to see how this generalizes to language modeling or machine translation, where RNNs are also heavily used. Third, the comparison to a smaller dense model (704 units) shows that pruning a larger model is better than training a smaller one from scratch, which is a nice result, but the paper doesn't explore why this is the case—is it because the initial dense training provides a better starting point, or because the pruning process itself acts as a form of regularization? Fourth, the persistent RNN discussion is interesting but speculative—the paper doesn't actually implement or benchmark the 146x speedup they claim, which feels a bit hand-wavy. Finally, the method doesn't incorporate any structural sparsity constraints, so the resulting sparse matrices are unstructured, which limits the efficiency gains on hardware that prefers block-sparse patterns. That said, this is a well-executed and practical paper that addresses a real deployment bottleneck, with clear results and a method that's easy to implement. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to provide more principled hyperparameter selection guidelines and to explore structural sparsity for even better hardware efficiency.

title: Lossy Image Compression with Compressive Autoencoders
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a new approach to the problem of optimizing autoencoders for lossy image compression. New media formats, changing hardware technology, as well as diverse requirements and content types create a need for compression algorithms which are more flexible than existing codecs. Autoencoders have the potential to address this need, but are difficult to optimize directly due to the inherent non-differentiabilty of the compression loss. We here show that minimal changes to the loss are sufficient to train deep autoencoders competitive with JPEG 2000 and outperforming recently proposed approaches based on RNNs. Our network is furthermore computationally efficient thanks to a sub-pixel architecture, which makes it suitable for high-resolution images. This is in contrast to previous work on autoencoders for compression using coarser approximations, shallower architectures, computationally expensive methods, or focusing on small images.
review: This paper tackles lossy image compression with autoencoders, and honestly, I think it's a significant step forward for the field. The core challenge—quantization being non-differentiable—is handled with a refreshingly simple solution: keep rounding in the forward pass but pass gradients through as if it were the identity. This is clever because it preserves the information bottleneck while still letting gradients flow, and it avoids the weird artefacts that additive noise or stochastic rounding introduce. The sub-pixel architecture is also smart—operating in downsampled space makes the network computationally efficient enough for high-resolution images, which is a big deal compared to RNN-based methods that are painfully slow. The results are genuinely impressive: they beat JPEG 2000 on SSIM and in a mean opinion score test, and they're competitive on PSNR. The incremental training strategy and scale parameter finetuning for variable bit rates are nice practical touches. However, I have some reservations. First, the gradient trick is essentially a hack—it works empirically, but the paper doesn't provide much theoretical justification for why the identity is the right choice, and I wonder if more sophisticated approximations could do even better. Second, the entropy model is just independent Gaussian scale mixtures, which is fine but not state-of-the-art; more powerful autoregressive models like PixelCNN could likely improve compression further. Third, the ensemble of multiple autoencoders for different bit rates is computationally expensive at encoding time—they have to run several networks and pick the best, which isn't ideal for real-time applications. Fourth, while the MOS test shows CAE beating JPEG 2000 at higher bit rates, the difference at 0.25 bpp is not significant, and the artefacts—like Gabor-like patterns and occasional discolouration—are noticeable in the examples. Finally, the paper doesn't explore perceptual metrics beyond SSIM, and optimizing for more sophisticated perceptual losses (like VGG-based features or GANs) is left as future work, which feels like a missed opportunity given how impactful those have been in super-resolution. That said, this is a well-executed, practical paper with strong empirical results and a method that's easy to implement. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to explore more powerful entropy models and perceptual losses in future work.

title: Structured Attention Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Attention networks have proven to be an effective approach for embedding categorical inference within a deep neural network. However, for many tasks we may want to model richer structural dependencies without abandoning end-to-end training. In this work, we experiment with incorporating richer structural distributions, encoded using graphical models, within deep networks. We show that these structured attention networks are simple extensions of the basic attention procedure, and that they allow for extending attention beyond the standard soft-selection approach, such as attending to partial segmentations or to subtrees. We experiment with two different classes of structured attention networks: a linear-chain conditional random field and a graph-based parsing model, and describe how these models can be practically implemented as neural network layers. Experiments show that this approach is effective for incorporating structural biases, and structured attention networks outperform baseline attention models on a variety of synthetic and real tasks: tree transduction, neural machine translation, question answering, and natural language inference. We further find that models trained in this way learn interesting unsupervised hidden representations that generalize simple attention.
review: This paper introduces structured attention networks, and honestly, I think it's one of the more thoughtful extensions to attention mechanisms I've seen in a while. The core idea—that standard soft attention is just a special case of a graphical model over latent variables, and that we can generalize it to CRFs and dependency parsers—is elegant and well-motivated. The paper does a great job laying out the framework, showing how to backprop through inference algorithms like forward-backward and inside-outside, and demonstrating that these structured layers can be dropped into existing architectures with minimal changes. The experiments are broad and generally convincing: on the synthetic tree transduction task, structured attention massively outperforms simple attention (99.2% vs 87.4% at depth 2, and the gap widens at deeper depths), which is a clear win. On Japanese-English translation, the segmentation CRF gives a solid 1.5 BLEU boost over simple attention on the character-to-word task, though the word-to-word gains are marginal. The QA experiments show that the binary CRF model matches or exceeds MemN2N on answer accuracy but crucially does much better at recovering the correct supporting facts—up to 2x better on some tasks—which suggests the model is actually learning the right reasoning chain rather than just exploiting spurious correlations. The NLI results are also positive, with structured attention outperforming both no-attention and simple-attention baselines, though the pretrained parser doing worse than training from scratch is an interesting and somewhat counterintuitive result. The technical implementation is solid—the algorithms for backprop through forward-backward and inside-outside in the signed log-space semifield are non-trivial and well-explained. However, I have some concerns. First, the computational cost is significant—structured attention is about 5x slower to train than simple attention in the NMT experiments, and the parsing model is O(n^3), which limits scalability to long sentences. Second, the improvements on the word-to-word translation task are tiny (14.3 vs 14.1 BLEU), which suggests the segmentation prior doesn't help much when the input is already segmented, and I wonder if the benefits are primarily on tasks with noisy or unsegmented inputs. Third, the CRF models in QA are fairly simple—just unary or pairwise potentials with linear interactions—and I'd like to see whether richer potentials or higher-order structure could yield further gains. Fourth, the paper doesn't deeply explore failure cases; for example, the syntactic attention layer learns plausible but imperfect parses, and it's unclear when the structured bias helps versus hurts. Finally, the connection to other work on differentiable inference and structured prediction could be stronger—there's related work on segmental RNNs and neural CRFs that the paper mentions but doesn't fully engage with. Overall, though, I think this is a well-executed paper with a compelling idea, strong empirical results across diverse tasks, and clear practical value. The framework is general and likely to be adopted by others. I recommend acceptance.

title: Zoneout: Regularizing RNNs by Randomly Preserving Hidden Activations
abstract: Abstract:###We propose zoneout, a novel method for regularizing RNNs. At each timestep, zoneout stochastically forces some hidden units to maintain their previous values. Like dropout, zoneout uses random noise to train a pseudo-ensemble, improving generalization. But by preserving instead of dropping hidden units, gradient information and state information are more readily propagated through time, as in feedforward stochastic depth networks. We perform an empirical investigation of various RNN regularizers, and find that zoneout gives significant performance improvements across tasks. We achieve competitive results with relatively simple models in character- and word-level language modelling on the Penn Treebank and Text8 datasets, and combining with recurrent batch normalization yields state-of-the-art results on permuted sequential MNIST.
review: This paper introduces zoneout, and honestly, I think it's a clever and well-motivated regularization technique for RNNs. The core idea—stochastically preserving hidden unit activations from the previous timestep instead of dropping them to zero—is simple but has a nice intuitive justification: it maintains information flow through time, which is exactly what you want in a recurrent network. The analogy to dropout as a special case (applying dropout to the state delta rather than the state itself) is elegant, and the connection to stochastic depth helps ground the method in existing literature. The empirical results are solid: on character-level Penn Treebank, zoneout achieves 1.252 BPC, which is competitive with state-of-the-art at the time (1.250 from HyperLSTM), and on Text8 it hits 1.336 BPC, beating both recurrent dropout and recurrent batch normalization. The pMNIST results are particularly striking—zoneout alone gives 6.9% error versus 7.5% for recurrent dropout, and when combined with recurrent batch normalization, they achieve 4.1% error, which was state-of-the-art. The gradient flow analysis is also compelling: the identity connections clearly propagate gradients much better to early timesteps than dropout does, which explains why zoneout works so well for long sequences. However, I have some reservations. First, the paper claims zoneout "significantly improves performance across tasks," but the gains on word-level Penn Treebank are modest—77.4 perplexity with zoneout plus non-recurrent dropout versus 78.4 with dropout alone, and they don't achieve the state-of-the-art 73.4 from variational dropout. Second, the method introduces additional hyperparameters (zoneout probabilities for cells and hidden states separately), and the optimal values vary widely across tasks—0.5 for cells on PTB but 0.15 for shared masks on pMNIST—which suggests the technique might be sensitive to tuning. Third, the paper doesn't provide a strong theoretical justification for why identity connections work better than zero-masking beyond the gradient flow argument, and I'd like to see a more formal analysis of how zoneout affects the optimization landscape or implicit regularization. Fourth, the comparison to stochastic depth in a recurrent setting is interesting, but they note it led to instability, and they don't fully explain why—is it because of parameter sharing, or something else? Fifth, the static identity connections experiment in the appendix shows that noise injection is essential, which is useful, but it also suggests that the benefits aren't just from the skip connections themselves but from the stochasticity, which muddies the interpretation a bit. Overall, though, this is a well-executed paper with a simple, effective idea, strong empirical results, and clear practical value. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to provide more guidance on hyperparameter selection and to explore the theoretical underpinnings further.

title: Deep Probabilistic Programming
abstract: Abstract:###We propose Edward, a Turing-complete probabilistic programming language. Edward defines two compositional representationsâ€”random variables and inference. By treating inference as a first class citizen, on a par with modeling, we show that probabilistic programming can be as flexible and computationally efficient as traditional deep learning. For flexibility, Edward makes it easy to fit the same model using a variety of composable inference methods, ranging from point estimation to variational inference to MCMC. In addition, Edward can reuse the modeling representation as part of inference, facilitating the design of rich variational models and generative adversarial networks. For efficiency, Edward is integrated into TensorFlow, providing significant speedups over existing probabilistic systems. For example, we show on a benchmark logistic regression task that Edward is at least 35x faster than Stan and 6x faster than PyMC3. Further, Edward incurs no runtime overhead: it is as fast as handwritten TensorFlow.
review: This paper introduces Edward, and honestly, I think it's a significant contribution to the probabilistic programming landscape. The key insight—treating inference as a first-class compositional object on par with modeling—is both elegant and practically powerful. Unlike traditional PPLs that treat inference as a black box, Edward lets users compose inference algorithms, swap out gradient estimators, build variational models that reuse the model's representation, and even do things like variational EM by alternating between two inference objects. The flexibility is genuinely impressive: the same language supports MAP, variational inference, MCMC, and GANs, all with a consistent, concise API. The integration with TensorFlow is a major win—the HMC benchmark showing 35x speedup over Stan and 6x over PyMC3 on logistic regression is dramatic, and the fact that Edward incurs "no runtime overhead" over handwritten TensorFlow is a strong engineering achievement. The examples are well-chosen and demonstrate real sophistication: VAEs with different gradient estimators, Bayesian RNNs with variable-length sequences, Dirichlet process mixtures with stochastic control flow. However, I have some reservations. First, the paper leans heavily on the "compositional" framing, but the theoretical foundations are somewhat shallow—they don't formally characterize what makes an inference algorithm composable or prove any properties about the resulting systems. Second, while the flexibility is a selling point, it's not clear how Edward handles the tricky parts of probabilistic programming like automatic differentiation of stochastic programs, or how it deals with non-differentiable inference (e.g., discrete latent variables beyond REINFORCE). Third, the stochastic control flow support is mentioned but the paper doesn't deeply address the challenges of inference on programs with dynamic structure—this is an open problem and the paper acknowledges it, but it limits the generality of the claims. Fourth, the "probability zoo" idea is nice but feels like a minor addition rather than a core contribution. Finally, the benchmarks are impressive but limited to HMC on logistic regression; I'd like to see more comprehensive comparisons on deep generative models or large-scale variational inference. That said, this is a well-executed, practical, and timely piece of work that bridges the gap between probabilistic programming and deep learning frameworks. The design is thoughtful, the implementation is solid, and the potential impact is high. I recommend acceptance.

title: LR-GAN: Layered Recursive Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Generation
abstract: Abstract:###We present LR-GAN: an adversarial image generation model which takes scene structure and context into account. Unlike previous generative adversarial networks (GANs), the proposed GAN learns to generate image background and foregrounds separately and recursively, and stitch the foregrounds on the background in a contextually relevant manner to produce a complete natural image. For each foreground, the model learns to generate its appearance, shape and pose. The whole model is unsupervised, and is trained in an end-to-end manner with conventional gradient descent methods. The experiments demonstrate that LR-GAN can generate more natural images with objects that are more human recognizable than baseline GANs.
review: This paper introduces LR-GAN, and honestly, I think it's a clever and well-motivated approach to image generation that explicitly models the layered structure of natural scenes. The core idea—generating background and foregrounds separately and recursively, with explicit factorization of appearance, shape (mask), and pose (affine transformation)—is elegant and addresses a fundamental limitation of standard GANs, which treat images as flat pixel arrays without any structural priors. The qualitative results are genuinely impressive: the model learns to disentangle foreground from background in a completely unsupervised way, producing clean object masks and contextually relevant placements (e.g., horses on grass, birds in the sky). The ablation studies convincingly demonstrate the importance of both the transformation and mask components—without transformations, the decomposition degenerates, and without masks, training on natural images fails to converge. The human evaluation results are strong, with LR-GAN being preferred 68.4% of the time over DCGAN on CUB-200, and the proposed Adversarial Accuracy and Divergence metrics provide a more principled way to compare generated distributions than the often-criticized Inception Score. However, I have some reservations. First, the model assumes the number of objects is known a priori, which is a significant limitation for real-world applicability—determining the number of layers dynamically would be a much harder but more useful problem. Second, while the results on CIFAR-10 show clear improvements over DCGAN, the generated images still have substantial artifacts and deformations; the fraction of non-recognizable images is 67.3% for LR-GAN vs 77.7% for DCGAN, but that's still far from the 11.4% for real images, so there's a long way to go. Third, the model is quite heavy—it has significantly more parameters than DCGAN (e.g., 27.3M vs 6.34M on CUB-200), and the training complexity is higher due to the recursive structure and multiple sub-generators. Fourth, the paper's reliance on pre-training a classifier for evaluation metrics introduces potential bias, and the Inception Score results are dataset-dependent (e.g., on MNIST, the scores are low because Inception is trained on ImageNet). Fifth, the conditional generation experiments (using LR-GAN for segmentation) are interesting but preliminary—the model learns to generate masks, but the quantitative evaluation is missing, and it's unclear how this compares to supervised segmentation methods.
