title: Sigma Delta Quantized Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Deep neural networks can be obscenely wasteful. When processing video, a convolutional network expends a fixed amount of computation for each frame with no regard to the similarity between neighbouring frames. As a result, it ends up repeatedly doing very similar computations. To put an end to such waste, we introduce Sigma-Delta networks. With each new input, each layer in this network sends a discretized form of its change in activation to the next layer. Thus the amount of computation that the network does scales with the amount of change in the input and layer activations, rather than the size of the network. We introduce an optimization method for converting any pre-trained deep network into an optimally efficient Sigma-Delta network, and show that our algorithm, if run on the appropriate hardware, could cut at least an order of magnitude from the computational cost of processing video data.
review: This paper introduces Sigma-Delta networks, and honestly, I think it's a clever and timely idea that addresses a real practical concern—the computational waste of processing every frame of video independently with a fixed-cost neural network. The core insight is elegant: by having neurons communicate discretized changes in activation rather than absolute values, the network's computational cost scales with the amount of change in the input rather than the network size. The mathematical equivalence proof showing that the Sigma-Delta network computes the same function as a rounding network is solid and gives the method theoretical grounding. The sparse dot-product decomposition (replacing multiplications with additions) is a nice efficiency trick, and the energy-saving numbers from Horowitz make a compelling case for potential hardware benefits. The Temporal-MNIST experiments clearly demonstrate the computational savings—the Sigma-Delta network uses significantly fewer operations than the rounding network on temporally redundant data for the same accuracy, and the VGG video experiment suggests roughly 4-11x savings on natural video, which is substantial. However, I have some reservations. First, the Temporal-MNIST dataset is a synthetic construction where similar frames are shuffled together; while it demonstrates the principle, it's a far cry from real video data with complex motion, occlusions, and scene changes. Second, the optimization method for finding the tradeoff between error and computation is heuristic—using straight-through estimation for gradients through rounding is standard, but the paper doesn't deeply analyze the stability of this optimization, and the authors note they had difficulty with VGG until they added uniform noise during training, which suggests brittleness. Third, the comparison to standard dense computation is a bit unfair because they count multiplications as expensive and additions as cheap, but on modern hardware (especially GPUs) matrix multiplications are highly optimized and memory bandwidth is often the bottleneck, so the actual speedup might be less dramatic than the FLOP counts suggest. Fourth, the VGG experiment only shows qualitative results on a few videos and doesn't provide a systematic evaluation across a large video dataset or a rigorous comparison to other efficient inference methods like sparsity-based approaches or early-exit networks. Finally, the paper doesn't address how to handle convolutions or other layer types beyond fully-connected networks in depth, though the VGG experiment suggests it's possible. Overall, I think this is a promising and well-motivated paper with a solid theoretical foundation and compelling proof-of-concept results, but the experimental validation is somewhat limited and the practical hardware implications are speculative. I'd recommend acceptance with encouragement to provide more extensive video benchmarks and a clearer discussion of how this method compares to other efficiency techniques.

title: A STRUCTURED SELF-ATTENTIVE SENTENCE EMBEDDING
abstract: Abstract:###This paper proposes a new model for extracting an interpretable sentence embedding by introducing self-attention. Instead of using a vector, we use a 2-D matrix to represent the embedding, with each row of the matrix attending on a different part of the sentence. We also propose a self-attention mechanism and a special regularization term for the model. As a side effect, the embedding comes with an easy way of visualizing what specific parts of the sentence are encoded into the embedding. We evaluate our model on 3 different tasks: author profiling, sentiment classification and textual entailment. Results show that our model yields a significant performance gain compared to other sentence embedding methods in all of the 3 tasks.
review: This paper introduces a structured self-attentive sentence embedding model, and honestly, I think it's a thoughtful and practically useful contribution to the sentence representation literature. The core idea—using a matrix of multiple attention heads instead of a single vector, with a regularization term that encourages diversity among the attention weights—is both elegant and effective. The penalization term (minimizing \(||AA^T - I||_F^2\)) is a clever way to force each row of the embedding to focus on different parts of the sentence while preventing redundancy, and the visualization capabilities that come with it are a genuine bonus for interpretability. The results are solid: on the Yelp sentiment task, the model achieves 64.21% accuracy versus 61.99% for BiLSTM+max pooling and 62.05% for CNN+max pooling; on the Age author profiling task, it gets 80.45% versus 77.40% and 78.15%; and on SNLI, it achieves 84.4%, competitive with the state-of-the-art NSE encoder's 84.6%. The ablation studies convincingly show that both the penalization term and the multi-vector matrix representation contribute to performance—the model with \(r=1\) (single vector) performs on-par with baselines, but performance jumps significantly when \(r\) is increased to 10 or more. The heatmap visualizations in Figures 2-4 are genuinely insightful, showing that the model learns to focus on sentiment-bearing phrases in reviews and that the penalization term reduces redundancy. However, I have some reservations. First, the model is supervised and task-specific—unlike SkipThought or FastSent, it can't be trained in an unsupervised setting, and the paper acknowledges this as a limitation without offering a clear path forward. Second, the improvements over baselines, while consistent, are modest—on SNLI, the gap to the state-of-the-art is only 0.2%, and the pruning experiments show that the performance gains come at the cost of a much larger model (55M parameters for the full model vs 4.1M for the pruned version, with a 0.35% accuracy drop). Third, the penalty term's effect is task-dependent—it helps on Yelp and Age but doesn't show a clear quantitative benefit on SNLI, which suggests the regularization might not be universally beneficial. Fourth, the model assumes a fixed number of attention hops \(r\), which is a hyperparameter that needs tuning, and the paper doesn't provide a principled way to choose it beyond empirical observation that values between 10 and 30 work well. Finally, the comparison to LSTMN is hand-wavy—the paper claims their attention is "less focused on relations between words" and more on "semantics of the whole sentence," but this distinction is not rigorously supported. Overall, I think this is a well-written paper with a clever idea, strong empirical results, and clear practical value, but the novelty is somewhat incremental and the model's reliance on supervision limits its generality. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to explore unsupervised variants and to provide more systematic guidance on hyperparameter selection.

title: Regularizing CNNs with Locally Constrained Decorrelations
abstract: Abstract:###Regularization is key for deep learning since it allows training more complex models while keeping lower levels of overfitting. However, the most prevalent regularizations do not leverage all the capacity of the models since they rely on reducing the effective number of parameters. Feature decorrelation is an alternative for using the full capacity of the models but the overfitting reduction margins are too narrow given the overhead it introduces. In this paper, we show that regularizing negatively correlated features is an obstacle for effective decorrelation and present OrthoReg, a novel regularization technique that locally enforces feature orthogonality. As a result, imposing locality constraints in feature decorrelation removes interferences between negatively correlated feature weights, allowing the regularizer to reach higher decorrelation bounds, and reducing the overfitting more effectively. In particular, we show that the models regularized with OrthoReg have higher accuracy bounds even when batch normalization and dropout are present. Moreover, since our regularization is directly performed on the weights, it is especially suitable for fully convolutional neural networks, where the weight space is constant compared to the feature map space. As a result, we are able to reduce the overfitting of state-of-the-art CNNs on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN.
review: This paper introduces OrthoReg, a novel regularization technique for CNNs, and honestly, I think it's a clever and well-executed idea that addresses a subtle but important limitation of existing decorrelation-based regularizers. The core insight—that penalizing negatively correlated feature weights is counterproductive because such correlations are actually useful for competitive learning and inhibitory connections—is both biologically plausible and empirically validated. The proposed local loss (eq. 7) with the squashing function that effectively ignores angles greater than π/2 is a simple but effective fix to the global cosine similarity loss used in prior work like DeCov. The results are solid: on MNIST, OrthoReg reduces error from 1.74% to 1.45%; on CIFAR-10 with a 110-layer ResNet, it improves from 6.55% to 6.29%; and on wide ResNet v2, it achieves 3.69% error on CIFAR-10 and 18.56% on CIFAR-100, setting new state-of-the-art results. The SVHN result of 1.54% is also impressive. I particularly appreciate the computational efficiency—regularizing weights rather than activations is orders of magnitude faster (Table 1), making this practical for large models. The toy 2D visualization (Figure 2) beautifully illustrates the difference between global and local regularization, and the analysis of AlexNet, VGG-16, and ResNet weights (Figure 3) shows that OrthoReg indeed reaches higher decorrelation bounds. However, I have some reservations. First, the improvements over strong baselines (especially with dropout and batch normalization already present) are modest—0.2-0.5% absolute error reduction on CIFAR-10, which, while statistically meaningful, may not be practically significant for many applications. Second, the paper doesn't deeply explore why negative correlations are useful beyond citing neuroscientific evidence; a more rigorous information-theoretic or optimization analysis would strengthen the contribution. Third, the hyperparameter λ is set empirically to 10, but the paper doesn't provide much guidance on how to tune it for different architectures or datasets. Fourth, the method assumes normalized weight vectors, which means the regularization only affects angles, not magnitudes—this is sensible, but the paper could discuss more explicitly how this interacts with weight decay. Finally, the experiments are on relatively small datasets (CIFAR, SVHN); I'd like to see results on ImageNet to demonstrate scalability. Overall, I think this is a well-motivated, technically sound, and practically useful contribution to the regularization literature. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to provide more theoretical justification for the local loss and to explore the interaction with different activation functions in future work.

title: The Concrete Distribution: A Continuous Relaxation of Discrete Random Variables
abstract: Abstract:###The reparameterization trick enables optimizing large scale stochastic computation graphs via gradient descent. The essence of the trick is to refactor each stochastic node into a differentiable function of its parameters and a random variable with fixed distribution. After refactoring, the gradients of the loss propagated by the chain rule through the graph are low variance unbiased estimators of the gradients of the expected loss. While many continuous random variables have such reparameterizations, discrete random variables lack useful reparameterizations due to the discontinuous nature of discrete states. In this work we introduce Concrete random variables -- continuous relaxations of discrete random variables. The Concrete distribution is a new family of distributions with closed form densities and a simple reparameterization. Whenever a discrete stochastic node of a computation graph can be refactored into a one-hot bit representation that is treated continuously, Concrete stochastic nodes can be used with automatic differentiation to produce low-variance biased gradients of objectives (including objectives that depend on the log-probability of latent stochastic nodes) on the corresponding discrete graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Concrete relaxations on density estimation and structured prediction tasks using neural networks.
review: This paper introduces the Concrete distribution, a continuous relaxation of discrete random variables via a softmax of Gumbel perturbations, and honestly, I think it's a significant and well-executed contribution to the stochastic gradient estimation literature. The core idea is both elegant and practically useful: replace the non-differentiable argmax in the Gumbel-Max trick with a softmax at a temperature λ, yielding a distribution over the simplex with a closed-form density, a simple reparameterization, and the property that its zero-temperature limit recovers the original discrete distribution. The theoretical analysis is thorough—Proposition 1 establishes key properties including the density, rounding behavior, and log-convexity for low temperatures, and the binary special case is handled cleanly. The experimental results are solid: on density estimation and structured prediction tasks with MNIST and Omniglot, Concrete relaxations are competitive with VIMCO, sometimes outperforming (e.g., on non-linear models for density estimation and broadly on structured prediction) and sometimes underperforming, but crucially they "just work" with automatic differentiation without special-casing. The paper also provides valuable practical guidance on implementing Concrete relaxations, including the use of ExpConcrete in log-space to avoid underflow and the importance of relaxing both the stochastic node and the log-probability terms in variational objectives. However, I have some reservations. First, the method introduces bias with respect to the discrete objective—the gradients are unbiased only for the relaxed continuous surrogate, not the original discrete graph—and the paper doesn't fully characterize when this bias is harmful or how it trades off against the variance reduction. Second, the temperature hyperparameter is critical and the choice is dataset- and model-dependent; the paper provides a conservative guideline (λ ≤ 1/(n-1) for log-convexity) but doesn't offer a principled way to tune it, and they don't explore temperature annealing, which could improve performance. Third, the experiments are limited to relatively small-scale models with binary and low-ary discrete variables; I'd like to see how this scales to larger discrete spaces or more complex architectures. Fourth, the comparison to VIMCO is fair, but the paper doesn't compare to other related relaxations like the straight-through estimator or the concurrent Gumbel-Softmax work (Jang et al. 2016), which the paper acknowledges but doesn't empirically contrast. Finally, the practical implementation details are somewhat buried in the appendix; the main paper could be clearer about the exact relaxed objective they optimize and how they handle the KL term. Overall, I think this is a high-quality paper with a clean theoretical contribution, practical utility, and solid empirical results, but the bias-variance trade-off and hyperparameter sensitivity warrant further investigation. I recommend acceptance.

title: Unrolled Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a method to stabilize Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) by defining the generator objective with respect to an unrolled optimization of the discriminator. This allows training to be adjusted between using the optimal discriminator in the generator*s objective, which is ideal but infeasible in practice, and using the current value of the discriminator, which is often unstable and leads to poor solutions. We show how this technique solves the common problem of mode collapse, stabilizes training of GANs with complex recurrent generators, and increases diversity and coverage of the data distribution by the generator.
review: This paper introduces unrolled GANs, and honestly, I think it's one of the most sensible and effective fixes to the mode collapse problem I've seen in a while. The core idea is beautifully simple—instead of updating the generator against the current discriminator (which encourages collapse to a point), backpropagate through several steps of discriminator optimization so the generator can anticipate how the discriminator will respond. This gives the generator an incentive to spread its mass, because the discriminator will "chase" any collapse and make it less rewarding. The theoretical framing via the missing gradient term (Eq. 12) is clear: standard GAN training uses only the first term, which causes collapse; the second term captures how the discriminator would react, and it disappears at K=0 and K→∞, but in between it provides useful stabilizing information. The empirical results are compelling across a range of setups—on the toy 2D mixture of Gaussians, unrolling turns a rotating, non-convergent mess into a stable spread covering all modes; on the challenging RNN generator + conv discriminator MNIST setup, unrolling rescues training entirely; and on the 1,000-mode augmented MNIST task, 10 unrolling steps cover 77% more modes and reduce reverse KL from 0.174 to 0.075. The CIFAR-10 experiments are particularly convincing—while visual quality is similar (Figure 4), the optimization-based reconstruction experiments (Figure 5, Table 3) show that unrolled models can reconstruct training images much better, indicating they cover more of the data manifold. The pairwise distance histograms (Figure 6) provide further evidence: the 0-step model's samples are skewed toward small distances (mode collapse), while 10-step models match the data distribution. I appreciate the ablation in Appendix B showing that the second gradient term matters when the discriminator lags behind the generator, and that historical averaging doesn't work as well. My main criticisms are: (1) the computational cost scales linearly with K, which is a real practical limitation; (2) the method is somewhat architecture-dependent—it works great on the RNN+conv mismatch but the CIFAR-10 gains are more modest; (3) the paper doesn't provide a principled way to choose K—it's empirical; (4) the "mode coverage" metrics in the augmented MNIST experiment rely on a pre-trained classifier, which could introduce bias; and (5) the paper could more clearly discuss the relationship to other stabilizers like gradient penalties or spectral normalization, which have since become standard. That said, this is a well-executed, theoretically grounded, and practically useful contribution that directly addresses one of GANs' most notorious failure modes. I strongly recommend acceptance.

title: TopicRNN: A Recurrent Neural Network with Long-Range Semantic Dependency
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we propose TopicRNN, a recurrent neural network (RNN)-based language model designed to directly capture the global semantic meaning relating words in a document via latent topics. Because of their sequential nature, RNNs are good at capturing the local structure of a word sequence â€“ both semantic and syntactic â€“ but might face difficulty remembering long-range dependencies. Intuitively, these long-range dependencies are of semantic nature. In contrast, latent topic models are able to capture the global underlying semantic structure of a document but do not account for word ordering. The proposed TopicRNN model integrates the merits of RNNs and latent topic models: it captures local (syntactic) dependencies using an RNN and global (semantic) dependencies using latent topics. Unlike previous work on contextual RNN language modeling, our model is learned end-to-end. Empirical results on word prediction show that TopicRNN outperforms existing contextual RNN baselines. In addition, TopicRNN can be used as an unsupervised feature extractor for documents. We do this for sentiment analysis on the IMDB movie review dataset and report an error rate of 6.28%. This is comparable to the state-of-the-art 5.91% resulting from a semi-supervised approach. Finally, TopicRNN also yields sensible topics, making it a useful alternative to document models such as latent Dirichlet allocation.
review: This paper introduces TopicRNN, a hybrid model that combines RNNs with latent topic models to capture both local syntactic and global semantic dependencies, and honestly, I think it's a well-executed and practical contribution to language modeling. The core idea is intuitive and effective: use a variational autoencoder to infer a document-level topic vector that biases the RNN's word predictions, with a clever stop-word mechanism to prevent semantically empty words from corrupting the topic representation. The architecture is clean—the topic vector enters as an additive bias to the softmax (not the hidden state), which provides a clear separation of global semantics and local dynamics, and the inference network (a feed-forward MLP on bag-of-words features) is simple yet effective. The results are solid: on Penn Treebank, TopicRNN achieves 166.7 perplexity with 10 neurons versus 187.4 for the contextual RNN baseline, and the gains hold at 100 and 300 neurons. On IMDB sentiment analysis, the model extracts unsupervised features that achieve 6.28% error, close to the state-of-the-art 5.91% from a semi-supervised method, and the visualizations of topics and generated text are qualitatively convincing. The end-to-end training is a clear improvement over previous contextual RNNs that required pre-trained topic features. However, I have some reservations. First, the stop-word detection is based on a pre-defined list, which is a bit ad-hoc—a learned, dynamic mechanism would be more principled and the paper acknowledges this as future work. Second, the inference network depends on the full document's bag-of-words, which means perplexity computation requires a sliding window approximation that isn't fully online; this is fine for offline evaluation but limits real-time applications. Third, the comparison to Mikolov and Zweig (2012) is somewhat dated; more recent baselines like larger LSTMs or Transformer-based models would be stronger comparisons, though I understand the paper is framing this as a contextual RNN extension. Fourth, the computational cost is non-trivial—the inference network adds significant overhead, and the 78-hour training on a MacBook Pro for the IMDB experiment suggests scalability might be an issue for larger datasets. Finally, the paper doesn't deeply explore the interaction between the topic vector and the RNN's hidden state—does the RNN learn to rely less on its own memory for long-range dependencies? Some analysis of hidden state dynamics would strengthen the contribution. Overall, I think this is a solid, well-motivated paper with clear empirical gains and an elegant integration of topics and RNNs. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to address the stop-word limitation and provide more analysis of the model's internal behavior in future work.

title: Frustratingly Short Attention Spans in Neural Language Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###Current language modeling architectures often use recurrent neural networks. Recently, various methods for incorporating differentiable memory into these architectures have been proposed. When predicting the next token, these models query information from a memory of the recent history and thus can facilitate learning mid- and long-range dependencies. However, conventional attention models produce a single output vector per time step that is used for predicting the next token as well as the key and value of a differentiable memory of the history of tokens. In this paper, we propose a key-value attention mechanism that produces separate representations for the key and value of a memory, and for a representation that encodes the next-word distribution. This usage of past memories outperforms existing memory-augmented neural language models on two corpora. Yet, we found that it mainly utilizes past memory only of the previous five representations. This led to the unexpected main finding that a much simpler model which simply uses a concatenation of output representations from the previous three-time steps is on par with more sophisticated memory-augmented neural language models.
review: This paper investigates memory-augmented neural language models and makes a simple but important observation: despite all the sophisticated attention mechanisms, these models end up paying attention mostly to the immediately preceding few tokens. The Key-Value-Predict attention model they propose—splitting the LSTM output into separate key, value, and prediction representations—is a clean and principled extension that outperforms existing attentive LMs on the Wikipedia corpus (75.8 perplexity vs 80.1 for RM+TM-g and 82.0 for standard attention). However, the real contribution is the negative result: when they analyze the attention weights, they find that even the best model only looks back about five steps, and a trivial N-gram RNN that simply concatenates the previous three output representations performs on par with the more sophisticated architectures (75.9 perplexity for the 4-gram RNN vs 75.8 for Key-Value-Predict). This is a valuable finding because it highlights a genuine challenge in training neural LMs to exploit long-range dependencies, despite the theoretical capacity of attention mechanisms. The experiments on both the Wikipedia corpus and CBT are thorough, and they carefully control for parameter count across models. I appreciate that they reimplemented several baselines (RM+TM-g, HORNNs) for a fair comparison. My main criticism is that the paper is somewhat frustrating in its own right—it tells us that attention fails to learn long-range dependencies but doesn't offer a compelling solution beyond the N-gram RNN. The analysis of why the attention fails (e.g., gradient issues, optimization difficulties) is shallow; they could have explored whether curriculum learning, different memory structures, or explicit regularization could encourage longer-term memory usage. Also, the CBT results are weaker because the models are evaluated as language models on a cloze task, and many of the comparisons are to QA-specific models that are not directly comparable. Overall, I think this is a well-executed paper with a clear, surprising, and important result that the community should be aware of. It's not groundbreaking in terms of new methods, but the negative result is genuinely useful. I recommend acceptance.

title: Recurrent Hidden Semi-Markov Model
abstract: Abstract:###Segmentation and labeling of high dimensional time series data has wide applications in behavior understanding and medical diagnosis. Due to the difficulty in obtaining the label information for high dimensional data, realizing this objective in an unsupervised way is highly desirable. Hidden Semi-Markov Model (HSMM) is a classical tool for this problem. However, existing HSMM and its variants has simple conditional assumptions of observations, thus the ability to capture the nonlinear and complex dynamics within segments is limited. To tackle this limitation, we propose to incorporate the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to model the generative process in HSMM, resulting the Recurrent HSMM (R-HSMM). To accelerate the inference while preserving accuracy, we designed a structure encoding function to mimic the exact inference. By generalizing the penalty method to distribution space, we are able to train the model and the encoding function simultaneously. Empirical results show that the proposed R-HSMM achieves the state-of-the-art performances on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
review: This paper introduces Recurrent HSMM, and honestly, I think it's a significant step forward for unsupervised sequence segmentation. The core idea—replacing the simplistic emission model of traditional HSMMs with an RNN that captures complex within-segment dependencies—is both natural and powerful, and the results speak for themselves: on the synthetic sine/GP tasks, R-HSMM achieves 2.67% and 12.46% error versus 41% and 41% for vanilla HSMM, and on real-world tasks like human activity and Drosophila it outperforms strong baselines by large margins (16.38% vs 41.59% for HSMM, 36.21% vs 47.37% for subHSMM). The structured VAE framework with a bidirectional RNN encoder is a clever way to approximate the expensive dynamic programming inference, and the 400x speedup with only a ~1-2% accuracy drop is practically important. I also appreciate the stochastic distributional penalty method for handling discrete latent variables in VAE—it's a novel extension of the penalty method to distribution space and seems to work better than off-the-shelf stochastic neuron techniques. The reconstruction visualizations convincingly show that the generative RNNs learn the distinct characteristics of different segment types. However, I have some reservations. First, the method requires pre-specifying the number of states K and maximum duration D, which limits applicability to truly unsupervised settings where these are unknown. Second, the penalty method with λ annealing is theoretically sound but adds complexity and hyperparameters; the paper doesn't thoroughly explore sensitivity to λ. Third, the comparison to CRF-AE is somewhat weak—that model is more similar to HMM than HSMM and doesn't model duration explicitly. Fourth, the baseline HSMM variants like HDP-HSMM and subHSMM use Gaussian emissions, which are clearly insufficient for the complex patterns in these datasets, so the improvement is perhaps not surprising. Fifth, the paper doesn't compare to more recent neural sequence segmentation methods like segmental RNNs or RNN transducers. That said, the combination of HSMM structure with RNN emissions is elegant and well-executed, the empirical results are strong across multiple domains, and the inference speedup is a genuine practical contribution. I recommend acceptance.

title: Deep Variational Bayes Filters: Unsupervised Learning of State Space Models from Raw Data
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce Deep Variational Bayes Filters (DVBF), a new method for unsupervised learning and identification of latent Markovian state space models. Leveraging recent advances in Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes, DVBF can overcome intractable inference distributions via variational inference. Thus, it can handle highly nonlinear input data with temporal and spatial dependencies such as image sequences without domain knowledge. Our experiments show that enabling backpropagation through transitions enforces state space assumptions and significantly improves information content of the latent embedding. This also enables realistic long-term prediction.
review: This paper introduces Deep Variational Bayes Filters (DVBF), and honestly, I think it's a significant and well-executed contribution to the unsupervised learning of dynamical systems from high-dimensional data. The core idea—backpropagating gradients through the state transition to force the latent space to obey Markovian state-space assumptions—is both elegant and effective, addressing a key limitation of prior work like Deep Kalman Filters where the transition is only softly regularized via KL divergence. The reparameterization of the transition (making it deterministic given stochastic parameters β_t) is a clever trick that enables gradient flow through time, and the results speak for themselves: on the pendulum experiment, DVBF learns a latent space where angular velocity is strongly encoded (R²=0.916 for velocity prediction), whereas DKF fails almost entirely (R²=0.035). The visualizations of the latent space are particularly compelling—the polar-coordinate embedding of the pendulum angle and the checkerboard encoding of the bouncing ball position show that the model is genuinely recovering the underlying physical state. The generative sampling results, with stable long-term predictions beyond training sequence length, are impressive and demonstrate that the model has learned a meaningful dynamical system rather than just a good autoencoder. I also appreciate the locally linear transition parametrization, which provides a nice balance between flexibility and interpretability. However, I have some reservations. First, the paper only compares to DKF and doesn't include other strong baselines like E2C or VRNN, which would help position the contribution more clearly. Second, the computational cost is significant—the annealing schedule and the need to backprop through long sequences make this expensive, and the paper doesn't discuss training time or scalability. Third, the experiments are on relatively simple simulated environments (pendulum, bouncing balls) with low-resolution images; I'd like to see results on more complex datasets or real-world data to assess generalization. Fourth, the locally linear transition assumption, while reasonable, is still a limitation—the model can't handle arbitrary nonlinear dynamics without a more flexible transition function. Finally, the paper could benefit from a more thorough ablation study (e.g., the effect of the annealing schedule, the impact of the transition priors). That said, this is a well-written, theoretically grounded paper with strong empirical results and clear practical implications for model-based reinforcement learning and control. I recommend acceptance.

title: Generative Multi-Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a framework for producing a generative model by way of a two-player minimax game. In this paper, we propose the emph{Generative Multi-Adversarial Network} (GMAN), a framework that extends GANs to multiple discriminators. In previous work, the successful training of GANs requires modifying the minimax objective to accelerate training early on. In contrast, GMAN can be reliably trained with the original, untampered objective. We explore a number of design perspectives with the discriminator role ranging from formidable adversary to forgiving teacher. Image generation tasks comparing the proposed framework to standard GANs demonstrate GMAN produces higher quality samples in a fraction of the iterations when measured by a pairwise GAM-type metric.
review: This paper introduces Generative Multi-Adversarial Networks (GMAN) with multiple discriminators, and honestly, I think it's a practical and well-motivated extension of the GAN framework that addresses a genuine training difficulty. The core observation—that a single overpowering discriminator can starve the generator of useful gradient information—is valid, and the proposed softmax aggregation over an ensemble of discriminators is a clean way to mitigate this. The fact that GMAN can be trained with the original generator objective \(\log(1-D)\) rather than the modified \(-\log(D)\) is a nice bonus, and the analysis showing that the gradient magnitude vanishes only when all discriminators agree (which is unlikely for large \(N\)) is a solid contribution. The GMAM evaluation metric is a reasonable extension of GAM for multi-discriminator settings, and the results show consistent acceleration: GMAN with 5 discriminators reaches steady state roughly 2x faster than standard GAN on MNIST, CelebA, and CIFAR-10, with reduced variance. The GMAN* variant that lets the generator automatically tune the softmax temperature \(\lambda\) is also clever—the plot in Figure 6 showing \(\lambda\) starting low (lenient teacher) and then increasing (harsher critic) as training progresses is exactly the kind of adaptive curriculum learning you'd hope for. The image samples look noticeably better at earlier epochs, and the GMAM scores indicate GMAN* outperforms fixed \(\lambda\) variants. However, I have some reservations. First, the diversity mechanism for discriminators—varying dropout and network depth—feels ad hoc; the paper doesn't provide a principled way to ensure discriminators are sufficiently diverse, and the boosting experiments failed, which suggests the approach is sensitive to how the ensemble is constructed. Second, the claim that GMAN "makes using the original GAN objective possible" is a bit overstated—you can use the original objective with a single discriminator too, it just suffers from vanishing gradients; GMAN mitigates this but doesn't eliminate it. Third, the evaluation is primarily on relatively simple datasets (MNIST, CelebA, CIFAR-10) and the Inception scores on CIFAR-10 are decent but not state-of-the-art (6.0 vs 7.0+ in modern methods). Fourth, the GMAM metric, while intuitive, relies on the aggregator function \(F\) which is model-specific, making cross-variant comparisons somewhat circular—a model that uses mean aggregation will naturally look better when evaluated with mean aggregation. Finally, the computational cost scales linearly with \(N\), which is a tradeoff the paper acknowledges but doesn't thoroughly quantify in terms of wall-clock time. Overall, I think this is a solid, practical paper with a clear contribution, thoughtful design choices, and convincing empirical evidence that multiple discriminators can accelerate and stabilize GAN training. I recommend acceptance.

title: Mollifying Networks
abstract: Abstract:###The optimization of deep neural networks can be more challenging than the traditional convex optimization problems due to highly non-convex nature of the loss function, e.g. it can involve pathological landscapes such as saddle-surfaces that can be difficult to escape from for algorithms based on simple gradient descent. In this paper, we attack the problem of optimization of highly non-convex neural networks objectives by starting with a smoothed -- or mollified -- objective function which becomes more complex as the training proceeds. Our proposition is inspired by the recent studies in continuation methods: similarly to curriculum methods, we begin by learning an easier (possibly convex) objective function and let it evolve during training until it eventually becomes the original, difficult to optimize objective function. The complexity of the mollified networks is controlled by a single hyperparameter that is annealed during training. We show improvements on various difficult optimization tasks and establish a relationship between recent works on continuation methods for neural networks and mollifiers.
review: This paper introduces mollified networks, a clever approach to easing optimization in deep neural networks via a continuation method that gradually transitions from a convex/linear objective to the original non-convex one. The core idea—using a stochastic depth-like mechanism with noisy activations controlled by a single annealing parameter p—is conceptually elegant and connects nicely to prior work on curriculum learning, continuation methods, and noisy activation functions. The empirical results are promising: on the 40-bit parity task, mollified networks converge faster than residual networks with batch norm; on CIFAR-10 with 110-layer convnets, they achieve 92.45% test accuracy vs 91.78% for ResNet (though stochastic depth does better at 93.25%); and on PTB language modeling, a mollified LSTM achieves 123.6 PPL vs 128.4 for a standard LSTM. The idea of starting with a simpler model and gradually increasing complexity is well-motivated, and the connection to mollifiers (smoothing kernels) is mathematically sound. However, I have several concerns. First, the paper is poorly written and extremely difficult to follow—the notation is inconsistent, the derivations are rushed, and Algorithm 1 is cryptic. The connection between the generalized mollifier definition and the actual implementation is not clearly established; in particular, the claim that p^l → 1 yields a convex objective is asserted but not proven. Second, the empirical gains are modest and the comparisons are not always fair—the LSTM language modeling experiment uses a 2-layer LSTM without any regularization, which is a weak baseline; the CIFAR-10 result is worse than stochastic depth, and the paper doesn't explain why their method might be complementary or how it compares to other modern techniques like scheduled sampling or gradient noise. Third, the annealing schedule depends on a moving average of the loss, which introduces an extra hyperparameter and could cause instability; the paper doesn't analyze sensitivity to this. Fourth, the method is computationally expensive due to the stochastic decisions at each unit and the noise sampling, but no runtime comparisons are provided. Finally, the theoretical contribution feels superficial—the paper defines mollifiers but doesn't provide a rigorous convergence analysis or characterize the optimization landscape of the mollified objective. Overall, while the idea is interesting and the results are positive, the paper lacks clarity, strong empirical validation, and theoretical depth. I'd recommend rejection in its current form, but I think the core concept has potential if the authors can clarify the method and provide more convincing experiments.

title: beta-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework
abstract: Abstract:###Learning an interpretable factorised representation of the independent data generative factors of the world without supervision is an important precursor for the development of artificial intelligence that is able to learn and reason in the same way that humans do. We introduce beta-VAE, a new state-of-the-art framework for automated discovery of interpretable factorised latent representations from raw image data in a completely unsupervised manner. Our approach is a modification of the variational autoencoder (VAE) framework. We introduce an adjustable hyperparameter beta that balances latent channel capacity and independence constraints with reconstruction accuracy. We demonstrate that beta-VAE with appropriately tuned beta > 1 qualitatively outperforms VAE (beta = 1), as well as state of the art unsupervised (InfoGAN) and semi-supervised (DC-IGN) approaches to disentangled factor learning on a variety of datasets (celebA, faces and chairs). Furthermore, we devise a protocol to quantitatively compare the degree of disentanglement learnt by different models, and show that our approach also significantly outperforms all baselines quantitatively. Unlike InfoGAN, beta-VAE is stable to train, makes few assumptions about the data and relies on tuning a single hyperparameter, which can be directly optimised through a hyper parameter search using weakly labelled data or through heuristic visual inspection for purely unsupervised data.
review: This paper introduces β-VAE, and honestly, I think it's a significant and elegant contribution to unsupervised representation learning. The core idea—simply increasing the weight β on the KL divergence term in the VAE objective to impose a stronger bottleneck and independence prior—is almost laughably simple, yet the results are genuinely impressive. The qualitative comparisons on CelebA, chairs, and faces clearly show that β-VAE learns far more disentangled representations than the standard VAE, and even outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised (InfoGAN) and semi-supervised (DC-IGN) methods. The fact that β-VAE discovers factors like chair leg style (which InfoGAN misses) and provides smoother, more continuous latent traversals is a strong indicator that the approach is doing something fundamentally right. I also appreciate the theoretical framing via constrained optimization—it gives the β hyperparameter a principled interpretation as a Lagrange multiplier regulating latent channel capacity. The disentanglement metric they propose is a sensible attempt to quantify what has been largely qualitative, and the results on the synthetic 2D shapes dataset demonstrate that β-VAE approaches the performance of a supervised DC-IGN despite being completely unsupervised. The analysis showing the inverted-U relationship between β and disentanglement, and the need to normalize β by latent and input dimensions, provides practical guidance for practitioners. However, I have some reservations. First, the metric requires knowledge of ground truth generative factors, which limits its applicability to synthetic datasets—it's a useful diagnostic but not a solution for evaluating real-world performance. Second, the paper doesn't fully address the practical challenge of choosing β in a purely unsupervised setting without any labeled data; the suggestion of visual inspection is heuristic and may not scale. Third, the trade-off between disentanglement and reconstruction quality is acknowledged but not deeply explored—there's a tension between wanting good representations and wanting sharp reconstructions, and the paper doesn't provide a principled way to balance these. Fourth, while the qualitative results are compelling, the quantitative improvements over InfoGAN on the synthetic dataset are significant but the comparison is somewhat limited—InfoGAN struggles on this dataset, and it's not clear how β-VAE would fare on more complex GAN-friendly benchmarks. Finally, the paper doesn't fully characterize the conditions under which β-VAE fails—the appendix hints that data continuity matters, but this could be explored more thoroughly. Overall, I think this is a well-written, impactful paper that introduces a simple but powerful modification to a widely-used framework, with strong empirical evidence and a thoughtful evaluation protocol. I strongly recommend acceptance.

title: Offline bilingual word vectors, orthogonal transformations and the inverted softmax
abstract: Abstract:###Usually bilingual word vectors are trained *online**. Mikolov et al. showed they can also be found *offline*; whereby two pre-trained embeddings are aligned with a linear transformation, using dictionaries compiled from expert knowledge. In this work, we prove that the linear transformation between two spaces should be orthogonal. This transformation can be obtained using the singular value decomposition. We introduce a novel *inverted softmax* for identifying translation pairs, with which we improve the precision @1 of Mikolov*s original mapping from 34% to 43%, when translating a test set composed of both common and rare English words into Italian. Orthogonal transformations are more robust to noise, enabling us to learn the transformation without expert bilingual signal by constructing a *pseudo-dictionary* from the identical character strings which appear in both languages, achieving 40% precision on the same test set. Finally, we extend our method to retrieve the true translations of English sentences from a corpus of 200k Italian sentences with a precision @1 of 68%.
review: This paper provides a clean theoretical and empirical contribution to offline bilingual word vector learning, and honestly, I think it's one of the more satisfying pieces of work I've seen on this topic. The proof that the optimal linear transformation between normalized word vector spaces should be orthogonal is elegant and intuitive—the cartographer analogy is apt, and the SVD solution (essentially the orthogonal Procrustes problem) is both numerically exact and computationally efficient. The inverted softmax is a clever and effective fix for the hubness problem that Dinu et al. identified, and the results speak for themselves: boosting Mikolov's original mapping from 34% to 43% precision on the English-Italian test set is a significant jump. The most striking result, however, is the pseudo-dictionary approach using identical character strings—achieving 40% translation precision without any expert bilingual signal is genuinely surprising and demonstrates the robustness of the orthogonal transformation to noisy or low-quality dictionaries. The Europarl experiments are also impressive: learning the transformation from aligned sentences via simple summed sentence vectors and then using it for both word translation (43% precision) and sentence retrieval (68% precision) shows the approach is flexible and scalable. I appreciate the thorough comparison to previous methods (Mikolov, Dinu, CCA) and the careful breakdown by word frequency. My main criticisms are relatively minor. First, the paper doesn't deeply explore the limitations of the pseudo-dictionary approach—how does it perform for language pairs that share fewer identical strings, like English-Chinese? Second, the inverted softmax introduces a hyperparameter n_s that is somewhat ad hoc; the paper could provide more guidance on tuning it or a theoretical justification. Third, the sentence vectors are simple bag-of-words sums, which is fine for proof-of-concept, but more sophisticated sentence embeddings could likely improve the Europarl results. Fourth, the paper doesn't compare to more recent bilingual vector methods like VecMap or more advanced CCA variants, though the work appears to be contemporaneous with some of these. Finally, while the theory is clean, the practical takeaway that "orthogonal transformations are more robust" is empirically demonstrated but not fully explained—some analysis of why would strengthen the paper. Overall, this is a well-written, theoretically grounded, and empirically strong paper that makes a clear contribution to the bilingual vector literature. I recommend acceptance.

title: Visualizing Deep Neural Network Decisions: Prediction Difference Analysis
abstract: Abstract:###This article presents the prediction difference analysis method for visualizing the response of a deep neural network to a specific input. When classifying images, the method highlights areas in a given input image that provide evidence for or against a certain class. It overcomes several shortcoming of previous methods and provides great additional insight into the decision making process of classifiers. Making neural network decisions interpretable through visualization is important both to improve models and to accelerate the adoption of black-box classifiers in application areas such as medicine. We illustrate the method in experiments on natural images (ImageNet data), as well as medical images (MRI brain scans).
review: This paper presents a prediction difference analysis method for visualizing DNN decisions, and honestly, I think it's one of the most thoughtful and practical contributions to the interpretability literature I've seen. The core idea—measuring how the prediction changes when patches are "removed" by sampling from a conditional distribution—is probabilistically sound and addresses the major weaknesses of previous approaches. The three improvements over Robnik-Sikonja & Kononenko's original method are substantial: conditional sampling (replacing the crude independence assumption with a patch-based conditional model) is a game-changer for images, multivariate analysis (removing patches rather than individual pixels) is essential for high-dimensional data, and the extension to hidden layers opens up entirely new avenues for understanding what networks are actually learning. The results are genuinely impressive—the signed visualizations (red evidence for, blue evidence against) provide much richer insight than the usual saliency maps, and the hidden layer visualizations in Figure 5 and 6 are fascinating, showing how different feature maps specialize to different types of patterns. The comparison between marginal and conditional sampling in Figure 3 clearly demonstrates the superiority of the conditional approach, and the network comparison in Figure 8 reveals real architectural differences—AlexNet relies more on context, while VGG pays more attention to specific object parts. The medical imaging application is a compelling demonstration of practical value, though the classifier accuracy is modest (69%), which limits the clinical utility. My main criticisms are: (1) the computational cost is prohibitive for interactive use—20-70 minutes per image on a GPU is a significant barrier; (2) the conditional distribution is modeled with a simple multivariate normal, which could be improved with a more powerful generative model; (3) the medical evaluation lacks expert validation; (4) the paper doesn't thoroughly discuss how the patch size \(k\) should be chosen or whether the results are robust to this hyperparameter; (5) while the method is clearly better than sensitivity analysis (as shown in the appendix), a direct comparison to more recent methods like LRP or Integrated Gradients would strengthen the paper. Overall, this is a well-executed, thoughtful paper with a principled approach, strong empirical results, and clear practical applications. I recommend acceptance.

title: Categorical Reparameterization with Gumbel-Softmax
abstract: Abstract:###Categorical variables are a natural choice for representing discrete structure in the world. However, stochastic neural networks rarely use categorical latent variables due to the inability to backpropagate through samples. In this work, we present an efficient gradient estimator that replaces the non-differentiable sample from a categorical distribution with a differentiable sample from a novel Gumbel-Softmax distribution. This distribution has the essential property that it can be smoothly annealed into a categorical distribution. We show that our Gumbel-Softmax estimator outperforms state-of-the-art gradient estimators on structured output prediction and unsupervised generative modeling tasks with categorical latent variables, and enables large speedups on semi-supervised classification.
review: This paper introduces the Gumbel-Softmax distribution for reparameterizing categorical variables, and honestly, I think it's a significant and practically useful contribution to the stochastic gradient estimation literature. The key idea—replacing the non-differentiable argmax in the Gumbel-Max trick with a softmax at temperature τ—is elegantly simple, and the fact that this distribution smoothly interpolates between continuous and categorical sampling makes it a natural fit for end-to-end training. The empirical results are strong: on structured output prediction with categorical latent variables, Gumbel-Softmax achieves 59.0 nats vs 63.0 for MuProp and 61.1 for Annealed ST; on VAE training with categorical latents, it hits 101.5 nats vs 107.0 for MuProp and 110.9 for ST. The Straight-Through variant also performs well, often outperforming other biased estimators. I particularly appreciate the semi-supervised learning experiments—the speedup over marginalization is dramatic (nearly 10x for 100 classes), and the classification accuracy (93.6% with ST Gumbel) matches the marginalization baseline while being far more scalable. The density derivation in the appendix is clean, and the connection to the concurrent Concrete distribution (Maddison et al.) is properly acknowledged, though the paper could more clearly distinguish its contributions (the ST variant and the empirical focus on categorical variables). My main criticisms are: (1) the temperature annealing schedule is somewhat heuristic—the paper doesn't provide a principled way to choose τ or the annealing rate; (2) the Gumbel-Softmax estimator is biased for non-zero temperature, and the paper doesn't thoroughly analyze the bias-variance tradeoff; (3) the comparison to VIMCO is missing (though the paper notes it's for multi-sample objectives); (4) the categorical VAE experiment uses a learned prior rather than a Gumbel-Softmax prior, which technically means the training objective is not a variational lower bound—this is a bit hand-wavy. Overall, this is a well-executed, practical paper that provides a simple, effective tool for training networks with categorical latent variables, with strong empirical validation across multiple tasks. I recommend acceptance without hesitation.

title: Online Bayesian Transfer Learning for Sequential Data Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###We consider the problem of inferring a sequence of hidden states associated with a sequence of observations produced by an individual within a population. Instead of learning a single sequence model for the population (which does not account for variations within the population), we learn a set of basis sequence models based on different individuals. The sequence of hidden states for a new individual is inferred in an online fashion by estimating a distribution over the basis models that best explain the sequence of observations of this new individual. We explain how to do this in the context of hidden Markov models with Gaussian mixture models that are learned based on streaming data by online Bayesian moment matching. The resulting transfer learning technique is demonstrated with three real-word applications: activity recognition based on smartphone sensors, sleep classification based on electroencephalography data and the prediction of the direction of future packet flows between a pair of servers in telecommunication networks.
review: This paper tackles an important and practical problem—subject variability in sequential data—and honestly, I think the proposed online transfer learning framework is a solid contribution. The core idea of learning basis HMMs for different individuals and then estimating a distribution over these basis models for a new target in an online, unsupervised manner is both well-motivated and technically sound. The extension of Bayesian Moment Matching from Gaussian mixture models to HMMs with GMM emissions is a non-trivial piece of work, and the derivations in the appendix appear correct. The empirical results are impressive: on the activity recognition task, transfer learning outperforms the baseline on 15 out of 19 individuals, often by large margins (e.g., Person 6: 96.43% vs 73.98%); on sleep stage classification, it consistently beats both the BMM baseline and EM across all 142 patients; and on flow direction prediction, it's competitive or superior in most domains. The comparison to RNNs is also interesting—the RNNs perform poorly on activity recognition but better on the simpler traffic prediction task, which highlights the challenges of training RNNs and the value of the more structured HMM approach. However, I have some reservations. First, the method is computationally expensive: the target domain update step scales as O(K^2 N^2), which could be problematic for large numbers of source domains or hidden states. Second, the paper doesn't compare to more recent transfer learning baselines like domain adaptation or multi-task learning, which could be stronger competitors. Third, the RNN comparison feels somewhat tangential—the paper is about HMMs, and the RNN results are mixed and not systematically optimized (though they do a reasonable grid search). Fourth, the claimed novelty of "first online transfer learning technique" is a bit overstated; there's prior work on online domain adaptation and online multi-task learning. Finally, the paper could benefit from a clearer discussion of when the method is expected to work—it assumes the target can be expressed as a convex combination of basis models, which may not hold if the target exhibits entirely novel patterns. Overall, I think this is a well-executed paper with a sound theoretical foundation, strong empirical results across diverse applications, and clear practical relevance. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to discuss the limitations more explicitly and to consider scalability improvements.This paper tackles an important and practical problem—subject variability in sequential data—and honestly, I think the proposed online transfer learning framework is a solid contribution. The core idea of learning basis HMMs for different individuals and then estimating a distribution over these basis models for a new target in an online, unsupervised manner is both well-motivated and technically sound. The extension of Bayesian Moment Matching from Gaussian mixture models to HMMs with GMM emissions is a non-trivial piece of work, and the derivations in the appendix appear correct. The empirical results are impressive: on the activity recognition task, transfer learning outperforms the baseline on 15 out of 19 individuals, often by large margins (e.g., Person 6: 96.43% vs 73.98%); on sleep stage classification, it consistently beats both the BMM baseline and EM across all 142 patients; and on flow direction prediction, it's competitive or superior in most domains. The comparison to RNNs is also interesting—the RNNs perform poorly on activity recognition but better on the simpler traffic prediction task, which highlights the challenges of training RNNs and the value of the more structured HMM approach. However, I have some reservations. First, the method is computationally expensive: the target domain update step scales as O(K^2 N^2), which could be problematic for large numbers of source domains or hidden states. Second, the paper doesn't compare to more recent transfer learning baselines like domain adaptation or multi-task learning, which could be stronger competitors. Third, the RNN comparison feels somewhat tangential—the paper is about HMMs, and the RNN results are mixed and not systematically optimized (though they do a reasonable grid search). Fourth, the claimed novelty of "first online transfer learning technique" is a bit overstated; there's prior work on online domain adaptation and online multi-task learning. Finally, the paper could benefit from a clearer discussion of when the method is expected to work—it assumes the target can be expressed as a convex combination of basis models, which may not hold if the target exhibits entirely novel patterns. Overall, I think this is a well-executed paper with a sound theoretical foundation, strong empirical results across diverse applications, and clear practical relevance. I recommend acceptance, though I'd encourage the authors to discuss the limitations more explicitly and to consider scalability improvements.

title: Latent Sequence Decompositions
abstract: Abstract:###Sequence-to-sequence models rely on a fixed decomposition of the target sequences into a sequence of tokens that may be words, word-pieces or characters. The choice of these tokens and the decomposition of the target sequences into a sequence of tokens is often static, and independent of the input, output data domains. This can potentially lead to a sub-optimal choice of token dictionaries, as the decomposition is not informed by the particular problem being solved. In this paper we present Latent Sequence Decompositions (LSD), a framework in which the decomposition of sequences into constituent tokens is learnt during the training of the model. The decomposition depends both on the input sequence and on the output sequence. In LSD, during training, the model samples decompositions incrementally, from left to right by locally sampling between valid extensions. We experiment with the Wall Street Journal speech recognition task. Our LSD model achieves 12.9% WER compared to a character baseline of 14.8% WER. When combined with a convolutional network on the encoder, we achieve a WER of 9.6%.
review:
This paper introduces Latent Sequence Decompositions (LSD) for sequence-to-sequence models, and honestly, I think it's a clever and practically useful idea with solid empirical results. The core insight—that fixed, pre-defined decompositions of output sequences (like characters or wordpieces) may be suboptimal, and that the decomposition should be a function of both the input and output—is well-motivated and addresses a real limitation of current seq2seq models. The framework is elegantly formulated: marginalizing over latent decompositions during training, using a biased but effective left-to-right sampling procedure with epsilon-greedy exploration to escape local minima. The results on WSJ speech recognition are compelling: LSD with a 4-gram wordpiece vocabulary achieves 12.9% WER versus 14.8% for the character baseline, a 12.7% relative improvement, and when combined with a deep CNN encoder, they hit 9.6% WER—which is state-of-the-art for end-to-end models without a language model at the time. The analysis of decomposition distributions (Figure 1) is also illuminating—it shows that the model learns to use multi-character tokens for about 55% of characters, validating the idea that characters alone aren't optimal. I also appreciate the comparison to the Maximum Extension baseline, which performs worse than the character model, demonstrating that the "longest possible token" heuristic is not the right inductive bias. However, I have several reservations. First, the training procedure is biased and relies on a heuristic epsilon-greedy strategy—the paper acknowledges this but doesn't provide a rigorous justification or analysis of the bias. Second, the sampling from the posterior

Third, the epsilon-greedy schedule and the mix between uniform and model distribution are not clearly specified—how sensitive are the results to these hyperparameters? Fourth, the comparison to other variable-length output methods (like BPE or the original wordpiece models) is missing; the paper only compares to characters and MaxExt, which is a strawman. Fifth, the computational cost is high—5 days on 8 GPUs—and the paper doesn't discuss inference efficiency, which could be a concern for deployment. Finally, the evaluation is only on WSJ; I'd like to see how LSD generalizes to other tasks like machine translation or image captioning. Overall, I think this is a strong paper with a novel idea, solid results, and clear practical relevance, but the training procedure's bias and the lack of broader baselines are notable weaknesses. I recommend acceptance, but I'd encourage the authors to address the training approximation more rigorously and to evaluate on additional tasks in future work.

title: Paleo: A Performance Model for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Although various scalable deep learning software packages have been proposed, it remains unclear how to best leverage parallel and distributed computing infrastructure to accelerate their training and deployment. Moreover, the effectiveness of existing parallel and distributed systems varies widely based on the neural network architecture and dataset under consideration. In order to efficiently explore the space of scalable deep learning systems and quickly diagnose their effectiveness for a given problem instance, we introduce an analytical performance model called Paleo. Our key observation is that a neural network architecture carries with it a declarative specification of the computational requirements associated with its training and evaluation. By extracting these requirements from a given architecture and mapping them to a specific point within the design space of software, hardware and communication strategies, Paleo can efficiently and accurately model the expected scalability and performance of a putative deep learning system. We show that Paleo is robust to the choice of network architecture, hardware, software, communication schemes, and parallelization strategies. We further demonstrate its ability to accurately model various recently published scalability results for CNNs such as NiN, Inception and AlexNet.
review: This paper addresses the problem of predicting the performance of deep neural network training and inference across a wide range of hardware, software, and parallelization strategies. I find the overall approach—decomposing execution time into computation and communication components derived from the network's declarative specification—both plausible and clearly explained. The paper's main strength is its analytical flexibility: by abstracting away implementation details and using simple FLOP counts and bandwidth assumptions, PALEO can quickly project scalability for architectures like NiN, Inception, and AlexNet, and the empirical validation against TensorFlow and FireCaffe is reasonably convincing. That said, I have some concerns. The reliance on a single "platform percent of peak" (PPP) constant to capture all framework inefficiencies feels overly simplistic and potentially brittle across different layer types or batch sizes; I'd like to see more discussion of how sensitive the model is to this parameter. Additionally, the communication modeling abstracts away many real-world complexities (e.g., message passing overhead, contention, heterogeneous links), and the case studies gloss over the fact that parameter-server schemes don't perfectly match AllReduce, so the comparison to TensorFlow's Inception results is a bit hand-wavy. Still, the paper offers a practical, lightweight tool that fills a gap between brute-force profiling and theoretical lower bounds, and the writing is crisp and to the point. I'd recommend acceptance with a request for more transparency on the PPP calibration and a deeper discussion of when the model is likely to break down.

title: Combining policy gradient and Q-learning
abstract: Abstract:###Policy gradient is an efficient technique for improving a policy in a reinforcement learning setting. However, vanilla online variants are on-policy only and not able to take advantage of off-policy data. In this paper we describe a new technique that combines policy gradient with off-policy Q-learning, drawing experience from a replay buffer. This is motivated by making a connection between the fixed points of the regularized policy gradient algorithm and the Q-values. This connection allows us to estimate the Q-values from the action preferences of the policy, to which we apply Q-learning updates. We refer to the new technique as â€˜PGQLâ€™, for policy gradient and Q-learning. We also establish an equivalency between action-value fitting techniques and actor-critic algorithms, showing that regularized policy gradient techniques can be interpreted as advantage function learning algorithms. We conclude with some numerical examples that demonstrate improved data efficiency and stability of PGQL. In particular, we tested PGQL on the full suite of Atari games and achieved performance exceeding that of both asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) and Q-learning.
review: This paper addresses the problem of improving data efficiency and stability in deep reinforcement learning by combining policy gradient methods with off-policy Q-learning, drawing experience from a replay buffer. The core idea—establishing a connection between the fixed point of entropy-regularized policy gradient and the Q-values, then using that to derive a Q-estimate and apply Bellman updates—is clever and technically sound. The theoretical analysis showing that the Bellman residual vanishes as the regularization temperature goes to zero gives a nice justification for the hybrid update. The empirical results on Atari are impressive, with PGQL outperforming both A3C and Q-learning on a majority of games, and the normalized scores tables show clear improvements in mean and median performance. However, I have some reservations. The equivalency claim between actor-critic and action-value methods in Section 3.3, while interesting, feels a bit overstated—the equivalence relies on replacing the fixed measure \(\mu\) with the current policy, which changes the learning dynamics in non-trivial ways, and the paper doesn't fully explore the implications of that substitution. The practical implementation details are also somewhat hand-wavy: the weighting parameter \(\eta\) is replaced by a learning rate ratio in the Atari experiments, and the choice of 0.5 times the actor-critic learning rate for Q-learning feels arbitrary without more ablation. The paper also acknowledges that PGQL performed poorly or collapsed in several games, which suggests stability isn't uniformly improved, and the explanation that hyperparameter tuning might fix this is a bit unsatisfying. The writing is clear and the presentation is engaging, but I'd like to see a more systematic study of the hyperparameter sensitivity and a deeper discussion of when the hybrid update helps versus hurts. Overall, the approach is plausible and the empirical gains are real, but the theoretical novelty is modest and the practical contribution, while solid, doesn't fully overcome the lingering questions about robustness. I lean towards acceptance but with reservations about the generality of the claims.

title: Density estimation using Real NVP
abstract: Abstract:###Unsupervised learning of probabilistic models is a central yet challenging problem in machine learning. Specifically, designing models with tractable learning, sampling, inference and evaluation is crucial in solving this task. We extend the space of such models using real-valued non-volume preserving (real NVP) transformations, a set of powerful invertible and learnable transformations, resulting in an unsupervised learning algorithm with exact log-likelihood computation, exact sampling, exact inference of latent variables, and an interpretable latent space. We demonstrate its ability to model natural images on four datasets through sampling, log-likelihood evaluation and latent variable manipulations.
review: This paper addresses the problem of unsupervised density estimation for high-dimensional continuous data, proposing a class of invertible transformations called real-valued non-volume preserving (real NVP) transformations. The core idea—building a sequence of affine coupling layers that leave part of the input unchanged while applying a simple, invertible scaling and translation to the rest, conditioned on the unchanged part in a complex way—is elegant and technically sound. The key advantage is that it enables exact log-likelihood computation, exact and efficient sampling, and exact inference, all with a tractable Jacobian determinant that doesn't require computing the Jacobian of the complex conditioning functions. I find the approach well-motivated and the exposition clear, particularly the multi-scale architecture that factors out dimensions at regular intervals to reduce computational cost and distribute the loss. The empirical results are solid: the model achieves competitive bits per dimension on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet (though not beating PixelRNN), and the samples are sharp and globally coherent, which is a nice contrast to the blurry samples typical of VAEs. The manifold visualizations and the attribute manipulation experiments on CelebA also provide compelling evidence that the learned latent space has some semantic structure. That said, I have a few concerns. The performance on log-likelihood is not state-of-the-art, and the paper doesn't fully address why the model underperforms relative to autoregressive models, especially given that it's also exact and tractable. The samples, while sharp, sometimes show artifacts (as the authors acknowledge), and the conceptual compression experiments in Appendix D suggest the latent space semantics are more about low-level texture than high-level concepts, which limits the interpretability claims. Additionally, the batch normalization variant with lag feels a bit ad-hoc, and the paper could benefit from a more systematic ablation study to understand the contribution of each design choice (e.g., multi-scale architecture, batch norm, number of coupling layers). Overall, this is a strong, well-executed paper that makes a useful contribution to the generative modeling toolkit, and I recommend acceptance, though I'd appreciate more discussion on the trade-offs between exactness, sample quality, and semantic representation compared to other approaches.

title: Recurrent Batch Normalization
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a reparameterization of LSTM that brings the benefits of batch normalization to recurrent neural networks. Whereas previous works only apply batch normalization to the input-to-hidden transformation of RNNs, we demonstrate that it is both possible and beneficial to batch-normalize the hidden-to-hidden transition, thereby reducing internal covariate shift between time steps. We evaluate our proposal on various sequential problems such as sequence classification, language modeling and question answering. Our empirical results show that our batch-normalized LSTM consistently leads to faster convergence and improved generalization.
review: This paper addresses the problem of effectively training recurrent neural networks by adapting batch normalization to the hidden-to-hidden transitions of LSTMs—a direction previously thought to be problematic or ineffective. The authors make a simple but crucial observation: previous failures were largely due to improper initialization of the batch norm scale parameter \(\gamma\), and by setting it to a small value (0.1), they can successfully normalize recurrent activations without destroying gradient flow. The technical contribution is straightforward but practically significant: they reparameterize the LSTM by applying separate batch norm to the input and recurrent terms, use timestep-specific statistics to preserve transient dynamics, and provide a clear analysis showing how \(\gamma\) controls the variance of pre-activations and thus the magnitude of backpropagated gradients. The empirical validation is thorough and convincing—they demonstrate faster convergence and better generalization on sequential MNIST (where they achieve state-of-the-art), character-level language modeling on Penn Treebank and text8, and the Attentive Reader for question answering, where their BN-equipped model dramatically improves training speed and achieves competitive results. The paper is well-written and the experiments are carefully executed, with proper ablations showing the sensitivity to \(\gamma\) initialization and the importance of timestep-specific statistics. My main criticisms are that the technical novelty is somewhat incremental—the core idea of applying batch norm to RNNs is not new, and the key insight about \(\gamma\) initialization, while important, feels like a practical fix rather than a deep theoretical breakthrough. Additionally, the paper could benefit from a more systematic analysis of why the proposed method works beyond just gradient flow, e.g., how it affects the loss landscape or optimization curvature.
