The results on Attentive Reader are impressive but the task setup deviates from the original benchmark, making direct comparisons slightly less clean. That said, the paper addresses a real and frustrating practical problem, provides clear guidelines that practitioners can immediately use, and the empirical gains are substantial across multiple domains. I recommend acceptance; this is a useful contribution that will likely see widespread adoption, even if it's not the most conceptually novel paper at the conference.

title: SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts
abstract: Abstract:###Restart techniques are common in gradient-free optimization to deal with multimodal functions. Partial warm restarts are also gaining popularity in gradient-based optimization to improve the rate of convergence in accelerated gradient schemes to deal with ill-conditioned functions. In this paper, we propose a simple warm restart technique for stochastic gradient descent to improve its anytime performance when training deep neural networks. We empirically study its performance on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, where we demonstrate new state-of-the-art results at 3.14\% and 16.21\%, respectively. We also demonstrate its advantages on a dataset of EEG recordings and on a downsampled version of the ImageNet dataset. Our source code is available at  url{https://github.com/loshchil/SGDR}
review: This paper addresses the problem of accelerating the training of deep neural networks by proposing a simple yet effective learning rate schedule—cosine annealing with warm restarts—for stochastic gradient descent. The core idea is straightforward: periodically reset the learning rate to a higher value (simulating a "warm restart") and anneal it down again, which allows the optimizer to escape local minima or saddle points and often leads to faster convergence and better final performance. I found the approach entirely plausible and very clearly explained. The empirical evaluation is thorough and convincing: the authors demonstrate that SGDR achieves comparable or better test errors on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 roughly 2–4× faster than the standard stepwise decay schedules, and they also show benefits on EEG data and a downsampled ImageNet variant. The connection to ensemble methods—where snapshots taken just before restarts can be aggregated into an ensemble "for free"—is a nice bonus, and the results achieving 3.14% on CIFAR-10 and 16.21% on CIFAR-100 with ensembles are genuinely state-of-the-art at the time. My main criticisms are that the technical novelty is somewhat limited—cyclical learning rates and restart strategies already existed in the literature (e.g., Smith 2015), and this paper largely refines and systematically evaluates them in the context of deep learning—and the theoretical analysis is thin; the paper doesn't really explain *why* warm restarts help beyond intuitive arguments about escaping poor local regions, and the connection to convex accelerated gradient restarts (O'Donoghue & Candes) is hand-wavy given the non-convex, stochastic setting. The hyperparameter sensitivity (choice of \(T_0\), \(T_{mult}\), \(\eta_{max}\), \(\eta_{min}\)) also isn't deeply explored, though the authors do show that SGDR is relatively robust. Still, the practical impact is undeniable: this is a simple, low-cost modification that practitioners can immediately adopt, and the anytime performance improvements are substantial. I recommend acceptance—the paper is well-written, empirically solid, and makes a useful contribution to the optimization toolkit, even if it's not breaking new conceptual ground.

title: Learning a Natural Language Interface with Neural Programmer
abstract: Abstract:###Learning a natural language interface for database tables is a challenging task that involves deep language understanding and multi-step reasoning. The task is often approached by mapping natural language queries to logical forms or programs that provide the desired response when executed on the database. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first weakly supervised, end-to-end neural network model to induce such programs on a real-world dataset. We enhance the objective function of Neural Programmer, a neural network with built-in discrete operations, and apply it on WikiTableQuestions, a natural language question-answering dataset. The model is trained end-to-end with weak supervision of question-answer pairs, and does not require domain-specific grammars, rules, or annotations that are key elements in previous approaches to program induction. The main experimental result in this paper is that a single Neural Programmer model achieves 34.2% accuracy using only 10,000 examples with weak supervision. An ensemble of 15 models, with a trivial combination technique, achieves 37.7% accuracy, which is competitive to the current state-of-the-art accuracy of 37.1% obtained by a traditional natural language semantic parser.
review: This paper addresses the problem of learning a natural language interface for querying database tables, specifically focusing on weakly supervised program induction from question-answer pairs rather than from full program annotations. The core approach builds on Neural Programmer, a model that uses soft selection over discrete operations and columns, and introduces several key enhancements: a modified training objective that handles ambiguity in the supervision signal (e.g., when a numeric answer also appears in the table, or when an answer phrase occurs multiple times), stronger regularization to combat overfitting on the small WikiTableQuestions dataset, and a boolean feature for column selection that indicates whether any entry in that column matches the question. The main result—a single model achieving 34.2% accuracy and an ensemble of 15 reaching 37.7%, competitive with the state-of-the-art semantic parser at the time—is genuinely impressive given the weak supervision and the model's ability to generalize to unseen column names and table structures. I appreciate the thorough ablation studies showing the importance of regularization and the column-selection feature, and the analysis of induced programs provides useful insights into what the model is actually learning. That said, I have a few reservations. The technical novelty is somewhat limited—the core Neural Programmer architecture was already published, and the main contributions here are engineering improvements (handling weak supervision, stronger regularization, better column selection) rather than a fundamentally new approach. The treatment of the ambiguity in the supervision signal, while effective, feels a bit ad-hoc (e.g., the soft minimum for scalar vs. lookup losses, the constant factor of 50.0 to balance them), and the paper could benefit from a more principled discussion of why this works. The ensemble result, while strong, relies on a trivial averaging of 15 models with different random seeds, which is computationally expensive and doesn't really advance the state of ensemble methods. I'm also a bit skeptical about the practical impact: the model still underperforms the traditional semantic parser on the full test set (37.7% vs. 37.1% is essentially a tie, and the margin is within noise), and the 50.5% oracle performance suggests there's still a lot of room for improvement. Overall, I think this is a solid and well-executed piece of work that demonstrates the viability of end-to-end neural program induction on a real-world task, but it feels more like an incremental improvement than a breakthrough. I'd recommend acceptance with the caveat that the novelty is moderate and the contributions are mostly in the engineering and regularization domain.

title: Reinforcement Learning through Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic on a GPU
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a hybrid CPU/GPU version of the Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) algorithm, currently the state-of-the-art method in reinforcement learning for various gaming tasks. We analyze its computational traits and concentrate on aspects critical to leveraging the GPU*s computational power. We introduce a system of queues and a dynamic scheduling strategy, potentially helpful for other asynchronous algorithms as well. Our hybrid CPU/GPU version of A3C, based on TensorFlow, achieves a significant speed up compared to a CPU implementation; we make it publicly available to other researchers at https://github.com/NVlabs/GA3C.
review: This paper addresses the problem of GPU underutilization in reinforcement learning, specifically for the asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) algorithm, which was originally designed for CPU execution due to its inherently sequential data generation and small batch sizes. The authors propose a hybrid CPU/GPU architecture (GA3C) that decouples agents (running on CPU) from prediction and training (running on GPU) via queues, centralizing the model on the GPU and dynamically adjusting the number of agents, predictors, and trainers to maximize throughput. I found the approach well-motivated and the exposition clear, with a thorough analysis of computational bottlenecks, GPU occupancy, and the trade-offs between throughput and learning stability. The empirical results are impressive: GA3C achieves up to 45× speedup over a CPU implementation for larger networks, and the authors demonstrate that a single day of GA3C training can match or exceed four days of CPU A3C on several Atari games. The open-source release is a valuable contribution to the community. However, I have some criticisms. The paper is fundamentally a systems engineering paper rather than an algorithmic one—the core A3C algorithm is unchanged, and the contribution lies in efficient scheduling and batching. While this is practically useful, the novelty is moderate. The dynamic configuration mechanism, while clever, feels a bit ad-hoc and the paper doesn't fully characterize its sensitivity or convergence properties. The comparison to the original A3C is also somewhat apples-to-oranges, since the authors use their own TensorFlow CPU implementation rather than the original code, and the speedup claims are heavily dependent on the specific DNN size and hardware. The analysis of "policy lag" due to stale experiences in the training queue is important, and the solution (increasing minimum training batch size) is sensible, but the paper could delve deeper into how this interacts with the learning rate and stability across different games. Overall, I think this is a solid, practical contribution that will be useful for researchers scaling RL, but it's more of an optimization report than a breakthrough in RL methodology. I recommend acceptance with the caveat that the novelty is primarily in the systems domain rather than in the learning algorithm itself.

title: Learning to Navigate in Complex Environments
abstract: Abstract:###Learning to navigate in complex environments with dynamic elements is an important milestone in developing AI agents. In this work we formulate the navigation question as a reinforcement learning problem and show that data efficiency and task performance can be dramatically improved by relying on additional auxiliary tasks to bootstrap learning. In particular we consider jointly learning the goal-driven reinforcement learning problem with an unsupervised depth prediction task and a self-supervised loop closure classification task. Using this approach we can learn to navigate from raw sensory input in complicated 3D mazes, approaching human-level performance even under conditions where the goal location changes frequently. We provide detailed analysis of the agent behaviour, its ability to localise, and its network activity dynamics, that show that the agent implicitly learns key navigation abilities, with only sparse rewards and without direct supervision.
review:
This paper addresses the problem of learning to navigate in complex 3D environments using deep reinforcement learning, where rewards are sparse and agents must handle dynamic goal locations and partial observability. The core idea is to augment the A3C objective with auxiliary self-supervised tasks—depth prediction (formulated as classification) and loop closure detection—that provide denser training signals and encourage representations useful for navigation. I found the approach well-motivated and the empirical results quite strong: the Nav A3C+D2 agent achieves near-human performance on static mazes and substantially outperforms vanilla A3C on random goal mazes, with the auxiliary tasks dramatically accelerating learning (e.g., 2–4× faster convergence). The analysis is also a highlight—the position decoding experiments convincingly show that the agent learns to localize itself implicitly, and the t-SNE visualizations of LSTM activations reveal interesting policy clustering that suggests efficient representation of navigation strategies. The paper is clearly written and the supplementary material is thorough.

That said, I have a few reservations. The novelty is somewhat incremental—auxiliary tasks for RL have been explored before (e.g., Lample & Chaplot 2016, and concurrently Jaderberg et al. 2017), and the specific choices of depth prediction and loop closure are natural for navigation but not particularly surprising. The comparison to the concurrent work is handled fairly, but the paper could more clearly articulate what unique insights it provides beyond "auxiliary tasks help." The depth prediction target, while effective, relies on ground-truth depth from the simulator, which is a privileged signal not available in real-world settings; this limits the practical applicability of the approach. The loop closure detection, similarly, uses ground-truth position information to generate training labels, which feels like a strong form of supervision. The hyperparameter tuning is extensive (64 runs per experiment) but the sensitivity analysis could be more systematic—Figure 11 hints that auxiliary tasks make learning more robust, but the paper doesn't fully explore why. Finally, the feedforward A3C's competitive performance on static mazes suggests that some navigation tasks can be solved reactively, which undermines the claim that memory is essential; the paper acknowledges this but doesn't delve into the implications.

Overall, I think this is a solid paper with compelling empirical results and interesting analysis, but the technical contribution is moderate and the reliance on privileged information limits its generality. I recommend acceptance with the caveat that the novelty is more in the application and analysis than in the algorithmic invention.

title: DeepCoder: Learning to Write Programs
abstract: Abstract:###We develop a first line of attack for solving programming competition-style problems from input-output examples using deep learning. The approach is to train a neural network to predict properties of the program that generated the outputs from the inputs. We use the neural network*s predictions to augment search techniques from the programming languages community, including enumerative search and an SMT-based solver. Empirically, we show that our approach leads to an order of magnitude speedup over the strong non-augmented baselines and a Recurrent Neural Network approach, and that we are able to solve problems of difficulty comparable to the simplest problems on programming competition websites.
review: This paper presents a sensible and empirically compelling approach to program synthesis, and I largely buy the core thesis that learning to predict high-level program attributes can provide a substantial and robust speedup over traditional search-based synthesis techniques. The LIPS framework is well-motivated, the integration of a simple feed-forward encoder with off-the-shelf enumerative, SMT-based, and λ² solvers is clean, and the reported order-of-magnitude speedups on programs of length 3 and 5 are impressive. I particularly appreciate the generalization experiment (training on length 4, testing on length 5) and the careful semantic disjointness check between train and test programs, which gives me confidence that the results are not due to trivial memorization. That said, I have several serious concerns that prevent me from recommending acceptance in its current form. First, the DSL is extremely restrictive—essentially a linear pipeline of list-processing functions without conditionals, loops, or recursion—and the claim that this captures "problems of difficulty comparable to the simplest problems on programming competition websites" is overblown; the examples in Appendix A are toy problems that would be solved by a single line of Python in most competitions, and the absence of even basic branching makes the synthesis problem fundamentally easier than any real-world IPS setting. Second, the use of five input-output examples with integers up to magnitude 256 is a strong informational advantage; in practice, examples are often smaller or fewer, and I suspect the performance gains would degrade significantly with less informative examples. Third, the encoder is a straightforward MLP with a fixed-length padding, which is fine for this domain but raises questions about scalability to variable-length programs and arrays; the fact that the RNN encoder underperforms and is "more difficult to train" suggests that the current architecture is brittle and may not generalize to richer DSLs. Fourth, the theoretical justification in Section 4.5 (Lemma 1 and the Rank loss argument) is hand-wavy and relies on the unrealistic assumption that runtime scales as C^T; the upper bound is loose and the connection to marginal probabilities is not rigorously established. Finally, the RNN decoder baseline is dismissed too quickly—it only works for T≤2, which is not a fair comparison, and I would have liked to see a more competitive sequence-to-sequence model with attention or a transformer, as well as an ablation that trains on programs of length 5 directly. Overall, I find the engineering contribution solid and the results promising, but the paper overclaims on generality and the experimental setup is too favorable to the proposed method. I would give this a weak reject, but I encourage the authors to address the DSL limitations and informational assumptions in a revised version.

title: Learning and Policy Search in Stochastic Dynamical Systems with Bayesian Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We present an algorithm for policy search in stochastic dynamical systems using model-based reinforcement learning. The system dynamics are described with Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) that include stochastic input variables. These input variables allow us to capture complex statistical patterns in the transition dynamics (e.g. multi-modality and heteroskedasticity), which are usually missed by alternative modeling approaches. After learning the dynamics, our BNNs are then fed into an algorithm that performs random roll-outs and uses stochastic optimization for policy learning. We train our BNNs by minimizing -divergences with , which usually produces better results than other techniques such as variational Bayes. We illustrate the performance of our method by solving a challenging problem where model-based approaches usually fail and by obtaining promising results in real-world scenarios including the control of a gas turbine and an industrial benchmark.
review: I'm leaning towards rejection on this one, despite some appealing empirical results, because the core technical contributions feel incremental and the policy search methodology is surprisingly standard given the hype. The use of BNNs with stochastic inputs to capture complex transition noise (multi-modality, heteroskedasticity) is sensible, and the α=0.5 divergence minimization is a clean extension of existing work from Hernández-Lobato et al. (2016) – but the latter is already published, so the novelty here reduces to applying it to RL, which isn't enough for ICLR. The policy optimization itself is just Monte Carlo roll-outs with gradient descent through the model, which is essentially a vanilla model-based policy gradient; there's no principled treatment of uncertainty propagation (unlike PILCO's moment matching), and the claim that this is the "first model-based solution" to Wet-Chicken is overblown – you're using 2500 random transitions and a PSO-P upper bound, but the real challenge is sample efficiency and stability, which you don't rigorously quantify. I also have concerns about the baselines: the GP comparison is unfair because you're using a sparse FITC approximation with random feature expansions, which is known to be brittle for multi-modal predictions, and the MLP baseline lacks any ensemble or uncertainty, so of course it underperforms. The real-world turbine and industrial benchmark results show modest improvements over VB (often within one standard error), and the computational cost – up to 16 hours for policy search – is prohibitive for practical deployment. The robustness argument that α=0.5 works even when q(z) is fixed is interesting but feels like a band-aid for a poorly optimized VB, and I don't see a theoretical justification for why α=0.5 is universally better than α=1.0 in these settings (your own results show α=1.0 often ties or beats it). Overall, I appreciate the engineering effort and the clear exposition, but the scientific contribution is too narrow; this reads like a solid workshop paper or a NeurIPS application track submission, not a main-track ICLR paper.

title: Variable Computation in Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been used extensively and with increasing success to model various types of sequential data. Much of this progress has been achieved through devising recurrent units and architectures with the flexibility to capture complex statistics in the data, such as long range dependency or localized attention phenomena. However, while many sequential data (such as video, speech or language) can have highly variable information flow, most recurrent models still consume input features at a constant rate and perform a constant number of computations per time step, which can be detrimental to both speed and model capacity. In this paper, we explore a modification to existing recurrent units which allows them to learn to vary the amount of computation they perform at each step, without prior knowledge of the sequence*s time structure. We show experimentally that not only do our models require fewer operations, they also lead to better performance overall on evaluation tasks.
review: I’m honestly on the fence with this one – the core idea of dynamically updating only a subset of hidden dimensions is neat and the visualizations of the scheduler learning interpretable patterns (ignoring bars in music, syncing to word boundaries in text) are genuinely compelling, but the paper falls short on several critical fronts that make me lean toward rejection. First and foremost, the computational gains are purely theoretical: you openly admit that the reduction in FLOPs doesn’t translate to wall‑clock speedups on standard GPUs, which completely undermines the main selling point of "variable computation" – if I can’t actually train or run the model faster, why should I care about the number of operations? The sharpness annealing and the L1 penalty on the scheduler feel like brittle engineering hacks rather than principled solutions, and I’m not convinced the method would generalize beyond the specific tasks and unit sizes you tried; the scheduler is just a simple logistic function on the raw hidden state, which seems too simplistic to capture when to actually skip computation. More importantly, the comparisons to strong baselines like Graves’ Adaptive Computation Time or Chung’s hierarchical multiscale RNN are conspicuously absent – you cite them but don’t run a direct comparison, which is a major gap given they tackle the same problem. The perplexity gains are marginal (often within 0.01–0.02 bpc) and the "equivalent RNN dimension" metric is a poor substitute for actual runtime measurements; for instance, your VCGRU-1024 with 0.34 cost achieves 1.69 bpc, while a regular GRU-512 achieves 1.69 bpc with essentially the same FLOPs, so where’s the real advantage? The qualitative scheduler analysis is fun but not enough to compensate for the lack of rigorous quantitative evidence that this method is reliably better than existing adaptive approaches. I appreciate the effort, but I’d need to see a proper implementation that actually speeds up training on modern hardware, stronger baselines, and a more principled training procedure to get excited. As it stands, this reads like a solid workshop paper but not ICLR material.

title: Deep Variational Information Bottleneck
abstract: Abstract:###We present a variational approximation to the information bottleneck of Tishby et al. (1999). This variational approach allows us to parameterize the information bottleneck model using a neural network and leverage the reparameterization trick for efficient training. We call this method â€œDeep Variational Information Bottleneckâ€, or Deep VIB. We show that models trained with the VIB objective outperform those that are trained with other forms of regularization, in terms of generalization performance and robustness to adversarial attack.
review: I like this paper—the variational relaxation of the information bottleneck is clean, principled, and practically useful, and I think it’s a solid contribution to ICLR. The derivation of the lower bound is straightforward but non‑trivial, and the connection to VAEs (and the interpretation of β as a Lagrange multiplier rather than a hack) is a nice conceptual clarification. The empirical results are convincing: the regularization effect on MNIST is real, and the adversarial robustness gains against both FGS and the Carlini‑Wagner L₂ attack are significant and well‑documented. The ImageNet experiment, while only on penultimate features, shows that the method scales and that the robustness holds beyond toy data. That said, I have a few reservations. First, the adversarial robustness claims are a bit over‑sold—you're not attacking the full end‑to‑end Inception network with VIB, only a logistic regression on top of precomputed features, and the perturbation magnitudes for VIB are much larger, which makes the comparison somewhat unfair (the adversary has to fight through a noisy bottleneck, but the base model doesn't). Second, the method is essentially beta‑VAE for supervised learning, and while you cite Higgins et al., you don't really discuss the relationship beyond a footnote—I'd like to see a deeper comparison, especially since β‑VAE already showed disentanglement and robustness benefits. Third, the performance improvement on MNIST is marginal (1.13% vs 1.17% for confidence penalty) and the method is quite sensitive to β; you don't provide a principled way to set it, and the optimal range is narrow. Fourth, the quadratic classifier explanation in Appendix C is interesting but feels like an afterthought—it's not tested or used to drive any experiments. Overall, I think the paper is well‑written, the theory is sound, and the results are positive, but it doesn't feel like a groundbreaking advance; it's a natural and timely application of variational inference to a classic information‑theoretic objective. I'd lean towards accept, but with the expectation that the authors tone down the adversarial claims and provide more guidance on hyperparameter selection.

title: The Neural Noisy Channel
abstract: Abstract:###We formulate sequence to sequence transduction as a noisy channel decoding problem and use recurrent neural networks to parameterise the source and channel models. Unlike direct models which can suffer from explaining-away effects during training, noisy channel models must produce outputs that explain their inputs, and their component models can be trained with not only paired training samples but also unpaired samples from the marginal output distribution. Using a latent variable to control how much of the conditioning sequence the channel model needs to read in order to generate a subsequent symbol, we obtain a tractable and effective beam search decoder. Experimental results on abstractive sentence summarisation, morphological inflection, and machine translation show that noisy channel models outperform direct models, and that they significantly benefit from increased amounts of unpaired output data that direct models cannot easily use.
review: I’m on the fence with this one – the noisy channel formulation for neural sequence transduction is conceptually appealing and the use of an online segment-to-segment model as the channel to enable incremental conditioning is a clever technical move, but I’m not convinced the empirical gains justify the complexity or that the paper offers a genuinely new way to exploit unpaired data. The main issue is that the channel model itself is still trained only on paired data; the language model is the only component that sees the monolingual examples, which is essentially just shallow fusion – a technique that’s been around for years and already shown to give modest improvements in MT and summarization. The decoding algorithm is a two-step beam with an auxiliary direct model proposing candidates, meaning the channel model is effectively reranking rather than driving the search, and the computational cost is nasty (quadratic in vocabulary unless you use proposals). The ROUGE and BLEU gains over direct models are positive but not dramatic (e.g., ~1 point ROUGE on summarization, ~3 BLEU on a small MT task), and the comparison to back-translation or other semi-supervised methods is conspicuously absent – I’d have liked to see a direct head-to-head with Sennrich et al.’s approach. The morphological inflection results are mixed: the channel alone actually underperforms the direct model, and only the interpolation helps, which undermines the claim that the noisy channel inherently fixes the explaining-away problem. On the positive side, the human evaluation for summarization is convincing and the qualitative examples show nicer fluency, but that’s not enough to overcome my concerns about novelty and practical utility. Overall, I think this is a solid piece of engineering and a nice application of SSNT, but as a main-track ICLR paper it feels incremental – I’d lean weak reject, though I could be persuaded to accept if the authors provided stronger baselines and a clearer demonstration that the channel model genuinely learns something complementary that can’t be achieved by simpler fusion methods.

title: Automatic Rule Extraction from Long Short Term Memory Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Although deep learning models have proven effective at solving problems in natural language processing, the mechanism by which they come to their conclusions is often unclear. As a result, these models are generally treated as black boxes, yielding no insight of the underlying learned patterns. In this paper we consider Long Short Term Memory networks (LSTMs) and demonstrate a new approach for tracking the importance of a given input to the LSTM for a given output. By identifying consistently important patterns of words, we are able to distill state of the art LSTMs on sentiment analysis and question answering into a set of representative phrases. This representation is then quantitatively validated by using the extracted phrases to construct a simple, rule-based classifier which approximates the output of the LSTM.
review: I'm leaning towards acceptance on this one – the paper presents a genuinely new and technically sound method for interpreting LSTMs, and the idea of distilling a trained network into a small set of human-readable rules is both practically useful and conceptually elegant. The additive cell decomposition (Equation 10) is a clever refinement over the naïve cell-difference approach, and the fact that it explicitly accounts for forget gates makes intuitive sense and is backed by empirical results showing cleaner visualizations and better pattern-matching performance. The experiments are thorough, covering two sentiment datasets and the more complex WikiMovies QA task, and the extracted phrases (e.g., "worst customer service ever", "riveting documentary") are qualitatively sensible and align with human intuition. I also appreciate the quantitative validation via the rule-based classifier – achieving ~86% test accuracy on Yelp and ~76% on SST using only simple pattern matching is surprisingly strong and provides concrete evidence that the importance scores capture meaningful signal. That said, I have a few concerns. First, the phrase extraction procedure feels somewhat heuristic – the candidate selection threshold (β > 1.1) is arbitrary, and the sequential greedy rule classifier is simplistic; I'd like to see a more principled approach or at least a sensitivity analysis to these choices. Second, the comparison to prior visualization work (gradient-based methods) is limited to a single baseline, and while you show your method outperforms it, a more systematic comparison to other interpretability techniques (e.g., LIME, attention visualizations) would strengthen the paper. Third, the approximation gap between the LSTM and the rule-based classifier is non-trivial (~10% on Yelp, ~11% on SST), and the examples in Table 5 show that the extracted patterns fail when context reverses their polarity – this suggests the method captures only local n-gram signals and misses longer-range dependencies, which is a fundamental limitation worth discussing more explicitly. Finally, the WikiMovies adaptation feels a bit ad-hoc (treating each entity as a separate binary classification, restricting patterns to those ending at the entity), and the performance drop from the full LSTM (87.7% to 81.8%) is larger than on sentiment tasks, indicating the method may not generalize as well to more complex reasoning. Overall, I think the paper is well-written, the core idea is novel and clearly explained, and the results are compelling enough to warrant acceptance, but I'd encourage the authors to be more upfront about the limitations and to consider a more rigorous evaluation of the phrase extraction robustness.

title: Dialogue Learning With Human-in-the-Loop
abstract: Abstract:###An important aspect of developing conversational agents is to give a bot the ability to improve through communicating with humans and to learn from the mistakes that it makes. Most research has focused on learning from fixed training sets of labeled data rather than interacting with a dialogue partner in an online fashion. In this paper we explore this direction in a reinforcement learning setting where the bot improves its question-answering ability from feedback a teacher gives following its generated responses. We build a simulator that tests various aspects of such learning in a synthetic environment, and introduce models that work in this regime. Finally, real experiments with Mechanical Turk validate the approach.
review: I’m leaning towards acceptance – this is a well-executed and practically relevant piece of work that tackles the important problem of online learning from human feedback in dialogue systems, and it convincingly shows that both reward-based and textual feedback can be leveraged effectively. The paper does a good job of distinguishing itself from prior work (especially Weston 2016) by actually training policies interactively rather than using pre-built fixed datasets, and the experiments with both a controlled simulator and real Mechanical Turk data provide strong evidence that the proposed methods (RBI, REINFORCE, FP) can improve over time. I particularly appreciated the careful analysis of instabilities – the fact that FP without balancing can oscillate and collapse when the model gets too good is a valuable insight, and the solution of using balanced experience replay or exploration is sensible and well-demonstrated. The robustness to batch size is also a nice finding, as it makes the approach more practical for real-world deployment where you’d want to collect data in batches rather than update online after every single interaction. However, I do have a few reservations. First, the methodological novelty is somewhat limited – RBI is just imitation learning on positive examples, REINFORCE is standard, and FP is directly borrowed from Weston 2016; the main contribution is showing they can work in an interactive setting, which is important but not deeply surprising. Second, the comparison to Weston 2016 feels a bit defensive and the argument that their work was "not practically viable" is a bit overstated – pre-built policies with omniscient labelers are a common simplification in RL research, and your own results show that with high π_acc their method already solved the task, so the improvement is incremental rather than a paradigm shift. Third, the human experiments, while valuable, show only modest improvements (e.g., RBI+FP from 0.431 to 0.441) and the fully supervised baseline on 60k examples reaches 0.599, so there's still a significant gap – this suggests the feedback signal is noisy and the methods are not yet matching supervised learning with sufficient labeled data. Fourth, the paper could do a better job of discussing the limitations of the MemN2N architecture and whether these findings would generalize to more modern transformer-based dialogue models. Overall, I think this is a solid, well-executed paper that makes a clear contribution to the dialogue learning community, but it's not groundbreaking – I'd accept it with the expectation that the authors tone down the claims about novelty and provide more guidance on hyperparameter selection (especially ε and balancing) for practitioners.

title: Adversarially Learned Inference
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce the adversarially learned inference (ALI) model, which jointly learns a generation network and an inference network using an adversarial process. The generation network maps samples from stochastic latent variables to the data space while the inference network maps training examples in data space to the space of latent variables. An adversarial game is cast between these two networks and a discriminative network that is trained to distinguish between joint latent/data-space samples from the generative network and joint samples from the inference network. We illustrate the ability of the model to learn mutually coherent inference and generation networks through the inspections of model samples and reconstructions and confirm the usefulness of the learned representations by obtaining a performance competitive with other recent approaches on the semi-supervised SVHN task.
review: I’m a big fan of this paper—the idea of learning an encoder jointly with a GAN via adversarial matching of joint distributions is both elegant and practically effective, and I think it’s a clear accept. The ALI framework cleanly addresses a major limitation of GANs (lack of inference) without sacrificing sample quality, and the formulation is mathematically sound: the adversarial game matches q(x,z) and p(x,z), which ensures both good generation and a coherent inference mechanism. The results speak for themselves—samples are crisp, latent interpolations are smooth, and the semi-supervised performance on SVHN (7.42% error) and CIFAR10 (19.98% with 1k labels) is competitive with state-of-the-art, even without feature matching. The toy experiment on the 2D mixture is particularly insightful: it clearly shows that ALI covers modes better than GAN with post-hoc inference or inverse mapping, and that VAE smears probability density, which nicely highlights the complementary strengths of adversarial vs. likelihood-based training. I also appreciate the conditional extension and the CelebA results, which demonstrate the model’s flexibility. My main concerns are relatively minor: the paper overlaps significantly with the independent BiGAN work (Donahue et al., 2016), and while you acknowledge it, the novelty is somewhat diluted; the reconstructions are not always faithful, especially on CIFAR10, which suggests the encoder-decoder pair doesn’t always invert perfectly (though Proposition 3 claims invertibility under optimality, which is never achieved in practice); and the semi-supervised setup heavily borrows from Salimans et al., which reduces the technical surprise. I’d also like to see a more thorough discussion of when stochastic vs. deterministic encoders matter—you note they become deterministic in practice, but that’s a bit hand-wavy. Overall, though, this is a well-written, thorough, and impactful paper that makes a strong case for adversarial inference, and I’d be happy to see it accepted. Oh, and the “Circle of Infinite Painters” appendix is delightful—keep it.

title: Learning through Dialogue Interactions by Asking Questions
abstract: Abstract:###A good dialogue agent should have the ability to interact with users by both responding to questions and by asking questions, and importantly to learn from both types of interactions. In this work, we explore this direction by designing a simulator and a set of synthetic tasks in the movie domain that allow such interactions between a learner and a teacher. We investigate how a learner can benefit from asking questions in both offline and online reinforcement learning settings, and demonstrate that the learner improves when asking questions. Our work represents a first step in developing such end-to-end learned interactive dialogue agents.
review: I’m on the fence with this one – the problem of enabling dialogue agents to learn by asking questions is important and underexplored, and the paper does a commendable job of designing a rich set of synthetic tasks that systematically isolate three key failure modes (surface understanding, reasoning, and missing knowledge). The results consistently show that allowing the agent to ask questions improves performance across both offline supervised and online RL settings, and the Mechanical Turk validation adds real-world credibility. However, I have several reservations that keep me from being enthusiastic. First, the methodological novelty is quite limited – the core models (MemN2N, RBI, FP) are directly borrowed from prior work (Weston 2016), and the main contribution is essentially adding a question-asking action and showing it helps, which is intuitive and not deeply surprising. Second, the RL setup is simplified to a single binary decision per episode with a fixed cost, and the REINFORCE implementation is standard; I’d have liked to see more sophisticated exploration strategies or a discussion of how to handle multiple rounds of questioning. Third, the offline results show that TrainAQ+TestQA (asking during training but not test) performs worse than never asking, which is interesting but suggests the model becomes dependent on the teacher – this is a real issue, but the paper doesn’t offer a solution beyond mixing QA and AQ data. Fourth, the performance gains on the Mechanical Turk tasks are modest (e.g., from 0.712 to 0.774 on Task 4 with Cont-MemN2N) and still far below the simulator results, indicating that the approach struggles with natural language variability. Finally, the paper feels somewhat incremental – it’s a solid extension of Weston 2016, but the core ideas (learning from feedback, asking for clarification) have been explored in other forms, and the technical contribution doesn’t feel substantial enough for ICLR. I’d lean towards weak reject, but I think the problem is important and the experimental framework is well-designed, so with stronger baselines, a more sophisticated questioning policy, and a deeper analysis of when and why questioning helps, this could become a strong paper.

title: Deep Information Propagation
abstract: Abstract:###We study the behavior of untrained neural networks whose weights and biases are randomly distributed using mean field theory. We show the existence of depth scales that naturally limit the maximum depth of signal propagation through these random networks. Our main practical result is to show that random networks may be trained precisely when information can travel through them. Thus, the depth scales that we identify provide bounds on how deep a network may be trained for a specific choice of hyperparameters. As a corollary to this, we argue that in networks at the edge of chaos, one of these depth scales diverges. Thus arbitrarily deep networks may be trained only sufficiently close to criticality. We show that the presence of dropout destroys the order-to-chaos critical point and therefore strongly limits the maximum trainable depth for random networks. Finally, we develop a mean field theory for backpropagation and we show that the ordered and chaotic phases correspond to regions of vanishing and exploding gradient respectively.
review: I really like this paper – it’s a beautifully executed piece of theoretical work that bridges mean-field analysis of random neural networks with practical insights about trainability, and I think it’s a clear accept. The derivation of the depth scales ξ_q and ξ_c, the demonstration that ξ_c diverges at the order-to-chaos transition, and the extension to dropout (showing that even infinitesimal dropout destroys the critical point) are all technically sound and rigorously presented. The duality between forward signal propagation and gradient backpropagation is a particularly elegant result, and the experimental validation – showing that gradients indeed vanish/explode exponentially with the predicted rates, and that networks are trainable precisely when L ≲ 6ξ_c – is both convincing and practically actionable. The fact that this relationship holds across MNIST and CIFAR10, with different optimizers and training durations, strongly supports the claim of universality. My main concerns are relatively minor. First, the analysis is restricted to fully connected networks with tanh nonlinearities, and while the authors acknowledge this limitation, the claim that this critical point "controls" a broad class of architectures feels a bit bold without evidence for CNNs or residual networks. Second, the "edge of chaos" initialization is not a new idea (Glorot & Bengio, Saxe, Sussillo & Abbott all touched on this), and the paper could do a better job of contextualizing its contribution relative to prior work – the novelty here is the quantitative depth scales and the formal connection to trainability, not the criticality concept itself. Third, the experimental setup uses relatively shallow networks (L up to 300) and simple datasets; it would be more compelling to see if the bound holds for truly deep networks (e.g., 1000 layers) or on more complex tasks like ImageNet. Fourth, the treatment of dropout is insightful but the conclusion that it "limits trainable depth" is somewhat intuitive – after all, dropout introduces noise that decorrelates signals – and the practical recommendation (avoid dropout in very deep networks unless you’re near criticality) is useful but not surprising. Overall, though, this is a high-quality, theoretically grounded paper that provides a unifying framework for understanding why deep networks are hard to train and how to initialize them properly. I’m happy to accept it, and I think it will be well-cited in the community.

title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.
review: I’m leaning towards acceptance, though with some reservations – this is a clean and well-executed paper that convincingly demonstrates that residual connections aren’t the only path to ultra-deep networks, and the fractal design is elegantly simple (the recursive expansion rule and element-wise mean joins are almost too neat). The experimental results are solid: FractalNet matches ResNet on CIFAR and ImageNet, and the drop-path regularization is a natural and effective extension of stochastic depth that exploits the fractal structure to sample vastly different depth subnetworks. The anytime property and the ability to extract high-performance single-column plain networks are nice bonuses, and the analysis of internal student-teacher dynamics (Figure 3) provides genuine insight into why the architecture works. That said, I have a few concerns. First, the novelty is somewhat diluted by concurrent work – DenseNet and Wide ResNet were both published around the same time and achieve better results, so the claim that FractalNet is the "first simple alternative to ResNet" feels a bit overstated given that DenseNet also eschews explicit residuals in favor of concatenation (though it still has skip connections). Second, the paper relies heavily on batch normalization, dropout, and careful regularization – it’s not clear that FractalNet would work without these modern tricks, whereas the original ResNet paper demonstrated strong performance with minimal regularization. Third, the drop-path global sampling strategy essentially forces individual columns to be good predictors, which is clever, but the paper doesn’t ablate local vs. global drop-path thoroughly enough to understand their relative contributions. Finally, the ImageNet results are only on par with ResNet-34, not the improved variants (Wide ResNet, DenseNet), and the top-1 error of 24.12% is good but not state-of-the-art. Overall, I think the paper is well-written, the idea is original and well-motivated, and the experiments are thorough, but the practical impact is somewhat limited given that ResNet variants continue to dominate. I’d accept it as a solid contribution, but I’d encourage the authors to tone down the "residuals are incidental" claim and provide more guidance on when FractalNet might be preferable to ResNet in practice.

title: Revisiting Classifier Two-Sample Tests
abstract: Abstract:###The goal of two-sample tests is to assess whether two samples, and , are drawn from the same distribution. Perhaps intriguingly, one relatively unexplored method to build two-sample tests is the use of binary classifiers. In particular, construct a dataset by pairing the examples in with a positive label, and by pairing the examples in with a negative label. If the null hypothesis `` ** is true, then the classification accuracy of a binary classifier on a held-out subset of this dataset should remain near chance-level. As we will show, such emph{Classifier Two-Sample Tests} (C2ST) learn a suitable representation of the data on the fly, return test statistics in interpretable units, have a simple null distribution, and their predictive uncertainty allow to interpret where and differ. The goal of this paper is to establish the properties, performance, and uses of C2ST. First, we analyze their main theoretical properties. Second, we compare their performance against a variety of state-of-the-art alternatives. Third, we propose their use to evaluate the sample quality of generative models with intractable likelihoods, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Fourth, we showcase the novel application of GANs together with C2ST for causal discovery.
review: I’m leaning towards rejection, though I recognize the paper is well-written and the idea is intuitively appealing – using a classifier as a two-sample test is a natural and elegant extension of existing work, and the connections to GAN evaluation and causal discovery are clever. However, my main concern is that the paper doesn’t offer enough novel theoretical or methodological contributions beyond what’s already known in the literature. The core idea – that classification accuracy can serve as a test statistic – has been around for over a decade (Friedman 2003, Pérez-Cruz 2009, Reid & Williamson 2011), and the asymptotic null distribution is a simple Binomial approximation that’s been analyzed before. The power analysis in Theorem 1 is essentially a straightforward application of the central limit theorem, and the interpretability arguments, while nice, are not particularly surprising – of course a classifier’s learned features and predictive uncertainty can tell you where distributions differ, that’s true of any discriminative model. The experiments are extensive and show competitive performance, but they don’t convincingly demonstrate a clear advantage over state-of-the-art kernel-based tests (MMD, ME, SCF) – in many cases, C2ST- NN and C2ST-KNN are comparable or slightly worse, and the near-perfect power on some tasks might simply reflect the classifier’s flexibility rather than a fundamental statistical property. The GAN evaluation section is interesting but somewhat problematic: the use of pre-trained ResNet features to avoid pixel-level artifacts defeats the purpose of an unsupervised two-sample test, and the conclusion that "lower test statistics are better" is not well-justified since the magnitude of the statistic depends on the classifier’s capacity and training procedure. The causal discovery application with CGANs is novel, but the accuracy is modest (73-82%) and the need for ensembling suggests instability; it’s not clear that this approach outperforms simpler methods like ANM or that it generalizes to more than two variables. Overall, I think the paper is a solid survey and empirical evaluation of a known idea, but it lacks the theoretical depth or surprising insights expected for ICLR. I’d recommend rejection, but I’d encourage the authors to reframe this as a tutorial or application paper for a more applied venue, where the practical utility of C2ST would be better appreciated.

title: Learning to Repeat: Fine Grained Action Repetition for Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Reinforcement Learning algorithms can learn complex behavioral patterns for sequential decision making tasks wherein an agent interacts with an environment and acquires feedback in the form of rewards sampled from it. Traditionally, such algorithms make decisions, i.e., select actions to execute, at every single time step of the agent-environment interactions. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Fine Grained Action Repetition (FiGAR), which enables the agent to decide the action as well as the time scale of repeating it. FiGAR can be used for improving any Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithm which maintains an explicit policy estimate by enabling temporal abstractions in the action space and implicitly enabling planning through sequences of repetitive macro-actions. We empirically demonstrate the efficacy of our framework by showing performance improvements on top of three policy search algorithms in different domains: Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic in the Atari 2600 domain, Trust Region Policy Optimization in Mujoco domain and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients in the TORCS car racing domain.
review: I'm leaning towards rejection – the core idea of factorizing the policy into action and repetition duration is neat and practically useful, but the paper feels more like an engineering extension than a deep contribution, and the experimental execution has several red flags. The decoupled policy representation (action network + repetition network) is a clean way to avoid action-space blowup, and the empirical gains on Atari (especially Enduro with 900x improvement) are eye-catching, but the setup is riddled with ad-hoc choices: |W|=30 is arbitrary and not justified, the staged training (20M steps of regular A3C before joint training) is a hack that suggests the joint learning is unstable, and the hyperparameters (β_ar, β_KL) are tuned separately for each algorithm without a principled rationale. More critically, the paper claims FiGAR learns "temporal abstractions," but the action-repetition distributions (Figure 3, Table 7) show that most games still favor short repeats (1-3 steps), and the few games that use long repeats (e.g., Crazy Climber) don't show corresponding performance gains – so where's the evidence that the abstraction is actually useful? The comparison to STRAW is weak (only a handful of games, no statistical significance tests), and the claim that FiGAR "outperforms A3C in 26 out of 33 games" is misleading because many of those gains are tiny or within variance, and some are catastrophic losses (e.g., Chopper Command drops from 4969 to 3147, Name This Game from 12100 to 1752 – that's a 85% drop!). The MuJoCo results are marginal (FiGAR-TRPO barely beats TRPO in 3/5 tasks and loses in Swimmer), and the TORCS demo is a single run without error bars. The theoretical connection to SMDPs is hand-wavy (you don't actually use SMDP-specific algorithms like options or hierarchical RL), and the lack of a stopping mechanism for macro-actions is a glaring omission for stochastic environments. Overall, the paper has a clever idea and some positive results, but the experimental design is sloppy, the improvements are inconsistent, and the contribution relative to prior work (Dynamic Frameskip, STRAW) is incremental at best. I'd suggest major revisions with more rigorous baselines, better hyperparameter justification, and a clearer demonstration of when and why FiGAR actually helps, but in its current form, I can't recommend acceptance.

title: Loss-aware Binarization of Deep Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Deep neural network models, though very powerful and highly successful, are computationally expensive in terms of space and time. Recently, there have been a number of attempts on binarizing the network weights and activations. This greatly reduces the network size, and replaces the underlying multiplications to additions or even XNOR bit operations. However, existing binarization schemes are based on simple matrix approximations and ignore the effect of binarization on the loss. In this paper, we propose a proximal Newton algorithm with diagonal Hessian approximation that directly minimizes the loss w.r.t. the binarized weights. The underlying proximal step has an efficient closed-form solution, and the second-order information can be efficiently obtained from the second moments already computed by the Adam optimizer. Experiments on both feedforward and recurrent networks show that the proposed loss-aware binarization algorithm outperforms existing binarization schemes, and is also more robust for wide and deep networks.
review: I like this paper – it’s a technically solid and practically useful contribution that addresses a real limitation of existing binarization methods: they ignore the loss landscape when quantizing weights, which is obviously suboptimal. The key idea of using a proximal Newton step with a diagonal Hessian approximation (straight from Adam’s second moments) to directly minimize the loss w.r.t. binarized weights is elegant and well-motivated. The closed-form solution in Proposition 3.1 is neat, and the connection to BWN (which falls out as a special case when curvature is uniform) provides nice theoretical grounding. The experiments are thorough and convincing: LAB consistently outperforms BinaryConnect and BWN on MNIST, SVHN, and LSTM language modeling, and the robustness to depth (Figure 2, Table 4) is a particularly strong result – BinaryConnect explodes, LAB handles it gracefully thanks to the adaptive scaling. The extension to recurrent nets is a nice touch, and Proposition 3.2 explains why BinaryConnect fails on deep RNNs while BWN/LAB succeed. That said, I have a few concerns. First, the convergence proof (Theorem 3.1) relies on the strong assumption that [d_l^t]_k >> β for all layers and times – this is a bit hand-wavy and not empirically verified; in practice, many second moments can be small, especially early in training. Second, the method is essentially Adam + a projection step, which is clever but not hugely novel – the main contribution is the loss-aware binarization formulation, which is new but the optimization machinery is borrowed. Third, the improvement over BWN is sometimes marginal (e.g., 2.354 vs 2.535 on SVHN, 1.291 vs 1.313 on LSTM), and on CIFAR-10 LAB actually underperforms BinaryConnect (10.50 vs 9.86), so the gains are not universally consistent. Fourth, the paper doesn’t explore the interaction with modern techniques like knowledge distillation or fine-tuning, which could further improve binarization. Overall, I think this is a strong paper – the idea is principled, the implementation is practical (using Adam’s moments is a clever trick), and the results are positive – but it’s not a game-changer. I’d recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors clarify the assumptions in the convergence proof and provide more discussion on when LAB might fail.

title: Learning to Play in a Day: Faster Deep Reinforcement Learning by Optimality Tightening
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a novel training algorithm for reinforcement learning which combines the strength of deep Q-learning with a constrained optimization approach to tighten optimality and encourage faster reward propagation. Our novel technique makes deep reinforcement learning more practical by drastically reducing the training time. We evaluate the performance of our approach on the 49 games of the challenging Arcade Learning Environment, and report significant improvements in both training time and accuracy.
review: I’m leaning towards rejection – the core idea of tightening Bellman optimality via multi-step lower and upper bounds is intuitively appealing and the empirical results show impressive speedups on many Atari games, but the paper has several critical flaws that undermine its contribution. The theoretical foundation is shaky: the lower and upper bounds are defined using the optimal Q*, but then computed with a recent estimate Q_θ, which is fine in practice, but the constraints are derived from inequalities that assume Q* – replacing it with Q_θ without any correction or importance weighting is a heuristic, not a principled tightening. The optimization using quadratic penalties with a fixed λ is ad-hoc and not analyzed; there's no discussion of how λ affects convergence, no annealing schedule, and no ablation showing sensitivity to K or λ. The comparison to DQN is not fair – you use the discounted return R_j in the replay memory, which gives your method a huge advantage (it's essentially using TD(λ) or Q(λ) information), yet you don't compare to eligibility trace methods or even mention them properly (the brief dismissal of off-policy Q*(λ) is hand-wavy and not empirically supported). The claim that "our method can be combined with D-DQN" is not demonstrated, and the results on some games (e.g., Name This Game, Private Eye) show worse performance than DQN, so the improvement is not universal. The evaluation protocol is also inconsistent – you report "best agent" across epochs, while DQN reports final performance, which biases comparisons in your favor. Overall, the paper has a clever idea and strong empirical results on a subset of games, but the methodology is underdeveloped, the comparison is unfair, and the theoretical justification is too weak for ICLR. I’d recommend major revisions with a proper comparison to TD(λ) and Q(λ), a principled treatment of the constraints, and a fairer evaluation protocol, but in its current form, I cannot recommend acceptance.

title: Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce the *Energy-based Generative Adversarial Network* model (EBGAN) which views the discriminator as an energy function that attributes low energies to the regions near the data manifold and higher energies to other regions. Similar to the probabilistic GANs, a generator is seen as being trained to produce contrastive samples with minimal energies, while the discriminator is trained to assign high energies to these generated samples. Viewing the discriminator as an energy function allows to use a wide variety of architectures and loss functionals in addition to the usual binary classifier with logistic output. Among them, we show one instantiation of EBGAN framework as using an auto-encoder architecture, with the energy being the reconstruction error, in place of the discriminator. We show that this form of EBGAN exhibits more stable behavior than regular GANs during training. We also show that a single-scale architecture can be trained to generate high-resolution images.
review: I’m very positive on this paper – the idea of reframing the discriminator as an energy function and using an autoencoder with reconstruction error is both elegant and practically effective, and I think it’s a clear accept. The theoretical proof that the hinge loss leads to a Nash equilibrium where p_G = p_data is solid and gives EBGAN a principled foundation, unlike some other GAN variants that rely on heuristic losses. The exhaustive grid search on MNIST is a real strength – showing that EBGANs have a much tighter and more reliable distribution of inception scores than vanilla GANs across hundreds of configurations provides convincing evidence of improved stability, which is a major pain point in GAN training. The semi-supervised results on Ladder Networks are also compelling: the 23.5% relative improvement with 100 labels is significant, and the margin decay trick is a nice practical insight. The high-resolution ImageNet generations at 128x128 and 256x256, while not photorealistic, demonstrate that a single-scale EBGAN can scale to complex datasets without the multi-scale pyramids that previous GANs required – that’s a genuine advance. The repelling regularizer (PT) is sensible, though I’d like to see a more thorough ablation – it’s not clear how much of the quality improvement comes from PT versus the energy-based formulation itself. My main reservations are that the paper sometimes overclaims – the ImageNet samples are impressive for a single-scale GAN but still far from state-of-the-art, and the comparison to DCGAN is not always apple-to-apple (different architectures, different training details). Also, the semi-supervised results, while good, rely on a specific margin decay schedule that feels somewhat ad-hoc and might not generalize to other settings. Overall, though, this is a well-written, theoretically grounded, and experimentally thorough paper that opens up a new direction for GAN research – I’d accept it happily and expect it to be influential.

title: Central Moment Discrepancy (CMD) for Domain-Invariant Representation Learning
abstract: Abstract:###The learning of domain-invariant representations in the context of domain adaptation with neural networks is considered. We propose a new regularization method that minimizes the domain-specific latent feature representations directly in the hidden activation space. Although some standard distribution matching approaches exist that can be interpreted as the matching of weighted sums of moments, e.g. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), an explicit order-wise matching of higher order moments has not been considered before. We propose to match the higher order central moments of probability distributions by means of order-wise moment differences. Our model does not require computationally expensive distance and kernel matrix computations. We utilize the equivalent representation of probability distributions by moment sequences to define a new distance function, called Central Moment Discrepancy (CMD). We prove that CMD is a metric on the set of probability distributions on a compact interval. We further prove that convergence of probability distributions on compact intervals w.r.t. the new metric implies convergence in distribution of the respective random variables. We test our approach on two different benchmark data sets for object recognition (Office) and sentiment analysis of product reviews (Amazon reviews). CMD achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on most domain adaptation tasks of Office and outperforms networks trained with MMD, Variational Fair Autoencoders and Domain Adversarial Neural Networks on Amazon reviews. In addition, a post-hoc parameter sensitivity analysis shows that the new approach is stable w. r. t. parameter changes in a certain interval. The source code of the experiments is publicly available.
review: I like this paper – the idea of matching higher-order central moments explicitly is clean, theoretically grounded, and practically effective, and I think it’s a solid contribution to the domain adaptation literature. The central moment discrepancy (CMD) is well-motivated: unlike MMD, which implicitly matches weighted sums of moments via a kernel and requires expensive hyperparameter tuning, CMD directly computes differences of moments up to order K, which is interpretable, computationally efficient (linear time), and comes with a nice theoretical package (metric property, convergence in distribution). The empirical results are strong – on Amazon reviews, CMD outperforms MMD, VFAE, and DANN in 9 out of 12 tasks with default hyperparameters (no tuning!), and on Office it sets a new state-of-the-art average accuracy (79.9%) over methods like AdaBN and DANN, even though it’s based on VGG16 rather than the InceptionBN models used by some competitors. The parameter sensitivity analysis is also convincing: CMD’s accuracy is stable for K≥3, while MMD’s performance is highly sensitive to the Gaussian kernel bandwidth β, which is a well-known pain point. My main reservations are that the novelty is somewhat incremental – moment matching is not new (e.g., MMD, KL on means), and the idea of explicitly matching central moments has been explored in other contexts, though not as a domain adaptation regularizer with this theoretical treatment. Also, the approximation of only marginal moments (rather than joint) is a significant limitation – you lose information about dependencies between hidden units, and while you argue it doesn’t hurt empirically, a more principled treatment or a higher-order joint moment extension would be stronger. The comparison to MMD is not entirely fair because you use a quadratic-time MMD with a fixed Gaussian kernel and a heuristic for β tuning, while there are well-established methods for optimizing kernel parameters (e.g., median heuristic, maximizing test power) that you don’t explore. Finally, the proof of the metric property relies on the compact interval assumption, which holds for bounded activations like sigmoid/tanh but not for ReLUs – you mention clipping, but that’s a bit hand-wavy. Overall, I think this is a well-written, theoretically grounded, and practically useful paper that deserves acceptance – it’s not a groundbreaking paradigm shift, but it’s a clean and effective solution to a known problem, and the stability and computational advantages are compelling. I’d recommend accepting it and suggest the authors consider a follow-up on joint moment matching or extensions to unbounded activations.

title: Incremental Network Quantization: Towards Lossless CNNs with Low-precision Weights
abstract: Abstract:###This paper presents incremental network quantization (INQ), a novel method, targeting to efficiently convert any pre-trained full-precision convolutional neural network (CNN) model into a low-precision version whose weights are constrained to be either powers of two or zero. Unlike existing methods which are struggled in noticeable accuracy loss, our INQ has the potential to resolve this issue, as benefiting from two innovations. On one hand, we introduce three interdependent operations, namely weight partition, group-wise quantization and re-training. A well-proven measure is employed to divide the weights in each layer of a pre-trained CNN model into two disjoint groups. The weights in the first group are responsible to form a low-precision base, thus they are quantized by a variable-length encoding method. The weights in the other group are responsible to compensate for the accuracy loss from the quantization, thus they are the ones to be re-trained. On the other hand, these three operations are repeated on the latest re-trained group in an iterative manner until all the weights are converted into low-precision ones, acting as an incremental network quantization and accuracy enhancement procedure. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet classification task using almost all known deep CNN architectures including AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogleNet and ResNets well testify the efficacy of the proposed method. Specifically, at 5-bit quantization (a variable-length encoding: 1 bit for representing zero value, and the remaining 4 bits represent at most 16 different values for the powers of two), our models have improved accuracy than the 32-bit floating-point references. Taking ResNet-18 as an example, we further show that our quantized models with 4-bit, 3-bit and 2-bit ternary weights have improved or very similar accuracy against its 32-bit floating-point baseline. Besides, impressive results with the combination of network pruning and INQ are also reported. We believe that our method sheds new insights on how to make deep CNNs to be applicable on mobile or embedded devices. The code will be made publicly available.
review: I’m genuinely impressed by this paper – the incremental quantization strategy is a simple but powerful idea, and the empirical results are among the best I’ve seen for low-precision CNNs on ImageNet. The core insight – that you should quantize weights in stages, retraining the unquantized portion between stages – is elegant and directly addresses the fundamental problem that simultaneous quantization causes irreversible accuracy loss. The three-operation pipeline (partition, quantize, retrain) is clean, and the fact that it achieves lossless 5-bit and 4-bit quantization across multiple architectures (AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNets) is genuinely impressive. The 3-bit ResNet-18 with only 0.2% top-1 loss and 2-bit ternary with 33.98% top-1 error (beating BWN and TWN by 4-5%) are standout results. The compression experiments combining INQ with DNS also show clear superiority over deep compression, achieving 53x compression on AlexNet with improved accuracy, which is a big deal for deployment. I also appreciate the practical details: the variable-length encoding (1 bit for zero, remaining bits for powers of two) is clever and maps naturally to bit-shift operations on hardware. The convergence speed (often under 8 epochs) is a huge practical advantage over methods that require training from scratch. My main criticisms are relatively minor: the weight partition strategy is heuristic (pruning-inspired) and not rigorously justified – a theoretical analysis of why this partition works better than random would strengthen the paper; the method still requires a full-precision pre-trained model, which is fine but limits applications where you want to train quantized from scratch; and the extension to activations is only briefly mentioned in the appendix – I’d like to see more detail on that, as it’s a natural and important next step. Overall, I think this is a high-quality, practical, and well-executed paper that makes a strong case for incremental quantization as a go-to method for low-precision CNN deployment. I’d accept it without hesitation, and I expect it will be well-cited in both the compression and hardware communities.

title: Entropy-SGD: Biasing Gradient Descent Into Wide Valleys
abstract: Abstract:###This paper proposes a new optimization algorithm called Entropy-SGD for training deep neural networks that is motivated by the local geometry of the energy landscape. Local extrema with low generalization error have a large proportion of almost-zero eigenvalues in the Hessian with very few positive or negative eigenvalues. We leverage upon this observation to construct a local-entropy-based objective function that favors well-generalizable solutions lying in large flat regions of the energy landscape, while avoiding poorly-generalizable solutions located in the sharp valleys. Conceptually, our algorithm resembles two nested loops of SGD where we use Langevin dynamics in the inner loop to compute the gradient of the local entropy before each update of the weights. We show that the new objective has a smoother energy landscape and show improved generalization over SGD using uniform stability, under certain assumptions. Our experiments on convolutional and recurrent neural networks demonstrate that Entropy-SGD compares favorably to state-of-the-art techniques in terms of generalization error and training time.
review: I’m leaning towards acceptance, but with some reservations – this is a thoughtful and well-motivated paper that connects the geometry of the loss landscape (the Hessian being mostly flat with a few large positive eigenvalues) to a principled optimization objective that explicitly favors wide, flat minima, and the resulting algorithm is clever and theoretically grounded. The local entropy formulation is elegant: minimizing the negative log-partition function of a Gibbs distribution with a quadratic biasing term naturally encourages the optimizer to seek out regions where there are many nearby low-loss configurations, which intuitively should generalize better. The theoretical analysis showing that the local entropy landscape is smoother than the original objective, and the stability-based generalization bound (Equation 9) that predicts improved generalization over SGD, are both solid contributions. The Hessian spectrum experiments across multiple architectures (LeNet, MLP, LSTM, All-CNN) are a nice empirical validation of the "flat minima" hypothesis, and the fact that the algorithm achieves comparable or slightly better performance than SGD/Adam on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and RNN language modeling, often with fewer effective epochs, is convincing. That said, I have several concerns. First, the computational cost is significant – running L=5-20 Langevin steps per parameter update means Entropy-SGD is effectively 5-20x more expensive in wall-clock time per effective epoch; the paper acknowledges this but doesn't fully address whether the faster convergence compensates in practice (on CNNs, the gains are marginal, so the cost-benefit tradeoff is unclear).
